Disguised vegetable truck, point-blank fire: how Israel captured Hamas' internal security chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:35:33 UTC
00:35:33 KST

Israel’s dramatic operation to capture Muin al-Arabid, described by Israeli officials as Hamas’ internal security chief in the Gaza Strip, involved days of preparations, disguised vehicles, a raid on a Gaza City villa, a close-range firefight and heavy Israeli air cover during the withdrawal, according to new details published Wednesday by Saudi newspaper Asharq Al-Awsat.
The operation ended with al-Arabid wounded and in Israeli custody after an hours-long raid that Israeli authorities said caused no casualties among the forces involved.
The surveillance
According to the report, the Shin Bet had tracked al-Arabid for an extended period, studying his daily routine and the routes he used until intelligence officers identified what they believed was a vulnerability.
Israeli officials have described al-Arabid as a senior figure responsible for Hamas counterintelligence, intelligence activity and the handling and movement of hostages and senior Hamas officials.
Asharq Al-Awsat reported that preparations on the ground began at least two days before Tuesday’s operation. An Israeli vehicle was reportedly brought into the area and left there, apparently to support surveillance and real-time intelligence collection.
The vehicle was not part of the convoy used on the morning of the raid.
The infiltration
Once operational conditions were in place, the mission was launched under Southern Command.
The special forces unit reportedly entered the area using disguised vehicles, including a white van and another vehicle carrying different kinds of vegetables.
One team stormed the villa where al-Arabid was staying with members of his family, while a second team remained outside to secure the perimeter.
The firefight
The raid quickly developed into an armed confrontation.
According to the Saudi report, two of al-Arabid’s sons opened fire at the force entering the home, while two bodyguards also confronted the Israeli troops.
The report said al-Arabid’s wife was shot in the head at close range and killed at the scene. His two sons and the two bodyguards were seriously wounded.
Al-Arabid himself was shot and wounded before being captured by Shin Bet forces.
The withdrawal
The Israeli Air Force provided heavy air cover to support the force’s withdrawal and prevent additional threats from reaching the area.
Fighter jets struck what Israel described as military targets in the vicinity in an effort to isolate the scene and remove threats to the troops.
Asharq Al-Awsat also reported that two children were killed during gunfire outside the house and the airstrikes accompanying the withdrawal.
Palestinian reports said four people were killed during Israeli strikes in Gaza City on Tuesday.
The Israeli vehicle that had been left in the area during the days preceding the operation was later struck by several missiles and completely destroyed during the withdrawal, according to the report, apparently to prevent equipment or intelligence from falling into Hamas hands.
The interrogation
The operation lasted several hours and ended without Israeli casualties, according to the IDF and Shin Bet.
The wounded al-Arabid was taken from Gaza and transferred to Israel for interrogation.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu referred to the capture during a visit Wednesday to the Yellow Line inside the Gaza Strip.
“Yesterday we took Hamas’ Shin Bet chief. We’ll probably learn a few things,” Netanyahu said.
Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz later held a security assessment at the Gaza Division, where they met the Shin Bet personnel who led the operation and praised what they described as a daring and successful mission.
The IDF and Shin Bet said Tuesday that the operation had been led by the Shin Bet and Southern Command and was intended to remove Hamas threats in northern Gaza.
“Special Shin Bet forces raided a building in the Gaza City area and arrested the head of internal security of the Hamas terrorist organization throughout the Gaza Strip,” the agencies said in a joint statement.
According to the statement, al-Arabid had recently been working to strengthen Hamas control in northern Gaza and promote attacks against IDF forces operating around the Yellow Line.
The military said the Air Force struck several military targets in the area during the operation to remove threats to the troops.
The IDF and Shin Bet said the operation was intended to weaken Hamas’ control in the area and disrupt planned attacks against Israeli forces and civilians, adding that Israeli security forces would continue acting against threats in accordance with the existing arrangement in Gaza.

Swedish far-right party’s rhetoric on Muslims taken to UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:29:15 UTC
00:29:15 KST

Breadcrumb
Swedish far-right party’s rhetoric on Muslims taken to UN
A Swedish political party has submitted evidence to three UN Special Procedures, urging them to take action over what it describes as Islamophobic rhetoric from the Sweden Democrats (SD), the country’s nationalist, right-wing populist party. The submission warns that such rhetoric could undermine Muslim religious rights as Sweden heads towards a general election.
Visionpartiet — or Visionparty in English — filed the 21-page submission on 26 August, raising concerns about alleged violations of religious freedom, xenophobia, racism and anti-Muslim targeting by the SD. It argues that the party’s rhetoric could affect Muslims’ ability to live openly and practise their faith in Sweden.
The local party, founded in early 2023 as a pro-minority group, accuses the hard-right SD of moving beyond rhetoric ostensibly focused on combating extremism and increasingly targeting Islam, Muslim institutions and Muslims in Sweden.
The submission focuses on SD MP Richard Jomshof, whose outspoken opposition to Islam has drawn criticism in Sweden.
The report criticises Jomshof over proposals he has previously advanced in the Riksdag, or Sweden's parliament, including measures to investigate and potentially ban foreign funding for Muslim congregations and mosques; prohibit calls to prayer from religious buildings; ban full-face Muslim veils in public places; and restrict veils and other visible religious symbols in schools and preschools.
In 2023, Jomshof faced criticism from opposition parties over social media posts targeting Islam and the Prophet Muhammad amid wider outrage over Iraqi Christian asylum seeker Salwan Momika's public burning of the Quran on several occasions after receiving permission from Swedish authorities.
"When senior politicians themselves put such ambitions into words, their words must be taken seriously," Adel Sadat, Party Secretary of Visionparty, said in a statement. "We see a systematic political pattern in which more and more aspects of Muslims’ religious and institutional presence are being turned into political problems. It can no longer be assumed that ordinary Muslims are outside the scope of what is being targeted."
Rhetoric and attacks on Muslim communities
Muslim community leaders across Sweden have warned that discriminatory rhetoric about Islam and Muslims by political figures has contributed to a higher frequency of threats and attacks against their communities.
Citing a 2025 national study on the vulnerability of religious communities, the party said Muslim and Jewish congregations were particularly exposed to recurring violent offences and vandalism. More than one in five Muslim congregations surveyed reported graffiti vandalism at least six times in a year, while many respondents said the graffiti contained anti-Muslim or racist messages.
The submission also referred to accounts from Muslim community representatives who said they had found anti-Muslim or racist graffiti on religious buildings. One representative warned that such incidents could escalate to "arson or shots at mosques".
Visionparty argued that recurring attacks and hostile rhetoric should be understood in the context of mounting concerns over intolerance towards religious minorities in Sweden. It cited earlier UN observations on minority rights, as well as concerns raised by Muslim and Jewish communities.
In December 2025, the UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) urged Sweden to strengthen efforts to combat racist hate speech and hate crimes. The committee expressed concern over the prevalence of racist rhetoric, hate crimes and negative stereotypes affecting protected groups, including Muslims, and called on authorities to publicly condemn and distance themselves from racist hate speech by public figures, including politicians.
Visionparty also called on Muslims, mosques, Muslim organisations, other minority communities and Swedish civil society to speak out and "draw a clear line".
The Sweden Democrats, a far-right, anti-immigration party with roots in Sweden’s neo-Nazi movement, are Sweden’s second-largest party in parliament. They do not hold ministerial posts but provide parliamentary support to Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s centre-right government.
The submission comes less than three weeks before Sweden’s 13 September parliamentary election, in which the Sweden Democrats are seeking to enter government for the first time if the right-wing bloc retains power. The party is currently polling at about 19–20 percent, making it Sweden’s second-largest party, although support is marginally below the 20.5 percent it won in the 2022 election.
The New Arab has contacted Richard Jomshof for comment on the party’s latest claims but had not received a response by the time of publication.

Ukraine to Introduce Yellow and Red Air Alert Levels

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:29:00 UTC
00:29:00 KST

Ukraine will introduce yellow and red air alert levels, with yellow generally warning of drone raids and red signaling missiles, ballistic or large-scale attacks, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Wednesday, Sept. 2.
According to a statement posted by Zelensky, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi briefed him on measures being prepared in response to Russia’s changing attack tactics, particularly its use of drones to disrupt civilian life and economic activity.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“People must understand absolutely clearly what exactly they need to respond to and how,” Zelensky said.
What will the yellow and red air alerts mean?
Yellow alerts will be generally issued during drone raids, while red alerts will indicate missile threats, including the risk of ballistic strikes, as well as large-scale attacks.
The General Staff and Ukraine’s Air Force, together with the Ukrainian government, defense ministry, interior ministry, and state emergency services, will determine which threats qualify for each level. The criteria will be reviewed weekly.
Different siren sounds are also being prepared for the two threat levels, allowing residents to identify the danger from the warning signal.
Ukraine has already stopped sounding the siren a second time to mark the end of an air alert. Sirens are now activated only when an alert begins, while information about the all-clear is provided through other warning channels.
Zelensky also ordered officials to introduce more precise geographic targeting of alerts so warnings and restrictions apply only to areas facing an actual threat.
Donbas: The Ukrainian Roots That Survived
“The main goal of these changes is to give people and businesses in Ukraine more predictability and an understanding of how to respond in each specific case,” he said.
However, Zelensky did not announce when the two-level system or the new siren sounds would take effect.
Yellow alerts
The government, military, local authorities, interior ministry, and state emergency services will also establish criteria allowing public institutions, businesses, and certain economic and social facilities to continue operating during yellow alerts.
Rules for schools and kindergartens will remain unchanged, Zelensky said.
The government and local authorities will update requirements for the placement of shelters in cities, communities, and infrastructure facilities, including mobile shelters.
Koretskyi was instructed to prepare additional business support measures to expand the installation of modular shelters and help companies adapt their premises to the updated safety requirements.
Kyiv transport and curfew rules
Kyiv’s Syretsko-Pecherska, or Green, metro line will operate in full during yellow alerts.
City authorities were also instructed to substantially increase the number of surface public transport vehicles to compensate for service interruptions on the Sviatoshynsko-Brovarska, or Red, line during alerts.
Additional surface transport is expected to duplicate the metro route between Lisova and Dnipro stations.
Authorities will also shorten Kyiv’s curfew, although Zelensky did not specify the new hours or when the change would begin.
Other Ukrainian cities will be encouraged to review their curfews based on security conditions and the needs of residents and businesses.
The government is set to provide additional financial assistance to medical facilities to maintain services, while officials will conduct weekly reviews of alert procedures and other protective measures.

As US influence wanes, China expands Middle East security role
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:29:00 UTC
00:29:00 KST

Breadcrumb
As war with Iran weakens US influence, China expands Middle East security role
The clearest example is the recent “Eagles of Civilisation 2026” military exercises with Egypt. The drills demonstrated capabilities that went beyond symbolic military diplomacy. China deployed J-16 fighter aircraft, a YY-20A aerial tanker, a KJ-500 airborne early-warning aircraft, an electronic warfare aircraft, and other support assets to Egypt.
For the first time, Chinese jet formations flew more than 6,000 kilometres beyond Asia to reach Egypt, with aerial refuelling conducted en route. Prior to this deployment, China had only sent the J-16 to the Russian Far East and Pakistan. As recently as last year, China-Egypt exercises involved smaller J-10C fighter jets and support aircraft.
Since then, Chinese and Egyptian pilots have conducted medium- and close-range air combat drills involving Chinese J-16s and Egyptian Rafales.
While the deployment does not suggest Beijing intends to fight a war in the Middle East, it demonstrates the People's Liberation Army's ability to operate alongside regional militaries and sustain forces far from China, well beyond its immediate neighbourhood.
China has also maintained a military presence in the wider region at sea. Since 2008, it has conducted naval escort operations in the Gulf of Aden and waters off Somalia. As recently as August, its 49th escort task force departed for the region. Officially, the mission is focused on protecting international shipping and conducting anti-piracy operations.
Beijing has also expanded its military engagement through joint exercises. In 2025, it held naval drills with Iran and Russia in the Gulf of Oman. This August, it conducted the fourth Falcon Shield air force training exercise with the United Arab Emirates.
These deployments have increasingly featured more sophisticated platforms, including J-10 fighters, KJ-500 airborne early-warning aircraft and YY-20A aerial tankers.
A growing Chinese footprint
China is also becoming an increasingly significant, albeit indirect, player in Middle Eastern security. This comes as its close partner Pakistan expands its defence ties across the Gulf through the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement (SMDA) with Saudi Arabia, the Mecca Pact involving Turkey and Saudi Arabia, and a recently confirmed defence agreement with Kuwait.
As Islamabad deepens these partnerships, Chinese-made military equipment is likely to play a growing role in regional security architectures. Pakistan relies heavily on Chinese defence technology and has recently deployed HQ-9 air defence systems and JF-17 fighter jets, which it jointly produces with China, to Saudi Arabia.
For Beijing, such developments provide an opportunity to showcase its defence industry without assuming a formal security role in the region.
Instead, Chinese military technology can expand its footprint indirectly through Pakistani deployments, while systems such as the Beidou satellite network, already used across parts of the Arab world, further support the integration of Chinese-made platforms into regional security networks.
Could Beijing assume a larger security role?
Commenting on the prospect of a larger Chinese security role in the Middle East, Theodore Karasik, a fellow on Middle Eastern Affairs at the Jamestown Foundation, told The New Arab that Chinese technology and drones are already deeply embedded across the region, a trend he expects to continue.
Karasik argued that Beijing has benefited from US-Iran tensions while maintaining what he described as a “position of relative comfort”. Through infrastructure projects, commercial investments and growing arms sales, China has steadily expanded its regional footprint. He noted that Beijing's involvement now extends to defence cooperation, including support for Saudi Arabia's ballistic missile programme.
He also argued that America's longstanding strategic focus elsewhere has created opportunities for China to deepen its engagement in the Middle East. Combined with platforms such as BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), he said, these developments point to an increasingly fragmented global order.
However, Karasik suggested that the future trajectory of China's regional role may depend largely on Washington's response. A renewed US effort to discourage partners from deepening ties with Beijing could constrain China's ambitions, even as American policymakers remain focused on domestic political challenges and war with Iran.
While the Trump administration may seek to increase economic pressure on China, Karasik questioned how effective such measures would be. He added that President Xi Jinping's anticipated visit to the White House could help shape Beijing's approach.
Limits of Beijing's emerging role
Lacking a network of alliances, bases, or permanently deployed forces comparable to those of Washington, China has little security infrastructure in the Middle East beyond its only officially acknowledged overseas military base in Djibouti. Therefore, even if Beijing seeks to keep Gulf waterways open or expand military cooperation, it lacks the capacity to deploy large-scale forces to defend Gulf states against Iran.
Moreover, China maintains similar close ties with multiple regional actors, including Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Iran and Egypt through Comprehensive Strategic Partnerships (CSPs), and an Innovative Comprehensive Partnership with Israel. Any steps Beijing takes are therefore likely to remain non-confrontational.
Zeeshan Shah, an analyst at FINRA in Washington, told The New Arab that China has adopted a more subtle approach since the US-Iran war began. However, “regardless of official Chinese pronouncements on securing international waterways, or recent military exercises with Egypt”, he argued that Beijing is unlikely to move towards a more muscular form of engagement.
In his view, China primarily sees competition with the United States through an economic lens. While the threat of US sanctions has irritated Beijing, China has historically refrained from enforcing other sanctions against Iran.
Shah also noted that, despite maintaining strong commercial relations with Israel, China has generally refrained from using that relationship to influence Israeli policy. Whether Beijing chooses to leverage those ties more actively in the future, he argued, remains an open question.
The Chinese perspective
China's position during the Iran war has highlighted both the opportunities and contradictions in its emerging regional role. Beijing has presented itself as a stakeholder in de-escalation, particularly as the conflict has threatened Gulf security and the free flow of energy.
On 24 August, Foreign Minister Wang Yi told Kuwait's foreign minister that the Middle East and Gulf had reached a "critical juncture" and called for a return to dialogue, while saying China was ready to strengthen coordination with Kuwait and contribute to regional peace and stability. China has also engaged directly with regional actors and mediators as it seeks to protect its economic interests and prevent the conflict from disrupting trade and energy supplies.
But Beijing's position is complicated by its alleged role in sustaining Iran's military capabilities. US officials and recent reporting have identified Chinese companies and intermediaries as suppliers of military equipment and components to Iran, including a reported deal for hundreds of Chinese-made QW-12 and FN-16 man-portable air-defence missiles during the conflict.
Chinese manufacturing has also been central to Iran's wider drone ecosystem, with Chinese firms and suppliers providing components used in Iranian systems. At the same time, Washington has increasingly targeted China-linked entities over support for Iran's missile, drone and oil sectors.
In other words, Beijing could assume a larger regional role if it chose to do so.
For a clearer understanding of China's intentions and the limits it places on its regional ambitions, The New Arab spoke to Li Chao, Deputy Editor-in-Chief of China Media Group (CMG) Middle East.
In his view, although China's role in Middle Eastern security affairs is expanding, Beijing has no desire to challenge, replicate the American model or become the region's new “policeman”.
Describing the shift as a move away from a relatively narrow focus on economic and diplomatic engagement, Chao said China is pursuing “a broader, more integrated, but still restrained form of security involvement”. Driven by practical interests such as energy, trade, investment and the presence of Chinese personnel in the Middle East, he argued that it has become “increasingly difficult to sustain the old model of deep economic engagement but limited security involvement”.
However, Chao stressed that Beijing is not pursuing military alliances or large-scale permanent deployments. Instead, it is expanding its security presence through low-intensity instruments that form a “mutually reinforcing framework”, which is intended not to replace the United States but to reduce the risks that regional instability poses to Chinese interests.
He argued that China's Middle East strategy is centred on the normalisation of security engagement rather than militarisation. At the same time, Chao acknowledged the limits of this approach, noting that China does not possess an extensive military network comparable to that of the United States.
As a result, Chao said Beijing is likely to follow "a model of limited commitment, selective participation and avoidance of formal alliances". He argued that China's role would only enter a more substantive phase if it began participating in multilateral security mechanisms or institutionalised security cooperation across the region.
Until then, China's expanding security footprint is likely to remain cautious, selective and largely shaped by its economic interests.

Businesses downgraded their assessment of their performance in August. Entrepreneurs noted the impact of losses caused by russian attacks on production, warehouses and logistics, the blockade of seaports, expensive fuel and a shortage of personnel. UNN writes about this, citing the NBU survey of September 2.
Details
In August 2026, the Business Activity Expectations Index (BAEI) stood at 48.3, down from 50.1 in July 2026 and 49.0 in August 2025.
The following factors constrained the economic activity of enterprises and negatively affected business sentiment:
-  significant losses from the large-scale destruction of production facilities, warehouse premises and logistics infrastructure; 
-  the blockade of seaports; 
-  high fuel prices 
-  a shortage of qualified personnel. 
At the same time, the following provided positive momentum for development:
-  resilient consumer demand; 
-  international financial support; 
-  budget funding for infrastructure restoration and road construction; 
-  a stable situation in the energy sector; 
-  seasonality.  
What businesses expect
Construction companies were the only surveyed sector to retain optimistic assessments of their performance, thanks to stable budget funding for road and infrastructure restoration, sustained domestic demand, and the seasonal factor.
By contrast, industrial enterprises were the most restrained, given the significant losses from the destruction of production facilities, complicated logistics and a shortage of qualified workers.
Respondents in most sectors (except construction) expected an acceleration in the growth rates of both purchase prices / prices for raw materials and supplies, and prices / tariffs for their own products / services, as well as the cost of goods purchased for resale.
What are the assessments in the trade sector
"Unlike the previous month, trading companies expected a decrease in the volume of trade turnover and purchases of goods for resale, as well as a further decrease in inventories / stocks of goods for resale," the NBU stated.
Respondents expected a further decline in their trade margins.
What is the situation on the labor market
The situation on the labor market remains difficult. Only construction respondents continued to assess the total number of employees positively, while enterprises in other sectors expected staff reductions, most notably in industry.
For reference
The monthly survey of enterprises was conducted from August 4 to 21, 2026. A total of 586 enterprises took part. The survey results reflect only the opinions of the respondents — heads of enterprises — and not assessments by the National Bank of Ukraine.

Teva Pharmaceuticals said on Wednesday that its experimental treatment for the disease is showing positive results. In a trial, adults with the disease were meaningfully protected from harm caused by gluten.
Celiac disease is an autoimmune disease affecting about one in every hundred people, damaging the small intestine when the sufferer is exposed to gluten. Currently, the only accepted treatment for the disease is a gluten-free diet.
The Israeli pharmaceutical giant, whose stocks rose about 2 percent after the announcement, is running a trial for its new antibody, "TEV '408." In the trial, it gave the antibody to 50 gluten-free celiac adults, and two weeks later, they began a daily gluten challenge for six weeks.
At the end of the eight weeks, the trial reported statistically significant and clinically meaningful prevention of gluten-induced damage. In a statement, the company said that the antibody "was well-tolerated, with no safety signals observed to date."
In a call with Wall Street analysts, Teva CEO Richard Francis said the company has no intention of developing the drug with partners.
Analysts were interested in the differences between Teva's trial and those of competing developments, in which higher doses of gluten were given to trial participants. Teva explained that it was important to give participants gluten doses they could tolerate, or else they might drop out of the trial.
In the next phase of the study, which is meant to provide sufficient data to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for approval, Teva expects it will need to give participants more gluten per day in a longer trial.
In July, Teva announced successful results in a trial for an experimental drug that treats the skin condition vitiligo.

Who is Zelensky threatening in Russian skies?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:24:16 UTC
00:24:16 KST

Who is Zelensky threatening in Russian skies?
Vladimir Zelensky has warned “every airline” using Russian airspace that the “safe days” are over, as Kiev looks to deploy swarms of drones to disrupt air travel in the country.
Foreign airlines, insurers and governments were told in no uncertain terms on Tuesday that Ukraine’s expanding long-range drone campaign would increasingly endanger civilian flights over Russia, specifically pointing to Moscow, St. Petersburg and other major cities.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has called the statement a move toward “state terrorism” and warned that Moscow would respond if Kiev’s threats resulted in tragedy.
But who exactly is Zelensky threatening, how many people could be affected, and can Ukraine really shut Russian skies?
How many people fly in Russia?
Despite Western sanctions and airspace restrictions imposed after 2022, Russia still has one of the world’s largest civilian aviation networks.
Russian airlines carried around 50 million passengers in the first half of 2026, including more than 36 million on domestic routes and almost 13 million internationally, amounting to roughly 272,000 passenger journeys every day.
Foreign airlines are expected to carry around 26 million passengers on Russian routes this year.
As for foreign passengers, nearly 3 million tourist visits were also recorded in the first half of 2026, or roughly 16,500 per day. And that’s not counting the number of foreign business travelers, workers, students and other visitors.
Which airlines still operate in Russia?
Many international airlines have halted flights to Russia after the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, as Western countries closed their airspace to Russian carriers and Moscow imposed reciprocal restrictions.
The move sharply reduced direct connections with Europe and North America, but Russia remains linked to dozens of countries. Airlines from Türkiye, Serbia, China, the Gulf, Central Asia, the Caucasus, the Middle East and Africa continue to operate.
Türkiye, Uzbekistan and the UAE alone account for more than half of Russia’s direct international flights. Turkish Airlines and Pegasus remain major foreign carriers, while Uzbekistan Airways, Qanot Sharq and Centrum Air operate extensive links with Central Asia.
Emirates, flydubai, Etihad, Qatar Airways and Air Arabia connect Russian cities with Gulf hubs, while Chinese carriers including Air China, China Eastern and China Southern operate regular routes. By spring 2026, Russia and China had around 270 to 285 direct flights per week.
Air Serbia also maintains regular Moscow-Belgrade services, one of Russia’s few remaining direct air links with Europe.
Belavia, Azerbaijan Airlines, FlyOne Armenia, EgyptAir, Ethiopian Airlines and other foreign carriers also remain active.
How often do drones disrupt Russian airports?
Throughout the conflict, Ukrainian UAVs have repeatedly forced Russian airports to suspend operations. In the first quarter of 2026, more than 290 temporary airport restrictions were recorded, according to the Association of Tour Operators of Russia. By April 20, the number had passed 450.
Moscow airports have been repeatedly affected, along with Sochi, Krasnodar, Gelendzhik, Kaluga, Saratov and St. Petersburg.
When incoming drones are detected, Russian authorities often activate the “Kover”, or “Carpet,” plan, under which aircraft are diverted, departures are stopped and the affected airspace is closed until the threat passes.
How long has Kiev planned this?
Zelensky’s latest statement follows reports that Kiev has long been considering a much larger campaign against Russian civilian aviation.
The Atlantic reported in August that Ukrainian officials had worked on a plan known as “M&Ms,” which envisaged sending swarms of thousands of AI-guided drones toward Moscow airports.
The goal was reportedly to force foreign airlines to stop flying to the Russian capital.
Zelensky was said to have been skeptical at first, fearing that a civilian aircraft could be hit and that such an attack could be viewed as “piracy.” Preparations nevertheless continued for several months.
Less than two weeks after the Atlantic report, Zelensky apparently abandoned his concerns and issued a direct threat to international airlines.
What have aviation experts said about Zelensky's threat?
Aviation experts have expressed doubt that Kiev can realistically close Russia’s vast airspace on the scale Zelensky has suggested.
Former pilot Cyrille de Lattre told RT that such an operation would require enormous resources and that drones would not be the most practical weapon for the task. However, he warned that the threat should still be taken seriously.
Russian aviation expert Roman Gusarov described Zelensky’s statement as a direct threat to civilian aircraft and airport infrastructure, but said its main purpose was intimidation.
“The main message was not for Russia, but for our partners,” he told RT, arguing that Kiev wants to frighten foreign airlines into stopping flights.
Gusarov called the statement an “act of desperation” and said Russian air defenses and aviation authorities already have procedures to keep civilian aircraft away from areas where drones are detected.
He also criticized the lack of reaction from international aviation bodies, including the International Civil Aviation Organization.
How have foreign airlines reacted?
So far, Zelensky’s threat has not prompted foreign airlines to abandon Russian routes.
Although there were some morning cancellations announced by Turkish Airlines, the company has since explained that they were temporary and linked to Kover restrictions at Russian airports. The carrier said its planned flights to Russian cities would continue.
Pegasus Airlines had also cancelled several overnight flights, but has similarly said they were temporary and due to operational issues. The company said no new cancellations are planned and has confirmed that its Russia schedule would continue.
Moscow’s Vnukovo airport said 16 aircraft had arrived from Türkiye during the day despite the temporary restrictions.
No major foreign airline has announced plans to suspend its Russian operations over Zelensky’s threat.
Kiev’s record of attacking public transport
Zelensky’s threat comes as Ukraine has already repeatedly used drones against other forms of civilian transport throughout the conflict. These attacks have included strikes on passenger buses, trains, ambulances, trucks and civilian cars.
On June 3, a drone struck a scheduled Moscow-Simferopol passenger bus in Enakievo in the Donetsk People’s Republic, killing seven people and injuring 11.
Two weeks later, a drone hit a bus carrying a Belarusian youth football team through Bryansk Region. The coach’s wife was killed and several passengers, including children, were injured.
Passenger trains have also been targeted. On June 4, a drone struck a commuter train traveling from Azovskoye to Kerch in Crimea, killing one person and injuring three. Four days later, another drone hit the locomotive of a Moscow-Simferopol passenger train, killing the assistant driver and injuring the driver.
How has Russia responded?
Putin has described Zelensky’s threat as a move toward “state terrorism” and has warned that Russia would respond if it led to civilian casualties. He also rejected Kiev’s calls for renewed talks, saying there could be no negotiations with terrorists.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova similarly noted that Zelensky’s remarks showed that the Ukrainian government had combined state institutions with “terrorist methods.”
Transport Minister Andrey Nikitin said Russian aviation authorities were preparing for the threat and would continue tightening security measures. Temporary restrictions may continue when drones approach, he said, but Moscow would not allow major disruptions to civilian aviation.

The firm resumed that audit the following year, and its preliminary report in 2023 painted a damning picture of the institution under long-serving former governor Salameh.
Salameh, who headed the bank from 1993 to July 2023, is widely viewed as a key culprit in the country's dramatic economic crash and is accused of having amassed a fortune during his time in the job.

Could GLP-1 weight-loss drugs help you live longer?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:23:17 UTC
00:23:17 KST

GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are transformational. From helping people lose weight to controlling their blood sugar to tamping down inflammation and improving heart health, these medications herald a new age of medicine. And now a new study in mice suggests that starting semaglutide, a GLP-1 (glucagonlike peptide 1) medication sold under the brand names Wegovy and Ozempic, in old age extends the lifespan by about 12 percent.
Not only that, but semaglutide outperformed dieting in terms of maintaining memory and keeping blood sugar in check. It’s an intriguing result: Scientists already knew that restricting calories seems to boost longevity and hold off the ill effects of aging. But sticking to such a diet is hard, and researchers have long looked for a drug that delivers the same benefits without the hunger. The new results, published in Nature, suggest they may have found it.
In the study, scientists gave semaglutide to female mice that were 20 months old—roughly equivalent in age to a woman in her 60s—and injected them with the drug for the rest of their lives. Against a comparison group of the same age that ate freely and received only saline shots, the mice’s median lifespan rose by about 12 percent—from 742 days to 834.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Semaglutide’s list of uses has grown long in recent years. Beyond being used to treat diabetes and obesity, it is approved to lower cardiovascular risk, slow kidney decline and treat fatty liver disease, with trial data piling up for sleep apnea and osteoarthritis. Why one drug works in so many seemingly unrelated conditions is a mystery. “I read in journals about all these benefits for all kinds of diseases, and I don’t think there was an answer in the scientific community,” says Danica Chen, a longevity researcher at the University of California, Berkeley, and senior author of the new study.
Chen has researched calorie restriction for two decades and thought that semaglutide might work as a dieting substitute because it also reduces calorie intake, albeit through appetite suppression rather than willpower and discipline. Perhaps, she reasoned, by slowing aging itself through the same calorie restriction effect, the drug would push back the diseases that aging can bring on. It worked.
Mice on semaglutide explored more, balanced longer on a rotating rod, ran farther on a treadmill and solved a maze faster—gains that held even after the researchers accounted for the animals just being leaner than their peers. Compared with the untreated animals, their tissues were less worn out and inflamed, and they died later.
Then Chen and her team set up a separate, five-month experiment in which a group of late-life mice got the drug while another group was simply fed 24 percent less—about the same amount of food as the treated mice had cut back on because of appetite suppression. Semaglutide treatment matched the diet on measures of muscle strength and coordination.
To see whether the drug works through the same biological mechanism as dieting, the team sequenced gene activity in the livers of treated mice and compared that to existing data on calorie restriction. The overlap was significant: both calorie restriction and the GLP-1 quieted down inflammation and fat processing, and both stepped up the genes for handling blood sugar and maintaining proteins. The results suggests semaglutide mimics calorie restriction but has an additional power: the GLP-1 mice had better memory scores, curiosity levels and blood sugar.
“In that sense, it’s more than just a calorie restriction,” Chen says. Why the drug apparently has this edge over dieting is unclear. “The short answer is: we don’t know yet,” she says.
The study doesn’t answer whether dieting or semaglutide extends the lifespan more. “Maybe calorie restriction increases the lifespan more?” wonders Nir Barzilai, a longevity researcher at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine who was not involved in the study. “The data is not there, and it bugs me.” It bugs Chen, too.
That experiment is currently ongoing, she says. “I don’t predict what the results might be. The results always surprise us.”

The risk of high blood pressure in pregnancy is rising—and the damage can be life-changing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:22:57 UTC
00:22:57 KST

It happened so fast.
It was 2019, and Megan O’Grady was 32 weeks pregnant with her first child. She took her dogs for a walk, just as she usually did. But that day, she was surprised by how tired she was. Then her chest started to hurt. Later, sitting in a restaurant with her husband, she felt miserable. She realized something was wrong. By the time she got to the hospital that night, her blood pressure was 220/120 millimeters of mercury (mm Hg)—dangerously high.
O’Grady was shocked: at a doctor visit just a few days before, her blood pressure was completely normal. But now she was suffering from severe preeclampsia—a potentially deadly pregnancy complication marked by high blood pressure and organ damage. She rapidly found herself with no choice but to give birth, more than a month before she was due.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“It was so scary,” she recalls. “He was born, and then they were having to check my blood pressure every hour after he was born. It was crazy.”
O’Grady is far from alone. The rate of high blood pressure in pregnancy has increased by 73 percent, between 2016 and 2024, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. This is a rate of about one in 10 women. What’s more, cases of gestational hypertension—high blood pressure that happens to someone for the first time while they are pregnant—have been rising since 1989, the first year the condition was recorded on birth certificates.
The increase can’t be easily explained by any single cause, says Sarah Kilpatrick, a maternal fetal medicine specialist at Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles. The average age of people’s first pregnancy is going up, and more people older than age 40 are having babies. More women are having twins and triplets more often because of in vitro fertilization. And women’s body mass indexes (BMIs) have been consistently going up.
Any one of these factors is a risk for high blood pressure, Kilpatrick says, and some people might have more than one. As pregnancies progress, gestational hypertension increases the risk of preeclampsia, which also leads to liver and kidney problems. The condition is diagnosed by blood pressure readings and signs of organ damage in urine or blood tests. It can be fatal: blood pressure problems during pregnancy are one of the leading causes of illness and death in U.S. mothers. And as with O’Grady, the high blood pressure aspect of preeclampsia can come out of the blue.
“If we don’t diagnose it soon enough or people stay pregnant too long, they can get really sick and, in the extreme, of course, die,” Kilpatrick says. “That’s the problem with the disease—it can be very insidious.”
The recent CDC report found that gestational hypertension in 2024 was highest among Native American and Black women. People age 40 and older and those whose BMI was considered “obese” were also most likely to have the condition. But in general, the rates of high blood pressure in pregnancy are rising, no matter what. Baha Sibai, a maternal fetal medicine specialist at in the University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston, believes the rate could be even higher because many birth certificates have incomplete data.
A piece of data that could help doctors better understand and manage hypertension in pregnancy involves tracking how many weeks the pregnancy reached before birth, Sibai says. Once diagnosed, he says, gestational hypertension is supposed to be monitored very carefully in the interest of the woman, not just the fetus.
“All of our focus before was managing the pregnancy,” he says. “Now there is a big emphasis on how we are going to reduce morbidity in the woman.”
Preeclampsia is, at its heart, a systemic response to the placenta. An abnormal increase in a protein called sFlt-1 (soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1), which slows down placental growth, Kilpatrick says. This seems to be the trigger that leads to preeclampsia later.
In 2023 the U.S. approved the first blood test to diagnose preeclampsia, measuring the ratio of sFlt-1 to another placental protein that doesn’t change. Kilpatrick was involved getting it approved.
“We’ve known it’s been increasing partially because of better recognition and diagnosis,” Kilpatrick says. Still, some women may not appreciate the risks of hypertension and preeclampsia. “It should be something women know about,” she says.
When O’Grady went to the hospital, she was diagnosed with a severe form of preeclampsia, a rare condition called HELLP syndrome (the acronym is based on symptoms: hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelet levels). The staff immediately gave her magnesium sulfate to prevent her from having seizures.
“I had no concept of what that was,” she says of HELLP syndrome, “no concept that my chest pain was my liver being pushed up” because of swelling and pressure.
High blood pressure in pregnancy carries lifelong consequences, raising the risk of cardiovascular disease and recurring hypertension. This is particularly true for preeclampsia.
O’Grady recovered from her first pregnancy, and she and her husband planned carefully for their second. She went on beta-blockers in case her blood pressure started creeping up again—it did.
At 24 weeks, her blood pressure started to climb, and eventually, she was admitted to a hospital for the remainder of her pregnancy. At 28 weeks, she delivered her baby. The nurses offered to play music in the delivery room. O’Grady chose the Beatles classic “Let It Be.”
“It’s out of your control,” she says, describing that moment years later, with her two sons running around the house. Now she follows a healthy lifestyle that she hopes will ward off the risk of heart disease. “You just have to listen to your doctors and trust in their advice. You kind of have to hope that everything will be okay.”

Iran threatens tougher strategy after US strikes kill 4 at wedding
Iran threatened to take a tougher line in its war with the United States on Wednesday after the heaviest exchanges in weeks left at least 19 Iranians dead, including four at a wedding -- an incident slammed as a "war crime" by Tehran.
A wave of Iranian attacks earlier targeted US bases in Jordan, the UAE, Kuwait, Bahrain and Iraq's autonomous Kurdistan region, after extensive US bombardment hit sites across Iran.
The flare-up deepens the ongoing impasse in the war, as Iran maintains a stranglehold on the Strait of Hormuz oil export route and the US presses its counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Iran reacted with fury after the Iranian Red Crescent said four people including a child were killed and more than 50 people wounded by a US attack that hit a wedding in Iran's south.
"The truth of this unlawful war of choice -- and the true face of the war crime -- is in Sirik, where a wedding ceremony was brutally bombed as part of America's desperate struggle to conceal its failure," foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei posted on X.
The US military did not address the incident directly.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) spokesman Tim Hawkins said "the US military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC", referring to Iran's Revolutionary Guards.
Iran's security chief warned the United States would face a "new strategy" from Tehran in the six-month war.
"You will soon see that Iran's new strategy on the battlefield, in diplomacy and in confronting the economic blockade will shatter your foundations," Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei wrote on X.
'Acts like Satan'
Iran's top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf lashed out at Washington over the wedding attack, calling the United States "Satan".
"If a power acts like Satan, picks targets like Satan, and kills like Satan, it's Satan," he posted on X.
The latest round of fighting began when Washington hit Iranian targets on Sunday, the first known strikes in several weeks.
Tehran's forces then targeted US troops in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates, and projectiles struck two oil tankers in unclaimed attacks, one of which killed two Filipino sailors, according to a Saudi shipping company.
Trump said the US strikes were "in retaliation for the Iranians' failed attempt at adding sea mines to the Strait" and for firing missiles at the base in Jordan.
More US strikes came on Tuesday, with Iranian state TV reporting explosions along the Hormuz and on an island in the Gulf, as well as an attack on an airport in the southern province of Kerman.
Seven people were killed and eight others wounded in a missile attack in the southern Khuzestan province, IRNA reported.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said four personnel were killed in a US strike in Kermanshah province, and three paramilitaries died on Lavan island in the Gulf. Another paramilitary was killed in the southern province of Fars, Iranian media said.
US President Donald Trump had warned of "much harder" attacks if Iran retaliated.
But Tehran's response was widespread, and included attacks targeting US interests in Erbil in Iraqi Kurdistan, and a US Marine training camp in Jordan near the Saudi and Israeli borders, according to Iranian media.
In the Gulf, air raid sirens sounded in Bahrain and Kuwait, where authorities said an Iranian drone set off a blaze at a residential complex.
'Very saddening'
Iranians expressed regret at the return to hostilities, including the deaths at the wedding. Hossein Moazami, 50, who is self-employed, called the attacks "truly distressing".
"I hope they all return to the negotiating table, because the only people suffering from this are the Iranian people," he said.
"The Americans are on the other side of the world, and nothing happens to them."
A video shared by an Iranian government account showed debris and damage at what it said was the wedding site in Sirik following the US strike, with people heard screaming in the background.
"It is a very saddening incident... Thank God the casualties were not higher," Ali Mallahi, father of the bride and owner of the building that was hit, said in a video carried by state TV.
The war began in late February with US-Israeli attacks on Iran that killed its supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
A fragile ceasefire collapsed after attacks on commercial ships in the Hormuz strait, through which one-fifth of world oil supplies previously flowed.
Incidents in the strait have continued. Iran's Guards said Wednesday that two oil tankers caught fire after hitting mines due to "the urging of the US military to transit via an illegal route".

Estonia quarantines emails from Russian domains over cyberattack risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:18:29 UTC
00:18:29 KST

Estonia is automatically diverting emails using Russia’s .ru internet domain into quarantine for additional security checks before they reach state institutions connected to the country’s secure government network, Justice and Digital Affairs Minister Liisa Pakosta told Estonia's public broadcaster ERR.
The measure is intended to protect Estonian government computer systems amid a post-2022 surge in cyberattacks that officials link to Russia. It applies only to institutions operating inside the secure state network, leaving local governments and some state bodies outside.
Many Estonian residents, particularly Russian speakers, still use .ru email services, ERR noted. Because the filter is triggered solely by the address ending, legitimate messages will be screened alongside potentially malicious ones and may take longer to arrive.
Pakosta said the safeguard was necessary because cyberattacks against Estonia had increased “exponentially” since 2022 and that many were linked to Russia. She said such attacks had not succeeded against Estonia, while major public-sector cyberattacks had succeeded in both Latvia and Lithuania.
The rerouting is automatic and handled centrally, so agencies do not need to take any action, Pakosta said. A large proportion of state institutions have already moved behind the government’s unified cyber shield, while the transition continues.
Pakosta described the quarantine as one small measure within Estonia’s wider cybersecurity work. Estonia’s courts have gone further, saying they will ask parties in legal proceedings to stop using .ru addresses for official communication, according to ERR.
How the Baltic states are hardening against Russia
Estonia's email quarantine forms part of a broader Baltic effort to limit Russian influence and strengthen defenses against military, cyber, and covert threats.
Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania are constructing a Baltic Defense Line, a planned network of bunkers, anti-tank ditches, and other barriers, along their borders with Russia and Belarus. Latvia has also banned imports of Russian and Belarusian books, clothing, toys, and other goods.
The threat extends beyond cyberattacks: an Estonian court found that Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU, ordered the 2024 firebombing of a Ukrainian restaurant in Tallinn, part of a wider Russian sabotage campaign targeting European supporters of Ukraine.

discarded aluminum blinds transform into cylindrical lighting system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:15:47 UTC
00:15:47 KST

Keker Collection by Reza Raeisifar repurposes discarded aluminum Venetian blind slats, originally designed to control and block light, as components for a modular system that directs and distributes illumination. By transferring a familiar architectural element into a new lighting application, the project uses recycled material to develop a family of adaptable lighting objects.
Keker began in 2018, when Raeisifar encountered an old, unused Venetian blind in a storage space and began exploring how its material and structure could be reused. The idea developed further through an invitation to propose a lighting design for the interior of the Afarinesh project at Shiraz University. The resulting system shifts the function of the aluminum slats from controlling incoming light to directing and diffusing an artificial light source, while using a limited amount of material.
The first iteration consists of three laser-cut acrylic sheets that form the structural framework. Longitudinally cut aluminum slats are inserted into grooves within the sheets, creating a repeated modular arrangement. An energy-efficient LED light source sits at the center and distributes light in 360 degrees, while the curved slats conceal the source from direct view. Their geometry produces changing patterns of light and shadow while maintaining visual comfort.
The construction system allows Keker to be configured into different forms and lighting types. Over time, the collection by designer Reza Raeisifar has developed into pendant, linear, ceiling, wall-mounted, and floor-standing versions, each retaining the same underlying construction principle. The first iteration of Keker was presented in 2019 at Ordibehesht Gallery in Tehran. In 2025, the different versions developed over the intervening years were brought together as a collection and presented at Design Gallery One in Tehran.

Ukraine’s New Defense Minister Tells Europe: $27B Needed Urgently
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:14:00 UTC
00:14:00 KST

Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara in his first official presentation to his European counterparts said his country needs $27 billion in support to defend itself from Russia, most of all for air defense weapons to protect his country’s civilian homes and businesses from mass Russian aerial attacks, a ministry statement made public on Tuesday said.
Khmara debuts at EU Defense Ministers informal summit
European defense ministry bosses and other top officials assembled in Druids Glen, County Wicklow, Ireland on Monday at an “informal gathering” listened to Khmara’s video presentation sympathetically and several later spoke in support – but there were no immediate declarations of new assistance to Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
A senior commando officer credited for running some of Ukraine’s most effective special operations missions behind Russian lines, Khmara has served as his country’s defense minister since July and met with a few of his Western counterparts bilaterally, but until Tuesday had never addressed the European national security leadership as a single audience.
Khmara told the gathering attended by among others NATO Deputy Secretary General Radmila Shekerinska and European Parliament defense committee chair Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermannthat Ukraine needs around $27 billion in additional defense funding and asked his audience to accelerate a $104 million equivalent EU military assistance loan that has been approved but not yet fully disbursed.
Donbas: The Ukrainian Roots That Survived
Ukraine is calling on Europe’s defense ministry heads to bring forward money earmarked in that loan for 2027 and transfer it to Ukraine immediately, Khmara said, because of intense Russian air attacks and dangerously low stocks of Ukrainian air defense weapons, particularly heavy Patriot interceptor missiles needed to stop Russian ballistic missiles, and light, hand-held anti-aircraft missiles needed to take on cheap Russian jet-powered kamikaze drones.
Ukraine also must deepen its stocks of air-to-air missiles fired by aircraft and reserves of modern fighter planes to carry the missiles in preparation for a mass Russian aerial bombardment campaign that is likely to begin in early winter, he said.
Mutual benefits of EU cooperation with Ukraine in wartime tech developments
Khmara said that defense cooperation between Ukraine and Europe is mutually beneficial and that his country is ready to transfer its top wartime-developed defense technologies to allies.
Thanks to years of actual combat experience against Russia, Ukraine’s drone, battle sensor, and war data fusion systems are often years ahead technologically, and usually orders of magnitude cheaper, than competing NATO-standard systems, Ukrainian military analysts agree.
“Every euro invested in Ukrainian defense is an investment in European security,” Khmara said.
Kaja Kallas, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, following the meeting, told reporters in Ireland that Russia is attacking Ukraine using “terror by design,” and that the Kremlin’s attempts to prevent European support to Ukraine would not work.
“They will not succeed. To the contrary, today, also in the discussions that we had, we will increase our support to Ukraine,” Kallas said. “Especially for Patriot missiles [in European army stocks] about to expire should be sent or sold to Ukraine.”
Helen McEntee, Ireland’s Minister for Defense and Foreign Affairs, said that most EU governments support Khmara’s request to accelerate the Ukraine loan. Ukraine has a hole in its air defenses and Europe needs to help fill it, she said.
“What I think was very clear from our presentation from the defense minister [Khmara] is that there is a gap,” McEntee said. “I do believe that there was a significant number of member states that supported that ask.”
Because the meeting was informal, no formal decision could be made, she added in comments to Irish reporters. Approving Ukraine’s loan advance request would require unanimous agreement by the member states and the European Commission, McEntee said.
European reporting on the EU Defense Ministers informal summit
According to European defense sector reports, behind the scenes, Kyiv and its closest supporters are pushing Greece and Spain to turn over their in-stock Patriot systems and interceptor missiles to Ukraine.
In both Athens and Madrid, there is some resistance to the idea because of limited stocks and potential threat of air attacks on the homeland, in Greece’s case by neighboring Turkey, and in Spain’s case by insurgents or terrorists based in North Africa.
The major European information platform Euronews filed reports on the meeting directly highlighting Khmara’s appeal for Ukrainian drone financing, Patriot interceptors and additional European funding.
The Irish Times reported McEntee’s assessment that the issue of Ukrainian air defense was no longer simply a Ukrainian security issue, because the Russian military aggression is, potentially, a threat to the entire continent.
Germany’s center-left government led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Tuesday charged Russia with “state-sponsored terrorism” for an Aug. 4 drone attack that attempted, unsuccessfully, to blow up a Ukrainian heavy cargo plane on the tarmac of Leipzig airport.
Kremlin officials have scoffed at the idea Russia had anything to do with it and accused Merz and his supporters of warmongering.
Germany politically split between center-left Ukrainian supporters and far-right nationalist detractors
Since coming to power in 2025, under Merz’s leadership, Germany became Ukraine’s single most generous supporting state, having contributed $10 billion of aid of all types that year. The next-most supportive, Britain, handed over slightly less than $6 billion.
Germany has local elections scheduled in September in the eastern Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern states, both regions dominated by Germany’s far-right, single most popular political party, the nationalist-right AfD (Alternativ fur Deutschland).
On Tuesday evening, during a Sat 1 Newstime Sommerinterview broadcast, the co-leader of the AfD, Tino Chrupalla, said that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky “gives him more stomach aches” than Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
Chrupalla went on to call Zelensky “a highly corrupt president” who wants to keep the war with Russia going so that he and members of his inner circle could make more money from Europe-financed defense contracting.
Chrupalla argued that Germany “should return to dialogue with Moscow” and dismissed Russia’s having invaded Ukraine as no worse than “illegal” wars launched by US and Israel.

Slovak government approves joining compensation commission for Ukraine despite Russian threats
The Slovak government has approved a proposal to join the Convention establishing the International Claims Commission for Ukraine, over which Russia's Foreign Ministry had contacted Slovakia.
Source: Slovak newspaper Denník N, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Slovakia had planned to join the convention earlier, but Prime Minister Robert Fico eventually withdrew his signature. However, he has now reconsidered his position, as demonstrated by the government's decision adopted on 2 September.
Fico confirmed that negotiations on the issue had been suspended last week on his instructions.
On Wednesday, after a government meeting in Nitra, the prime minister said that "it is perfectly normal" for another state to express disagreement with a particular decision.
"Yes, it is true. Yesterday I learned from our ambassador about information from the Russian side that they do not like this convention on the claims commission," Fico acknowledged, as quoted by Teraz.sk.
Meenahwile, he dismissed the "opposition's hysteria", which he said is evident in this case. "Last week, we suspended negotiations on the issue to clarify some details, and today we approved it," he said.
He stressed that the creation of the claims commission is provided for by a Council of Europe convention and, although the commission's subsequent decisions are not legally binding, he described the convention as a strong political gesture.
Slovakia's accession to the convention still requires parliamentary ratification.
Background:
- Previously, Slovak politician Ivan Novotný from the opposition Freedom and Solidarity (SaS) party said that Russia may have pressured Robert Fico's government not to join the Convention establishing the International Claims Commission for Ukraine.
- Novotný said Slovakia was due to sign the Convention establishing the International Claims Commission for Ukraine in July this year.
- However, Fico eventually withdrew his signature. According to Novotný, Russia had threatened Bratislava into making this move.
- The Convention establishing the International Claims Commission within the institutional framework of the Council of Europe is the second component of the international compensation mechanism, alongside the Register of Damage.
- The document was opened for signature on 16 December 2025 during a high-level diplomatic conference in The Hague. At the time, 35 states and the European Union signed it – a record number. Among EU countries, Slovakia, Hungary and Bulgaria did not sign the document.

Ukraine Eliminates Russian Mercenaries From Zimbabwe and Colombia on Lyman Front
Ukrainian forces have eliminated foreign nationals from Colombia and Zimbabwe fighting in Russian ranks on the Lyman front, where foreigners now account for roughly 30% of personnel in newly deployed Russian units, Ukraine’s 66th Separate Mechanized Brigade said on September 2.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the brigade, the Colombian and Zimbabwean fighters were killed by soldiers of its 3rd Mechanized Battalion “Fireflies” and the “Siverska Sich” Motorized Infantry Battalion.
The brigade said the proportion of foreign nationals serving in Russian formations within its area of responsibility has continued to increase, particularly among newly deployed units. Many come from African and Latin American countries and, according to the Ukrainian military, were recruited into Russian service through deception.
The September 2 statement follows an assessment provided several days earlier by Vasyl Denysiuk, spokesperson for the 66th Separate Mechanized Brigade, who told Suspilne on August 29 that foreign personnel were increasingly common among Russian reinforcements arriving on the Lyman axis.
According to Denysiuk, the recruits come from Latin America, Africa, and Southeast Asia. He said that when Russia deploys a fresh company into the brigade’s area of responsibility, approximately one platoon can consist entirely of foreign personnel.
Denysiuk also said the recruits generally receive limited military preparation before being deployed on combat missions. The brigade has linked this practice to an increase in cases of foreign fighters surrendering to Ukrainian forces.
At the same time, Russian forces have continued reinforcing the Lyman sector with assault troops and drone crews while attempting to identify vulnerable sections of the Ukrainian defensive line, Denysiuk told Suspilne.
The latest cases add to a broader pattern of foreign nationals serving in Russia’s military. On August 4, Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Liubinets said Ukraine had captured citizens of 51 countries while they were fighting in Russian ranks.

Zelensky announces new air alert system as Russia strikes Kyiv for seventh consecutive day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:12:28 UTC
00:12:28 KST

Zelensky announces new air alert system as Russia strikes Kyiv for seventh consecutive day
Ukraine will change how air raid alerts operate amid relentless Russian drone strikes on Kyiv for the seventh consecutive day, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sept. 2.
Currently, a single air raid alert is used for any type of aerial threat in a particular region.
Under the new plan, alerts will be divided into red and yellow levels. The yellow level corresponds to incoming drones, whereas the red level indicates threats from missiles, including ballistic missiles, and massive combined attacks, according to Zelensky.
For each threat level, the air raid alert sirens will sound a different signal. The warnings should also be more localized according to the area of the threat, Zelensky added.
The measures are intended to give people in Ukraine greater predictability and clearer guidance on how to respond to different threats, Zelensky said.
Russia has attacked the Ukrainian capital with drones and missiles in a relentless barrage for seven consecutive days. The accompanying air raid alerts sound throughout the day and night, and the Russian strikes have taken a toll on residents.
"We’re tired. We’re very, very tired," Diana To Hang, a student, told the Kyiv Independent on Sept. 2 following more Russian strikes on Kyiv.
During a yellow alert, public transport in Kyiv will be altered, but not stopped, with some metro lines working partially or fully, and curfew restrictions will also be revised, according to Zelensky.
The General Staff, together with the Air Force, the Cabinet, the Defense Ministry, the Interior Ministry, and the State Emergency Service will determine the specific thresholds for the yellow and red levels weekly, Zelensky said.
Zelensky also announced an effort to update the standards and localities of air raid shelters, "in particular mobile shelters to protect people."
Only the measures regarding schools and kindergartens are to remain unchanged, the President said. For thousands of Ukrainian children, the new school year began on Sept. 1.

Russia arrests children’s hospice director over army criticism
LONDON - Russian police on Sept 2 arrested the head of a children’s hospice on suspicion of spreading “false information” about the army, her lawyer told AFP, as Moscow cracks down on critics of its Ukraine offensive.
Lida Moniava, 38, is the founder and director of a Moscow-based charity that provides end-of-life care to children and young adults.
Her arrest stems from a Telegram post she made in 2023 marking the first-year anniversary of the war, in which she alluded to UN data showing thousands of civilian casualties, her lawyer Mikhail Biryukov said.
Prosecutors accuse her of having been “motivated by political hatred”, Biryukov told AFP.
She faces up to 10 years in prison if found guilty.
Russia’s Investigative Committee, which prosecutes serious crimes, announced she had been charged with “knowingly spreading false information regarding the use of the Russian Armed Forces”.
“Moniava has been detained. During questioning, she did not admit guilt regarding the alleged offence,” it said.
Amnesty International described Moniava’s arrest as “another brazen attempt by Russia’s authorities to crackdown on any expression of anti-war sentiment.”
Since Moscow launched its offensive in February 2022, Russian police have detained thousands of people for speaking out against the war – Europe’s deadliest since World War II.
Prosecutors often accuse those publishing criticisms of the Russian army of spreading “fake news”.
Russia’s media regulator has ordered domestic news outlets to use only “official Russian sources” when reporting on the conflict, limiting them to information provided by the Russian defence ministry. AFP

Russian TV channels are required to give airtime to debates before elections. The parties just don’t show up.

Russian TV channels are required to give airtime to debates before elections. The parties just don’t show up.
Televised debates for candidates in elections to the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, have begun airing on Russian television. Russian law requires state TV channels to give parties and candidates free airtime, but they cannot fill all of it with campaign ads — at least half must go to joint campaign events such as discussions, roundtables, and debates.
Public debate in modern Russia has been in decline for years. Vladimir Putin has never once taken part in a debate during his time in power, and many United Russia candidates have followed his lead. By the 2026 campaign, substantive political discussion had all but disappeared — though some of this year’s debates are still worth watching.
In Ryazan, the channel Russia 1 spent two days straight trying — and failing — to get State Duma candidates into its studio. On both occasions, the host said goodbye to viewers right after her opening remarks, with all six lecterns around her standing empty.
In Buryatia, by contrast, Bair Tsyrenov, a candidate from Russia’s Communist Party (KPRF), did make it into the studio. On air, he called on his United Russia opponent to join him in open debates. But before he could finish, the broadcast cut away to a government meeting with Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin.
Some candidates split the difference between skipping the debate and delivering a fiery speech: they simply stay silent on air. Alexey Chernov, a candidate from the Direct Democracy Party, took 25 seconds to answer the moderator’s question, then stood silently in front of the camera for another 35 seconds. The moderator tried to coax him along, saying, “maybe something will come to mind,” but Chernov said nothing else would.
Clips from these debates have spread widely on social media, but watching live remains the surest way to see them. Journalists have noted that TV channels delete recordings of debate broadcasts “at the request of the copyright holder.”

BANGKOK, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Thailand and Singapore agreed on Wednesday to elevate their strategic partnership at their first leaders' retreat in 11 years, pledging closer cooperation as the two countries prepare to take consecutive chairmanships of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and his Singaporean counterpart Lawrence Wong welcomed a joint statement on a forward-looking strategic partnership after talks during the fifth Thailand-Singapore Leaders' Retreat in Bangkok and agreed to work on four further agreements covering the digital economy, transnational crime, food security, and supply chain resilience.

China to continue hydrological information sharing with Nepal to support disaster response
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
23:07:10 CST
00:07:10 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- China will continue to share information on barrier lake risks, glacial lake risks and emergency hydrological monitoring with Nepal to support disaster rescue and relief efforts, an official with the Ministry of Water Resources said Wednesday.
A fast-moving chain mudslide, triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal, struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region on Aug. 26, causing severe damage to the port and destroying hydrological monitoring facilities.
As of Wednesday noon, 21 people had been confirmed dead and 541 others remained missing, according to the latest update from the Xizang regional government.
The disaster-hit area poses significant challenges for hydrological monitoring, as it is surrounded by high mountains, deep valleys and numerous glaciers and glacial lakes, the ministry said.
China's emergency hydrological monitoring team is working to restore the damaged monitoring stations, establish an early warning system, and closely monitor key risk areas. It is also continuing to share hydrological monitoring information with Nepal.
The ministry is now providing Nepal with daily updates on the development of a barrier lake above the Gyirong Port, cascading risks associated with the Cuojian River impact crater in Nepal, glacial lake risks in the Gyirong Zangbo River basin, the development and risk forecasts of new barrier lakes, and emergency hydrological monitoring.
The geological conditions in the Gyirong disaster-hit area remain highly unstable, with risks of further landslides, rockfalls and other secondary hazards, the ministry warned. The large number of glacial lakes in the surrounding area is also adding to the uncertainty.
The timely information provided by the ministry offers Nepal much-needed technical support, helping its authorities carry out rescue and emergency response efforts, evacuate residents in a timely manner and reduce casualties, the ministry said.
Looking ahead, China will work with Nepal to promote the signing of an agreement on hydrological information sharing for transboundary rivers and establish a regular cooperation mechanism, with the aim of jointly strengthening disaster prevention and mitigation, it added. ■
