Feature: Amid war, a library of "Impact" rises from rubble in Gaza
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
23:06:52 CST
00:06:52 KST

GAZA, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Inside a modest tent in Deir al-Balah, in the central Gaza Strip, Mohammed Saad sits surrounded by thousands of books that survived the war.
He picks up a book, gently wipes the dust from its cover, and flips through its pages before placing it among rows of novels, historical works, scientific publications and philosophical books.
For Saad, 58, this is more than sorting books. It is an attempt to bring back to life a part of his world that he thought had been buried beneath the rubble.
A father of five, Saad spent 35 years collecting books. Before the war, he owned between 80,000 and 100,000 books in Beit Lahia, northern Gaza, some of which he sold in front of the Islamic University in Gaza City.
When his home and warehouse were destroyed during the Israeli war on Gaza, he believed his entire collection was gone.
About three months ago, he returned to his ruined home and began searching through the debris.
"I didn't care about my house or my personal belongings," Saad told Xinhua. "The first thing I started searching for among the rubble was my books and my library."
For weeks, with help from neighbors, he recovered more than 30,000 books and transported them to Deir al-Balah.
"I couldn't believe I had saved so many books," he said. "I truly cried. For me, they are not just books; they represent life, history and happiness."
After the books arrived in Deir al-Balah, Saad refused to keep them stacked away, safe from damage but out of readers' reach.
Instead, he established "al-Athar Library," Arabic for "the Impact," a modest space where people can read, buy, or borrow books.
"I'm not looking for money or material gain," Saad said as he continued dusting and arranging the books. "All I want is for these books to reach people so they can read, learn and benefit from them."
The library still lacks a proper building, adequate shelves, and suitable storage facilities. Yet readers have begun to arrive.
"Women and children are among the most interested visitors, particularly those looking for novels and stories, while young people often seek cultural, historical and educational books," Saad said.
For many, the library offers more than books. It is a rare escape from a daily reality of displacement, destruction, and uncertainty.
Among its regular visitors is 25-year-old Mohammed al-Deeb, who comes to browse and buy books, particularly works by Arab authors.
"For me, reading has become a refuge, especially during the long periods of internet and electricity outages," al-Deeb told Xinhua.
Sometimes he takes novels back to his tent and reads them with his family. "Reading has become one of the few things we can do together under these circumstances," he said. "We need things to remind us that our lives aren't just about war."
Ibrahim Abu Amsha, 30, also visits the library from time to time. He sees the library as a small but vital revival of Gaza's cultural life, which has sharply declined during the war.
His interests include novels, Palestinian history and children's books. But displacement, the destruction of libraries and the shrinking of cultural spaces have made finding books increasingly difficult.
"Before the war, accessing books was easy, and libraries were located in various areas," Abu Amsha said. "Now, finding a book you like requires effort."
"The war took many things from us, but it shouldn't take reading from us too," he added, expressing hope that the library would continue to grow and expand.
The establishment of the library comes as Gaza's cultural infrastructure has suffered extensive damage since the outbreak of the Israel-Hamas conflict in October 2023.
According to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics, the Gaza Strip had 87 public libraries and library institutions before the war, all of which have suffered total or partial damage during the conflict.
Against this backdrop, Saad sees every recovered book as more than a salvaged object. To him, the books preserve fragments of a collective memory that war cannot be allowed to erase.
"The war destroyed many things, but we must bring books back to life and bring children back to culture, science and school," he said. "If there is no science and culture, we will collapse." ■

Kenyan students depart for China under Chinese language education program
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
23:06:41 CST
00:06:41 KST

NAIROBI, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- A send-off ceremony for Kenyan students preparing to pursue further studies in China was held Wednesday at the Confucius Institute at the University of Nairobi, bringing together government officials, teachers, students, and parents.
A total of 23 students have completed two years of study at the University of Nairobi under a 2+2 joint program for international Chinese language education and will travel to Tianjin Normal University to continue their studies.
Graduates are expected to teach Chinese at secondary schools across Kenya in the future, contributing to the development of Chinese language education in the country.
Zhang Zhizhong, charge d'affaires of the Chinese Embassy in Kenya, said the program is far more than a language-training initiative.
"Its birth and continued success reflect a much larger story," Zhang said, adding that it was born out of growing enthusiasm among Kenyan students for learning Chinese, made possible by the integration of Chinese into Kenya's national education system, and sustained by rising demand for Chinese-speaking talent as more Chinese enterprises invest and operate in Kenya.
Wahome Rureri, deputy director in Kenya's State Department of Higher Education and Research within the Ministry of Education, said the University of Nairobi and its Confucius Institute are playing a vital role in teacher training, and the 2+2 program has been a successful collaboration between China and Kenya.
With Chinese-language education in Kenya continuing to grow, Kenya plans to launch pilot schools and further improve both the number and quality of locally trained Chinese language teachers, Rureri said.
Ayub Gitau, vice chancellor of the University of Nairobi, said scholarship programs and cooperation with local partners have created valuable opportunities for young Kenyans to learn Chinese and contributed to the development of Chinese language education in the country.
He said the program is well-designed to train Chinese language teachers within the broader context of competency-based education in Kenya and has been designed to respond to educational needs and teacher-certification requirements.
In December 2023, the University of Nairobi, the Center for Language Education and Cooperation under China's Ministry of Education, and Tianjin Normal University signed a tripartite agreement on the joint training of students majoring in international Chinese language education, officially establishing the 2+2 dual-degree scholarship program. ■

China to advance development of new-type power grids
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
23:06:39 CST
00:06:39 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- China will advance the high-quality development of its new-type power grids during the 2026-2030 period to ensure the safe and stable operation of the country's power system, the National Energy Administration (NEA) said Wednesday.
The new-type power grid, as defined by the NEA, encompasses both the construction of a backbone grid and the coordinated development of power grids at all levels, with its operation powered by information technology. Its development is a key step in China's efforts to build robust, intelligent and digitalized power grids.
The NEA said that during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), China's power demand is expected to grow at an average annual rate of around 5 percent, and the demand for high-quality green power from high-end industries will grow steadily, placing higher requirements on the construction of new-type power grids.
To meet the growing demand, efforts should be made to strengthen power infrastructure, said Wang Hongzhi, head of the NEA. Wang called for measures to enhance the safety and stability of the country's large power grids, fully leverage distribution networks as public platforms, and promote flexible and diverse interactions within smart microgrids.
Wang also stressed innovation-driven development, calling for accelerated research and development of new technologies, including artificial intelligence and intelligent grid management.
The construction of a new-type power grid links upstream projects, such as renewable energy generation, with downstream industrial and commercial sectors as well as households, Wang said, noting that its broad reach and large scale make it a strong driver of investment.
Approvals for major power grid projects, such as power transmission corridors, should be accelerated, Wang said. He added that grid companies should fully leverage these types of projects to spur investment, while local energy authorities should expedite the implementation of related supporting measures.
"The NEA will encourage private enterprises nationwide to actively invest in the development of new-type power grids and benefit from the opportunities they create," he said.
New-type power grids are part of China's "six networks" initiative, which aims to boost domestic demand and support steady economic growth.
The initiative covers six types of networks: water networks, new-type power grids, computing power networks, next-generation communication networks, urban underground pipeline networks and logistics networks. ■

Hinton’s Views on Consciousness: Explained
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:01:50 UTC
00:01:50 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
In recent interviews, Hinton has unabashedly spoken of AI being conscious, among many other claims, such as worrying that AI will fool humans into ceding power to AIs against our best interests, and that AIs ‘really understand’ us.
Here are some short videos of these claims in action.
What strikes me most about these conversations as a philosopher of mind is the complete absence of any explanation as to why Hinton thinks any of this.
Consider, for example, Hinton’s argument for why AI really understands. He states that anybody who regularly uses a chatbot knows that AI understands, using a kind of reductio ad absurdum to make his point. Anyone who denies AI lacks understanding is committed to believing an AI can give you the correct answer to a question without understanding the question. This is absurd, he says, so it’s not true.1
Something must be capable of understanding a question to answer a question. This argument alone might not move you, though the claim itself is not entirely unreasonable. In fact, I’d be willing to accept the claim, though I’d draw a different conclusion to Hinton. I wouldn’t concede AI consciousness on these grounds. Id respond that AI doesn’t actually answer questions. It produces outputs given inputs.
But this is beside the point, because Hinton’s views on AI are rooted in a lot more than the arguments offered in these videos, and that’s what’s frustrating.
What’s absent from the conversation is Hinton’s beliefs on the nature of understanding, how the human brain works, and how these views of his inform his views on AI consciousness and intelligence. That’s what we’ll get into here.
What Does Hinton Think the Brain is Like?
The Symbolic View and The Connectionist View
There are two big views on how the brain works: a symbolic view of the brain (it goes by other names too) and a connectionist view of it.
Hinton is a connectionist. He essentially believes that the human brain is one big neural network, and that, as such, it processes information very similarly to LLMs. Of course, Hinton and everyone else recognises that LLMs learn differently to humans, but he believes that fundamentally the human brain and LLMs are both non-symbolic distributed weight systems (these points are hinted at in the videos above, just not explained in any detail).
According to a connectionist model of the brain, we can explain human cognition in terms of neuronal connections, specifically, in terms of the patterns of activations that emerge across networks of neurons and the strengths of those patterns.
This view of the brain is sharply contrasted with a symbolic view in cognitive science, according to which the brain is like a digital computer. On this view, human cognition is understood in terms of the manipulation of symbols using formal rules.
Consider, then, what it means according to each view, to ‘understand’ something.
The Classic Symbolic View
To understand something according to a classic symbolic view of the brain, one needs to correctly manipulate a specific representation of whatever it is you’re trying to understand (a ‘representation’ of something is basically a fancy word for a physical symbol that carries information about that thing. e.g, that the concept bachelor contains information about males and marriage)
To understand what a bachelor is, you need to possess the appropriate rules to correctly use the term bachelor. Such a rule might be bachelor = unmarried adult male. Possessing an understanding of the concept bachelor on this view, just is the ability to check whether something is a male, is unmarried, and is an adult, and to return an appropriate output, namely, that ‘X is a bachelor’ or that ‘X is not a bachelor’.
The Connectionist View
According to a connectionist view, the brain has no rules and has no physical symbols in this sense. All it has are patterns of activations across neurons and varying strengths among those different patterns. In our last example, the concept bachelor does not consist of any information stored in symbols. And understanding what a bachelor is does not require possessing rules to manipulate that symbol.
It consists of the right neuronal patterns of activations, and those neuronal patterns of activations, further standing in the right relationships to other patterns of neuronal activations that are relevant to the concept.
E.g., to understand what a bachelor is requires the right patterns of neurons to activate to identify a bachelor (e.g., when you encounter one) and to have this neural pattern overlap with other appropriate patterns, for example the activations for ‘unmarried’, ‘male’ and ‘adult’, while diverging from unrelated ones, like ‘women’, ‘child’ and ‘married’.
Why Hinton Thinks AI’s ‘Understand’
For a brief overview of how LLMs work, see section 1 of this article before reading further
Now you’re in a better position to understand why Hinton thinks AIs ‘understand’. He’s a connectionist. He views the brain as one enormously vast and complex neural network, which, though not identical to an LLM, is built of the same basic principles.
LLMs, like the brain, is built on distributed representations and learned weights. So when we ask what it means for an LLM to understand something for Hinton, it more or less means exactly the same thing as what it means for a human to understand something. Once an LLM has been appropriately trained, and its ‘representations’ —that is, its patterns of activations across its MLP and attention layers —stand in the right relationships to the relevant concepts (i.e., other activation patterns) then an LLM understands these concepts. That is why Hinton thinks LLMs understand you when you ask it a question and it gives you the ‘right’ answer.
Now, I want to be clear, connectionism as a theory does not claim to explain consciousness. Moreover, I don’t mean to suggest that all connectionists believe that ‘understanding’ can necessarily be reduced to the picture I have described above (instead, I am interested in offering a possible way of understanding Hinton’s own claims about AI). So, Hinton’s view on consciousness are unexplained based on his connectionism beliefs alone. With that said, I do think we are in a better position to understand his views on consciousness if we consider his connectionist beliefs.
Hinton is well known for having built and designed foundational neural network models. He has even won the Nobel Prize “for foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks”2
Now, if you remember that Hinton believes LLMs share the same basic foundational architecture as human brains, it is not too difficult to see how he might believe AIs are conscious. To be honest, if I were convinced the brain was a neural network —and I am really not convinced of this — I would at least consider it incumbent on me to seriously consider whether AI is conscious too.
Now, here comes the kicker. I really don’t see any reason to believe connectionism about the brain is true. But that’ll be a post for another time.
In the meantime, let me say that what is desperately missing in the media is any kind of educational content, or even laying out of background assumptions, to explain the views of people like Hinton. There is no denying Hinton is a man of genius, talent, and exceptional accomplishment. That is all the more reason to make very clear what his background beliefs are. Since, we are already conditioned to believe what he says.
Thank you for being here. If you found this article valuable, consider a free or paid subscription. Behind the paid tier you’ll find work that spells out my own philosophical views, analysis of AI lab papers, videos where I share ideas in progress and more. Plus, you’ll be helping support the existence of rigorous independent philosophical writing on AI consciousness, something we all desperately need today.
See this argument in the first minute of the second video linked here.
See: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2024/hinton/facts/

China’s Xi visits Egypt’s el-Sisi: Why it matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:00:30 UTC
00:00:30 KST

China’s Xi visits Egypt’s el-Sisi: Why it matters
Xi’s historic visit to Egypt aims to strengthen China-Egypt ties amid rising Middle East tensions.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is visiting Egypt for the first time in a decade, as Cairo looks to foster deeper economic and military ties with Beijing while maintaining its long-standing relationship with Washington.
The visit comes as the US-Israel war on Iran and resulting disruption to global trade have prompted US allies in the region to reassess their strategic relationships. Most recently, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye announced the Mecca Joint Deterrence Agreement, a mutual defence pact.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3China’s Xi makes first visit to Egypt in a decade, amid regional turmoil
- list 2 of 3China’s Xi makes his first visit to Egypt in a decade
- list 3 of 3Xi, Modi and Putin attend SCO summit: What’s on the agenda?
Seeking closer ties with Beijing, therefore, is part of an effort to further what President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has called Cairo’s “independent foreign policy”.
For China, Egypt offers an important foothold in the Middle East with its large economy, control of the Suez Canal and diplomatic influence across the Arab world and Africa.
Here is what you need to know:
What is the visit about?
Xi’s three-day visit, which began on Tuesday evening, includes talks with el-Sisi that are expected to focus on the regional conflict and its consequences for maritime trade security, as well as expanding Chinese investment in Egypt.
The two countries are expected to sign economic agreements covering areas including artificial intelligence (AI), transport and manufacturing.
The visit marks 70 years of diplomatic relations between Egypt and China. Egyptian state-run media reported that Xi has called for the two countries to “expand the scope of pragmatic collaboration”, while el-Sisi praised Chinese investment in Egypt and reiterated Cairo’s support for Beijing’s position on Taiwan, the island nation that China claims as part of its own territory.
Military cooperation is another increasingly important part of the relationship.
In August, Egypt and China held joint air exercises including Chinese J-16 fighter jets and Egypt’s French-made Rafale aircraft. It was the first time the J-16s had taken part in a combat exercise alongside the Rafales.
Why is this state visit important?
Xi’s visit highlights Beijing’s efforts to expand its influence in a region where the US has been the dominant military power for decades.
Egypt is a key Middle East ally for Washington, and the second-largest recipient of US military aid.
The meeting comes at a time of considerable geopolitical instability, with Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, the US-Israel war with Iran, and disruption around the Red Sea caused by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis targeting Saudi-linked ships all raising questions about the durability of the existing US-led regional order, experts say.
Rob Geist Pinfold, a lecturer in international security at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera, “China is trying to position itself as an increasingly important economic and diplomatic actor in that environment, particularly as a counterweight to the US, as a more responsible and more hands-off regional actor.”
Egypt has a population of 110 million and is an important market for Chinese goods and investment. It is also particularly important to Beijing because it controls the Suez Canal, Pinfold said, adding that the waterway has become even more critical amid disruptions to shipping in the crucial Bab el-Mandeb and Hormuz straits.
Iran has effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz for the past six months in retaliation for US-Israeli strikes. Prior to the war, more than one-fifth of the world’s oil and petroleum products were shipped through the strait, which is the only sea route to the open ocean available to Gulf producers.
China offers Egypt opportunities to develop investment, infrastructure and technology, while bilateral ties have also expanded into areas including defence and artificial intelligence.
But the growing relationship should not be interpreted as Egypt pivoting away from the US entirely, Pinfold said, noting that “instead, el-Sisi’s approach is better understood as one of diversification and strategic autonomy”.
“In short,” Pinfold said, “as the Gulf states have done in recent years, he is trying to hedge without alienating or annoying Egypt’s indisputably most important ally, the US.”
How strong are Egypt-China relations?
Relations between Cairo and Beijing have deepened significantly since 2014, when el-Sisi visited China and the two countries signed a strategic partnership agreement.
China is now Egypt’s largest trading partner in non-petroleum goods, with bilateral trade reaching nearly $20.7bn by the end of 2025, according to Egypt’s State Information Service (SIS).
Data from the country’s Central Agency for Public Mobilization and Statistics (CAPMAS) shows a nearly 200 percent increase in Egyptian exports to China, at $840.8m in the first half of 2026, while imports stood at $10.4bn.
Beijing has also invested more than $10bn in Egypt, including in the New Administrative Capital east of Cairo and an electric rail line serving industry in the Nile Delta.
Chinese companies have also invested in container ports, green hydrogen, iron pipes, tyres and satellites.
Chinese investments in Egypt are focused mainly in the Suez Canal area and the China-Egypt TEDA cooperation zone in Ain Sokhna, part of Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative, which hosts about 200 companies with investments exceeding $3.8bn, according to Egyptian state media.
In 2023, Egypt joined BRICS, the bloc of Global South nations including Brazil, Russia, India and China.

Best Pizza Cheese for Melting and Stretchiness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:00:29 UTC
00:00:29 KST

Best Pizza Cheese for Melting and Stretchiness
When it comes to pizza, cheese is not just a topping; it is the foundation of texture, flavor, and visual appeal. The perfect pizza cheese should melt smoothly, stretch generously when sliced, and complement the crust and sauce. Achieving that iconic cheese pull depends on protein structure, moisture content, fat levels, and how the cheese is processed. Below is a detailed guide to the best cheeses for melting and stretchiness, along with why they work so well on pizza.
Mozzarella, The Gold Standard!
Mozzarella is widely considered the best pizza cheese for both melting and stretchiness, and for good reason. But why is it that good? Because it has high moisture and an elastic protein structure allow it to melt evenly, and Casein proteins form long strands when heated, creating the classic cheese pull. Also, Mild flavor lets the sauce and dough shine. Calindairy Mozzarella cheese is the best for American or Italian-style pizza.
Types of mozzarella
- Low-moisture mozzarella (whole milk): The most common choice for professional pizzerias. It melts smoothly, stretches well, and releases less water than fresh mozzarella.
- Low-moisture mozzarella (part-skim): Slightly less creamy but still very stretchy. Often used for cost efficiency.
- Fresh mozzarella: Soft and delicate with excellent melt, but high moisture can make pizza watery unless properly drained and baked at high temperatures.
Provolone, Stretch with Extra Flavor!
Provolone is a semi-hard Italian cheese that melts beautifully and stretches well, though slightly less than mozzarella. This cheese had a similar protein structure to mozzarella. Higher fat content adds richness, and more pronounced flavor enhances depth.
Best use of Provolone Cheese
- Blended with mozzarella for better flavor complexity.
- Excellent on Sicilian, Detroit-style, or pan pizzas.
Fior di Latte, Artisan-Level Stretch!
Fior di latte is a fresh mozzarella made from cow’s milk, commonly used in traditional Italian pizzas. Has exceptionally smooth melt, Clean, milky stretch with a soft bite, and Balanced moisture when baked properly.
Best use
- High-temperature ovens.
- Thin-crust pizzas where ingredient quality is the focus.
Oaxaca Cheese, Outstanding Stretch Alternative!
Oaxaca cheese, traditionally used in Mexican cuisine, is one of the stretchiest cheeses available, so you can use it in your next pizza recipe and enjoy the ultimate and extraordinary cheese pull. The pasta filata (stretched curd) process is similar to that of mozzarella. This cheese creates dramatic, long cheese pulls and has a mild flavor that works well with tomato-based sauces.
Normally Can be used for:
- Fusion-style pizzas.
- Home cooks seeking maximum stretch with minimal effort.
Monterey Jack, Smooth Melter with Elasticity!
Monterey Jack melts easily and smoothly, producing moderate stretch. The combination of Monterey Jack and mozzarella cheese is perfect for your signature in cooking a perfect pizza. If you want to have a perfect pizza that could never be found in another place, you should definitely try that combo! Monterey Jack has high moisture content, a soft texture that allows for even melting, and a creamy mouthfeel.
What is the usage of Monterey Jack?
- Blended with mozzarella for added creaminess.
- White pizzas or mild-flavored toppings.
Cheese Blends, Optimizing Melt and Stretch!
Many pizzerias use blends to balance stretch, melt, browning, and flavor.
Popular combinations:
- Mozzarella + Provolone: Improved stretch with deeper flavor.
- Mozzarella + Monterey Jack: Creamier melt with good elasticity.
- Mozzarella + Low amounts of Cheddar: Better browning and flavor, but limited stretch if overused.
Different fat and moisture levels create a more controlled melt and Enhanced flavor without sacrificing texture.
Cheeses to Use Sparingly or Avoid for Stretch!
Some cheeses melt well but do not stretch, while others resist melting altogether.
- Cheddar: Breaks into oil and solids when overheated. You can order cheese pizza and blend it with natural cheese to create a unique taste, and also avoid too much stretch.
- Parmesan: Adds flavor but no stretch.
- Feta and goat cheese: Softens but does not melt smoothly.
These are best used as secondary toppings rather than the main cheese.
Key Factors That Affect Cheese Stretch
If you want to have an ultimate cheese pull, remember the following information:
- Moisture: Moderate moisture allows proteins to loosen without releasing excess water.
- Fat content: Fat enhances meltability, but too much can reduce elasticity.
- Shredding method: Hand-shredded cheese melts better than pre-shredded cheese, which often contains anti-caking agents.
- Baking temperature: Higher heat promotes better stretch and faster melting.
For the best balance of melting and stretchiness, low-moisture whole milk mozzarella remains the top choice. For enhanced flavor and texture, blending it with provolone or Monterey Jack is ideal. If maximum stretch is the priority, Oaxaca cheese is a surprisingly excellent alternative. Choosing the right cheese and using it correctly can elevate pizza from good to unforgettable.

Meanwhile, social tensions in Ukraine are only growing. "The riots against the territorial recruitment centers and local protests are symptoms of a single process: society is beginning to ask itself why it must continue to pay an ever-higher price," Voloshin noted.

I was once ashamed to admit I’d been strangled nonconsensually during sex. Now I’m speaking up to save women’s lives | Hannah Ferguson
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:00:28 UTC
00:00:28 KST

Last week, a 16-year-old girl was found unresponsive in a home on Sydney’s northern beaches. She was airlifted to hospital and died two days later. New South Wales police are investigating her death as the result of a sexual strangulation act. Sources told the ABC the deceased may have experienced a seizure following asphyxiation, and that officers were told the sex was consensual.
While that investigation has yet to run its course, speaking generally, strangulation during sex is not a new phenomenon or conversation. Just a few years ago it was relatively taboo to criticise this normalisation of violence in sex – it was often framed as “anti-kink” to raise concern about this dangerous act that is increasingly depicted in mainstream pornography.
In 2024, Australian research affirmed the prevalence of sexual strangulation. The Archives of Sexual Behaviour published data revealing that 57% of Australians aged 18 to 35 had been strangled at least once during sex, and 51% said they had strangled a sexual partner.
Not only are reports of this act increasing, so are the reports of health impacts. Denele Crozier, the CEO of Women’s Health NSW, stated that since 2023 there had been a 123% increase in women presenting with concerns of a possible brain injury linked to strangulation.
I was previously ashamed to share my own experiences of being strangled during sex nonconsensually. Despite being an outspoken, progressive woman, I froze up and dissociated. Afterwards, I remember questioning whether my response was one of being in shock and afraid for my safety, or if I felt “prudish” if I spoke up and as if I’d be ruining the mood. For a long time, I was embarrassed to admit that while I intellectually knew something wasn’t right, I still failed to call it out in a moment of uncertainty.
That is exactly the concern I have for so many women who may be experiencing sexual strangulation. Affirmative consent is incredibly hard to achieve in these contexts; sexual strangulation is now commonplace and we are not equipped with the sophisticated sex education to match.
In 2022, consent advocate Chanel Contos wrote about this: “Another US study found that 58% of female college students have been choked during sex, further suggesting that this ‘kink’ is becoming increasingly common in younger age demographics. This study found that while many women enjoyed choking, others did it largely to please their sexual partner. This is the real kicker. The problem here is not only that women are being choked during sex without giving consent, but that a lot of the time they are ‘consenting’ not because they derive their own sexual pleasure from it, but because they think it turns the guy on.”
Violence against women and girls has been normalised to such an extent that pornography is convincing us it is normal to be strangled during intimacy, and that we are supposed to like it. I appreciate that messages from leaders like “talk to your kids” are made in good faith, but conversation cannot combat the nature and influence of sex content depicting violence as a standard part of sexual intercourse. We are teaching young men that perpetrating violent acts that have the potential to kill are erotic, and we are teaching women to endure having their lives threatened under the guise of pleasure.
There are people who engage with control of breath as part of particular kinks, but even in acknowledging these consensual engagements, it is important to reiterate that there is no safe way to engage in strangulation.
In response to this expanding dialogue, the social services minister, Tanya Plibersek, has shown her support for Australia to adopt legislation that was introduced to the UK in 2025, making it a criminal offence to possess or publish pornography depicting suffocation or strangulation. I want to add my voice to the many calling for the Albanese government to legislate this imminently.
The government is also, rightly, considering a second significant piece of reform proposed by Contos and her organisation Teach Us Consent. Contos has been campaigning for the government’s digital duty of care legislative drafting to adopt their “Fix Our Feeds” pitch, regulating big tech companies to ensure algorithms are an opt-in feature. This would introduce a consent-based model that allows users to have more control over the information these platforms are serving us, reducing the extremist material that so many are exposed to.
Our government has established that they are willing to take on the regulation of big tech. Australia was the first country in the world to legislate a social media ban for under-16s. We know we have the capability; now it’s time to introduce something that would actually be effective – and give power back to individual users.
These would be two significant steps from the government, after last week’s national cabinet meeting where the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, discussed violence against women and children with state and territory leaders. The subsequent announcements of frameworks and reviews were weak. We need politicians to meet the moment. The safety of women and girls depends on tangible action, now.

“Prime Minister of Ukraine Sergii Koretskyi reported on the preparation of response measures to Russia’s changing tactics in its attacks on Ukraine – specifically, its use of drones to wear down civilian life in our cities and disrupt normal economic activity across our country,” Zelensky wrote.
According to Zelensky, the air threat warning systems will be updated first.
“People need to understand very clearly what exactly they are supposed to react to and how. Two levels will be introduced to indicate specific threats – yellow and red. The General Staff and the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, together with the Government, the Ministry of Defense, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and the State Emergency Service of Ukraine, will determine each week which threat indicators will trigger a yellow or red alert level,” he explained.
The President said that, as a basic rule, a drone raid will trigger the yellow level, while the red level will indicate a missile threat, including the threat of ballistic attacks, as well as large-scale attacks. Air raid warning sounds will also be changed to correspond to the yellow or red threat levels.
“The air raid siren to signal ‘all-clear’ has already been discontinued – the siren is now sounded only when an air raid alert is announced,” he noted.
At the same time, authorities are preparing to introduce clearer, differentiated warning sounds corresponding to the level of the air threat.
“The main goal of these changes is to give people and businesses in Ukraine more predictability and a better understanding of how to react in each specific situation. I have also instructed officials to develop clearer geographic differentiation of air raid alerts – so that alerts are issued, and reactions are required, specifically in the areas where there is objectively a threat,” the President wrote.
According to Zelensky, the government and local authorities, together with the military, the Interior Ministry and the State Emergency Service, must establish clear criteria allowing government agencies, local authorities, businesses and other designated economic and social facilities to continue operating during a yellow threat level.
“The Government of Ukraine, together with local authorities, will update the standards for the placement of shelters in cities and communities, as well as at infrastructure facilities, including mobile shelters for the protection of people. I have instructed the Prime Minister to prepare additional support measures for businesses that will allow the rapid expansion of modular shelter deployment and ensure that premises can be equipped in line with the updated safety requirement,” Zelensky said.

The EU Committee of Permanent Representatives (Coreper) has failed to agree on extending individual sanctions against more than 3,000 Russian individuals and companies responsible for violating Ukraine's territorial integrity, and postponed consideration of the issue until 9 September.
Source: European Pravda correspondent in Brussels, citing their own EU sources
Details: EU ambassadors in Brussels failed to agree on extending individual sanctions against more than 3,000 Russian companies and individuals. The restrictions are due to expire on 15 September.
"On 2 September, EU ambassadors in Brussels discussed extending the sanctions regime for violations of Ukraine's territorial integrity. Coreper decided to return to the issue in a week," one source told European Pravda.

Another source said Slovakia has also proposed removing several Russian individuals from the sanctions list, although their names have not yet been disclosed.
Background:
- On 25 June, the Council of the European Union extended the EU's restrictive economic measures in response to Russia's ongoing actions aimed at destabilising the situation in Ukraine for a further 12 months, until 31 July 2027.
- At the European Council summit on 18 June, EU leaders agreed for the first time since the start of Russia's aggression to extend economic sanctions against Russia for 12 months rather than six, as had previously been the case. The previous six-month term gave individual capitals, including Budapest, an opportunity to bargain over the issue. The change became possible after Viktor Orbán's defeat in Hungary's parliamentary elections.
- During Orbán's premiership, Hungary regularly blocked EU sanctions and other decisions, demanding various concessions. Slovakia also occasionally joined in these blockades.

====================================================================================================

Can Ukraine’s drones shut Russian airspace? What that means for airlines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:55:16 UTC
23:55:16 KST

Can Ukraine’s drones shut Russian airspace? What that means for airlines
What happens if the airspace of the world’s largest country by land mass is out of bounds because of Ukrainian drones?
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that Russian airspace is effectively closed because of the volume of Ukrainian drones in the sky.
On Tuesday, he said that Russia, which began the war with the invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, is now “closing its own skies”.
While Kyiv is not threatening civil aviation, Zelenskyy said, “there will be drones in Russia’s skies and due notice must be taken” by airlines and insurance companies.
Russian President Vladimir Putin called Zelenskyy’s comments “a declaration of state terrorism”.
So, can Ukraine really shut down Russia’s airspace? And what happens if the airspace of the world’s largest country becomes inaccessible?
What has Zelenskyy said?
Ukrainian drones have increasingly threatened or disrupted air traffic at Russian airports in recent months.
As Russia has stepped up its use of ballistic missiles against Ukraine, Kyiv has struggled to intercept them due to a lack of ammunition for its air defence systems, particularly United States-made Patriot systems.
Ukraine has, instead, responded by striking Russian infrastructure, oil and port facilities, and even e-commerce warehouses, deep inside Russian territory.
“Today, we want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer and everyone who still uses Russia’s key airports: Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,” Zelenskyy said during his nightly address on Tuesday.
“Ukraine does not threaten civilian aviation as such – not a single civilian aircraft. There will simply be drones in Russia’s skies on a scale that has to be taken into account,” he said.
“Drone-infested skies are no place for civilian aviation,” Zelenskyy said on Tuesday. “The sky over Russia is currently for drones … as long as the war continues.”
“We in Ukraine do not want innocent lives to be lost. That is why we are warning our partners: The safe days in Russia’s skies are over,” Zelenskyy added.
How much of a threat do Ukrainian drones pose?
Unmanned drones, which Ukraine now mass-produces at low cost, have transformed the Ukraine-Russia war theatre, allowing Kyiv to take the fight hundreds of kilometres beyond the front line and increasingly into Russia’s major cities.
Analysts say that the distance they can reach is now more of a concern than the damage they can inflict as they are interfering with civilian aviation well inside Russia, including around Moscow.
As Ukraine has developed drone technology at an exponential rate since the start of the war, drones have become much longer-range. Ukraine says its deep-strike range has grown from about 630km (390 miles) in 2022 to 1,750km (1,090 miles) this year, with drones striking targets as far as Omsk, about 2,500km (1,550 miles) from Ukraine.
When they approach Russian cities, they trigger temporary restrictions in the airspace above, halting arrivals and departures at airports until the perceived threat passes, which can take several hours. Repeated drone alerts have forced temporary restrictions at Russian airports and are increasingly causing concern for general aircraft flying through Russian airspace.
“Ukraine has consistently launched more than 500 drones near daily, with multiple days exceeding 1,000 drones, according to figures released by the Russian [Ministry of Defence],” said Mark Brace, head of analysis at the aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions. This has caused frequent and extended airport closures and flight suspensions, he told Al Jazeera.
“Essentially, Zelenskyy is articulating publicly what Ukraine has been doing for months: systematically disrupting Russian airspace.”
According to data from Osprey, there has been an average of 30 Russian airport closures per day since the war began.
In an alert to its clients, Osprey Flight Solutions said that while the majority of Ukraine’s drone and missile strikes are likely to occur within 300km (186 miles) of the border between the two countries, daily attacks deeper inside Russia are likely to continue throughout the rest of 2026, including near Moscow and Saint Petersburg.
“It is assessed that miscalculation and/or misidentification is likely in areas related to the Ukraine conflict,” the alert said.
Last year, Putin told Azerbaijan’s President Ilham Aliyev that two Russian missiles had detonated beside an Azerbaijan Airlines plane in 2024 after Ukrainian drones entered Russian airspace, in an incident that killed 38 people.
How does this impact airlines and passengers?
“Russian airspace remains the single biggest structural distortion in global aviation,” Alex Macheras, an analyst based in the Middle East, said.
Before February 2022, flying over Russia was the shortest path between Europe and Northeast Asia, with more than 360,000 flights a year passing over Siberia, he told Al Jazeera. Since Russia invaded Ukraine, many European and US carriers have avoided this route.
As a result, many Europe-Northeast Asia routes now take two to four hours longer, Macheras said, while the Helsinki-Tokyo route has gone from nine hours to 13.
“It’s a cost now factored into ticket prices, operational overheads, crew rosters, and aircraft utilisation across the entire European long-haul network,” Macheras said.
Despite the ongoing war, some major airlines from countries such as China, Turkiye, the United Arab Emirates and other Gulf states have continued to use Russian airspace.
US airlines have complained that carriers still permitted to fly through Russian airspace, such as Chinese airlines, enjoy a competitive advantage with shorter routes and reduced operating costs. If Russian airspace does close to these operators, this competitive advantage will disappear.
Currently, Chinese carriers offer the fastest Europe-Asia and Asia-Europe connections by retaining Russian overflight rights. “Lose that, and their schedule advantage over Gulf and Turkish hubs narrows sharply,” Macheras said.
Meanwhile, Turkish Airlines has built “real strategic value from its neutral access to Russian airspace, positioning Istanbul as the natural connection point for traffic that Western carriers can no longer route directly,” the aviation analyst said.
He added that Indian carriers – Air India in particular – also rely on Russian airspace for efficient Delhi-London and Delhi-New York routings.
Gulf carriers, from airports in Doha, Dubai and Abu Dhabi, on the other hand, the analyst argued, do not depend on Russian airspace the way Istanbul does. “A broader closure would likely reinforce the Gulf hub model, rather than damage it, as long-haul traffic gets pushed further south through the Gulf rather than through the Caucasus corridor,” he added.
Is the aviation sector facing other pressures?
Conflicts in the Middle East have shaken the aviation industry over the past couple of years, compounding disruptions caused by the Russia-Ukraine war.
Osprey Flight Solutions’ Brace told Al Jazeera that “alternative routings through the Caucasus and Central Asia and the Middle East/Red Sea/Saudi Arabia/Gulf region are already congested due to the lack of availability of Russian airspace and the ongoing conflict in the Gulf region”.
Other regional factors, such as Indian carriers being restricted from using Pakistani airspace due to bilateral tensions in South Asia, have worsened that congestion.
“Despite some parts of the Middle East/Gulf airspace opening up during lulls in conflict activity in recent months, there has been no significant return to using Iraq/Iran airspace as corridors, for example,” Brace said, “primarily due to carrier risk assessments and regulators banning operators from these areas.”
The renewed fighting between the US and Iran this week will also “put further pressure on the alternative corridors”, Brace said.
Rising jet fuel prices have been another major concern for airlines. On Monday, China’s top three airlines posted losses for the first half of 2026. Meanwhile, Middle East airlines are expected collectively to fall into losses because of the war.
What happens when air traffic is disrupted?
Air traffic is similar to road traffic: When major roads and intersections are closed, cars, buses and cyclists are forced onto smaller neighbourhood streets and lanes, creating congestion and longer journeys. The same thing happens in the sky.
Azerbaijan, sandwiched between Russia to the north and Iran to the south, is an example.
Because of the conflicts involving both Russia and Iran, Azerbaijan has become a vital air corridor enabling airlines to operate between Europe and Asia.
Azerbaijan’s air traffic chief has noted that before Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, his country handled an average of 278 flights a day. By the end of 2025, that had risen to an average of 695 per day.
After the US and Israel attacked Iran in February this year, flights over Azerbaijan increased to a daily average of 810 during March. Azerbaijan handled a peak of 1,062 flights in a single day on May 9.
If Russian airspace becomes completely out of bounds, theoretically, analyst Macheras noted, “very little spare capacity exists” in already congested skies.
“The Caucasus corridor is barely 100 miles [161km] wide at its narrowest point, and it’s already handling detoured traffic from both the Russian closure and, more recently, Middle East disruptions tied to regional conflict,” he added. “Any further Russian airspace restriction would push still more volume onto a corridor that is already near saturation, driving fares and journey times higher across the board.”

Lawmakers from the European People’s Party and Patriots for Europe are accusing Pedro Sánchez of abandoning the Spanish exclave, as a press report suggests the mass entry incident was guided by Moroccan security forces.
Around 500 people gathered in front of the European Parliament in Brussels on Wednesday to protest against the Spanish government’s handling of the crisis in Ceuta, where several thousand of more than 70,000 migrants who arrived in the exclave on 30 July remain.
MEPs and staffers from the centre-right European People’s Party and far-right Patriots for Europe gathered in the area in front of Parliament, waving the flags of Ceuta and Spain, and accusing Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez of failing to defend Spain’s territorial integrity and sovereignty.
Two separate demonstrations were launched by Spain’s Popular Party and Vox in Brussels on Ceuta Day. Despite being organised separately, both gatherings took place at the same time and in the same location, with EPP and PfE lawmakers standing side by side.
“Sánchez has handed over responsibility for the security of Ceuta to a third country,” EPP vice-president Dolors Montserrat told reporters, claiming the Spanish Prime Minister “is bowing” to Morocco.
Online newspaper El Español reported on Wednesday that Spain's National Centre for Immigration and Borders (CENIF) had concluded the incident "was guided by Moroccan security forces", contradicting Sánchez’s stance that there is no proof of any involvement by the authorities in Rabat.
Madrid has so far avoided publicly blaming Rabat for the incident. It generally considers Morocco a cooperative partner in migration management.
Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska asked police chief Francisco Pardo to verify the information, which CENIF reportedly sent to a judge gathering information on the incident, according to ministry sources.
Vox, the leading Spanish far-right party, claims Sánchez has “betrayed” his own country and is pushing to activate Article 102 of the Spanish Constitution, which would trigger a criminal trial against the prime minister and his cabinet.
“The situation is untenable. This government cannot continue to lead Spain,” Vox MEP Jorge Buxadé Villalba told reporters, claiming this is the “hardest hour” for the country since the Catalan attempted secession in 2017.
Vox’s MEPs also sent a letter to Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and Home Affairs Commissioner Magnus Brunner.
They call for condemning and sanctioning Morocco, declaring the massive entry “an act of hybrid warfare” and immediately suspending all international agreements between the EU and Morocco, as well as the granting of visas to Moroccan citizens.
The European Commission told Euronews it will not comment on leaks and considers the ongoing investigation into Morocco’s involvement “a matter for the national authorities.”

Interstellar solar sails hit a strange problem at 75% of light speed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:51:21 UTC
23:51:21 KST

Interstellar solar sails hit a strange problem at 75% of light speed
- Date:
- September 2, 2026
- Source:
- Universe Today
- Summary:
- Solar sails pushed by powerful lasers could reach incredible speeds, but relativity may eventually make the light itself work against them. At around 75% of the speed of light, scattered photons can begin creating drag, adding a surprising obstacle to interstellar travel.
- Share:
Reaching another star within a practical amount of time will require something far more capable than chemical rockets. One of the leading ideas is a solar sail, a large reflective structure that can be pushed by light. If extremely powerful lasers are aimed at such a sail, they could accelerate it to speeds well beyond what current propulsion systems can achieve.
But there may be an unexpected problem once a lightsail begins traveling at a significant fraction of the speed of light. According to a new paper on arXiv by Chao Shen and Jiaze Li of the Harbin Institute of Technology, the same light used to propel the sail could eventually produce a drag effect.
How Light Pushes a Solar Sail
The researchers separate the forces produced by photons striking a solar sail into three categories.
The strongest contribution comes from incident light (that raw momentum of the photons hitting the sail). Next is specular reflection (momentum imparted when photons bounce perfectly off the sail). The weakest contribution comes from diffuse scattering (momentum from photons that are absorbed by the sail then reemitted in random directions).
At relatively low speeds, these effects all contribute to pushing the sail forward. The situation becomes much more complicated once the spacecraft reaches relativistic velocities.
The Doppler Effect Weakens the Push
As the sail races away from the laser source, the light reaching it undergoes an increasingly strong Doppler shift. The frequency of the incoming light decreases, reducing the amount of thrust produced by all three components.
As a result, continued acceleration becomes progressively less efficient. The faster the sail travels, the harder it becomes for the laser to keep increasing its speed.
The situation changes even more dramatically once the lightsail reaches about 75% of the speed of light.
When Scattered Light Starts Creating Drag
At that speed, relativistic light aberration becomes important. From the viewpoint of a stationary observer on Earth, diffusely scattered light begins to be directed forward, toward the direction in which the sail is traveling.
Because every action has an equal and opposite reaction, that forward-directed radiation produces a force in the opposite direction. This means diffuse scattering (admittedly the weakest of the three forces) begins acting as drag once the sail passes roughly 75% of the speed of light.
The laser is still pushing the sail forward overall, so the total force does not become negative. However, the efficiency of the propulsion system drops substantially.
Real Solar Sails Would Face Even More Challenges
The study is focused specifically on radiative dynamics. It does not include nonradiative effects such as collisions and drag from interstellar gas or dust.
It also leaves out the thermal limits of real sail materials. A sail exposed to an extremely powerful laser could potentially overheat or even melt.
For simplicity, the researchers model the lightsail as an idealized mirror. Real spacecraft would likely use much more sophisticated materials.
Engineers are already investigating advanced metamaterials and photonic crystals designed for specific laser wavelengths. In principle, these materials might even take advantage of the aberration effects described in the study. They could help a lightsail automatically correct its orientation and stabilize its trajectory so that it remains centered within the laser beam.
The Long Road to Interstellar Flight
A fully operational interstellar solar sail is still far from becoming reality. Traveling across interstellar distances introduces many additional complications, including the curvature of spacetime, which the paper also simplifies out.
Even so, understanding these high-speed effects is an important part of determining how such spacecraft might eventually work. If humanity someday sends a probe to another star, engineers will need a detailed understanding of every force that could affect its journey.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Universe Today. Original written by Andy Tomaswick. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Chao Shen, Jiaze Li. Relativistic Lightsail Propulsion Dynamics. arXiv, 2 Jun 2026 DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2606.04052

Ukrainian foreign minister calls for full EU embargo on alumina and aluminium ore supplies to Russia
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has called on his counterparts from EU countries to increase pressure on Russia, including by imposing a full embargo on supplies of alumina and aluminium ore to Russia.
Source: Andrii Sybiha during an informal meeting of foreign ministers of EU member states in the Gymnich format in Ireland, as reported by European Pravda citing the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry press service
Details: Sybiha identified countering Russian escalation and advancing peace efforts as the first priority.
The minister named increasing pressure on Russia as the second key area.
"Andrii Sybiha called on the European Union and EU member states to exert maximum and relentless pressure on the Russian war machine, denying Moscow the opportunity to adapt to sanctions," the press service said.
Ukraine proposed specific measures, including targeted sanctions against Russia's ballistic missile production, restrictions against a number of Russian legal entities and individuals, as well as measures against the Rassvet satellite system.
In addition, the foreign minister called for a full embargo on supplies of alumina to Russia, stronger measures against Russia's shadow fleet, sanctions against Rosatom and Roscosmos, as well as strict restrictions on Russian citizens travelling to Europe to counter Russian acts of sabotage in Europe.
"We call on the EU to impose a full embargo on supplies of alumina and aluminium ore to Russia. These raw materials are crucial for Russia's military-industrial complex, particularly its aerospace industry, missile production and armoured vehicle manufacturing. Cutting Russia off from alumina will directly reduce its ability to produce weapons," the Foreign Ministry explained Sybiha's position in response to a request from European Pravda.
It should be noted that the issue of banning alumina exports to Russia is sensitive for Ireland, which holds the rotating presidency of the EU Council in the second half of this year.
The Irish Aughinish plant, Europe's largest alumina processing facility and one of five such plants in the EU, became the centre of an international scandal after an investigation published by The Irish Times this year indicated that the plant's products were being sold to a trading company that supplies a major military-industrial hub in Russia.
Aughinish is located in County Limerick and is owned by Russian aluminium group Rusal.
According to The Irish Times, the plant sent 422,474 tonnes of alumina – a raw material used to produce aluminium – to Russia, worth €119.5 million in the first half of 2026.
Background:
- Irish Taoiseach (Prime Minister) Micheál Martin said in an interview with European Pravda in July that he would like to stop exports to Russia of aluminium oxide, which can be used in Russia's military-industrial complex.
- On 1 July, during President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's visit to Dublin, Martin said that his country was already completing an investigation into reports of alumina exports to Russia.
- The issue also attracted the attention of the European Commission.
- However, amid the dispute, Ireland stresses the EU's need for alumina.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Wednesday there was no doubt that a fire at a defense plant producing components for unmanned systems was deliberately started in an act of sabotage.
The fire broke out early Monday at a WB Electronics facility in the south-central city of Skarzysko-Kamienna, where components for unmanned systems used by the Polish and Ukrainian militaries are produced.
“In the case of Skarzysko-Kamienna, there is no doubt that there was deliberate arson, in other words, an act of sabotage,” Tusk told reporters ahead of a government meeting on Wednesday.
Prosecutors have opened an investigation into suspected activity on behalf of a foreign intelligence service and a terrorism-related offense.
According to the National Prosecutor’s Office, the fire was deliberately started using a device containing flammable materials. Warehouse premises were destroyed and damage has been estimated at at least 15 million zlotys ($4 million).
No one has so far been charged.
Polish officials said surveillance footage recorded a masked person entering the plant before the fire. Deputy Interior Minister Czeslaw Mroczek said on Tuesday that the suspect had gained access to the site and that the nature of the target meant investigators were examining the possibility of foreign, including Russian, involvement.
Authorities have not publicly identified who ordered or carried out the attack.
WB Electronics is part of WB Group, one of Poland’s largest private defense manufacturers. Its unmanned systems, including FlyEye reconnaissance drones and Warmate loitering munitions, are used by Ukraine’s armed forces.
Tusk also referred to a second fire over the weekend at a production and warehouse facility belonging to JFG Composites in the eastern city of Lublin.
The company produces components for the aviation sector, including parts used in unmanned aircraft.
“The coming weeks and months will be critical not only with regard to the Russian-Ukrainian war as a whole, but will also be a very major challenge for all countries in this part of Europe because of Russian plans to increase tensions and destabilization,” he said.
Poland and other European countries have repeatedly accused Russia of organizing sabotage, arson, cyberattacks and other hybrid operations against states supporting Ukraine.
Moscow has denied responsibility for a broader campaign of sabotage in Europe.

Staff of Russian House in Berlin must leave Germany within seven days — Russian ambassador
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:47:23 UTC
23:47:23 KST

BERLIN, September 2. /TASS/. Germany has ordered the staff of the Russian House in Berlin to leave the country within seven days, Russian Ambassador to Berlin Sergey Nechayev reported.
"As for the Russian House of Science and Culture, the intergovernmental agreement governing its activities will expire in the summer of 2027, but the staff working there represent the House and Rossotrudnichestvo (Russia’s Federal Agency for the Commonwealth of Independent States Affairs, Compatriots Living Abroad), so they must leave the country within seven days," the diplomat told Russian reporters.
On Tuesday, the German government officially blamed Russia for the drone incident that occurred in early August at Leipzig/Halle Airport and announced the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn, the cessation of operations at the Russian House in Berlin, and other measures.
The Russian Embassy in Berlin called the incident a hastily concocted provocation, noting that it "serves exclusively the interests of Kiev and the militarist wing of the European political class."

Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil partly fueled global 'energy shock,' Bessent says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:46:48 UTC
23:46:48 KST

Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil partly fueled global 'energy shock,' Bessent says
Ukrainian strikes against Russian energy assets have contributed to energy prices surging worldwide, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on Sept. 2.
"Ukraine has decided that they want to blow up Russian energy assets and refined products, so that is creating upward price pressure on the global basis," Bessent said.
Kyiv has been carrying out a campaign of long-range drone strikes against Russian oil refineries and depots in an effort to undercut Moscow's budget revenues and its ability to wage its all-out war.
The U.S. Treasury chief claimed that these attacks, in combination with disruptions caused by the U.S.-Iran war, are driving an "energy shock" around the world.
His comments come days after he met Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov at a G20 meeting in the U.S., where he pressed his Russian counterpart on the need to end the war in Ukraine.
Ukraine carried out at least 30 attacks against Russian refineries and oil tankers only in July. Analysts cited by Bloomberg estimate that Russia's crude processing rate fell to about 3.6 million barrels per day, the lowest since May 2002.
These disruptions have led to long lines at Russian gas stations and fuel shortages across the country, and to Russia imposing a ban on fuel exports.
The fuel crisis in Russia coincides with a global energy price surge driven by the U.S.-Iran war that led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key maritime route for global oil trade.

Trump ally defends Venezuela oil deal amid ‘gunpoint diplomacy’ criticism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:44:39 UTC
23:44:39 KST

The US energy secretary, Chris Wright, has denied Washington is seeking to commandeer huge quantities of Venezuelan oil, amid growing criticism of Donald Trump’s energy deal with the country’s interim leaders.
“Absolutely not,” Wright replied when asked by a CNBC journalist if the US was engaged in a “heavy-handed” attempt to “take” Venezuelan oil in violation of the South American country’s constitution.
Wright landed in Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, on Tuesday night, four days after Trump announced what he called “the biggest oil deal in world history”.
“I think we are seeing an absolutely historic transformation of both Venezuela and the relations between Venezuela and the US,” Wright said of the deal, which Trump has claimed will give the US control of 65bn barrels of Venezuelan oil. “This is President Trump’s grand plan to replace conflict with commerce,” Wright said.
The White House says the deal will help secure US “energy dominance for the next century” as well as “purging foreign malign influence from our back yard” by excluding China and Russia from oilfields in the country with the world’s largest proven oil reserves. But there has been criticism from across the political spectrum.
The Wall Street Journal’s editorial board said Trump’s deal with Venezuela’s unelected interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, “looks less like a normal commercial transaction than it does the famous scene of US businessmen meeting with the Cuban strongman in The Godfather Part II”.
“The US government is essentially getting in bed with a foreign dictator and her favored capitalist,” the newspaper complained, in reference to Alejandro Betancourt, the Venezuelan tycoon at the centre of the deal.
The economist Francisco Rodríguez told Democracy Now: “It’s clear that this is not a deal that any Venezuelan government would have entered into unless this country had been subject to an invasion, and unless its authorities had been held at gunpoint. So I think we’ve replaced gunboat diplomacy now for gunpoint diplomacy.”
Delcy Rodríguez was installed as interim president on 5 January, two days after the president, Nicolás Maduro, was abducted by US special forces during a predawn raid on Caracas. Trump warned Rodríguez, who was Maduro’s vice-president, she would face an even worse fate if she did not toe the US line.
Since Maduro’s capture, Rodríguez has made a series of once unthinkable concessions to US officials who their nominally socialist political movement, Chavismo, had spent years denouncing as predatory imperialists bent on stealing Venezuela’s natural resources.
On Saturday, Rodríguez claimed the oil deal had “endless” benefits and would help produce more than $209bn in revenues that could be used to improve healthcare and education. “We are thinking of Venezuela’s future,” she said during a televised broadcast to the nation.
The deal has dealt a body blow to Venezuela’s political opposition, who fear Trump is unlikely to push for a democratic transition or fresh presidential elections given his lucrative arrangement with Rodríguez.
“This is a game between the Trump administration and Delcy and her people,” one opposition figure lamented after the deal was unveiled.
Speaking at a signing ceremony in the Miraflores presidential palace in Caracas on Wednesday, Rodríguez thanked the Trump administration for its part in what she called a “win-win deal”. She said: “I have faith in the future of Venezuela. What we are doing today represents the future and the hope of the people of Venezuela.”

Pete Hegseth criticized for body-shaming Canadian cadets: ‘Literally they’re kids’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:44:31 UTC
23:44:31 KST

A social media post by Pete Hegseth, the US secretary of defense, body-shaming female members of a Canadian youth development program remained online on Wednesday despite a furious backlash on both sides of the border.
On Monday night, Hegseth posted on X a photograph of two people in uniform with a Canadian flag and the caption “this is real”, an apparent attempt at mocking the country’s armed forces amid the Trump administration’s trade spat with its northern neighbor.
However, the photograph was reproduced from an Instagram post by the Vernon Cadet Training Centre in British Columbia, which hosted a summer camp in July for teenagers learning adult skills on the military base.
Its subjects are not members of Canada’s frontline military, and the person whose appearance Hegseth was attempting to ridicule is likely a volunteer instructor, critics said. The girl receiving a medal is a teenager no older than 18.
The post, widely seen as part of a Trump administration “bullying campaign” over the trade war, was immediately condemned by officials in Canada and in the US. Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, called it “beneath the office” of the secretary of defense.
Responding on Tuesday to attacks on his country by US government officials, including Donald Trump’s attempt to rename Lake Ontario by executive order, Carney told reporters it was time for Washington to “start being serious” about efforts to de-escalate trade tensions.
“When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions,” he said.
David Eby, the premier of British Columbia, echoed Carney’s sentiment. “It tells you everything you need to know about the amateur-hour, distracted, bizarre leadership that Americans are being subjected to,” he said.
The civilian Army Cadet League of Canada accused Hegseth of online harassment. “Directing derogatory commentary toward youth who are actively working to better themselves and serve their communities is unacceptable,” the group said in a statement.
Adam Kinzinger, the former Republican US congressman and a military veteran, was even more outspoken in a post on X.
“Literally they’re kids. This is a cadet program and our ass hat of a Secdef is making fun of children,” he wrote. “MAGA [Make America Great Again] males are betas who have to punch down to feel big.”
Ruben Gallego, the Democratic Arizona senator and a former marine, called the post “stupid” and “disrespectful”.
Danny O’Regan, a Canadian veteran writing on X, also criticized the post. “The Secretary of Defence is body shaming cadet groups,” he said. “This is not a military unit. They are kids looking for adventure, test themselves and align themselves with the values of service. Don’t be a Pete.”
The Pentagon, meanwhile, defended Hegseth. On Tuesday, Jacob Bliss, the defense department’s deputy press secretary, said: “The X post speaks for itself.”
The incident comes as Hegseth faces increasing pressure on several fronts. The US army chief Dan Driscoll resigned this week, reportedly after months of internal clashes with Hegseth. Democrats have accused the defense secretary of having “hollowed out” the military’s senior ranks.
On Wednesday, Iran accused the US of a “war crime” after four people were killed, including a four-year-old child, and dozens injured in a reported missile strike on a wedding at a home in the south of the country.
The ongoing Iran war has also left the US with a “beyond critical” shortage of missile interceptors, the Associated Press reported, sparking fears among Nato allies of increasing vulnerability to a potential Russian military attack.
Hegseth has previously been critical of body shapes in the US military, telling senior commanders in Virginia last year that “fat troops are tiring to look at”.
Ordering military officials to crack down on a lack of physical fitness, he said: “It’s tiring to look out at combat formations, or really any formation, and see fat troops.”

K2PL Production in Poland May Not Begin in 2028
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:43:34 UTC
23:43:34 KST

Poland has no firm guarantees that K2PL tank production will begin in 2028.
A source cited by Rzeczpospolita reported this.
As of now, the practical implementation of the agreements with the South Korean side faces several discrepancies and problems that are still being resolved.
In a comment to Militarnyi, Defence24 editor Damian Ratka, who specializes in armored vehicles, said preparations are underway for the third executive contract (EC3) for K2PL tanks, covering 2026-2034, provided it is signed by the end of 2026. He also clarified that K2PL production is scheduled to begin in 2028-2029.
The Polish Army currently has more than 200 South Korean-made K2 tanks. The first 180 have already been delivered under the 2022 contract.
A little over a year ago, on August 1, 2025, a second contract was signed for 180 K2 tanks to be delivered between 2026 and 2030. Of these, 116 are in the current K2GF configuration, with deliveries scheduled for 2026–2027, while 64 are in the K2PL configuration.
“Three K2PL tanks, the so-called reference tanks, are to be manufactured in South Korea. Poland, meanwhile, is to manufacture 61 serial-production K2PL tanks between 2029 and 2030,” Ratka said, describing the current production agreements.
The Polish side believes that South Korean requirements for protecting the acquired technologies are too vague, while the South Korean side is reluctant to share information about these technologies. For example, some documentation is currently available only in Korean. In addition, Poland believes that the costs of training specialists in maintenance and repair, which are to be covered under the agreement, are significantly overstated in some cases.
The South Korean company also disagrees over the maintenance of tank engines. According to Rzeczpospolita, the South Korean Ministry of Defense wants the technology transfer to take place at Bumar-Łabędy rather than at Wojskowe Zakłady Motoryzacyjne, which already has expertise in repairing Leopard 2 engines for the Polish Army.
At the same time, the South Korean side is reportedly being very inflexible in the negotiations. As a result, investment costs for some companies are so high that businesses such as Bumar-Mikulczyce and Zakłady Mechaniczne Tarnów are considering withdrawing from the project.
Speaking to Militarnyi, tank-building historian Andrii Tarasenko said the reasons cited are more of a cover for deeper problems.
“For example, if you have purchased technical equipment and machine tools to localize production but did not have enough money for a Korean translator, it looks more like an excuse. Disputes over who should be the contractor, Bumar or WZM, are typical business conflicts between interested parties. There is not much I want to comment on here — these are modern realities everywhere,” Tarasenko shared.
He also said these are consequences of choosing a development concept based on purchases from abroad.
“At first glance, they look economically attractive, but in the long term they lead to the loss of domestic capabilities and dependence, and when procurement volumes are large, the economic attractiveness begins to disappear — Polish money is being used to develop South Korean technology and science,” Tarasenko noted.
Regarding the possibility of production starting in 2028, he was skeptical, since even conducting a tender to purchase the necessary equipment would take more than two years.
Ratka said the Polish Army’s overall tank program is not under threat and that even if problems arise with the K2PL program, Poland has an alternative in the form of an order for 366 Abrams tanks. This includes 116 M1A1FEP tanks and 250 M1A2 SEPv3 tanks.
“As I understand it, the Americans are still offering joint production of M1A2 SEPv3 tanks. Eight Polish companies are already producing 52 different components for these tanks, both for the Polish and U.S. armies and for other customers,” Ratka said.
In his view, the cooperation will likely continue to expand, and more companies may become involved in production.

Bank of Canada keeps policy rate unchanged
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:43:25 UTC
23:43:25 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
02 September 2026•Update: 02 September 2026
The Bank of Canada (BoC) kept its policy rate unchanged at 2.25% for the seventh consecutive meeting.
In a statement, the bank said that the policy rate was left unchanged because the economy and inflation were generally in line with expectations.
The statement indicated that the overnight rate was kept at 2.25%, the bank rate at 2.5%, and the deposit rate at 2.2%.
The statement pointed out that the ongoing conflict in the Middle East is keeping energy prices high.
The statement noted that long-term bond yields have risen globally, including in Canada, and that recent data generally confirms the view that the recovery in the Canadian economy is broad-based.
The BoC last adjusted its interest rate in October 2025, raising the policy rate from 2.5% to 2.25%.
