How Many Patriot Missiles Can Ukraine Actually Get for $2.3 Billion?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:24:37 UTC
23:24:37 KST

- Category
- World
How Many Patriot Missiles Can Ukraine Actually Get for $2.3 Billion?
A $2.31 billion Patriot order sounds straightforward—until export pricing turns it into a question of whether Ukraine gets 190 missiles or nearly three times as many.
Ukraine has asked the European Commission for permission to direct €2 billion ($2.31 billion) toward Patriot air defense missiles, potentially setting up one of Kyiv’s largest interceptor purchases of the war, depending on what price Washington ultimately approves; the same funding could buy fewer than 200 PAC-3 MSE interceptors—or potentially close to 600, according to Defense Express on September 1.
But the amount of money alone does not reveal how many missiles Ukraine could actually receive.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Kyiv submitted the request under a broader $104.2 billion European loan framework.
Another $4.63 billion from the portion of the financing available for defense procurement is expected to be directed toward weapons manufactured in EU countries and Ukraine.
Defense Express noted that the size of the proposed Patriot allocation makes it possible to estimate the potential number of PAC-3 MSE interceptors Ukraine could purchase. The problem is that there is no single PAC-3 MSE price.
The anti-ballistic interceptor is commonly quoted at around $4 million-$5 million per missile, but those figures generally reflect procurement for the US military rather than foreign customers.
In September 2025, the Pentagon ordered 1,970 PAC-3 MSE interceptors and associated equipment for $9.8 billion.
Dividing the overall contract value by the number of missiles produces a figure of roughly $4.97 million per interceptor. For Ukraine, obtaining anything close to that price would make an enormous difference.
At US military procurement levels, Kyiv’s approximately $2.31 billion allocation could theoretically cover roughly 460 to 580 PAC-3 MSE interceptors, depending on the final contract structure and associated services.
Foreign customers, however, can pay considerably more. Germany provides a useful European comparison.
Berlin allocated roughly $796 million at the exchange rate cited when the procurement was announced, for 120 PAC-3 MSE interceptors at the end of 2024. That worked out to approximately $6.61 million per missile.
If Ukraine received comparable European pricing, its $2.31 billion allocation would purchase roughly 315 interceptors.
A more pessimistic example comes from Saudi Arabia. In February 2026, the US approved a potential sale of 730 PAC-3 MSE interceptors and associated equipment with a maximum estimated value of $9 billion.
On paper, that represents about $12.3 million for each missile if the entire package value is simply divided by the number of interceptors.
That figure was an authorization ceiling, however, not the final value of a signed contract, and included more than just the missiles themselves. Still, using that upper-end figure illustrates the enormous effect export pricing can have.
At around $12.3 million each, Ukraine’s $2.31 billion would cover only about 190 PAC-3 MSE interceptors.
The difference is striking: essentially the same pool of money could potentially buy about 190, 315 or as many as 580 missiles depending on procurement terms.
For Ukraine, however, cost may ultimately be only part of the problem. Even an order of roughly 315 PAC-3 MSE interceptors would represent an extraordinary share of annual production, Defense Express noted.
That means finding enough missiles to buy could prove just as difficult as finding the money to pay for them.
PAC-3 MSE is among Ukraine’s most important defenses against Russian ballistic missiles, which remain among the hardest aerial threats for Ukrainian air defenses to intercept.
Earlier, reports emerged that US forces may have used as many as 96 to 128 PAC-3 interceptor missiles in a single night while defending military bases in Jordan from an Iranian ballistic missile attack—potentially consuming up to 17% of estimated US stocks.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Zelenskyy: Two levels to be introduced to indicate specific threat – yellow, red levels
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
17:23:03 EEST
23:23:03 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced an update to the warning systems regarding existing threats in light of changes in the enemy’s tactics – two levels of threat designation (yellow and red) will be introduced.
Zelenskyy stated about this on Telegram on Wednesday following a conversation with Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky.
First, the president said, the threat alert systems will be updated. "People must understand absolutely clearly what exactly they need to react to and how. Two levels of threat alerts will be introduced – yellow and red," Zelenskyy said.
The General Staff and the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, together with the government, the Ministry of Defense, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and the State Emergency Service, will determine on a weekly basis which threat indicators will be classified as yellow and red alert levels.
"Generally speaking, the yellow level applies to drone incursions, while the red level applies to missile threats – including the threat of ballistic attacks – as well as massive attacks," Zelenskyy said.
According to him, the audio signals for air raid alerts will also be modified to correspond to the yellow or red threat levels.
"The practice of sounding the air raid siren a second time to signal the end of the alert has now been abolished – currently, the siren is sounded only when the air raid alert is first declared. We are preparing to introduce clearer air raid warning siren signals that are differentiated by threat level," Zelenskyy added.
"The main goal of these changes is to give people and businesses in Ukraine more predictability and a better understanding of how to respond in each specific situation. I have also instructed officials to work out a clearer geographic differentiation of alerts so that alerts are issued and responses are carried out precisely in those areas where there is an objective threat," the president said.

Xi calls on Mideast nations to be ‘masters of their own affairs’ in rare Egypt visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:22:36 UTC
23:22:36 KST

Xi calls on Mideast nations to be ‘masters of their own affairs’ in rare Egypt visit
Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday called on "the people of the Middle East" to oppose "externalinterference" and consider reshaping the region's security order during a visit to Egypt. The rare visit by the Chinese leader comes as Beijing aims to expand its influence in the region as the Iran war tests the reliability of the traditional US security umbrella in a vital geostrategic zone.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday urged countries to oppose "external interference" in the Middle East and said Beijing was ready to work with regional states to safeguard maritime shipping, jeopardised by the US-Iran war.
Xi's remarks to his Egyptian counterpart Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, on his first visit to Cairo in a decade, come as Beijing seeks a greater foothold in the region, expanding investment while managing fallout from the war.
"We must uphold the principle that the people of the Middle East are the masters of their own affairs, oppose external interference [and] support regional countries in strengthening dialogue on peace and security," Xi said in a meeting with Sisi, according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua.
Xi was greeted by Sisi and a 21-gun salute for talks at the opulent Ittihadiya Presidential Palace in the Egyptian capital.
The talks covered the six-month US-Iran conflict, with both presidents urging "diplomatic solutions" to reach a "comprehensive agreement to end the war", according to a statement from Sisi's spokesperson.
Sisi's office also said the two BRICS members signed an agreement to launch the third phase of the Egyptian-Chinese industrial zone at the Suez Canal, which officials say already hosts 200 companies and investments worth around $4 billion.
The new investments – for which Egypt has not announced a figure – give Beijing even greater influence in the canal zone, a critical artery of global trade, as conflict in the region chokes other conduits.
Read moreGlobal shipping firms to avoid Suez Canal as attacks from Yemen's Houthi rebels increase
Xi said China "stands ready to work with countries in the region to safeguard the security of international shipping lanes, advance development cooperation... and eliminate the breeding grounds for conflict".
A series of additional agreements were also signed, though Egyptian officials did not provide details.
'Independent foreign policy'
Beijing is eyeing a greater foothold in the Middle East, at a time when "the United States looks like it can't really make up its mind whether it wants to withdraw from the region or be more engaged", Mirette Mabrouk, a senior fellow at the Washington-based Middle East Institute, told AFP.
China sees Egypt as a key partner and an entry point to more regional influence.
For Egypt, closer ties with China are part of a broader effort to diversify partnerships rather than align with a single power, Mabrouk said.
Sisi, in an op-ed published in Egyptian media on Tuesday, highlighted Cairo's "independent foreign policy", days after the Emirati branch of Egypt's second-largest bank, Banque Misr, was targeted by US sanctions.
Washington vowed last month to isolate Iran economically, threatening expanded sanctions that could also hit Chinese banks, among others.
China, a major buyer of Iranian oil, has vowed to safeguard its interests.
In the lead-up to an expected meeting between Xi and US President Donald Trump this month, it has also sought to shore up ties with US-friendly regional nations.
Cairo is one of the largest recipients of US military aid, and historically a key Middle East mediator.
Egypt – which under Sisi's administration became one of the world's top weapons buyers – hosted major joint air combat exercises with the Chinese military in August, featuring Beijing's powerful J-16 fighter jet.
China is a major exporter to Egypt, with its trade surplus reaching $12 billion in the first seven months of 2026, according to Chinese customs data.
Across Cairo, a megalopolis home to over 26 million people, major streets have been lined with Chinese and Egyptian flags, as well as billboards showing Sisi and Xi.
Xi is expected to head to the Grand Egyptian Museum overlooking the Giza Pyramids later on Wednesday.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Putin says Russia is 12 km from Sumy—1.5 km farther than in June
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:19:02 UTC
23:19:02 KST

On 1 September, Russian President Vladimir Putin said during a conversation with journalists that Russian troops had 12 km left to reach Sumy. Censor.NET estimated from DeepState’s map that Russian forces were approximately 17 km from Sumy’s administrative boundary.
Russian military commanders have systematically exaggerated their gains on the battlefield. The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) describes such claims as part of a Kremlin information campaign aimed at creating the impression of major Russian gains. In this case, the Russian president cited exaggerated gains that, compared with his previous claims, appear to be a setback.
What Putin said
“The ‘North’ group of forces continues to create a security belt along the Russian-Ukrainian border in the border areas of the Sumy region... There are 12 km left to Sumy, to the Sumy ring road,” Putin said during the press conference.
Censor.NET reported that Russian forces were about 17 km from Sumy without specifying the reference point, while Putin did not say which section of the city’s ring road his 12 km figure referred to.
Putin previously gave a different distance
On 28 June, during an interview with Russian propagandist Pavel Zarubin, Putin said that Russian troops had “about 10.5 km” left to reach Sumy. At the time, he also explained the offensive as the creation of a “security zone” along Russia’s border.
Putin’s claimed distance to Sumy therefore increased by approximately 1.5 km in just over two months, contradicting the Kremlin’s portrayal of a continuing advance.
Other exaggerations
In July 2026, Putin claimed that Russian forces had “completely captured” Kostiantynivka. Ukraine’s General Staff rejected the claim, saying Ukrainian forces continued defensive operations in the city. ISW also said some videos of Russian flags being raised in Kostiantynivka were likely AI-altered.
On 2 December 2025, Putin claimed that Russian forces had captured Pokrovsk in Donetsk Oblast. ISW found no evidence confirming the city’s complete capture and assessed that its fall would not enable Moscow to achieve a significant breakthrough.

Venice Film Festival: Clooney, conflicts and competition dominate as ceremonies begin

Awards, artificial intelligence, conflicts and climate change. Much of the opening talk at the start of the 83rd Venice Film Festival has revolved around geopolitics, propaganda and the future of cinema.
George Clooney is the undoubted star of the show as the Venice Film Festival opens for its 83rd edition.
In the nearly 30 years since he first stepped onto the Lido Out of Sight, he’s become something of a staple fixture. It’s a city where he’s enjoyed many significant moments, from his wedding at the Aman Venice to the debut of Good Night, and Good Luck, which earned him his first Oscar nomination for best director.
Now, the actor, director and producer is due to receive a lifetime achievement award but when facing the press, he didn't appear to want to talk much about the journey that's led him to be the centre of the spotlight at the world's oldest celebration of cinema.
Ahead of the prize-giving ceremony on Wednesday, the 65-year-old wanted to discuss anything and everything it seemed but his life on or behind the camera.
Whether it was talk of artificial intelligence,climate change, power brokers in Hollywood and beyond and the state of journalism today, Clooney had two cents and more to spend on a range of topics.
"There’s a great word, kakistocracy, which is a country run by the least qualified people,” he said. “I think maybe we have a kakistocracy right now. But we’ll get through it.”
On artificial intelligence, Clooney said that his industry is going to have to find ways to survive, and that he would “like to avoid being in a tampon commercial 20 years after I’m dead.”
He also criticised the fact that some of the world's richest men own The Washington Post and X and said that the proposed merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. was “a complicated thing because I don’t know how this works out, I don’t know how it goes through."
The state we are in
Clooney was by no means alone is decrying the state of current affairs. Jury president Maggie Gyllenhaal also made her feelings clear on a variety of subjects including, sexism, politics and conflicts.
“Look, we could say how are we possibly here talking about movies right now when the world is in a state of emergency,” Gyllenhaal said. “To me the answer has something to do with empathy.”
She also addressed the dearth of female directors in the competition lineup, with only one film directed by a woman. Perhaps in response to critics, just last week, NAZA - a documentary about Gaza co-directed by a woman - was added to the lineup.
“I guess it’s just finally become clear that men make better movies than women do,” Gyllenhaal joked, before speaking about the systemic issues facing female directors, like financing and preconceived notions about high art.
Over the course of 11 days, many stars and celebrities from Hollywood and beyond are expected on the red carpet, from Robert Pattinson to Noel and Liam Gallagher of Oasis.
The sprawling lineup also includes documentaries about , Elon Musk (Musk) and independent Russian journalists covering the war in Ukraine (My Undesirable Friends — Part II: Exile) as well as Palestinian films and a short about U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Minneapolis.
The festival will open with Danny Boyle's Ink a competition title featuring Guy Pearce as media baron Rupert Murdoch and Jack O'Connell as tabloid newspaper editor Larry Lamb. The movie dramatises Murdoch's acquisition of The Sun newspaper in 1969 and how Lamb reversed its fortunes from a failing venture into Britain's bestselling daily.
The Venice Film Festival runs until Saturday 12 September.

UNEP urges sustained action to cap global warming, avert climate breakdown
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
22:17:26 CST
23:17:26 KST

NAIROBI, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Governments, industries, and societies must take radical measures to prevent global temperatures from breaching the 1.5-degree-Celsius warming limit set by the Paris Agreement and avert widespread calamities such as extreme heatwaves and ecosystem collapse, according to a United Nations Environment Program (UNEP) report launched in Nairobi on Wednesday.
The report "Limiting Overshoot: Navigating exceedance of 1.5 degrees Celsius and pathways towards return" warns that failing to curb runaway warming will plunge humanity into a perilous future marked by climatic shocks, hunger, disease outbreaks, and economic collapse.
UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen noted that while global temperatures are increasingly likely to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels in the near term, avoiding a permanent breach of the threshold remains entirely possible.
"Now is the time we must double down on climate action. We can -- and must -- get on the right path by cutting greenhouse gas emissions, strengthening resilience and adaptation, and ensuring that any exceedance of 1.5 degrees Celsius is as small and short-lived as possible," Andersen said.
She noted that preventing even a fraction of a degree of warming each year will save lives, protect fragile ecosystems, and reduce economic losses.
Despite national net-zero commitments, the UNEP report warns that breaching the Paris Agreement's temperature threshold is increasingly likely, escalating risks of accelerated sea-level rise, coral reef collapse, catastrophic wildfires, and glacier loss.
The report warns of an elevated risk of triggering irreversible tipping points such as the collapse of the West Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets, the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, and the Amazon rainforest, with catastrophic consequences for planetary stability.
Unabated emissions of greenhouse gases, including methane and carbon dioxide, could cause temperatures to continue rising, threatening small island developing states and low-lying coastal cities with partial or total submersion, the report notes.
The report says that runaway warming will drive up energy costs and insurance premiums, straining financial systems worldwide.
Stressing that a climate crisis is still preventable, the report emphasizes that nations must transition to clean energy while cutting emissions of methane and other short-lived climate pollutants.
Limiting temperature spikes will require simultaneous adaptation and mitigation efforts, backed by multilateral cooperation, political resolve, effective policies, and sustained financing, according to the report.
The report calls for implementing simultaneous adaptation and mitigation measures, backed by multilateral action, political goodwill, effective policies, and sustained financing, to curb global temperature spikes. ■

Xi calls on China, Egypt to enhance mutual support, deepen cooperation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02

Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan pose for a group photo with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi and his wife Entissar El-Sisi in Cairo, Egypt, Sept. 2, 2026. Xi held talks with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi in Cairo on Wednesday. (Xinhua/Yin Bogu)
CAIRO, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday called on China and Egypt to support each other, deepen cooperation, and continue advancing the building of a China-Egypt community with a shared future amid a turbulent international and regional landscape.
Xi made the remarks during his talks with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi, noting that Egypt was the first Arab and African nation to establish diplomatic ties with the People's Republic of China in 1956.
The older-generation leaders of the two countries led their peoples in fighting side by side for national independence and against imperialism and colonialism, forging an unbreakable bond of friendship, Xi said.
Over the past seven decades, China-Egypt relations have weathered challenges and developed distinctive features of equality and mutual trust, friendship and mutual learning, solidarity and mutual support, as well as win-win cooperation, he said.
Xi said the China-Egypt comprehensive strategic partnership has achieved leapfrog development in recent years under the guidance of the two heads of state. The two sides share similar views and have closely aligned strategies in pursuing development and revitalization, improving people's well-being, and upholding international fairness and justice, he added.
Xi emphasized that China and Egypt should firmly support each other, maintain the momentum of high-level exchanges, enhance exchanges and cooperation in all fields and at all levels, and strengthen exchanges and mutual learning on governance experience.
Xi said the two sides should promote mutually beneficial cooperation, better align their development strategies, tap the potential for cooperation in traditional fields such as infrastructure development, power, agriculture and communications technology, and foster new highlights of cooperation in green energy, electric vehicles, aerospace, the digital economy and modern agricultural technology.
The two sides should promote people-to-people exchanges, comprehensively expand exchanges and cooperation in culture, education, science and technology, health, sports and other fields, and facilitate personnel exchanges and enhance people-to-people bonds, Xi said.
The two sides should strengthen security cooperation, jointly combat transnational crime, deepen international cooperation in anti-corruption, firmly support each other's anti-terror efforts, and safeguard their common security, Xi said.
The two sides should strengthen multilateral collaboration, further enhance coordination and cooperation on multilateral platforms such as the United Nations and the BRICS, jointly promote the development of the China-Arab States Cooperation Forum and the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation, jointly oppose unilateralism and acts of bullying, and promote a more just and equitable global governance system, Xi said.
For his part, Sisi welcomed Xi's historic state visit to Egypt on the occasion of the 70th anniversary of diplomatic ties between the two countries.
Sisi said that since the establishment of diplomatic relations, bilateral ties have developed in a sound and steady manner, and cooperation across various fields has yielded fruitful results.
Egypt firmly adheres to the one-China principle and is committed to further advancing the Egypt-China comprehensive strategic partnership, Sisi added.
Egypt is ready to work with China to deepen cooperation in trade and investment, manufacturing, infrastructure development, finance, science and technology, and new energy, strengthen military and security exchanges, and promote closer people-to-people exchanges, so as to benefit the two peoples and contribute to regional development and prosperity, Sisi said.
Sisi said China, as a permanent member of the UN Security Council, plays an important and constructive role in international affairs. Egypt is ready to strengthen coordination with China at multilateral platforms, jointly address global challenges, and work together to uphold international fairness and justice, he added. ■

Feature: Ebola casts shadow over school reopening in eastern DR Congo
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
22:17:18 CST
23:17:18 KST

BUNIA, DR Congo, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- As schools reopened across the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) for the new academic year, pupils returning to classrooms in the Ebola-hit east found themselves facing a school routine shaped as much by the epidemic as by lessons and textbooks, with handwashing stations, temperature checks and restrictions on close physical contact becoming part of the first days back.
In Bunia, capital of the eastern Ituri Province and the epicenter of the outbreak, pupils in uniform returned to schools across the city on Tuesday, some accompanied by their parents, but several classrooms visited by Xinhua remained only partly filled, reflecting continued hesitation among families over whether it was safe to send children back while Ebola transmission remained active.
In Beni, in neighboring North Kivu Province, the concern was visible in a different way, as pupils washed their hands before entering school, had their temperatures checked and were encouraged to avoid hugs and embraces with classmates after the holiday, while some schools also adjusted seating arrangements to reduce close contact.
The reopening comes as nearly 31 million pupils are expected to attend school across the country this academic year, according to DRC Minister of State for National Education Raissa Malu, who officially launched the new school year Tuesday in the capital Kinshasa against a national backdrop marked by both armed insecurity and serious public health risks.
"Some parts of our country remain confronted with insecurity and conflicts, while others face health risks. But our duty remains the same: to keep schools functioning wherever possible," Malu said at the opening ceremony.
The DRC Ministry of National Education has introduced a three-tier system -- green, orange and red -- based on the intensity of Ebola transmission. Some 2,890 schools are considered at high risk, according to authorities.
In green and orange zones, in-person classes will continue with corresponding preventive measures. In red zones, where transmission remains active, regular classroom teaching will be temporarily replaced by home-based learning materials and educational programs broadcast on radio and television.
That challenge is particularly acute in eastern DRC, where the Ebola outbreak has crossed the threshold of 3,000 deaths. According to the latest situation report issued Wednesday by the country's health authorities, 6,186 confirmed cases and 3,007 deaths had been recorded as of Aug. 31, while 1,409 patients had recovered.
The epidemic remains active in six provinces: Ituri, North Kivu, Haut-Uele, Tshopo, South Kivu and Bas-Uele, with Ituri continuing to bear the heaviest burden and accounting for more than four-fifths of confirmed cases recorded nationwide since the outbreak began.
Children have also been heavily affected. According to a report by the United Nations Children's Fund in August, those aged 17 or younger represent about 21 percent of confirmed Ebola cases but around 33 percent of reported deaths.
In Bunia, those concerns had already been voiced before the first day of class, with some parents and members of the teaching community questioning whether sanitary conditions were sufficient to ensure the safety of pupils and teachers.
At Mwanga Beabo primary school, however, Nkwasa Jonathan, a father of two, said he had decided to send his children back, arguing that families had already been living with the epidemic for months and could continue schooling if preventive measures were respected.
"It is true that the epidemic continues to spread in the province, but we are calling on all parents not to give in to fear. We have been living with this situation for months. We continue to protect ourselves by respecting the health measures," he told Xinhua.
For Jonathan, keeping children at home would risk interrupting their education once again, but other parents in the city remain far less confident about the timing of the reopening.
Wawina Rachelle, a pupil's mother, said she believed schools had reopened too soon while cases were still being reported, drawing a comparison with restrictions imposed during the COVID-19 pandemic.
"I am against this school reopening because the cases continue to increase here. During COVID-19, the children stayed at home, the schools and churches were closed and gatherings were banned. We should have waited this time as well in order to reduce the risk of infection," she said.
Schools in Bunia have nevertheless introduced a range of preventive measures in an effort to reassure parents and reduce the risk of transmission. At the Pierre Jacques Dufort school complex, pupils are required to wash their hands and have their temperatures checked before entering, while at the Fabia school complex, a room has been prepared to receive possible suspected cases, and at Shalom school, recess has been suspended in order to limit contact among pupils.
Local authorities have so far chosen to follow the national academic calendar, with Bunia Mayor Jean-Bosco Mbuyi Kola saying the authorities did not want the health crisis to derail an already established national school program.
"We, as authorities, decided to open the schools because we do not want to compromise an already established national school program. Despite the persistence of the epidemic, we therefore decided to open the schools on the scheduled date throughout the country," he said.
In Beni, where Ebola transmission is also active, the reopening has brought preventive measures directly into pupils' daily routines, particularly at the Institut de l'Avenir school complex, where handwashing facilities have been installed, temperatures are checked and seating arrangements have been adjusted to reduce close contact.
Zakindu Musulu Christele, a pupil at the school, said the measures had changed the way students interacted after returning from the holidays, but she considered them necessary given the risks posed by the epidemic.
"We think this is a good measure because the epidemic can be transmitted particularly through physical contact, hugs and embraces," she said.
According to Zakindu, the school has about 15 handwashing stations, roughly one in front of each classroom, with water available to allow pupils to wash their hands regularly during the school day.
"I would not want to see a friend fall ill or die because of this epidemic. I therefore have to protect myself and protect others," she said.
Education authorities in Beni say they are coordinating with health officials to strengthen prevention measures, with Robert Kibonge, head of the Beni educational sub-division, saying officials had been asked to identify the areas most affected by Ebola while some partners had promised to provide additional prevention equipment to schools.
He also stressed the role of teachers in reinforcing awareness among pupils, noting that although many educators already had some knowledge of Ebola dating back to the 2018 outbreak, further sensitization was still needed so that they could pass accurate prevention messages on to children.
"We must strengthen this awareness so that teachers can, in turn, transmit the right information to our children and help them better protect themselves against the disease," Kibonge said. ■

FIS has returned Russians to competition under a neutral flag — Ukraine welcomed the decision
Kyiv • UNN
FIS will allow athletes from Russia and Belarus to participate under a declaration of neutrality. They may compete only individually and without national symbols.
The International Ski and Snowboard Federation (FIS) has simplified the procedure for admitting athletes from Russia and Belarus to international competitions. UNN reports this with reference to FIS.
Details
As stated by the federation, a decision was adopted on the conditions under which athletes of Belarusian and Russian sporting nationality will be allowed to participate in FIS competitions during the 2026/27 season.
In view of the recent decisions of the International Olympic Committee on this issue, the FIS Council analyzed the situation and decided that athletes and support personnel from these two countries may be granted permission to participate in FIS competitions provided that they sign a declaration of neutrality based on a set of principles established by FIS. Compliance with these principles of neutrality will be continuously monitored, and sanctions will be imposed in the event of violations
The federation added that athletes' participation is limited to individual competitions and is subject to the condition that no national symbols—such as flags, anthems, or uniforms—may be displayed. Athletes must also comply with all applicable anti-doping requirements.
The Ski Federation of Ukraine welcomed this decision.
In recent years, the Ski Federation of Ukraine has systematically worked to ensure that Ukraine's position is heard and taken into account at the international level. We thank FIS for a decision that upholds the principles of neutrality and contributes to preserving the integrity and fairness of sport
We remind you
The International Olympic Committee temporarily lifted restrictions on the Russian Olympic Committee, which had been imposed after the ROC incorporated the Olympic committees of the occupied territories of Ukraine into its structure.

NATO vows to defend every inch. Svalbard is where Russia plans to prove it won’t.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:16:46 UTC
23:16:46 KST

US Central Intelligence Agency Director John Ratcliffe's visit to Moscow has triggered much speculation. The main thesis is that Russia may be preparing to conduct an act of aggression against a NATO member in the relatively near term to invalidate NATO's Article 5.
According to sources cited by the Wall Street Journal, Ratcliffe delivered a warning to Russia not to attack NATO countries. Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania were singled out in a Politico report on 26 August, citing two "sources familiar with the matter."
Every warning names the Baltics. Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania are where the CIA pointed, where the intelligence assessments focus, where NATO has massed its tripwire forces. But the Baltics are defended. The one piece of NATO territory Russia could seize before anyone could stop it—and that hands hesitant Western capitals a ready-made excuse not to respond—lies far to the north. It is Svalbard.
The timeline
On 6 August, citing new US intelligence reports, the Wall Street Journal reported that "US intelligence is warning that Russia may attempt to test NATO's resolve by carrying out a limited strike against one of the Alliance's member states within the next few years." US intelligence assessments indicate that any action by Russia could occur between this autumn and 2029. This is only the latest in a series of warnings of the risk of war with Russia. Leaders of NATO's eastern flank countries recently issued public warnings, citing intelligence that Russia is preparing provocations on their territory.
On 29 August, the Polish Prime Minister said there were signs that Russia was seriously preparing for an escalation and that the next seven to eight months could be critical for the security of Ukraine, Poland, and the entire region.
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) argues that a CIA director's personal visit to deliver a message is unusual and generally reserved for sensitive matters of the highest importance. Ratcliffe's arrival in Moscow on a C-17 military transport aircraft and his use of an American motorcade suggest that the US regarded its intelligence as urgent and sensitive—not a warning of a distant threat. The visit indicates concern about a much shorter timeline than the US intelligence reports of early August suggested.
Latvia just moved from “Russia might attack” to “here’s where you report if it does”
That timeline is shaped by Europe's urgent effort to close its critical military vulnerabilities by 2030. Russia is unlikely to wait until Europe has regained its strength.
The last CIA director's trip to Moscow was in November 2021, when William Burns made a final effort to deter Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. To state the obvious: Burns' effort failed—and he served a president friendly to NATO and to international law. Ratcliffe serves a president who treats Europe as a strategic adversary; his warning is unlikely to shift Moscow at all.
The threat: sub-threshold is over
The EU White Paper describes Russia as the "fundamental threat" to European security for the foreseeable future, citing its war economy, industrial mobilization, nuclear posture, and cooperation with Belarus, Iran, and North Korea.
According to assessments by several EU intelligence services, Russia's rapidly expanding military-production capacity could give it the ability to test the unity of Western countries and the effectiveness of Article 5 within the next three to five years. The US recently warned Poland that Russia is planning an armed provocation on Polish soil designed to test NATO's commitment to collective self-defense.
Let us be clear: Russia has been testing the unity of Western countries and the effectiveness of Article 5 for years already.
It is waging an ever-escalating hybrid war that could—and arguably should—have triggered Article 5 long ago. It is attacking critical infrastructure, conducting sabotage and cyberattacks, running influence and information operations, violating NATO airspace with missiles and drones, and flying UAV intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance missions over allied territory. On 23 August, The Telegraph reported, citing Western intelligence sources, that Russia has launched a new wave of attacks on weapons factories in Europe, recruiting members of local criminal gangs and testing NATO's response.
None of it has forced a response. That is the point. To test NATO's commitment to collective defense—rather than merely its patience—Russia must escalate beyond the sub-threshold. It must stage the one thing it has so far avoided: a military operation that forces NATO to confront Article 5.
The window for doing so is closing. On 11 December 2025, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte warned that Russia could attack a NATO country within five years, adding that the Alliance must "be prepared for the scale of war our grandparents or great-grandparents endured"—the first time since World War II that a secretary general has raised the prospect of a full-scale war on NATO soil. NATO's generals warn of war by 2029; Europe will not be ready until 2035. Russia has every incentive to act inside that gap, before it narrows.
The gap is real. These assessments have emerged against a backdrop of critical munitions shortages: Patriot interceptors, long-range precision-guided missiles, tactical ground-launched missile systems, 155mm artillery shells, and Stinger short-range surface-to-air missiles. US stocks have been badly depleted by weak defense-industrial production and by the Israel–US confrontation with Iran. NATO has since named Integrated Air and Missile Defense a top priority for the Alliance's survival and deterrence, calling for a 400 percent increase in air- and missile-defense capabilities. That is the measure of the shortfall. Worse, recent exercises have shown the Alliance is nowhere near ready to fight a drone war with Russia.
Most analysis fixes on the Baltics. In my opinion, there is a more likely scenario: the seizure of Norwegian sovereign territory in the High North.
Why Svalbard: the tripwire it lacks
Admittedly, no intelligence service has ranked Svalbard above the Baltics. That is puzzling, given that while the Baltic states are a challenge for Russia, Svalbard is a challenge for NATO.
Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania are defended by a standing tripwire. NATO permanent battlegroups operate in each—the UK leads in Estonia, Canada in Latvia, Germany in Lithuania—backed by a forward-defense posture built to stop any incursion at the border rather than liberate territory afterward. In response to Russian airspace incursions, drone provocations, and GPS jamming, NATO stood up the Eastern Sentry initiative; after repeated undersea cable cuts, it added Baltic Sentry to patrol the sea and guard the infrastructure. The Suwałki Gap—the 60-kilometer land corridor linking Poland to Lithuania between Belarus and Kaliningrad—is heavily fortified and rehearsed in large multinational exercises.
An attack on the Baltic countries hits allied forces on day one, forcing the Alliance to act, and it requires a force buildup that telegraphs intent and escalates toward exactly the general war Russia wants to avoid.
Svalbard offers the opposite. There is no permanent garrison and no fortification, because Article 9 of the 1920 Svalbard Treaty bars naval bases, fortifications, and any "warlike" use of the archipelago. Norway retains the sovereign right to defend it—Coast Guard and naval vessels call at Longyearbyen, and defensive measures under Article 5 are permitted—but there is no standing tripwire, and the treaty ensures there never will be.
That is the vulnerability: Russia can seize the archipelago by surprise and present a fait accompli before any force can reach it.
And it hands hesitant Western capitals a ready-made excuse. Svalbard is Norwegian sovereign territory, and Norway holds—correctly—that Article 5 applies to it. The land-territory question is not genuinely ambiguous; Russia manufactures the ambiguity, contesting Norway's interpretation and pointing to the treaty's demilitarized character to argue that any response is itself a violation. But in a strategic environment where Western leaders seek any reason not to engage Russia, that manufactured doubt—remote outpost, unpopulated rock, a "demilitarized" treaty—is enough.
Trending Now
The excuse is political, not legal. And the excuse is the objective: a visibly divided Alliance, unable to agree whether or how to respond, is the entire purpose of a Russian move against a NATO member.
If Russia achieves surprise, it will meet no opposing force. The Northern Fleet operates in the area routinely; Russia's Arctic forces—roughly 15,000 to 20,000 troops across motor-rifle and naval-infantry brigades, with cold-weather armor and layered anti-access/area-denial systems—are already in place. Svalbard sits within range of Russian tactical aviation flying from the Kola Peninsula, which could establish air control fast enough to keep NATO from landing at all.
What Russia would gain
The occupation would also pay for itself many times over, shifting the balance across the entire Arctic and North Atlantic.
The primary military incentive is nuclear. The Kola Peninsula houses Russia's strategic ballistic-missile submarines, and holding Svalbard would close the shallow Barents Sea into a protected bastion where those submarines—the core of Russia's second-strike deterrent—could operate insulated from NATO. Control of the archipelago also locks the "Bear Gap," the stretch between Svalbard and Norway's North Cape. Anti-ship and anti-air batteries on the islands would let Russia choke off NATO surface and anti-submarine forces from the Barents Sea while guaranteeing its Northern Fleet unhindered breakout routes into the North Atlantic.
The archipelago is also a forward platform. Using existing infrastructure such as Longyearbyen's airport, Russia could base tactical aircraft and long-range maritime patrol aircraft hundreds of kilometers further west than its current fields on Franz Josef Land. Seizing SvalSat—one of the world's largest commercial satellite ground stations—would let Moscow blind or repurpose a hub critical to Western environmental, civilian, and dual-use satellite operations. And by holding the "gateway to the Arctic," Russia would gain physical leverage over the western entrance to the Northern Sea Route, an increasingly viable shipping lane as the ice retreats.
These are gains Russia would want under any circumstances. They are not why Svalbard is the likely next target—that case rests on the tripwire it lacks and the window that is closing. But they explain why, of all the ways to test Article 5, this one carries no offsetting cost.
Conclusion
The map confirms the logic. Baltic officials and government-affiliated analysts stress that NATO should take the Russian threat seriously but that their immediate assessment has not changed—there is no large-scale buildup along the Russian border with the Baltic states. The only NATO territory open to invasion without such a buildup is Svalbard.
According to the Norwegian Intelligence Service, Russia "will remain intent on preventing NATO from making military use of the archipelago" and aims "to increase Russian scope for action in Svalbard, to influence attitudes to Norwegian defence policy, to instil fear, polarisation and political apathy in the population and to undermine trust in Norwegian authorities—in addition to weakening support to Ukraine." Norway's proximity to the Arctic, its energy supply to Europe, and its role as a logistics and reception hub for allied forces all make it a target.
A limited attack on NATO's northern flank would aim to invalidate Article 5 by producing a situation the North Atlantic Council—which must vote unanimously to honor the mutual-defense clause—cannot resolve. Moscow would choose the operation most likely to leave NATO unable to unify on a decisive response, and thus unable to come to the aid of the member attacked.
A failure to invoke Article 5, or to act on it, would gut the credibility of the guarantee—one of Vladimir Putin's longest-standing strategic objectives beyond Ukraine.
Retaking Svalbard would mean moving NATO amphibious forces more than 1,000 kilometers across open ocean patrolled by Russian submarines and dominated by Russian aviation—an extremely risky and costly endeavor, with no guarantee of success. A Russian occupation would also feed an unhinged American president's fixation on Greenland, eroding Alliance cohesion further still.
Attacking the Baltics—defensively prepared, reinforced by allied forces, and offering none of Svalbard's advantages—makes no comparable sense.
The information war has already started. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov published an article on 31 August accusing NATO of militarizing the Far North in a "direct threat" to Russian security and an attempt to turn the Arctic into a "new front" against Russia—laying the groundwork to frame any Russian move as a pre-emptive defense. The same day, Russia's Ambassador to Norway, Nikolay Korchunov, claimed that Norway's "creeping abandonment of its own guiding principles regarding foreign military activity on its territory undermines the country's sovereignty" and warned of "a slide into direct military conflict."
NATO has committed, repeatedly and at every level from the Strategic Concept to the Secretary General, to defend "every inch of Allied territory." Svalbard is where Russia intends to prove that commitment empty.
Russia has exhausted the sub-threshold; forcing the Article 5 question now requires a discrete military act, and the window for it closes as Europe rearms. The one place that act can be staged—without a telegraphing buildup, against territory with no tripwire, offering a built-in political excuse for NATO to hesitate—is Svalbard.
That is why, if Russia moves, the logic points north.

WHO's Tedros says Ebola response must be scaled up to tackle Congo outbreak

WHO's Tedros says Ebola response must be scaled up to tackle Congo outbreak
GENEVA, Sept 2 - The head of the World Health Organization on Wednesday said the Ebola response needs to be scaled up to tackle the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, with tracking the chains of transmission still posing a challenge.
"Until every chain is found and broken, the epidemic will continue and will continue to pose a threat to DRC, its neighbours and the region as a whole," the WHO's director-general, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, told reporters in Geneva.
The number of deaths in Congo's Ebola outbreak has surpassed 3,000, government data showed on Wednesday, as the country's worst epidemic continues to spread across its northeast.
The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, became the largest and deadliest in Congo's history after surpassing the 2018-2020 epidemic.
It is now second only to the 2014-2016 West African outbreak, which infected over 28,600 people and killed more than 11,000 across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
But there is now hope of possible progress in treatments and vaccinations. The WHO aims to start clinical efficacy trials of potential vaccines next month or in November, and trials on treatments are under way.
FUNDING NEEDED FOR MORE BEDS
However, Tedros said many deaths were among people who were not on a list of known contacts.
"That means there are chains of transmission we don't know about," he said, adding that many of those who died were still being buried unsafely, which is fuelling transmission.
He urged the international community to increase and accelerate funding for the Congolese government-led Ebola response plan, which is seeking $1.3 billion.
While the WHO has managed to ship 320 tons of supplies, and has increased testing capacity to 3,000 tests per day, it needs further funding to help support its response - including to increase bed capacity at Ebola treatment centres.
Luca Fontana, technical officer for health and technical logistics with the WHO, said it costs $15 million per month for a 1,500 bed treatment centre.
"We know that we are making this request at a time when financing for humanitarian assistance has contracted," Tedros said. "But as we know from previous Ebola outbreaks, we can control this epidemic if we choose to."
CLINICAL TRIALS
More than 300 Ebola patients have been enrolled for a trial of two treatments, Tedros said.
Trials are also under way of the antiviral drug obeldesivir among people considered high-risk contacts of Ebola cases, to assess if it is effective in preventing disease after exposure to the virus.
Two new vaccines against Bundibugyo virus are in safety trials in Britain and Canada. It is not known whether an approved vaccine against the Zaire Ebola virus would be effective against Bundibugyo virus, so it requires clinical efficacy trials, the WHO said.
"WHO is working with partners to progress all three vaccines to efficacy trials in DRC, starting in October or November," Tedros said. REUTERS

How Trumpism is changing the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02

How Trumpism is changing the world
This US presidency is rewriting the rules of global governance and ushering the world into a new era.
The post-World War II era was dominated by idealism that gave birth to a dense architecture of multilateral institutions and Western-led governance frameworks.
That order has now reached a decisive historical inflection point. The foreign policy paradigm forged during the two administrations of United States President Donald Trump — marked by unilateralism, transactional nationalism, and a recalibration of historic alliances — represents a sharp break from prior international norms. Combining coercive leverage with strategic media manipulation, this shift has heralded a new foreign policy phenomenon: Trumpism.
By combining assertions of national sovereignty with an anti-establishment tone, Trumpism systematically challenges the core assumptions that had underpinned global governance for generations.
At its core, it represents a deliberate move away from grand, Western-dominated global leadership towards a decentralised, issue-specific, and deeply transactional international order.
The pillars of transactional statecraft
Trumpism’s operational strategy has replaced traditional multilateral commitments with a hardheaded focus on economic statecraft and national interest. Foreign policy engagements have been explicitly tethered to domestic economic priorities: reindustrialisation, a revitalised defence industrial base, energy dominance, balanced trade, and leadership in the financial sector.
To achieve these aims, the Trump administration has eschewed expansive multinational agreements in favour of bilateral bargains, deploying aggressive tariffs, coercive trade measures, and sanctions as primary instruments of state power.
The administration’s reliance on expansive sanctions regimes and aggressive extraterritorial enforcement has ignited fierce global debates regarding international law, state sovereignty, and the legitimate limits of national jurisdiction.
Under the banner of “peace through strength”, Trumpism has integrated legal, economic, and security mechanisms to pressure allies and adversaries alike. Law enforcement operations and national security objectives have been routinely repurposed as direct tools of foreign policy.
This transactional posture has extended directly into collective defence and security architectures, most notably NATO. Trumpism has brought intense scrutiny to Western defence burden-sharing arrangements, highlighting severe imbalances where the US had borne a disproportionate share of costs and strategic risks.
Institutional disruption and systemic paralysis
The systemic consequences of Trumpism have reverberated across every layer of the global governance hierarchy.
In multilateral forums, the administration has displayed unprecedented ambivalence and unpredictability, frequently reneging on established international agreements and disengaging from multilateral institutions.
This volatile leadership style has exposed deep vulnerabilities within global governance, accelerating the fragmentation of the post-Cold War liberal international order.
A prominent casualty of this institutional disruption has been the United Nations, particularly the UN Security Council. Trump’s policies have magnified existing debates over the UNSC’s legitimacy, representation, and effectiveness.
Observers have noted that entrenched geopolitical rivalries, institutional inertia, and structural hierarchies rooted in the colonial era had already left the UNSC paralysed—trapped in a pre-contemplation stage of reform rather than delivering substantive structural changes. US institutional disengagement has further compounded this inertia, raising fundamental questions about the long-term durability and authority of international security bodies.
While proponents have argued that the Trump administration is seeking to drive necessary institutional reform through selective, high-level engagement—such as collaborating with like-minded allies and engaging the UN secretary-general on shared priorities—critics have viewed these moves as prioritising immediate national interests over global stability.
The rise of a multipolar and regionalised order
As the US is stepping back from global stewardship, the resulting power vacuum is catalysing a profound restructuring of international politics. Middle powers and regional blocs are increasingly stepping forward to bridge governance gaps.
These actors have begun constructing regional frameworks and issue-specific coalitions, casting them as vital supplements — or direct alternatives — to traditional Western-dominated institutions.
This global pivot has ignited a fierce debate among international relations scholars and policymakers regarding Trump’s legacy.
On the one hand, some argue that the disruptions he has caused are a catalyst for reform and systemic resilience. By forcing middle powers and non-Western nations to take greater ownership of regional security and economic coordination, Trumpism is fostering a more plural, inclusive, and realistic global order capable of addressing modern geopolitical realities.
Others are warning that US disengagement from multilateral commitments has shattered collective security arrangements and degraded institutional legitimacy. From this viewpoint, weakened Western leadership has paved the way for sustained strategic competition, regional instability, and dangerous governance voids across critical international forums.
Redefining great power
The foreign policy of the Trump presidency cannot be dismissed as a temporary aberration or a simple shift in personal political style; it warrants the enduring label Trumpism because it has established a distinct, reproducible paradigm of international statecraft.
By deliberately weaponising unpredictable diplomacy, prioritising national prosperity over institutional continuity, and asserting absolute national sovereignty against global governance constraints, Trumpism fundamentally is redefining how a great power can exercise leverage in the modern era.
Trump’s foreign policy will leave an indelible imprint on the contemporary international system. By challenging the foundational premises of the liberal international order, it will permanently alter the balance of power, forcing the world into a new era characterised by decentralised authority, heightened regionalism, and a continuous search for new governance models.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Palestinians in fear as Israeli forces mount pogroms on West Bank mosques
Palestinian witnesses recount the coordinated Israeli army and settler attacks on mosques in the occupied West Bank.
Naim Ahmed Faraj, along with dozens of worshippers, was standing for the evening (Isha) prayers, when Israeli forces threw tear gas canisters inside their mosque in Madama village near Nablus. Faraj, 66, who suffers from joint and heart ailments, collapsed due to suffocation.
Faraj’s son, Mohammed Naim, says his father fell semiconscious and his condition deteriorated after inhaling tear gas. The 66-year-old regained consciousness gradually after he was rushed home inside a car as there were no ambulances available, according to Naim.
“The mosque is supposed to be a safe haven where people can pray without being attacked. But lately – and for a long time now – the mosque has become a source of anxiety,” Naim told Al Jazeera, adding that worshippers now fear while going to mosques for prayers amid escalating violence in the occupied West Bank.
A suffocating island
The Madama attack is part of a sharply rising wave of Israeli settler and military pogroms across the occupied territory, which Palestinian sources say are emboldened by extremist government ministers like Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.
Naim described these raids as daily occurrences, deliberately timed during prayer hours to maximise panic. He noted that soldiers and settlers regularly collaborate to “terrorise” the local population.
“Our village has become like an island surrounded from all sides by settlements, the bypass road, and the army, and we do not have any outlet or area we can go to,” Naim said, pointing out the expansion of illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, which cut through Palestinian towns and villages.
More than 750,000 settlers live in illegal settlements throughout the occupied Palestinian territory, and their numbers continue to rise as top Israeli leaders, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, publicly oppose the establishment of a sovereign Palestinian state.
The anti-Palestinian rhetoric and physical attacks have particularly exploded in recent weeks as Israeli politicians campaign for next month’s general elections. Last week, far-right Israeli Knesset member Zvi Sukkot stormed Madama village and smashed a Palestinian memorial with a sledgehammer.
Arson and racism
Hours after the attack in Madama, Israeli settlers launched a separate violent raid on the Imad al-Din Zanki mosque in the nearby town of Bazariya in the occupied West Bank.
Attackers poured flammable liquids onto the ground floor of the building and ignited it.
Taysir Safarini, the former head of the Bazariya village council, recounted the frantic response.
“Neighbours woke up, of course, to the burning flames, and informed the civil defence crews in Anabta, and tried to extinguish the fire themselves to stop [it] from spreading,” Safarini told Al Jazeera.
The settlers also sprayed Hebrew graffiti on the walls, including threats to kill Arabs and a mocking message directed at the United States ambassador to Israel reading: “Huckabee, greetings from the terrorists.”
Mike Huckabee, a staunch ally of Israel who has voiced support for Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, recently called the settlers “terrorists“.
Following the attacks, the office of Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas warned that such violations risk triggering a catastrophic religious war.
Religious targeting
The Palestinian Ministry of Religious Affairs condemned the continued pogroms, describing the targeting of mosques as a flagrant violation of international law.
The ministry documented that at least 13 mosques have been vandalised or burned by Israeli settlers and forces since the start of the year.
This targeting extends far beyond rural villages; in a detailed August report, the ministry recorded 26 incursions into the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound and 155 instances in which the call to prayer was banned at the Ibrahimi Mosque in Hebron.
The human toll of these pogroms is high.
According to the United Nations, at least 76 Palestinians, including 18 children, have been killed in the territory this year, and some 3,800 people have been displaced.
The UN recorded more than 1,450 settler attacks resulting in roughly 1,040 injuries, while the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission estimates the total number of attacks exceeds 6,000.
For Palestinian residents, the relentless violence has shattered any semblance of safety, forcing families to make choices about their basic movements.
“For example, I do not allow my son to go to the mosque or anywhere else out of fear for him, and I keep him at home and tell him do not go out in these times due to the daily incursions,” Naim told Al Jazeera.

Nepal rescuers delayed by mud and water in tunnels – PM
Mud and water have almost completely blocked hydropower tunnels in Nepal’s flood-hit north, complicating efforts to reach the more than 600 workers feared trapped underground, Prime Minister Balendra Shah has told parliament.
Shah said the floodwaters had carried large amounts of mud and soil into the tunnels in the Bhote Koshi-Trishuli corridor last week, creating an unusual and difficult rescue environment. Nearly 4,000 people remain missing in the country as authorities continue search and rescue efforts eight days after the floods.
The death toll from the flood is now 1,114, the country’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said on Wednesday. Nearly 12,000 people have been rescued to date.
Across Nepal, families are starting to carry out symbolic funerals as hopes dim for the retrieval of the remains of their loved ones.
Nepalese authorities are also carrying out mass burials of unidentified flood victims as morgues run out of space. The bodies are being buried with identification markers, after collecting DNA samples, to facilitate their future identification.
The total morgue capacity in the Himalayan nation is only 350.
Rescue teams need the weather to improve and the mud to dry sufficiently before stable space can be created for personnel and equipment, Shah said.
He also said the tunnels offered limited space to deploy the heavy equipment needed to remove the mud and rocks.
The prime minister’s comments come as some families of those believed trapped in the tunnels question delays in the rescue effort.
At the 60-megawatt Upper Trishuli-3A project, 42 people are believed to be trapped inside an underground powerhouse, while more than 557 people remain missing from the Upper Trishuli-1 project.
The government only recently began involving technical teams from hydropower developers directly in rescue operations.
Upper Trishuli-1 Managing Director Giriraj Adhikari said the developer’s technical team should have been mobilized from the outset but joined the effort only on Monday, Kathmandu Post reported. At the Langtang Khola project, promoter Vijay Mohan Bhattarai said only one company representative had been allowed at the site until Monday.
Nepal has approached the board of the UN-backed Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, seeking financial assistance for the damages from the flood, reports said. Nepalese Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said the aid should be treated as “moral liability” and “not charity.”
“We are paying the ultimate price for a global crisis we did not create,” he was reported as saying.
”The major industrial emitters – such as China, which is the world’s top emitter, the United States at number two, and India at number three – have a historical responsibility to compensate vulnerable nations like Nepal.”

Russian “Syrian Express” Moves East Through Mediterranean With AIS Signals Turned Off
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:14:07 UTC
23:14:07 KST

A Russian naval group consisting of the Admiral Levchenko destroyer, the Sparta cargo ship, and the General Skobelev tanker is moving east through the Mediterranean with its AIS signals switched off.
OSINT observers from the Russian Forces Spotter reported this on September 1, publishing photographs of the Russian vessels.
Their AIS signals disappeared after the vessels passed through the Strait of Gibraltar on August 27.
According to the observers’ estimates, based on the group’s speed, the “Syrian Express” could reach Port Said, Egypt, or Tartus, Syria, around September 5-6.
Sparta’s official destination is listed as Port Said. At the same time, Russia has previously used the port as a formal destination for vessels that were actually bound for Tartus. Therefore, the current group may also be heading to Syria.
The “Syrian Express” is an informal name for Russia’s military maritime logistics route that supplied Russian forces in Syria for years. It transported military equipment, weapons, ammunition, fuel, and other supplies between Russian ports and Tartus.
Tartus was the key hub of this logistics network, where Russia maintained a naval facility. After the start of Russia’s military operation in Syria in 2015, Moscow modernized it. Another important facility was the Khmeimim air base near Latakia.
Maritime logistics along the “Syrian Express” supplied these facilities for years. Vessels operated by Oboronlogistika, including Sparta, regularly transported military cargo.
After the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime in December 2024, Russia began withdrawing some of its forces and equipment from Syria as the future of its military facilities became uncertain.
In January 2025, Russia started evacuating equipment from Tartus. Satellite imagery showed military equipment being loaded onto the Sparta and Sparta II transport vessels. Meanwhile, Syria’s new authorities terminated an agreement with a Russian company to manage the port of Tartus.
Despite reducing its military presence, Moscow continued negotiations with Damascus over the future of its facilities. Throughout 2025-2026, Russia gradually withdrew from secondary positions.
As of August 2026, a limited Russian contingent remains at Khmeimim and Tartus. It consists primarily of technical personnel, security forces, and a limited aviation group.
In August, Syria and Russia signed a memorandum of understanding to reorganize Russia’s military presence. Civilian facilities are to be transferred to Syrian control, while Russian military bases are planned to be converted into joint training and qualification centers. The transition process is to take up to three months.
Meanwhile, the current movement of Sparta, along with Admiral Levchenko and General Skobelev, may be related to the continuation of Russian maritime logistics in the region. However, the group’s exact destination and the nature of its cargo remain unconfirmed.
Turning off AIS signals after passing through Gibraltar makes it harder to determine the vessels’ actual route.

EU readies fresh cash for Ukraine’s air defence as Patriot stocks run low
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:11:32 UTC
23:11:32 KST

The EU is weighing a multibillion-euro Ukrainian request for PAC-3 Patriot interceptors as Russia steps up air attacks. Brussels hopes to approve the funding as early as next week, with talks also underway over a possible NATO contribution.
Brussels is assessing a new payment request from Kyiv worth several billion euros to bolster Ukraine’s air defences, as Russia intensifies its aerial attacks and Ukraine seeks more US-made Patriot interceptors.
“We have received a new payment request. It is worth several billion euros and would cover Ukraine’s air defences, including the highly advanced PAC-3 Patriot air defence systems,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said at a joint press conference with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.
EU countries now need to approve a derogation from the conditions of the Ukraine Support Loan, which limits non-European sourcing to 35% of the value of a defence product unless no European alternative is available.
The Commission president did not disclose the exact amount requested, as doing so could have put pressure on member states to approve the full sum sought by Kyiv, a Commission official who asked not to be named told Euronews.
Part of the payment could also come from NATO, although discussions were still ongoing, the official added. No other derogations were requested under this payment apart from the one covering the Patriots.
Russia has intensified its aerial attacks on Ukraine in recent weeks, at times launching as many as 30 ballistic missiles in a single night and further straining Kyiv’s already depleted stocks of interceptors.
Patriots are among the most advanced systems available for intercepting ballistic missiles. They take considerable time to manufacture, while stocks have been depleted by more than four years of war in Ukraine and by the US-Iran conflict earlier this year, which forced Gulf states to use large numbers of their own interceptors.
At an informal meeting of EU defence ministers in Ireland earlier this week, EU officials lobbied member states with significant remaining stockpiles to share them with Kyiv. So far, however, the pressure has failed to produce the hoped-for results.
“Member states are currently looking at Ukraine’s request, but I can say it’s going in the right direction,” von der Leyen said.
According to Ukrainian media reports, Kyiv has asked the European Commission to allow it to spend around €2 billion on Patriot interceptor missiles. The number of missiles that sum could purchase would depend primarily on the terms of the deal.
For Kyiv, however, the main challenge is not funding but availability.
In July, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine would need at least 140 Patriot interceptors to defend against a single Russian attack involving around 70 ballistic missiles.
Ukraine has already secured a derogation for US-made Patriots under the €90 billion loan, alongside another allowing the procurement of Chinese drone components, even as France ramps up pressure to phase out non-European suppliers.
National representatives are due to discuss the request on Monday, with a view to approving it as early as next week. The Commission would then need signed procurement contracts before it could disburse the payment.
Von der Leyen also pointed to Freya, a pan-European anti-ballistic missile defence project led by Ukraine’s Fire Point and involving several European companies, as a potential way to help close a critical gap in Europe’s air-defence capabilities.
“Since June, we have issued €8.5 billion for drones and missiles for Ukraine from this loan. And this money would also buy fighter jets from European industry,” she said.

Trump aides seek 'quiet' in Iran war but say attacks may intensify after November elections

2026-09-02

23:08:34 KST

Top aides to U.S. President Donald Trump are pushing to keep the Iran war from escalating before November's midterm elections to staunch Republican electoral losses, four people familiar with the discussions said, a strategy already under strain as the U.S. and Iran exchanged back-and-forth attacks overnight.
White House officials will consider ramping up military action after the November 3 vote, said the sources, who requested anonymity to describe internal thinking, though any return to full-scale conflict is far from a given. The U.S. military said its latest strikes were retaliation for recent attacks on American forces and marine traffic in the region.
For now, the sources said, the administration wants to rely on applying more economic pressure on Iran in an effort to extract concessions in any future negotiation that months of military action failed to secure.
"We are keeping the pressure on Iran," one White House official said. "But November is a priority."
Keeping the war mostly contained until then would help prevent the unpopular conflict from dominating the news as Trump's Republicans campaign to defend thin majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives, said the sources, three of whom are White House officials.
Only 31% of Americans approve of the war, while some 63% disapprove, according to a late August Reuters/Ipsos poll, and voters are particularly unhappy about high gas prices.
A tactical pause could also give the U.S. military some breathing room to replenish its heavily depleted munitions stockpiles, the sources said.
But pulling off the play-it-cool strategy looks more difficult by the day. While the conflict remains much less intense than it was during the spring or during a flare-up in the middle of the summer, both sides have exchanged tit-for-tat strikes in recent days.
Iran's leaders, emboldened after months of disrupting traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and facing little internal unrest, will likely keep striking at U.S. and allied Gulf targets, including military bases, vessels and energy infrastructure, at least periodically, analysts said.
The U.S. will face pressure to retaliate, potentially leading to an escalatory spiral that brings both sides back to a full-scale air war - whether the administration wants it or not.
Over the weekend, the U.S. struck rocket launchers on Iran's Larak Island, prompting Iran to fire missiles toward Jordan and the United Arab Emirates. The U.S. hit more Iranian targets around the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday in the biggest outbreak of fighting since July, a fresh outburst of violence that killed military personnel and civilians in Iran.
"The regime has every incentive to disrupt the 'calm' - which is no real calm, after all, since the administration's explicit aim is to increase economic pressure massively on Iran," said Barbara Leaf, who served as the top State Department official for the Middle Eastunder former President Joe Biden.
Another wild card is Trump himself.
The president's approval rating has fallen from 40% to 33% since the conflict began, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling. Sources said he is not currently interested in escalation, but he is famously prone to changing his mind and could change course in response to events.
Trump threatened on Tuesday to escalate the conflict if Iran hits back against the latest U.S. strikes.
"If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings," he wrote on his Truth Social platform.
Constrained by logistics and politics
Trump has publicly said the upcoming elections were not factoring into this Iran strategy.
But as the war enters its seventh month, his White House finds itself increasingly constrained by logistical and political realities.
"The timetable has changed," one senior White House official said. Another added that the "calendar is driving Iran."
Reuters reported in August that the military had used "virtually all" of its supply of certain precision missiles. The Washington Post reported on Sunday that the heads of the Army, Navy and Air Force warned Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth in a written assessment that prolonging the war was unsustainable and would diminish the military's readiness in other theaters.
The Pentagon has said the military had "everything it needs to execute" its mission.
“President Trump has destroyed Iran’s military capabilities and is crippling what’s left of its abysmal economy with the most powerful naval blockade in world history and crushing sanctions," White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales said. "The President will continue to advance America’s interests at home and abroad and will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon."
America's Gulf allies - some of whom had pushed for aggressive action against Iran earlier in the war to weaken their main regional adversary - roundly urged the White House to deescalate after a recent round of attacks in late July, regional diplomats said.
Currently, two White House officials said, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are among the high-ranking Trump aides who are on board with the idea of trying to keep the Iran conflict relatively "quiet" until November.
In recent weeks, administration officials have instead intensified an economic isolation campaign, during which the U.S. has threatened to slap countries that trade with Iran with massive sanctions, while maintaining its own blockade on the Strait of Hormuz.
The trade-focused strategy, however, has its own limits, analysts and officials said.
Iran has spent decades under layers of U.S. and international sanctions that have battered its economy but have not deterred its leadership.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that the pressure campaign may cause Iran to lash out militarily, raising the prospect that the economic campaign could itself stoke military escalation.
Additionally, some major world powers, like China, have not joined Washington's bid to isolate Iran, prompting questions about the campaign's effectiveness.
"The purpose of the new sanctions package is meant to add economic pressure on top of that being caused by the blockade to force Iran back to the table, after the administration determined it was a better option than returning to kinetic action," said Alex Plitsas, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council.
"Iran is concerned about it, but China has already indicated that it's not willing to play ball, which calls into question how effective it will be."
