Rial-based trade mechanism with neighbors being designed: TPO official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:01:03 UTC
21:01:03 KST

Rial-based trade mechanism with neighbors being designed: TPO official
TEHRAN- The Deputy for Commercial Services of Iran's Trade Promotion Organization (TPO), referring to the country's plans to expand trade with neighboring countries, said: To facilitate trade exchanges with countries such as Iraq and Afghanistan, proposals have been made to establish a rial-based trade mechanism, and this matter is being reviewed in cooperation with the banking system and exchange offices.
Mohammad Sadegh Ghannadzadeh stated on Wednesday in an exclusive interview with IRNA: A significant portion of Iran's exports go to countries like Iraq and Afghanistan, and in some cases, traders from these countries obtain rials to purchase goods from Iran. Therefore, we have proposed that a clear procedure be established for this type of exchange with neighboring countries.
He added: Although exports must ultimately generate foreign currency, to resolve existing problems and facilitate trade with neighboring countries, we are designing mechanisms with the help of the banking system and exchange offices, and the necessary proposals have also been submitted to the Central Bank. Currently, the final procedure has not yet been implemented at the Central Bank, and the matter is under review.
Ghannadzadeh noted the government's plan to develop trade with neighboring and aligned countries and explained: For different countries, tailored to the conditions and capacities of each, programs have been designed in the areas of trade, transportation, financial and banking systems, payment methods, and alternative trade methods.
He continued: These programs are being pursued on a country-by-country basis through working groups, joint committees, joint commissions, and exchanges of trade delegations, in order to resolve issues and obstacles in the path of developing trade relations.
The Deputy for Commercial Services of Iran's Trade Development Organization, referring to negotiations with Pakistan, said: Recently, we have followed this process with Pakistan, and subsequently, necessary negotiations and actions will also be carried out for Iraq, Turkey, Afghanistan, and other target countries.
Assessing the state of Iran's foreign trade after the recent war, Ghannadzadeh stated: It was natural that after the war, the country's trade would face a decline, and this reduction was largely unavoidable due to increased risk in the international arena, especially in the field of transportation and maritime logistics.
He added: A significant portion of the country's trade is conducted via sea routes, and given the tensions that arose and the reduced movement of the transport fleet, part of the country's trade was affected.
Ghannadzadeh continued: To manage these conditions, especially in the area of imports, the government prioritized essential goods, staple commodities, and raw materials needed for production, so that the trade decline would mostly affect commodity groups that do not cause serious damage to the economy.
He emphasized: Although the total volume and value of imports and exports faced a decline, we tried to ensure that the reduction in trade for essential goods and production raw materials was smaller, so that the country would not face serious strain in meeting basic needs and maintaining the operation of production units.
Beyond the immediate mechanisms for settling trade payments, Iran is pursuing a broader strategic realignment of its commercial relations with neighboring states. The government recognizes that traditional trade routes and banking channels, long dominated by dollar-based transactions, are no longer sufficient—or reliable—given the shifting geopolitical landscape. In response, Tehran is designing country-specific trade packages that go far beyond simple currency arrangements. These comprehensive plans address transportation corridors, customs facilitation, joint production partnerships, and barter-style exchanges where appropriate.
For Pakistan, recent negotiations have focused on reopening land border crossings and streamlining customs procedures to reduce transit times. With Iraq, the emphasis is on formalizing the rial-based payment system that already operates informally through exchange houses. Turkey remains a priority for expanding overland trucking routes and industrial cooperation, while Afghanistan presents opportunities for food and construction material exports through simplified trade protocols.
Crucially, the government is also exploring alternative trade mechanisms such as countertrade, commodity swaps, and direct investment exchanges with resource-rich neighbors. These approaches aim to reduce dependency on hard currency while deepening economic integration across the region. By treating each trading partner individually—through joint commissions, delegation exchanges, and sector-specific working groups—Iran hopes to build resilient commercial ties that can withstand external pressures and supply chain disruptions, ensuring that trade with neighbors becomes a stable pillar of the national economy.

Brussels will not mediate between US and Canada, EU trade chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:00:56 UTC
21:00:56 KST

Maroš Šefčovič said the Commission is ready to explore a wide range of options to deepen cooperation with Ottawa as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney calls for a closer partnership with the EU.
In an exclusive interview, European Union Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič told Euronews that the EU is not in a position to mediate in the trade war between Canada and the United States following the collapse of their trade talks.
Ten days ago, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney walked away from the negotiations with the Trump administration, blaming them for pressuring Canada over the use of the French language.
In the following days, US President Donald Trump announced 50% US tariffs on Canadian cars and trucks, to which Ottawa retaliated with tariffs on more than 700 US imports, worth about $20 billion (€17.2 billion).
“I don't think that we are in a position to mediate,” Šefčovič said. “At the same time I know that they [Canada and the US] have such a close economic relationship that, despite the current tension, sooner or later there will be attempts to resolve it.”
The Commissioner added that “tariffs are taxes which are paid in the end by the economic operators or by the citizens”, a message he has reiterated several times over the last year during the EU's own trade dispute with Washington.
“We clearly support free and fair trade with the lower or no tariffs at all,” he told Euronews.
Ready to cooperate
Since the trade talks stopped, Carney has called for a closer relationship between Ottawa and Brussels and announced he will attend European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's State of the Union in Strasbourg in mid-September, one of the main events in Brussels' political calendar.
An EU-Canada summit is also scheduled for later this autumn.
Šefčovič said the Commission is ready to explore “all possibilities” to increase cooperation with Canada, but he added that any new arrangements “would very much also depend on how comfortable the Canadian side would feel and what is its level of ambition”.
He pointed out that after Brussels clinched a trade deal with Ottawa in 2016, trade between the EU and Canada grew by 75% – but he also suggested that the deal could be pushed further.
“On both sides, we have certain elements which we can improve, still certain barriers, certain sensitivities for the products. I really think that we can explore much more that.”
Šefčovič said that a digital agreement might be signed with Canada before the end of the year, and he also cited coming cooperation in critical raw materials with potential joint investments.
Ottawa is seen by Brussels as a like-minded partner sharing its vision of the new global trade order, and Šefčovič hopes to have its backing to get closer to members of the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), which has liberalised trade between 12 countries in the Asia-Pacific region and the Americas, including Canada – but not the US. The UK became the pact's first and to date only European member in 2024, with Canada ratifying its full accession as of 1 September.
“Canadians are very important partners for forging a new level of cooperation with the CTPPP," Šefčovič said, "which represents together 40 percent of global trade.”

Brain scans shed light on how practice and genetics combine to influence reading ability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:00:50 UTC
21:00:50 KST

Reading is a complex skill that relies on a combination of innate genetic traits and physical brain changes driven by practice. Recent research provides evidence that our foundational ability to process sounds and meaning is strongly inherited, while the brain connections that stitch these skills together are sculpted by reading experience. These insights, published in Cerebral Cortex, suggest that differences in reading ability across the general population exist on a continuous spectrum of brain anatomy.
Learning to read involves teaching the brain to link written symbols to spoken language and concepts. This process generally relies on two complementary networks. The phonological route maps written letters to speech sounds, a task heavily dependent on the auditory cortex. The auditory cortex is a brain region located on the upper sides of the temporal lobes, just above the ears, and is responsible for processing sound.
The semantic route maps whole words directly to their meanings. This pathway leans on the anterior temporal lobes, which are structures located near the front tips of the temporal lobes that act as hubs for organizing semantic knowledge and recognizing objects.
Connecting these gray matter areas are white matter tracts, which serve as the brain’s information highways. The arcuate fasciculus is a bundle of nerve fibers that connects sound-processing areas to speech-production areas. The inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus bridges visual regions at the back of the brain to language and meaning hubs in the front.
Past studies have often looked at structural differences in these regions to understand conditions like dyslexia. For instance, a 2026 review highlighted that about half of the variation in language and reading outcomes in children is driven by genetics, but that environmental exposure heavily influences how those skills develop. However, researchers have primarily focused on broad anatomical measures or distinct clinical diagnoses. By looking closer at the micro-level structure of specific functional zones within the auditory cortex and anterior temporal lobes, scientists can better understand how neurodevelopmental variation shapes reading ability in the wider population.
“It fascinates me how the brain’s microstructure reflects individual skills and how it builds complex networks of information,” said study author Mikael Roll, a professor at the Centre for Languages and Literature at Lund University. “I wanted to understand which aspects of this structural ‘hardware’ are partly inherited and which may be more strongly shaped by experience.”
Roll told PsyPost that reading is an especially useful model for this question. “Reading is particularly intriguing because it is a relatively recent cultural invention that requires the brain to bring together sounds, visual forms, and meaning,” he explained.
To investigate this, the research analyzed brain imaging and behavioral data from 1,068 young adults who participated in the Human Connectome Project. The participants, aged 22 to 37, were typical readers without severe clinical impairments. To separate genetic influences from environmental ones, the sample included a subgroup of 396 twins. The researchers used high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging to measure cortical surface area, cortical thickness, and a specific image ratio called T1w/T2w, which serves as an indicator of myelin content.
Myelin is the protective sheath around nerve fibers that helps signals travel faster. Participants completed a standardized oral reading recognition test that evaluated their ability to pronounce letters and words. The research team then looked for statistical relationships between reading scores and the structural features of specific subregions in the auditory cortex and anterior temporal lobes.
The findings point to a dual-route system where genetics and experience play distinct roles. In the phonological route, the researchers found that a higher myelin proxy in the left medial belt of the auditory cortex was associated with lower reading scores.
While this physical brain trait was predominantly shaped by environmental factors rather than being highly heritable, its specific relationship with reading ability showed a stable genetic correlation. The medial belt processes basic sound rhythms and syllable boundaries, which is an early step in learning to decode words. In contrast, cortical thickness in the auditory core, the area responsible for processing fine-grained sound details like individual consonants and vowels, was positively associated with reading ability. This increased thickness did not show a genetic link, which suggests it builds up through the experience of reading.
A similar division appeared in the semantic route. A larger cortical surface area in two specific meaning-processing hubs, the left anterior middle temporal gyrus and the right dorsal temporal pole, was positively associated with better reading skills. Twin comparisons indicated that this expanded surface area was strongly heritable. Follow-up tests showed that these exact brain areas predicted how well participants performed on a vocabulary comprehension task, linking the heritable brain trait specifically to semantic processing.
“The genetic relationships between reading skill and regions in the anterior temporal lobes surprised me,” Roll noted. “These areas are involved in accessing word meaning and identifying faces and familiar visual forms. It is possible that partly inherited differences in these systems give some people an advantage when they begin learning to identify written words and connect them with meaning.”
The team also analyzed the brain’s white matter tracts in a subset of 1,036 participants. They found that the structural integrity of the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus and the arcuate fasciculus predicted reading ability independently of genetic influences. This indicates that as people practice reading, the communication pathways that integrate sound and meaning become optimized through experience.
Ultimately, these physical and genetic variations translate into distinct learning styles. “Our different starting points and experiences shape the brain’s routes to reading, producing a unique reading experience for each of us,” Roll said. “Some people may rely more strongly on an inner voice, while others may connect written word forms more directly to meaning.”
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2025, which observed that better reading ability across the general population was associated with a thicker left auditory cortex and a larger left anterior temporal lobe. The current study also aligns broadly with another study covered by PsyPost in 2025 that linked genetic factors to altered white matter and brain volume in language areas. That earlier study, however, specifically examined genetic risk scores for dyslexia rather than directly measuring heritability and continuous reading ability.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The image ratio used to estimate myelin is an indirect measure. While it generally correlates with myelin content, it can also reflect other cellular variations like the density of brain cells or the orientation of nerve fibers.
“Some of the brain features associated with reading ability in this study have previously been linked to dyslexia,” Roll pointed out. “Importantly, I found continuous relationships with reading ability across the population in a group without known dyslexia. This does not diminish the difficulties experienced by people with dyslexia, but suggests that there may also be a broader gray zone of less striking reading difficulties that deserves attention.”
He also cautioned that the structural correlations, while systematic, are not massive. “The effects are modest, which is what we would expect for a complex ability like reading that depends on many biological and environmental factors,” Roll explained. “But they were detected in a large sample of more than a thousand people and reveal systematic differences across the population.”
It is also important to note that the study looked at a single snapshot in time using young adults. Because the researchers compared twins to estimate heritability, they can confidently say certain traits have a genetic basis. However, estimating how much a brain structure changes purely due to reading experience over a lifetime would require tracking the same individuals from childhood through adulthood.
Future studies might look at how these specific structural differences respond to reading interventions in children. Because the study provides evidence that reading relies on both sound-based and meaning-based brain hubs, educators might find that mixing phonological training with vocabulary building helps support the diverse natural brain profiles found in any classroom. “One practical message is that we should recognize that children come to reading with different starting points and may need different kinds of support,” Roll added.
“I would like to extend this approach beyond reading and map more specific language abilities onto genetic and fine-grained measures of brain structure,” Roll said regarding his future research. “I am particularly interested in the structural basis of auditory abilities involved in analyzing speech sounds and speech melody. Ultimately, I would like to understand how inherited differences and experience interact to build the brain networks that support language.”
The study, “Heritable and experience-dependent cortical traits of reading ability,” was authored by Mikael Roll.

Adversarial Collaboration in Philosophy (guest post)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:00:32 UTC
21:00:32 KST

Adversarial Collaboration in Philosophy (guest post)
“Philosophical work would be better with adversaries collaborating to keep each other honest.”
Why is that? What would it look like?
In the following guest post, members of the Mind and Morality Lab at Boston University—Victor Kumar (Boston University), Derek Anderson (Boston University), Emilia Lacy (Boston University), Josh May (University of Alabama, Birmingham), Rachel McKinney (Suffolk University), Tino Themelis (Boston University), and Velana Valdez (Boston University)—explain adversarial collaboration and offer answers to those questions.
Adversarial Collaboration in Philosophy
by Victor Kumar, Derek Anderson, Emilia Lacy, Josh May, Rachel McKinney, Tino Themelis, and Velana Valdez
Scientists, being only human, often collect and analyze data in ways that unintentionally skew the results in their favor. Thankfully, this occupational disease has a known cure.
In adversarial collaboration, researchers with conflicting hypotheses lay down their arms, joining forces to work out a study design and statistical criteria—not eliminating confirmation biases, just neutralizing them in the aggregate. Then they run the study and accept the results, come what may.
As philosophers, we applaud this development. It’s about time, really. We’ve been practicing adversarial collaboration ourselves since circa 387 BC, haven’t we?
Not exactly. Adversarial collaboration isn’t just the Socratic method. It’s a commitment to abide by prespecified evidence. And how could we agree in advance about what would settle philosophical disputes? We don’t run experiments, nor do we have any data to crunch. (Mostly.) You can’t precommit to a thought experiment: by the time you pose one, the results are already in.
The idea seems like a non-starter, but in fact, adversarial collaboration can be adapted for philosophy. The first step is to isolate its true functions in science.
The Method
The late Nobel laureate Daniel Kahneman argued that scientific disagreement was too combative. Scientists rarely change their minds. So in the late 1990s, he thought: if you can’t beat ’em, join ’em. (And he did. Many times.)
Kahneman’s final adversarial collaboration was on income and happiness. Previously, he’d found that happiness rises with income but only until about $75,000. Another researcher, Matthew Killingsworth, found no plateau at all. Instead of trading criticisms, they decided to analyze the data together. What they found is that the plateau is real but only for the least happy fifth of people: unless you’re miserable and already somewhat wealthy, more money does mean more happiness.
Adversarial collaboration of this kind makes sense if, as Hugo Mercier and Dan Sperber argue, a primary function of reasoning is to justify yourself to others. We’re biased when we produce arguments but much sharper when we evaluate someone else’s. So if you’re not in close dialogue with people who disagree, you risk fooling yourself about how much the evidence supports your position.
Decades after Kahneman pioneered adversarial collaboration, the practice was renewed by Cory Clark and Philip Tetlock, who saw it as a solution to science’s methodological woes.
The replication crisis in science has been driven by so-called Questionable Research Practices like “p-hacking.” Classically: run a study, peek at the results periodically, and end data collection once you hit statistical significance. Other QRPs include generating post-hoc hypotheses to suit the data; choosing statistical criteria that best support your hypothesis; selectively reporting only significant results; and removing outliers.
Open Science can address some QRPs. For example: preregistering a hypothesis before running a study that tests it. But adversarial collaboration is another effective solution. A research team won’t be motivated to skew the results in one direction if each side has opposing priors. What’s more, Clark and Tetlock’s team argued, adversarial collaboration can also address other methodological problems that Open Science leaves untouched, such as when scientists “operationalize theoretical constructs in ways that load the dice.”
Clark and Tetlock didn’t just argue for adversarial collaboration. They institutionalized it. The Adversarial Collaboration Project at Penn funded studies, fostered multilab collaborations, created dedicated special issues in journals, and carried out a meta-study on the outcomes of completed projects. And unlike Kahneman, Clark and Tetlock saw how adversarial collaboration could improve scientific inquiry that bears on politically contentious issues.
Political Research
What are the effects of affirmative action? The risks of gender-affirming care? The benefits of neurodiversity? It’s natural and perhaps even vital for moral and political commitments to guide research on these topics. In their absence, important topics would be neglected or misunderstood.
Problems arise when these commitments lead to dogmatism. Politically motivated scientists are susceptible to confirmation bias—reinforced by like-minded intellectual communities—and more likely to fall into QRPs. Yet as standpoint theorists themselves often suggest, intersubjective coordination across standpoints can increase objectivity. This is what adversarial collaboration brings to the table.
Through such collaboration, research on politically contentious questions can provide answers that are not only more objective but also more trustworthy. Policymakers, journalists, and the general public often don’t trust political research because the scientists behind it are (or appear to be) biased, especially as science has grown more politicized. Neutralizing those biases can restore trust in science.
Gender biases in academia are a case in point. When do feminist researchers have special insights into the ways that female academics are professionally disadvantaged? And when do they see illusory patterns that confirm their preconceptions? A group of researchers with conflicting hypotheses and diverging political orientations decided to find out by running an adversarial meta-analysis.
Gender bias is difficult to study because of confounding variables. For example, male and female job candidates differ in many ways beyond their gender. One study finds that women in philosophy are 10-17 percentage points more likely than men to land a permanent job, but that might be just because they have to be more talented and determined to push through all the sexism in the field. To really test the idea, you have to match candidates on overall quality.
That’s exactly what the adversaries did. They found no biases in grant funding, journal acceptances, and recommendation letters. Women do get worse student evaluations and are paid less. But even when matched on quality, female candidates are more likely to be hired.
Women in academia experience other disadvantages, such as sexual harassment, hostile climates, and obstacles related to pregnancy and childcare. Yet adversarial collaboration enabled the researchers to uncover the biases their method could detect—and recognize what it couldn’t.
If only this method could be exported.
Why Export It to Philosophy?
If Kahneman thought scientists are too combative, imagine what he must have thought about philosophers. We’re regularly in “soldier mindset” rather than “scout mindset,” defending our positions rather than mapping the terrain. We often act like “lawyers for a view,” especially for political topics. Empirical research (by one of us and others) also suggests that philosophical views are often shaped by personality and other psychological traits. All of this helps explain why philosophical dialogue rarely changes minds.
And like science, philosophy has its own QRPs. Philosophers cherry-pick thought experiments that support their theories, leaving out the variants that don’t; bite the bullet selectively; and treat opponents uncharitably, ignoring the strongest version of their arguments. So the conditions that call for adversarial collaboration in science also exist in philosophy. Philosophical work would be better with adversaries collaborating to keep each other honest.
There’s another reason to export adversarial collaboration to philosophy. When philosophers write about politically contentious topics—gender identity, policing, AI—it’s reasonable for the public to discount their conclusions as motivated. Philosophical work that comes from both sides would be not only higher quality but more trustworthy.
Some philosophers have answered the call—but so far mostly just in subfields that involve collecting or closely analyzing empirical data. Opponents have joined forces in experimental philosophy and some areas of philosophy of mind. Christoff Koch and David Chalmers engaged in “adversarial forecasting” about the science of consciousness. Why not in more abstract areas of philosophy? Why not in ethics or political philosophy?
It’s hard to see how this could work in practice. Generally, philosophers analyze concepts, run thought experiments, explore logical implications, and synthesize evidence. We don’t know what evidence we’re seeking until we already have it, so we can’t decide how to approach the evidence in advance. Moreover, it’s routine for unanticipated evidence to arise in the course of inquiry.
The challenge runs deeper. Tetlock and Mitchell argue that adversarial collaboration is hardest under certain conditions: unclear falsification criteria, methodological disagreement, and background intellectual or political tribalism. All of these conditions hold in philosophy.
And yet, adversarial collaboration is viable in philosophy, once you see how it actually works in science.
From Science to Philosophy
In theory, adversarial collaboration can resolve scientific disagreement. In practice, though, it’s rare for one side to be vindicated; more often, the research uncovers middle ground (as in Kahneman’s final adversarial collaboration on income and happiness). In part, that’s because research can settle the results without settling the correct interpretation of those results.
So what’s the purpose of adversarial collaboration in science? To answer that question, best to go straight to the sources.
Here’s Kahneman and collaborators:
The authors did not agree when they began the collaboration, nor do they agree now. But [such] agreement is not necessary for a successful adversarial collaboration. Success should be gauged by the extent to which joint efforts yield surprising results, insightful discussions, and testable hypotheses about outstanding issues.
And here’s Isch, Tetlock, and Clark:
Rather than producing a clear “winner,” the most common outcome was a deeper understanding of the problem space through the integration of opposing perspectives.
This is precisely what good philosophy does. Decisive resolutions are rare in philosophy, but they’re rare in scientific collaborations too. Rather, adversarial dialogue can clarify disagreement, refine arguments, identify presuppositions, disambiguate terms, and map logical space. Sounds familiar.
But wait. Philosophers already engage in adversarial dialogue: back-and-forth in journals, Q&As during colloquia, author-meets-critics sessions at conferences, journal refereeing, feedback on draft papers, and informal discussion at the bar. What would distinguish adversarial collaboration from existing practices in philosophy? Now that we have a clearer picture of the practice in science as adversarial dialogue, haven’t we been doing it since circa 387 BC, after all?
How to Do It in Philosophy
Not exactly. Adversarial collaboration in philosophy isn’t just business as usual. It’s a structured method through which philosophers with genuine disagreements commit to investigating a topic together—cooperating rather than competing.
The collaborators agree to be intellectually open rather than attached to one side; calm rather than combative (avoiding “fighting words”); transparent about their assumptions; willing to revise; oriented toward truth-seeking rather than victory. These are possible in ordinary philosophical practice, of course. But it’s not enough to personally commit to these values. They have to be built in, structurally. How?
Through a philosophy lab (aka a research group).
The collaborators are then invested members of the same intellectual tribe rather than opposing tribes. They have buy-in: as members of the same lab, they’re practiced at constructive inquiry that aims to refine one another’s ideas rather than shoot them down. They’re open to being convinced and seeking compromise. As topics shift from essay to essay, collaborators’ allegiances shift naturally, and they can avoid factionalism.
This is a far cry from Reviewer 2. It would also avoid the pitfalls of Scott Alexander’s adversarial collaboration contest, where most groups bailed: lacking a prior relationship, they couldn’t successfully cooperate. Members of the same lab give more credence to conflicting opinions and countervailing arguments.
Philosophers can’t precommit to study design and statistical methods, but they can and should precommit to certain values, norms, and rules. Our own collaborative practice suggests the following possibilities for orienting a lab’s approach:
Values: trust; respect; good faith; fallibility.
Norms: Disagree without being disagreeable; attempt to give no offense and take no offense either; be constructive rather than destructive (“yes-and” rather than “no-but”); seek objections that aim to strengthen a view rather than defeat it; avoid seeing views only in terms of your commitments or identity; aim for nuance rather than a decisive verdict; avoid treating answers to questions as objects of status or esteem competition.
Rules: Roughly equal representation on all sides; commit to authorship, wherever the argument leads; land on ideas that some lab members disagree with; no edits without track changes; assign final cut to a managing editor (who may change from project to project so that no one person monopolizes authorial control).
Such values, norms, and rules support collaboration, but the work has to be adversarial too. For example, a lab might attempt to capitalize on political diversity among its members. Academia is politically much more homogeneous than the general public, yet diversity does exist. In our lab, there is real disagreement between doomers and anti-doomers; between democratic socialists and free market liberals; between those more or less sympathetic to social justice politics of the last 10-15 years; between those who are pessimistic about AI and those who are optimistic (or, er, only mildly pessimistic).
That’s the idea, but what would a philosophy lab produce?
Two Types of Essays
One type of essay is written in a single voice. A lab meeting begins with an idea or just a topic. As a thesis forms through discussion, it attracts supporters and dissenters. If there are students in the lab, they must be encouraged to voice their disagreements rather than defer to faculty. Ideally, you want a roughly even split, though what’s necessary is just a critical mass on each side, with faculty spread between them. Then open-minded discussion between adversaries yields arguments, objections, and replies. They go off and do some research and come back to discuss. Rinse and repeat.
In the end, the essay has only one voice, though it may express nuance that reflects internal difference of opinion. And it’s shaped by not just those who endorse it but those who dissent too. It’s even possible for the essay to become an expression of the lab’s “collective mind,” such that no individual endorses it entirely. No one, then, would be fully accountable. (Is that troubling? Or freeing?) Perhaps it leads to spin-off essays from dissenters—as happened after our lab’s first single-voice essay. (We’ve been using this method to write public-facing essays, but it could also be used for journal articles.)
The main strength of the single-voice model is that the essay takes a familiar form, making it straightforwardly readable. The main weakness is that the essay must reflect some sort of consensus view.
A second type of essay is written in many voices, divided into multiple sections. Debate books have been doing something like this for decades, at least when authors provide feedback on one another’s draft chapters. Examples include Walter Sinnott-Armstrong vs. William Lane Craig on atheism and Gilbert Harman vs. Judith Thomson on moral objectivity and moral relativism. What about collaborating within a single essay?
It could have a thesis section endorsed by one side, an antithesis section endorsed by the other side, and then a synthesis endorsed by both—as in our first many-voices essay. Or it begins with the main argument from one side, a dissenting opinion, and then a reply. Or it’s a philosophical dialogue, a classic form and perhaps the best way to let readers decide.
Another version of an essay with many voices mimics a format in science. A lab member who serves as a neutral arbiter writes the introduction; each side gives its argument; then the arbiter writes a final, evaluative section. (Some of us think it would be interesting to enlist an LLM as arbiter; others are skeptical.)
The many-voices model has the advantage of clearly reflecting both sides, though the essays might tend to look more like a traditional debate rather than a collaboration with synthesis. Then again, perhaps the real value of adversarial collaboration is the process rather than a legible product: fewer essays of higher quality.
Ultimately, we don’t know which model to prefer, and probably neither is uniquely best. Our goal is to continue pursuing both and see what results.
Another goal is for the practice to spread. Adversarial collaboration could even be institutionalized, with philosophy journals hosting special issues, funders incentivizing it, and skeptical philosophers publishing criticisms. But before all that, other labs can try running their own experiments. If you find something, let us know.

Trump’s ridiculous bullying of Canada is backfiring | Robert Reich
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:00:24 UTC
21:00:24 KST

What do bullies do when someone stands up to their bullying and punches them in the face? They look for someone weaker to bully who won’t punch back.
Presumably that’s why Donald Trump has now taken on Canada, after Iran punched back so hard in the cage match the US president began more than six months ago as to leave him humiliated and baffled.
Trump wants to be the bully who humiliates others and forces them into submission. Needing to assert his dominance, Trump has now started a trade war with our northern neighbor, friend, second-largest trading partner (after Mexico) and, at least until now, reliable ally.
He’s hammering Canada on his Truth Social and in media appearances, saying Canada has “ripped off” the US for years, and signing an order to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America”.
This is pure bunk, of course – more empty Trump bravado and ignorant belligerence. Canada? Really? If Mel Brooks were still making movies, this would be a comedy. But as all else with Trump, it’s no laughing matter.
Trump apparently assumed that Canada would quickly surrender because it had more to lose. The tariffs Trump has imposed on Canada – along with those he’s threatening if Canada retaliates – affect a tiny portion of the US’s total imports but a huge portion of Canada’s total exports.
Jamieson Greer, Trump’s US trade representative, says the duties are too small to pose a problem for the US and are “more [Canada’s] emergency than ours”.
But bullies like Trump rarely think about the effects of their bullying on the thinking and attitudes of their targets.
Trump’s bullying of Iran has not only reinforced its hardline regime but shown them that control over the strait of Hormuz is an effective means of gaining concessions from other Gulf states as well as the US, and likely strengthened their resolve to build a nuclear weapon.
Trump’s bullying of Canada, meanwhile, is igniting a patriotism that has often eluded that nation, which separatist factions have long threatened to pull apart.
Mark Carney’s decision to stand up to Trump – through “dollar for dollar” retaliation on goods coming from key industries in states including Ohio and Texas with competitive Senate elections – has led to a surge of support for the prime minister’s Liberal party. Liberals won three special by-elections on Monday.
Trump’s trade war with Canada has also dimmed the prospects of Canada’s separatist movements, at least in the short term. A candidate from Carney’s Liberal party edged out a Quebec separatist in one of Monday’s special by-elections, in a district hit hard by US tariffs.
This is a good omen for Canada before 5 October’s vote in Quebec on whether the province’s secessionist party, Parti Québécois, gains additional seats in the province’s legislative body, and 19 October’s vote in Alberta on whether to hold a referendum to secede from the rest of Canada.
Trump may also have underestimated the negative reactions to his trade war at home. According to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll, 57% of Americans oppose Trump’s moves to impose tariffs on Canadian imports. About 63% oppose his peevish order to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America”. Only 20% support the higher tariffs on Canadian goods.
The negative response is especially pronounced in border states whose economies are tightly interconnected with Canada.
In Michigan, for example, where overwhelming majorities oppose Trump’s tariffs on Canada, Democrats have launched new attack ads on the Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers for refusing to denounce the tariffs. The Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed called Trump an “asshole” for launching the trade war.
There’s still time for the US and Canada to avoid the worst of the economic and political fallout from this. Carney’s “dollar for dollar” retaliation goes into effect on 8 September but Trump’s counter-counter measure – threatened 50% tariffs on autos and auto parts – won’t go into effect until New Year’s Day.
Still, no one should expect an easy resolution to what may go down in history as the stupidest of all the stupid foreign policies Trump has initiated. And given the extent of Trump’s dumb international moves, that is saying something.
- 
  Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

How to turn past-their-best bananas into a glorious ice-cream – recipe | Waste not
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:00:24 UTC
21:00:24 KST

With two young kids, we get through a lot of bananas in our household. Perhaps surprisingly, though, most of them are frozen: our daughters eat them straight from the freezer most evenings, with frozen berries and yoghurt, for pudding. We normally order a stack of bananas every Saturday, and before the end of the week they inevitably start to turn brown. At this point, we peel, slice and freeze them for the children’s evening yoghurt, though sometimes, when we have a real excess, I turn them into today’s incredibly satisfying “ice-cream”. Its silky-smooth texture really hits the spot, and satisfies any ice-cream cravings without recourse to added sugar or excessive fat. The trick is to freeze the bananas in a single layer on a flat tray, so they don’t freeze into a homogeneous mass, then transfer to a container to enjoy as and when.
Brown banana ‘ice-cream’
This has to be in my top five everyday desserts, not least because brown bananas are very gooey and sweet, have a rich and creamy texture and a satiating flavour. Portion for portion, it feels luxurious and indulgent, even without the extra sugar, saturated fat, gums and stabilisers found in much commercial ice-cream and other ready-made desserts. Of course, blended fruit is itself a readily absorbable sugar, but the trade-off is worth it for the extra fibre, potassium, manganese and other vitamins. It’s also a fraction of the price of shop-bought ice-cream.
This is best eaten fresh from the blender, but if you need to store a bumper batch, remember to take it out of the freezer at least 10 minutes before you want to scoop it.
1 or more brown bananas
Half the bananas’ weight in liquid – water, yoghurt, milk or a plant-based alternative
Toppings, all optional and to taste
Chopped nuts
  Coconut flakes
  Grated chocolate
Peel and chop the bananas into 2cm-thick slices (this makes them easier to blend later), then spread out on a tray and freeze for at least five hours. Once frozen, store in a sealed container in the freezer.
To make the ice-cream, weigh the amount of banana you’ve taken out, then add half its weight in liquid – that is, water, yoghurt, milk or a plant-based alternative. Transfer to a jug blender and blitz smooth, but not for too long or the fruit will melt too much; stir, if need be, to get an even blend. Serve immediately as it is, or leave to soften like a Mr Whippy-alike soft serve, or freeze for an hour or more for a firmer, scoopable texture, adding any optional toppings of your choice.

Freelancers are getting buried with ‘soulless’ AI slop cleanup: ‘It’s a shame we need to do it’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:00:23 UTC
21:00:23 KST

Lisa, a freelance graphic designer based in Spain, noticed a shift in her work after the release of ChatGPT in 2022. She went from receiving slow one-off jobs creating logos and packaging to an onslaught of requests asking her to fix versions that were generated by artificial intelligence – from sharpening fuzzy images for printing to turning flawed designs into usable files.
By 2025, Lisa, who asked not to be fully named to avoid solicitations, said 90% of her incoming logo and packaging design requests required cleaning up AI-generated content, work that accounted for 60% to 70% of her annual income. But the grind was exhausting. Clients lowballed her;' some AI-generated designs were so flawed that she had to recreate them from scratch and she worried about being complicit in AI-driven copyright infringement. By the end of the year, she began turning those jobs down.
“It was just so soulless,” said Lisa, who now focuses on “human-made designs”.
Lisa is part of a growing group of creative freelancers being hired to clean up AI slop, a term used to characterize low-quality, AI-generated output. As businesses use tools like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude to produce marketing copy, illustrations, books and videos, they are hiring creative professionals to humanize AI-generated copy, repair botched images and salvage flawed footage.
The work serves as a stopgap in an increasingly challenging job market, supplementing income for those who freelance full-time or on the side. But clients often underestimate the time and skill involved, expecting cleanup to be quick and cheap when it can require as much work as creating something original, freelancers said. And while the high volume of cleanup gigs can be lucrative, freelancers are divided over the trade-off. Some find it tedious and creatively unfulfilling, while others enjoy the challenge. As AI improves, freelancers question how long the demand will last and where they’ll turn once the jobs dry up.
For now, demand for AI cleanup work is growing.
On Freelancer.com, a contract work platform with more than 88 million users, job listings tagged with phrases such as “correct AI”, “AI hallucination” and “AI error” rose 87% to 10,760 globally between August 2025 and June 2026, according to internal data shared with the Guardian. The jobs were concentrated in graphic design, followed by video editing, proofreading and content writing. Upwork saw AI remediation gigs jump 70% year over year, and Fiverr saw keyword searches for “AI cleanup” services grow more than 20 times between 2023 and 2026, according to data shared with the Guardian.
The specter of AI could spell trouble for the creative freelance labor market. Listings for freelance jobs exposed to automation fell 21% in the eight months after ChatGPT launched and image-creation gigs dropped 17% after AI image generators arrived, according to a 2025 study published in the academic journal Management Science. And those losses have continued, according to a 2026 study.
Meanwhile, more workers are turning to freelance work as companies cut staff and hire less, intensifying competition. The average project on Freelancer.com drew 54 bids in 2025, up 8% from the year before, according to the site’s annual report.
But as companies cut costs, they’re changing the nature of freelance assignments, from requests for creative work to sprucing up AI output. Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com, said the cleanup work is often commissioned by small companies and entrepreneurs using AI to produce a first pass, only to run into problems they don’t have the expertise to solve.
“[AI output] needs a human to turn it into something polished that can actually be used,” he said. The time and money saved on the first draft can be eaten up by the “incredibly time-consuming” work of preparing it for commercial use.
The rise of the AI cleanup crews
For some freelancers, cleanup is taking up a growing share of their workload and traditional creative projects are becoming harder to find.
Todd Van Linda, a full-time freelance illustrator in Florida, began taking AI cleanup gigs in 2023 as his usual work drawing illustrations, video game art and architectural plans became less steady. The work typically involves filtering out visual noise, improving resolution, and hunting for glitches like an extra toe.
“Money”, Van Linda said of his motivation. “The jobs were there to be done.”
Though some clients expect AI cleanup to cost less than original work, Van Linda won’t lower his rates. When one prospective client offered about $500 to repair 13 to 15 AI-generated illustrations for a children’s book, with the expectation that each should take about 15 minutes, he turned it down. He said projects can take between a few hours of work to days depending on the scope. His rate is $65 an hour and “doesn’t go down from there”, he said.
For Kym Dunbar, a freelance writer and editor based in Australia, AI cleanup now accounts for about 60% of her workload, as writing work like blogs and website copy have dwindled. As a result, Dunbar said her monthly earnings from writing original content have fallen to roughly a third of what she made during the pandemic.
Dunbar stumbled into cleanup work in 2024, when a client asked her to revise an AI-generated article. She quickly learned to spot recurring problems, from repetitive language and awkward paragraph structures to a lack of emotional nuance. Since then, she has worked on about 40 AI-generated nonfiction books, longform articles and technical papers.
“There’s a lot less good projects available for writers and editors these days,” Dunbar said.
But “cleanup” can understate how much work is involved.
Nathan McConnell, a multimedia editor who freelances on top of his full-time job, started editing AI-generated videos in 2023. His work has ranged from removing reflections from AI real estate videos to fixing robotic voiceovers and malformed 3D models. The requests have increased from two or three projects in 2023 to eight to 10 so far this year, he said.
One client brought him roughly 100 AI-generated images of humanoid animals for a tarot deck riddled with extra fingers, two left feet and other mistakes. McConnell spent two to three hours repairing each image in Photoshop, expecting the project to take nearly two weeks to finish. But after making the first 10 cards, he called the project off because of health issues and constant changes requested from his “persnickety” client.
Not everything that lands in McConnell’s inbox can be saved, he said. That could look like videos where the physics feel off, like shadows falling the wrong way, or animations that repurpose another creator’s work without permission.
“I’ve told a client before that it’s ‘too’ slop,” McConnell said. “There’s no way I can fix this.”
While McConnell and Van Linda would rather make original work, not everyone finds fixing AI outputs dispiriting. Dunbar considers it “interesting” and “challenging”, and takes satisfaction in turning a weak draft into polished prose.
What troubles her is that people increasingly see AI not as a tool, but as the “be-all and end-all” of the creative process.
“I just feel it’s a shame we need to do it,” Dunbar said.
Slop cleanup jobs may not last
It’s unclear whether cleaning up AI-generated slop will remain a viable source of work.
Dunbar isn’t convinced it will. She believes much of the work humanizing AI could dry up within five to 10 years as models improve and allow businesses to generate usable content themselves.
McConnell sees it differently, arguing that AI still needs to be “babysat” to catch mistakes an untrained eye might miss, from logos that violate brand guidelines to objects that appear and disappear in videos. “We need people [to fix] problems that AI is creating,” he said.
But Van Linda is already creating a different path. After he stopped taking AI cleanup gigs late last year, he has seen more clients, some of whom have been dissatisfied with AI, seeking original, hand-drawn work.
“Quite frankly, this kind of thing has gotten extremely distasteful to me,” he said about AI cleanup work.
Though Lisa, the freelance graphic designer, updated her profile to say she no longer works with AI-generated images, she still gets requests to edit them. She occasionally takes cleanup gigs for clients who come to her after getting poor results with AI. But some clients “straight up lie” and pass off the images as original creations.
“They say ‘I don’t use AI,’ but there’s a “[Google] Gemini logo on the bottom,” she said.
But just in case AI makes her job obsolete, she has a plan. Lisa has begun returning to the canvases, watercolors and other physical art she practiced before she pursued a career in graphic design. She predicts that within “another year or two”, AI will be able to do logo and packaging design as well as she can, leaving only “the best of the best” able to make a living.
“I don’t know if I’m good enough to survive the digital stuff,” she said.

How Japan aims to convert ageing warships into leverage to counter China
Tokyo plans to send retired destroyers to Manila and Jakarta, but it may not demand alignment against China as part of deal
Such transfers, they said, fit into Tokyo’s broader security assistance toolkit to strengthen partners’ capabilities and forge longer-term defence relationships through equipment, training, maintenance and interoperability – expanding Japan’s regional influence without demanding alignment against Beijing.

Killing at Sea
Three families, two bombings and a hidden war: uncovering the lives behind Operation Southern Spear’s dead.

Russia secretly helps Iran develop engines for hypersonic cruise missiles, FT reports
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:00:00 EEST
21:00:00 KST

Russia secretly helps Iran develop engines for hypersonic cruise missiles, FT reports
Russia is secretly helping Iran develop a new class of hypersonic cruise missiles.
Source: the Financial Times in an investigation based on leaked Russian correspondence, experts' travel data and an analysis of military patents
Details: The FT says the years-long secret programme is codenamed C430L.
"The main purpose of C430L is to help Iran to develop a ramjet propulsion system, an engine that allows a cruise missile to sustain flight at several times the speed of sound," the FT says.
Missile and military experts said the technology is almost certainly intended for anti-ship cruise missiles and cruise missiles for strikes against ground targets. They estimate that such weapons could pose a threat to US aircraft carriers and other warships in the Middle East.
"Iran has built and flight-tested the ramjet propulsion system, although there is no evidence that a Russian-assisted supersonic cruise missile has yet been deployed," the FT says.
The programme was coordinated by Russian state arms exporter Rosoboronexport and NPO Mashinostroyenia. The C430L contract with Iran's Ministry of Defence and Armed Forces Logistics was signed in November 2023.
By 2025, NPO Mashinostroyenia had received a substantial amount of technical material from Iran on the ramjet engine. Russian engineers analysed data from Iranian flight tests, particularly the performance of the fuel system, combustion stability, air intake and engine nozzle, after which they sent questions and recommendations to the Iranian side.
In April 2025, Rosoboronexport proposed sending around two dozen Russian experts to Iran for technical consultations as part of C430L.
The FT established that senior experts from NPO Mashinostroyenia were involved in the programme, including designers who had worked on naval cruise missiles, ramjet engines and high-speed missile systems.
Nicole Grajewski, a professor at Sciences Po University in Paris, said the secret ramjet programme "shows Russia is trying to broaden the Ukraine war and draw the US into different theatres". "Russia doesn't care as much about the red lines in the region," the professor added.
According to the FT, the programme continued in 2026. In June, Rosoboronexport and the Iranian side were still discussing elements of the next stage of development and Russian technical reports. However, the outlet was unable to establish whether the next stage of the programme had begun.
The Kremlin, Rosoboronexport, NPO Mashinostroyenia and the Iranian government did not respond to the Financial Times' requests for comment on the programme.
Background: Earlier, the FT reported that Iran had signed a secret €495 million deal with Russia for the supply of 500 Verba man-portable air-defence systems and 2,500 missiles for them. The contract was also signed through Rosoboronexport.

Sudan: Air attack destroys food aid for families in South Kordofan
Two truckloads of food aid destined for hungry families in South Kordofan state, Sudan, were destroyed in an aerial attack over the weekend, the World Food Progamme (WFP) said on Wednesday.
The UN agency strongly condemned the attack which occurred on 30 August outside the city of Dilling.
The trucks carried 50 metric tonnes of WFP food including cereals, yellow split peas, vegetable oil and salt—enough to provide lifesaving assistance to 5,800 people for one month.
They were heading to Kadugli, where WFP is supporting nearly 58,000 people facing emergency levels of food insecurity or worse, and were clearly marked with its banners and flags.
End ‘unacceptable’ attacks
WFP said the attack was the latest example of the complex operating environment facing it and other humanitarian agencies in Sudan.
The UN has repeatedly called for an end to the war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and former allies the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) which erupted in April 2023.
As a result of the conflict, some 30 million people required humanitarian assistance last year.
Since January, WFP has recorded eight aerial attacks that have damaged its premises and disrupted operations.
“Attacks on aid workers and humanitarian operations are unacceptable and must stop,” WFP said, urging all sides to uphold international humanitarian law by protecting civilians, aid workers and humanitarian assets.

From scientific research to running their own business in Europe. Two stories of Ukrainian entrepreneurs
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:57:24 EEST
20:57:24 KST

From scientific research to running their own business in Europe. Two stories of Ukrainian entrepreneurs
Kyiv • UNN
From scientific research to running their own business in Europe. Two stories of Ukrainian entrepreneurs.
An academic career can become the foundation for one's own business—especially in finance, where one has to work not only with business models but also with licensing, financial monitoring, data protection, and other regulatory requirements.
Among the Ukrainians creating financial and technology companies in Europe are entrepreneurs with academic backgrounds. Vladyslav Zaporozhchenko and Tetiana Dashevska came to business by different paths: he began with banking research, while she spent years working in banking and fintech.
Vladyslav Zaporozhchenko: from banking research to the payments business
At first, banking was a research subject for Zaporozhchenko. As a student, he studied banking supervision and the payment card market, completed an internship at the NBU's administration, and prepared more than 30 materials on fintech. After his studies, he worked at banks—in lending, payments, and corporate products. His research subject became his daily work: he saw how financial products depend on operations and regulatory requirements.
Later, he says, it became interesting not only to analyze changes but also to create products himself and take responsibility for their operation. His own projects required skills from academic work: working with primary sources, testing assumptions, assessing risks, and documenting decisions.
The next step was the European market: procedures there are more predictable, but they require financial-monitoring, KYC, and compliance policies, risk assessment, and flow planning. In 2018–2021, Zaporozhchenko became the founder of the Czech company AMERO PAY; from 2021, he has been the director of the British QIUNTEXBANK TECHNOLOGY LTD; and in 2022, the Polish company Qiuntex Pay was entered in the KNF register of small payment institutions.
Working in different countries showed how much regulatory approaches can differ: he dealt with the requirements of the Czech National Bank, the UK's FCA, Canada's FinTRAC, Switzerland's VQF, and other regulatory and professional organizations.
In 2022, together with Yulia Raubishke, he founded the British consulting company INTERNATIONAL FINTECH BUSINESS LTD, which provides financial licensing and regulatory support. The company was registered on October 20 of the same year. This was where his previous experience in banking, fintech, and working with regulators found practical application.
Tetiana Dashevska: from a banking career to her own platform
Dashevska's path was different. She entered entrepreneurship after more than twenty years in banking and fintech. With a PhD in economics and an MBA, she spent a significant part of her career launching digital banking products—in other words, she saw from the inside how every new service begins.
Over the years, Dashevska says, she repeatedly ran into the same problem. Every new neobank or payment service had to build a substantial part of its technological infrastructure independently: customer identification, transaction processing, and reporting took months, sometimes years, as well as significant resources. What surprised her most, she says, was the repetition itself—companies were writing things that dozens of companies before them had already written.
Eventually, she decided that this work did not need to be repeated every time—and that is how the idea of a platform made up of ready-made modules emerged, adaptable to the needs of different companies. In 2023, Dashevska and Yevhen Pavlenko founded SoftBees. The company operates in Ukraine and Poland and develops such a platform for launching and developing digital financial services. The model is the same as Zaporozhchenko's: the team remains at home, while the legal entity operates within the European legal framework.
The European market added requirements concerning information security, risk management, personal data protection, and financial monitoring to the technological tasks. In Dashevska's experience, the academic method here means formulating assumptions, checking risks, and documenting decisions. In 2025, SoftBees completed certification of its information security management system under ISO 27001.
What these stories have in common
The stories of Zaporozhchenko and Dashevska do not indicate that an academic degree is a necessary condition for business success. They show how academic and professional experience can find application in entrepreneurship.
In fintech, decisions have to be made while taking technology, finance, and regulatory requirements into account simultaneously. That is why experience working with data, research, and complex documentation becomes a practical tool. For Zaporozhchenko, the journey began with research into the banking system; for Dashevska, it began with many years of work in banks. At first, knowledge helps one understand the problem, and later experience suggests how to turn that understanding into a product or company.

Iran accuses US of ‘war crime’ after missile blast kills four people at wedding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:56:00 UTC
20:56:00 KST

Iran has accused the US of a war crime after a missile blast killed at least four people and injured 68 who were attending a wedding at a private home in a coastal city of southern Iran, as the fresh exchange of strikes prompted fears of a wider renewal of hostilities.
Iranian media said that the wedding ceremony was being held in a home in the city of Kuhestak, Hormozgan province, late on Tuesday when a US missile struck, with shrapnel and debris from the strike killing and injuring people.
Among the dead was a four-year-old child, Amir-Ali Karimi, and a 16-year-old, Mohammad Mollahi.
“It’s a terrible thing. I’m extremely worried and upset about what happened – really upset,” Ali Mollahi, the father of the bride, told Mehr News.
A video of the aftermath shows colourful wedding streamers and decorations strewn across the ground, and shoes abandoned in the rush to escape the attack.
“You wicked people have attacked people’s homes and turned their wedding ceremony into a funeral,” said a man filming the aftermath of the strike, shared by Fars news agency.
The deputy of the provincial government, Ahmad Nafisi, said first responders had headed immediately to the scene and transferred the wounded to the hospitals.
Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson called the US attack a “war crime” and said Iran “will respond to these savage crimes with firmness”.
The chief Iranian negotiator, Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf, said the attack had killed families with children, and called the US the “great Satan”.
“If a power acts like Satan, picks targets like Satan and kills like Satan, it’s Satan. Shields a junior Satan that does the same? It’s THE Great Satan,” Ghalibaf said in a post on X.
The US attacks followed strikes on Sunday, ending a month-long uneasy truce between the US and Iran, and appeared to signal a resumption of another cycle of escalation. US Central Command (Centcom) said the overnight strikes focused on Iranian military targets, including air defence sites, radars and maritime assets.
Iran responded by launching drones and missiles on US bases across the Middle East, including in Bahrain, Kuwait and the UAE. Iran’s military spokesperson, Lt Col Ebrahim Zolfaghari, vowed “heavier, broader, and more crushing and devastating” retaliation.
Videos of the aftermath of the strike show a caved-in roof, blown-out windows and ground riddled with debris, as well as walls pockmarked with what appeared to be holes from shrapnel. Footage from a nearby hospital showed women in wedding attire watching as injured children were being treated.
“When we arrived there, an explosion occurred. It was very intense. Bricks, stones and cement hit me in the face and head, and many others were injured,” a child who was injured at the wedding told the state-affiliated Fars news agency.
A woman with her hands decorated in henna for the nuptials posted a video on Instagram after the attack, saying “my hands and feet are still shaking”.
A spokesperson for Centcom, Tim Hawkins, said the US was aware of reports of civilian casualties, but the “US military never targets civilians, unlike the [Iranian Revolutionary Guards Corps]”.
In February, a strike on an elementary school killed at least 156 people, including more than 120 schoolchildren. Independent investigations concluded that the US likely carried out the strike with the assistance of AI, though the US government said the incident remained under investigation.
Pictures of shrapnel collected at the site of Tuesday’s attack were published on Iranian state media, and appeared to show the internal components of US munitions. Trevor Ball, an independent weapons analyst, identified some of the remnants as belonging to the Standoff Land Attack Missile-Expanded Response (Slam-Er) missile, which is made by the US weapons company Boeing. The Slam-Er is a 1,500-pound, GPS-guided missile touted by Boeing to be “extremely accurate”.
It was unclear if the home where the wedding was being held was struck directly, or if a missile hit close to the home and debris from the strike hit the home and its occupants. CCTV footage captured at least six strikes in the area within a minute. A separate strike appeared to hit a communications tower about 150 metres away from the home.
Authorities said that several “telecommunications and internet towers and sites were also seriously damaged in the latest strikes”.
The US has been targeting communications and radar infrastructure along Iran’s coast to try to stop its blockade on the strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint which prior to the US-Iran war was a transit point for at least 20% of the world’s oil supply.
Iran has virtually closed the strait since the start of the Iran war, frustrating the US president, Donald Trump, who is facing a midterm election with expensive gas prices and knock-on inflation across the board.
In recent weeks, the US has focused on trying to degrade Iran’s capacity to strike ships transiting the strait to reopen the waterway for traffic.

From infrastructure to military drills, China deepens footprint in Egypt as Xi visits Cairo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:53:49 UTC
20:53:49 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping’s return to Cairo comes as Egypt and China push their relationship beyond infrastructure and trade into technology, defence and a broader strategic partnership with regional implications.
Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Egypt on Tuesday for his first visit since 2016, as the two countries mark 70 years of diplomatic ties and push their relationship into new areas in what Beijing has described as a "comprehensive strategic partnership".
Since his last visit, some of Beijing's megaprojects have become part of Egypt’s landscape.
Chinese companies have helped build the central business district of Egypt’s New Administrative Capital. Built by China State Construction Engineering Corporation, it consists of 20 skyscrapers.
At its centre stands the 385.8-metre Iconic Tower, Africa's tallest building.
A light rail system built with Chinese involvement connects Cairo’s eastern outskirts with new urban centres, and a China-Egypt industrial zone near the Suez Canal now hosts more than 200 companies.
The industrial zone created more than 10,000 direct jobs, according to Chinese figures. Chinese reporting puts total investment at more than $4.7 billion (€4.05bn).
The scope is now widening.
AI, advanced manufacturing and technology transfer are increasingly part of the economic agenda, while Chinese and Egyptian fighter aircraft have been training together in the second joint air force exercise between the two countries.
Trade grows, but so does the imbalance
Bilateral trade reached $11.3 billion (€9.75bn) in the first six months of 2026, up 21.5% year on year, according to Egypt's Central Agency for Public Mobilisation and Statistics.
Egyptian exports to China almost tripled to $840.8 million (€725.4m), driven by fuel, mineral oil, fruit, vegetables and cotton.
But imports from China reached $10.4 billion (€8.97bn) over the same period — machinery and electrical equipment alone accounting for $4.1 billion (€3.5bn), followed by vehicles, iron and steel, plastics and chemicals.
Egypt wants Chinese investment and technology, but also wants more Chinese companies to manufacture inside Egypt and greater access for Egyptian goods to the Chinese market.
A five-year programme agreed for 2024-2028 calls for local production and technology transfer in electric vehicles, electronics, solar panels, chemicals and modern agricultural technology, with artificial intelligence also listed as a priority.
El-Sisi said ahead of the visit that Egypt wanted to attract Chinese investment in EVs, battery storage, renewable energy and shipbuilding, while expanding technology transfer in telecommunications, AI and space sciences.
Military ties move into view
Defence links are also becoming more visible. China and Egypt are holding the second edition of their Eagles of Civilisation joint air force exercise, running from mid-August into early September at Egyptian air bases. The first was held only last year.
Chinese officials said the 2026 drills would include air combat tactics, air superiority operations, combat search and rescue and joint force deployment.
The US remains Cairo's key longstanding security partner, providing large-scale military assistance and supplying a significant part of Egypt's diversely sourced military equipment.
Washington has not publicly commented on the Chinese exercises. The Pentagon has previously flagged concerns about Chinese military engagement with US partners across the Middle East and Africa.
The exercises fit Egypt's wider policy of diversifying its defence partnerships, a deliberate balancing act that also encompasses its involvement in BRICS, the New Development Bank and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation alongside continued reliance on Western economic and security support.
Next phase of relations crucial
Ahead of the visit, Xi described the country as an important link between the Arab world and Africa and called for deeper China-Arab and China-Africa cooperation through Egypt.
For China, Egypt combines a market of more than 100 million people with a strategic position on the Suez Canal and political weight across the Arab world and Africa.
The two governments have also taken similar positions on several regional issues, including support for a Palestinian state, while Egypt maintains its One China policy.
Egypt was the first Arab and African country to establish diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China in 1956.
El-Sisi has travelled to China eight times since taking office in 2014, most recently in May 2024.
The agreements announced during Xi's visit are expected to provide more detail on newer areas of cooperation, particularly technology transfer and advanced manufacturing, where Egypt has pushed hardest to move beyond the construction and infrastructure model that defined the relationship's first decade.

Türkiye ready to show effort to end Ukraine war: Erdoğan

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:52:21 UTC
20:52:21 KST

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has told Russian leader Vladimir Putin that Türkiye is ready to exert all kinds of efforts to end the war between Moscow and Kiev, reiterating that the continued armed conflict since 2022 did not benefit either side.
“Türkiye plays a role in the peaceful resolution of conflicts in our region. In particular, it is our expectation, and Mr. Putin’s, that the war between Russia and Ukraine will end peacefully as soon as possible,” Erdoğan told reporters aboard his flight back from Kyrgyzstan on Sept. 2, where he held a bilateral meeting with Putin on the sidelines of a Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit.
Describing his meeting with Putin as very fruitful and sincere, Erdoğan said they discussed all the aspects of bilateral ties as well as the ongoing war.
Türkiye’s wish is to see the establishment of peace and stability in the region with the termination of the war, Erdoğan said. “It is obvious that this war does not bring any positive outcome to either side, to the region and the world. Is Mr. Putin happy about this? No, he is not. He, too, is hopeful that the war will end,” he added.
Erdoğan noted that he has “expressed our readiness to do our best for peace. It is a reality that peace will prevail and not war. We are ready to exert efforts to this end.”
Black Sea security is important for Türkiye.
On a question about increased attacks on civilian ships, including those with Turkish flags, Erdoğan underscored the importance of uninterrupted maritime security for Türkiye in the Black Sea.
“The conflict between the warring sides should not escalate to a point where it jeopardizes the safety of civilians and businesses. For these reasons, we are acting with a much broader perspective. We need to solve this problem,” he said.
Erdoğan reiterated the need for the establishment of a new mechanism to secure the shipment in the Black Sea, urging for a speedy resolution before a food security crisis erupts mostly in Africa due to insufficient supply of grain.
Greece should not arm islands.
Another important question Erdoğan answered was on Greece's attempts to arm the Aegean islands with demilitarized status at the expense of ruining ties with Ankara. Greece and Israel have recently signed a multibillion-dollar agreement to bolster the former’s air defense system.
“Greece must reverse the change and course and stop arming islands that have demilitarized status. History is a very good guide for those who learn from it. We will continue to work for peace, security, and stability in our region,” he stated.
Türkiye has always been acting in a constructive way, but it did not receive the same from Greece, Erdoğan said. “Whoever interprets Türkiye’s calm and responsible approach as weakness is making a serious mistake.”
Talks for F-35s continue.
On a question about Türkiye’s plans to return to the F-35 program after transferring its Russian-made S-400 air defense systems, Erdoğan said he discussed all the matters with Putin during their bilateral meeting.
“As you know, Türkiye was part of the F-35 program and delivered an enormous contribution to it. Our talks for Türkiye’s return to the program continue. We think that this issue will be solved following the accomplishment of the processes in the U.S.,” he stated.
Türkiye was expelled from the F-35 joint fighter program in 2019 after it purchased and deployed S-400 air defense systems from Russia. The U.S. laws require that Türkiye end its possession of the S-400 systems to return the purchase of F-35s.
Erdoğan said Türkiye, in the meantime, is accelerating its efforts to create its own jet fighter, Kaan, and other air defense systems. “This is the road map of strong Türkiye,” he added.
‘Terror-free Türkiye’ projects advances
Erdoğan also commented on the implementation of his government’s “terror-free Türkiye” project after an interagency security committee was formed to oversee the process.
“We, as the state, have a road map, a plan, and a timing. Our institutions are working in coordination,” he stated.
“For the law to be implemented, the terror organization must actually lay down its arms and be dissolved. The procedures for this process are well defined. The process is proceeding step by step,” he added.
The president said the state and all other relevant bodies are running the process with care in a bid not to give any room for those who want to ruin it.
