&quot;Turnkey service&quot; for $50,000–70,000: Lubinets spoke about a new corruption scheme during mobilization
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
14:12:59 EEST
20:12:59 KST

"Turnkey service" for $50,000–70,000: Lubinets spoke about a new corruption scheme during mobilization
Kyiv • UNN
According to the ombudsman, a "turnkey" service exists in border regions, where TCC employees, for $50,000–70,000, transported people out of Ukraine. Information about the illegal removal of people who had already been mobilized is being verified.
The Office of the Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights is verifying information about a new alleged corruption scheme in the mobilization sector, under which a person who has already been taken away by representatives of a territorial recruitment and social support center may be illegally transported outside Ukraine for $50,000–$70,000. This was stated by Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets in an interview with Ukrainska Pravda, reports UNN.
Details
According to him, this concerns a so-called "turnkey" service. The information is currently being verified, so Lubinets did not name the specific region where such a scheme may have operated.
At the same time, he clarified that he was referring to Ukraine's border regions.
One of the latest stories—they tell me, we are currently verifying this information, I will not even name the region now, although everyone understands that we are talking about the border regions—is that there is a new service, the so-called "turnkey" service, when a person can pay between $50,000 and $70,000, and then that person, who has already been taken away in a van, may now be transported directly outside Ukraine
The Ombudsman links the emergence of such schemes to widespread corruption in the mobilization system. According to him, the cost of illegally evading mobilization has only increased over time. He also noted that there are fewer people able to pay large sums, but at the same time, because the risks are increasing, they are willing to pay more.
There are fewer people; there are fewer people who are able to pay, but people understand that the danger, well, is increasing, so they are willing to pay even more for this
According to the Ombudsman, corruption schemes in the mobilization system previously involved considerably smaller, although still substantial, sums. In particular, he said that around $10,000 was charged for the opportunity to "/get out of the van, $15,000 for getting out of the premises of a territorial recruitment and social support center, and $20,000 at the stage of undergoing a military medical commission.
$10,000 for getting out of the van, $15,000 from the premises of the territorial recruitment and social support centers, $20,000 at the stage of the military medical commission—these figures are not going anywhere. Moreover, month after month, this price tag only increases
In his assessment, the conditions for the spread of corruption arose, in particular, because of an approach under which the performance of the mobilization system is assessed primarily by the number of people who need to be mobilized. The Ombudsman explained that, at one point, the relevant structures were tasked with ensuring the mobilization of approximately 30,000 citizens per month throughout Ukraine.
Let's set a target that we need to recruit approximately 30,000 Ukrainian citizens per month throughout Ukraine. Moreover, no one was interested in who these people were. The main thing was to set the target. And they began taking everyone indiscriminately
In Lubinets's view, this system itself contributed to the emergence of corruption mechanisms: people who were physically capable of serving could try to buy their way out, while the numerical targets had to be met at the expense of other citizens.
The Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights also criticized the approach under which the effectiveness of territorial recruitment and social support centers is assessed by the number of people mobilized, rather than by how many people, after mobilization and training, actually reach military units. He recommended analyzing the effectiveness of each regional territorial recruitment and social support center based precisely on the final result.
In my view, effectiveness should be determined not by the number of people whom you mobilized as if they were checkmarks, but by the number of people whom you mobilized and who reached the front line
He also claims that various stages of the system currently are in fact responsible only for meeting their own formal indicators: territorial recruitment and social support centers are responsible for the number of mobilized people transferred, and training centers for their training, while the final result in the form of the actual replenishment of combat units is not properly analyzed. Lubinets believes that changing this approach could simultaneously improve the quality of military replenishment and reduce corruption risks.
The Ombudsman emphasized that the problem of corruption and violations of citizens' rights during mobilization must be addressed systematically. In his assessment, the lack of an adequate response to illegal actions in previous years became one of the factors behind the growing social tension.
At the same time, Lubinets emphasized that he condemns both the unlawful actions of certain employees of the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers and attacks on servicemen and representatives of the recruitment centers.
I condemn both attacks on employees of the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers and, equally emphatically, criminal offenses committed by employees of the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers. One cannot pretend that some are allowed to act outside the law while others are not
We remind you
In August 2026, the head of the Mykolaiv Regional Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center was detained for a $15,000 bribe.

China, Egypt sign agreements, MoUs to deepen bilateral cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:12:26 UTC
20:12:26 KST

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el Sisi and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping on Wednesday witnessed the signing of an agreement and memorandums of understanding between Egyptian and Chinese entities, according to the Egyptian Presidency.
The agreements and memorandums cover cooperation in several fields, including industrial development, investment and other areas aimed at strengthening economic ties between the two countries, said a presidency statement.
Sisi said that the two countries have a “clear political will to elevate the prospects of bilateral cooperation, particularly through localising industry and transferring technology,” according to the statement.
He also said the two countries are launching a new phase of cooperation in renewable energy, automotive manufacturing, textiles and chemical fibers, while announcing the launch of the third phase of expansions at the China-Egypt industrial zone in the Suez Canal Economic Zone.
The two presidents also affirmed their support for efforts to reach a comprehensive agreement to end the war in the region, Egypt's state-linked Al-Qahera News reported.
Xi said Beijing is “keen to elevate relations with Egypt to broader horizons” and will continue “encouraging Chinese companies to increase their investments in the country and benefit from the advantages of the Egyptian market.”
The two leaders held talks in the Egyptian capital Cairo following an official reception ceremony for Xi at Al-Ittihadiya Palace, according to an Anadolu correspondent.
The ceremony included the playing of the national anthems of Egypt and China, while artillery fired ceremonial shots in honour of the visiting president.
Xi’s visit is the first by a Chinese president to Egypt in 10 years.
Egypt and China established diplomatic relations in 1956, making Egypt the first Arab and African country to recognise the People’s Republic of China.
Beijing backed Cairo during the 1956 Suez Crisis, while Egypt supported China’s restoration of its seat at the UN in 1971.
The countries established a strategic partnership in 1999, which was elevated to a comprehensive strategic partnership in December 2014 during Sisi’s visit to Beijing.

NATO member Turkey would consider taking its relations with the China and Russia-led security bloc, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, to a higher level, President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said on Wednesday.
"Turkey's prospect of (full) membership to the organization does not imply a breakaway from any other bloc or from the West," Erdogan said, according to a transcript of remarks he made to journalists on his return flight from Kyrgyzstan.
Erdogan attended a summit of the SCO, of which Turkey is a "dialog partner," in Bishkek on Tuesday.
Erdogan also said on Wednesday that a mechanism is needed to permanently ensure the safety of commercial maritime transport in the Black Sea before a grain crisis escalates.
Earlier this week, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Turkey had prepared a plan for the safe passage of grain via the Black Sea, and that it was in contact with both Russia and Ukraine regarding it.
Erdogan and Russian President Vladimir Putin held talks on Tuesday in Bishkek on the sidelines of the SCO summit, and Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said Putin had discussed the situation in the Black Sea with Erdogan.
In remarks to journalists on his return flight from the trip to Kyrgyzstan, Erdogan said a grain crisis had resurfaced, particularly in Africa, and action needed to be taken before the problem escalated further, according to a transcript shared by his office on Wednesday.
"The safety of all civilian maritime transportation in the Black Sea is important to us. The fighting between parties should not escalate to a point where it undermines the safety of civilians and commercial life," Erdogan said. "We need to resolve this issue," he added.
Turkey, UN help mediate Russia-Ukraine Black Sea Grain Initiative in 2022 after outset of war
In July 2022, Turkey and the United Nations helped mediate the so-called Black Sea Grain Initiative to allow the safe export of nearly 33 million metric tons of Ukrainian grain via the Black Sea, despite the war.
However, Russia withdrew from the agreement in 2023, complaining that its own food and fertilizer exports faced serious obstacles.
In comments on recent efforts to reach a deal, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Grushko said on Wednesday that Moscow sees no grounds for the Black Sea grain agreement to resume.

Taiwan targets NT$8 trillion in semiconductor output this year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:04:35 UTC
20:04:35 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan aims to raise semiconductor industry output above NT$8 trillion (US$251.8 billion) this year, as demand for AI and high-performance computing continues to drive growth, UDN Money reported.
The semiconductor industry covers a wide range of businesses, including chip design, wafer manufacturing, and packaging and testing. Its total output has grown from about NT$4.3 trillion in 2023 to NT$5.3 trillion in 2024 and NT$6.5 trillion last year, according to the Cabinet and the Taipei Exchange.
The government is working to strengthen Taiwan’s capabilities across chip design, semiconductor equipment, and advanced packaging. Chiou Chyou-huey (邱求慧), director general of the Industrial Development Administration, said Wednesday that the agency has assisted 84 chip design and semiconductor equipment companies with technology development.
On the equipment side, the agency has worked with major chipmakers and packaging companies, including TSMC and ASE, to help 29 suppliers develop new equipment and validate their equipment on production lines.
Companies supported by the program include Gallant Micro Machining Co., Scientech Corp., MPI Corp., Skytech Inc. and Usun Technology Co. These suppliers have become important equipment providers for the country‘s growing advanced packaging industry and are expected to help lift domestic semiconductor equipment output above NT$270 billion this year.
Advanced packaging is one area where equipment makers are seeing growing business opportunities as AI chips become larger and combine more types of components. As a result, accurately positioning and bonding chips has become increasingly important to maintaining production yields, the department said.
With government support, Gallant has developed a panel-level packaging system that can process chips of different sizes and orientations on a single machine, removing the need to transfer them between multiple machines. An image-based alignment system precisely positions each chip before bonding, reducing processing time by 50%, according to the department.
The agency is also supporting domestic chip designers as they develop products for a broader range of industries. One example is Alltek Marine Electronics Corp., which has developed a chip for maritime communications.
The chip incorporates a maritime communications technology that can transmit nearly 30 times more data than traditional automatic identification system technology. It is designed to support communication among ships, shore stations and satellites, with potential applications in vessel positioning and emergency communications at sea.

Trump aides, fearing a midterm crash, push to keep Iran war 'quiet' for time being

20:04:13 KST

Top aides to US President Donald Trump are pushing to keep the Iran war from escalating before November's midterm elections to staunch Republican electoral losses, four people familiar with the discussions said, a strategy that is already under strain as the United States and Iran resume their back-and-forth attacks.
White House officials will consider ramping up military action after the November 3 vote, said the sources, who requested anonymity to describe internal thinking, though any return to full-scale conflict is far from a given.
For now, they said, the administration is focused on tightening the economic pressure on Iran in an effort to extract concessions in any future negotiation that months of military action failed to secure.
"We are keeping the pressure on Iran," one White House official said. "But November is a priority."
Keeping the war mostly contained until then would help prevent the unpopular conflict from dominating the news as Trump's Republicans campaign to defend thin majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives, said the sources, three of whom are White House officials.
Only 31% of Americans approve of the war, while some 63% disapprove, according to a late August Reuters/Ipsos poll, and voters are particularly unhappy about high gas prices.
A tactical pause could also give the US military some breathing room to replenish its heavily depleted munitions stockpiles, the sources said.
But pulling off the play-it-cool strategy looks more difficult by the day. While the conflict remains much less intense than it was during the spring or during a flare-up in the middle of the summer, both sides have exchanged tit-for-tat strikes in recent days.
Iran will likely keep striking US assets
Iran's leaders, emboldened after months of disrupting traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and facing little internal unrest, will likely keep striking at US and allied Gulf targets, including military bases, vessels and energy infrastructure, at least periodically, analysts said.
The US will face pressure to retaliate, potentially leading to an escalatory spiral that brings both sides back to a full-scale air war - whether or not the administration wants it.
Over the weekend, the US struck rocket launchers on Iran's Larak Island after a month of relative calm, prompting Iran to fire missiles toward Jordan and the United Arab Emirates. On Tuesday, the US hit more Iranian targets around the Strait of Hormuz.
"The regime has every incentive to disrupt the 'calm' - which is no real calm, after all, since the administration's explicit aim is to increase economic pressure massively on Iran," said Barbara Leaf, who served as the top State Department official for the Middle East under former President Joe Biden.
Another wild card is Trump himself.
The president's approval rating has fallen from 40% to 33% since the conflict began, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling. Sources said he is not currently interested in escalation, but he is famously prone to changing his mind and could change course in response to events.
Trump threatened on Tuesday to escalate the conflict if Iran hits back against the latest US strikes.
"If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings," he wrote on his Truth Social platform.
Constrained by logistics, politics
Trump has publicly said the upcoming elections were not factoring into this Iran strategy.
But as the war enters its seventh month, his White House finds itself increasingly constrained by logistical and political realities.
"The timetable has changed," one senior White House official said. Another added that the "calendar is driving Iran."
Reuters reported in August that the military had used "virtually all" of its supply of certain precision missiles. On Sunday, the Washington Post reported that the heads of the Army, Navy and Air Force warned Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth in a written assessment that prolonging the war was unsustainable and would diminish the military's readiness in other theaters.
The Pentagon has said the military had "everything it needs to execute" its mission.
“President Trump has destroyed Iran’s military capabilities and is crippling what’s left of its abysmal economy with the most powerful naval blockade in world history and crushing sanctions," White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales said. "The President will continue to advance America’s interests at home and abroad and will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon."
America's Gulf allies -- some of whom had pushed for aggressive action against Iran earlier in the war to weaken their main regional adversary -- roundly urged the White House to deescalate after a recent round of attacks in late July, regional diplomats said.
Currently, two White House officials said, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are among the high-ranking Trump aides who are on board with the idea of trying to keep the Iran conflict relatively "quiet" until November.
In recent weeks, administration officials have instead intensified an economic isolation campaign, during which the US has threatened to slap countries that trade with Iran with massive sanctions, while maintaining its own blockade on the Strait of Hormuz.
The trade-focused strategy, however, has its own limits, analysts and officials said.
Iran has spent decades under layers of US and international sanctions that have battered its economy but have not deterred its leadership.
On Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the pressure campaign may cause Iran to lash out militarily, raising the prospect that the economic campaign could itself stoke military escalation.
Additionally, some major world powers, like China, have not joined Washington's bid to isolate Iran, prompting questions about the campaign's effectiveness.
"The purpose of the new sanctions package is meant to add economic pressure on top of that being caused by the blockade to force Iran back to the table, after the administration determined it was a better option than returning to kinetic action," said Alex Plitsas, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council.
"Iran is concerned about it, but China has already indicated that it's not willing to play ball, which calls into question how effective it will be."

"Deeply emotional day for every Uttarakhandi": CM Dhami pays tribute to 1994 Mussoorie firing victims
Uttarakhand Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami on Wednesday said September 2 is a deeply emotional day for every Uttarakhandi as it marks the anniversary of the 1994 Mussoorie firing incident.Speaking to ANI, CM Dhami said, "Today is a deeply emotional day for every Uttarakhandi, as it marks the anniversary of the 1994 Mussoorie firing incident. It is a day to pay tribute. This major movement took place here in protest against the Khatima firing incident, which had occurred on September 1, 1994."Recalling the incident, he further added, saying, "On that day, lathis and bullets were used barbarically against unarmed agitators, resulting in the loss of six lives. I offer my heartfelt tributes to all those andolankaris."The Chief Minister reiterated his resolve to build the state as per the dreams of the martyrs. "We further strengthen our resolve to build an Uttarakhand that aligns with the dreams of those who sacrificed their lives and fought for the cause; we pledge to work ceaselessly without stopping or tiring to make Uttarakhand the best state in the country," he added.
September 2, 1994, remains a painful day in the history of Uttarakhand. On this day, the peaceful valleys of Mussoorie were shaken by gunfire when police opened fire on protesters demanding a separate Uttarakhand state.
Six protesters--four men and two women--were killed, while a police officer also lost his life in the incident.The Mussoorie firing became a major turning point in the Uttarakhand statehood movement. Although the demand for a separate state had been raised since the 1970s, the movement gained momentum and took a violent turn during the 1990s.The firing on peaceful protesters in Mussoorie on September 2, 1994, left many injured and claimed six lives. Decades later, the names of those who lost their lives are still remembered, while their families and friends continue to ask whether their sacrifices have truly been honoured.

A shootout involving Ukrainian security personnel in Kyiv left several people wounded on 2 September, with Ukrainian authorities now saying the confrontation occurred during an investigation into an alleged Russian plot to assassinate a Russian opposition figure in Ukraine.
The incident took place overnight in Kyiv’s Dniprovskyi district, amid reports that Stepan Kaplunov, deputy commander for combat operations of the Russian Volunteer Corps (RDK), had been abducted.
Shootout follows reported abduction
Ukrainska Pravda reported, citing Kaplunov’s lawyer Taras Borovskyi, that law enforcement officers arrived at the serviceman’s home after his reported disappearance.
According to Borovskyi, Kaplunov’s fellow soldiers came to the location after being alerted, after which gunfire broke out. The lawyer also published video from the scene, Ukrainska Pravda reported.
The RDK had previously said that unknown individuals abducted Kaplunov from the courtyard of his home.
Ukraine’s State Bureau of Investigation confirmed to Ukrainska Pravda that it had received a complaint from Kaplunov’s lawyers alleging his abduction and was examining it for possible registration as a criminal proceeding.
Ukrainska Pravda, citing sources in Ukraine’s security services, reported that the confrontation involved the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) and Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR). Its sources said three HUR personnel had been wounded as of Wednesday morning.
SBU links confrontation to Russian plot
The SBU later said the confrontation occurred during an investigation into an alleged terrorist attack organized by Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB).
The agency said its investigators were conducting a search at one of the addresses connected to the case when a group of people launched an armed attack on them. The group allegedly blocked the investigators’ vehicles with cars and attempted to prevent the search.
The SBU said its Alpha special operations unit was deployed to stop the armed resistance. Officers used their weapons, and several people who resisted were wounded, according to the agency.
The attackers were detained, the SBU said. Initial investigative work found that they belonged to one of Ukraine’s Defense Forces units, while weapons and documents were seized from them.
The agency did not identify the detainees or their military unit.
Alleged assassination attempt
Earlier on 2 September, the SBU said it and HUR had jointly foiled an FSB plot to assassinate a leader of a Russian opposition nationalist political movement who had traveled to Ukraine for Independence Day.
The SBU did not name the alleged target or provide details of the planned attack.
RBC-Ukraine, citing sources, reported that the target was Kaplunov. The outlet also reported that HUR later deleted a statement about the foiled attack.
The SBU’s later statement about the shootout did not name Kaplunov or explicitly identify the armed group involved as HUR personnel.
The Russian Volunteer Corps is a unit operating within Ukraine’s military intelligence structures and composed of Russian nationals fighting against Russia’s invasion.
Budanov calls for investigation
Kyrylo Budanov, head of Ukraine’s Presidential Office, said the incident should be thoroughly and impartially investigated, according to RBC-Ukraine.
He said no one should be allowed to abduct servicemen, open fire in Ukrainian cities, or give or carry out criminal orders with impunity.
The Prosecutor General’s Office has opened a pretrial investigation into threats against and an attempt on the life of a law enforcement officer, the SBU said.
Authorities have not publicly provided a full account reconciling the different reports surrounding the incident. Investigative actions are ongoing.
Ukraine and Russian opposition figures
Ukraine has become a base for some Russian opposition figures and anti-Kremlin activists since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion. Some have joined Ukrainian military units or otherwise supported Ukraine’s war effort.
That has also made some of them targets for Russian intelligence operations.

Brain waves reveal how alcohol cues hijack decision-making in addiction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:00:47 UTC
20:00:47 KST

People with alcohol use disorder experience automatic emotional reactions to alcohol-related images that disrupt their basic decision-making processes. Research published in Progress in Neuropsychopharmacology & Biological Psychiatry suggests that the brain attempts to offset these cognitive disruptions by increasing activity in regions associated with deliberate thought.
According to biological models of addiction, chronic substance use creates a disconnect between the brain’s reward centers and its executive control hubs. Over time, the brain assigns a disproportionate motivational weight to the addictive substance. This means that environmental cues, such as the sight of a bottle or a familiar bar, become highly stimulating and command the brain’s attention.
In alcohol use disorder, seeing a picture of a drink can trigger an immediate, positive emotional association. These latent affective connections operate beneath conscious awareness and encourage the individual to seek out alcohol. They often lead to a relapse by making it harder to implement cognitive strategies for resisting cravings.
Traditional psychological tests measure how fast or accurately someone reacts to a stimulus. These basic metrics do not fully capture the hidden cognitive steps involved in making a choice. To separate these underlying components, researchers use computational frameworks that break down the milliseconds of decision-making into distinct mathematical variables.
This computational approach quantifies how much information a person needs before acting, how fast they process that information, and how long they spend physically executing a response. The biological side of these automatic reactions also requires precise measurement. Scientists use electroencephalography, a method of recording electrical activity on the scalp, to track brain waves known as event-related potentials.
These electrical signals correspond to specific cognitive events and happen in fractions of a second. Early brain waves reflect automatic, unconscious attention. Later waves indicate top-down cognitive control, which involves conscious effort to evaluate a situation and guide behavior.
Researchers wanted to understand the sequence of these neural and behavioral events in people with alcohol use disorder. Zijing Wang, Jiang Du, Tianzhen Chen, and Min Zhao at the Shanghai Mental Health Center, along with colleagues at the Third People’s Hospital of Fuyang, conducted the research. They aimed to map exactly how early emotional biases affect later cognitive control, and how these brain wave patterns correlate with real-time decision-making speeds.
The team recruited 47 men diagnosed with alcohol use disorder and 32 healthy control participants. Because the total sample included 79 participants, this is considered a small study. The individuals with alcohol use disorder were hospitalized and in the withdrawal phase of recovery, having abstained from alcohol for two weeks to six months.
Participants sat in a sound-attenuated room and completed an emotional association task on a computer. In each trial, they viewed a picture for one second. Half of the images depicted alcohol, while the other half depicted healthy activities. Immediately after the picture disappeared, a word appeared on the screen.
Participants had one second to press a key categorizing the word as either positive or negative. The underlying logic of the test is that if a preceding picture elicits a positive emotional state, the participant will categorize a positive word more quickly due to a priming effect. Throughout the task, participants wore sensor caps containing electrodes that recorded their brain’s electrical activity in real time.
The researchers fed the behavioral data into a computational model to separate the decision-making process into three distinct parts. First, they looked at the decision threshold, which represents how much evidence a person needs to make a choice. Second, they analyzed the drift rate, which measures how fast a person accumulates that sensory evidence. Third, they measured non-decision time, which covers the physical execution of the button press and basic sensory encoding.
For positive words that followed alcohol pictures, the men with alcohol use disorder showed a lower decision threshold than the healthy controls. This indicates that they made choices more impulsively, requiring less mental evidence to trigger a response. At the same time, their drift rate was slower, meaning they were less efficient at actually processing the visual information on the screen.
The group with alcohol use disorder also exhibited a longer non-decision time during the alcohol trials. They spent more time physically or perceptually preparing to press the button. The researchers suggest that the emotional weight of the alcohol images likely caused a cognitive conflict that disrupted their basic motor responses.
The electroencephalography data provided a real-time map of the brain’s electrical activity during these delayed responses. The researchers focused on an early brain wave that peaks around 200 to 260 milliseconds after a stimulus appears. This wave tracks automatic emotional processing and early visual attention.
When viewing alcohol-related images, the group with alcohol use disorder showed a heightened electrical response in this early wave compared to the healthy controls. This heightened neural activity points to an unconscious, automatic sensitivity to alcohol cues. Such immediate biological engagement can overwhelm a person’s ability to shift their attention elsewhere.
The team also examined a later brain wave that occurs 600 to 800 milliseconds after a stimulus. This late-stage electrical activity is tied to cognitive reappraisal and the conscious reallocation of mental resources. For the images depicting healthy activities, the men with alcohol use disorder showed a larger late-stage brain wave response than the healthy controls.
The researchers propose that this increased late-stage activity represents a compensatory effort. Because healthy activities lack the dominant emotional pull of alcohol for these individuals, their brains had to exert more conscious cognitive control to process the non-addictive stimuli. This reveals an imbalance in the brain, where high automatic reactivity is paired with an increased need for deliberate mental effort.
Finally, the researchers ran a statistical analysis to see if the brain wave activity directly influenced the behavioral delays. They looked specifically at the relationship between the delayed non-decision time and the late-stage brain waves during the alcohol trials. They found that higher amplitudes in the late-stage brain waves were associated with a reduction in the non-decision time delay.
Even though the men with alcohol use disorder generally had slower physical response times, those who generated stronger late-stage electrical activity managed to speed up their reactions slightly. The brain’s evaluative systems were actively working to suppress the behavioral deficit caused by the emotional distraction. This indicates that enhanced conscious processing can partially counteract the impairments caused by automatic emotional reactions.
The study relied on a small sample of exclusively male participants. Brain responses and emotional association patterns might differ in women. All the individuals with alcohol use disorder were hospitalized and experiencing the withdrawal phase of recovery.
The observed neural and behavioral patterns may not reflect the cognitive processes of people actively consuming alcohol or those in long-term abstinence. Future research will need to track individuals over time to see how these cognitive and biological markers shift as a person transitions from early withdrawal into sustained recovery.
The study, “Neurocognitive mechanisms underlying alcohol-related emotional association bias among alcohol use disorder: Evidence from a hierarchical drift-diffusion model and event-related potentials,” was authored by Zijing Wang, Dapeng Zhang, Jiayi Zhu, Fanfan Luo, Dongli Fan, Luxing Cai, Fei Cheng, Jing Tian, Shiyan Qu, Jiang Du, Tianzhen Chen, and Min Zhao.

American forces strike IRGC targets in Iran

US forces have carried out a wave of strikes against Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targets inside Iran, hitting air defence sites, radar systems, maritime assets and other military facilities, according to US Central Command.
CENTCOM announced on 1 September that the strikes had been completed against a range of Iranian military targets. Targets identified by CENTCOM included Iranian air defence positions and radar systems, along with maritime assets and facilities, mine-laying capabilities and communications sites.
CENTCOM stated: “U.S. forces struck Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets including air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities, and communications sites.”
The command added: “The strikes follow recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members.”
The Strait of Hormuz is the narrow maritime passage connecting the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea. It is used by commercial shipping operating between Gulf ports and international markets and is also regularly patrolled by US and allied naval forces.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps maintains its own naval, aerospace and ground forces alongside Iran’s regular armed forces. Its naval element operates extensively in and around the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz. The target set identified by CENTCOM covered several elements of Iranian military infrastructure. Air defence and radar installations form part of Iran’s ability to detect and respond to aircraft and other aerial activity, while communications sites support military command and coordination.
CENTCOM also specifically identified mine-laying capabilities among the targets attacked. Iranian forces have long maintained naval mine capabilities for operations in the waters around Iran, including approaches to the Strait of Hormuz.
The United States currently has more than 50,000 military personnel deployed across the Middle East, according to CENTCOM. US Central Command is responsible for American military operations across a region covering the Middle East and parts of Central and South Asia, including the Persian Gulf and surrounding waters.

Trump’s threat against an NBC journalist is an attack on reality | Margaret Sullivan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:00:22 UTC
20:00:22 KST

With his approval ratings tanking, the crucial midterm elections looming, and his war with Iran turning into a quagmire, Donald Trump has entered full freak-out mode.
It’s not hard to tell. Just look at what happened this week when he lashed out at Kristen Welker, the well-respected host of NBC’s Meet the Press, and one of the best-known journalists in the nation.
Welker observed recently that Trump – while having significant influence – has a “mixed record” on making successful endorsements this year. An innocuous statement, made in advance of the Sunday show during her analytical comments to a network affiliate station in Washington.
But not harmless in Trump’s opinion.
Furious, he called on the Federal Communications Commission to go after Welker, saying she “will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment”.
In fact, as the Hill newspaper reported this week, while Trump “boasts a 100 percent record in Senate Republican primary contests this election cycle, several of his high-profile gubernatorial picks have lost”.
That sounds like a mixed record, doesn’t it? Not to Trump, who called Welker’s comments “purposeful inaccuracy”.
“The Press is a Disgrace to our Nation, and I hope that Chairman Brendan Carr, and the fine people of his Commission, will take this Threat to our Country very seriously,” he wrote on Truth Social. He later added: “FCC to the rescue.”
The threat is absurd. It would seem even more so if Trump had not already been using the agency as a weapon in his long-running campaign against the reality-based press.
Carr is a partisan, fully devoted to Trump’s mission, and he has shown himself more than willing to do the bidding of the president who appointed him during this second presidential term.
The FCC is intended to be bipartisan and independent but under Trump, it has skewed heavily Maga – and clearly political.
Carr himself seems to embrace without embarrassment the role of Trump’s media attack dog. He has warned that he would use the FCC’s power to issue broadcast licenses to go after what he and his boss call “fake news”.
The skirmishes are widespread. ABC has sued the FCC, charging that the agency’s early review of eight local broadcast licenses violates the first amendment.
The FCC is supposed to adhere to first amendment restrictions in dealing with broadcast licenses or in any punitive measures at all. “While the FCC has the limited ability to revoke stations’ broadcast licenses, it has not done so in over 40 years and its powers do not include revoking licenses because of a disagreement over a viewpoint expressed on the station,” the Washington Post noted this week.
It’s no surprise that Trump has singled out Welker for this unwarranted attack. He has a long and shameful history of going after female journalists and seems to particularly relish criticizing female journalists of color. In his first term, his targets included Yamiche Alcindor, then of PBS, April Ryan of American Urban Radio and Abby Phillip of CNN.
In one particularly vicious moment, he went after Welker herself during an interview earlier this year, saying: “You’re either crooked or you’re stupid.”
This new attack on Welker brings together some of his favorite techniques – trashing a Black female journalist, cracking down on free speech in apparent violation of first amendment protections and using what should be an independent government body (including, of course, the justice department) to carry out his retaliation efforts.
Although this new chapter is part of a well-established pattern, it feels especially desperate when seen in context.
In recent days, Trump’s efforts to control the media through threats and punishment have ramped up. The administration has barred reporters from three major news organizations from covering the G20 meetings, even as top journalists at Stars and Stripes, the military newspaper with a long history of independence, have been fired.
Trump’s reality has turned sour, so he certainly doesn’t want that reality reflected in the news media.
Threatening Kristen Welker – like so much of what he’s doing – is obvious over-reach.
If the FCC does somehow attempt to punish her or her network, there’s a solid first amendment case to be made in response. NBC, which has staunchly defended Welker, is likely to make it.
Welker did nothing wrong, not in terms of the facts and not in terms of her journalistic role.
As for Trump, his attacks against the mainstream media will continue.
Pointless and misguided as his media revenge tour is, it seems to be all he knows how to do.
- 
  Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture

6 Signs Your Venting Is Straining Your Relationships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:00:02 UTC
20:00:02 KST

Twenty minutes ago, you called a friend to complain about something your boss said. Since then, you’ve reconstructed his exact tone—don’t you hate it when someone says “interesting” like that?—supplied three years of relevant backstory, and pulled up six Slack messages that prove this wasn’t an isolated incident. Your friend has contributed the occasional “ugh” and “wow.” You are nowhere near finished.
Sometimes, it just feels good to say the petty, uncharitable thing out loud to someone who won't forward it to HR. A venting session can be validating, cathartic, and even productive if it helps you figure out your next steps.
“Venting is discrete,” says Jenny Martin, a psychologist and founder of Gemstone Wellness, a trauma-informed practice in Chicago. “It has a beginning, a middle, and an end.”
But venting can also keep you stuck—not to mention, exhaust the person listening. The distinction isn’t whether you complain, get worked up, or talk for a long time. It’s whether the conversation eventually moves somewhere, and whether the other person still feels like a participant rather than an audience member trapped in the front row.
So how can you tell when blowing off steam has started straining your relationships? Therapists—who listen to people vent for a living—say there are a few consistent tells.
It’s a monologue, not a dialogue
Genuine, healthy venting isn’t one-sided. You talk; the other person asks a question, winces in solidarity, or says the same thing happened to them. Maybe they offer a perspective you hadn’t considered. Then you keep going from there. (There are, after all, far more exciting things to discuss, like the tacos and drinks you’ll be enjoying after work on Friday.)
When venting starts straining a relationship, that dynamic changes. “It’s more just a monologue as opposed to a dialogue,” says Stephanie Mahalec, a therapist in Los Angeles. When the listener asks a question, it registers as an interruption—and any advice is flicked away like lint from a sleeve. If they try to share a similar experience, you quickly steer the conversation back to yours.
That doesn’t mean every vent needs to be perfectly balanced. Sometimes a friend gets 45 minutes because their day was objectively worse. Look at the pattern instead: When you finish talking, could you summarize anything your friend said—or only what you told them?
The conversation has no off-ramp
A useful vent has an ending. You get it out, feel understood, and eventually move on, perhaps to the considerably more entertaining gossip your friend has been waiting to share.
That beginning-middle-end structure Martin describes can be easiest to spot in reverse: The listener keeps trying to supply the ending, and the speaker keeps reopening the case.
Perhaps your friend offers a natural exit—“Well, at least you don’t have to see him until Monday”—and you respond by introducing an entirely new piece of evidence. They try to change the subject, and three minutes later, you’re back to your boss. The conversation ends only because somebody has to attend a meeting, make dinner, or claim an urgent need to wash their hair.
One complaint turns into every complaint
You begin with the dishes that have been in the sink all week—but soon you’re talking about the laundry, the trash, and the fact that nobody seemed to care what restaurant you wanted to go to on your birthday.
Listen for two words: always and never. “You’re definitely talking about the past, because you’re not talking about the dish in the sink anymore,” says Matt Cartwright, a therapist in New York. What started as one irritation has opened the file drawer containing every related grievance going back years.
That expansion makes the problem feel bigger and harder to solve. A friend might have useful thoughts about today’s inconsiderate comment; there’s considerably less they can do with “This always happens to me, and nobody has ever respected me.”
When you notice one complaint expanding into a sweeping conclusion, Cartwright suggests pausing and telling yourself—or the person you’re venting to—“The story I’m telling myself is…” For example: “The story I’m telling myself is that because the dish is still in the sink, what I asked for didn’t matter.” Admittedly, it doesn’t exactly roll off the tongue. But that’s part of why it works: The phrase forces you to separate the dirty dish from the much larger case you’ve built around it.
You feel worse than when you started
A good vent doesn’t have to produce a solution. Cartwright describes venting as a “quick release”—sometimes feeling heard is the entire point. But ideally, something has shifted by the end: You’re calmer, clearer about why you’re upset, or have a better sense of what you want to do next.
Unproductive venting does the opposite. Cartwright says it can “activate the memory bank,” turning one offense into a reminder of every similar slight. You replay what happened until it feels freshly committed, then remember three incidents that make it even worse. That doesn’t release frustration; it exacerbates it.
The person listening can intensify the spiral, too. “Now we’ve got two people who can feel flooded, and depending on the dynamics of the relationship, it just feeds each other,” Cartwright says. Psychologists sometimes call this co-rumination: dwelling on a problem and its negative emotions together. Research suggests that it can make people feel closer while also being associated with greater anxiety.
If the listener matches every complaint with a more outraged one—“He said what? I would never put up with that”—the two of you may keep winding each other up. By the time you hang up, your boss hasn’t merely irritated you; he’s become a threat to justice everywhere.
Check in with your body afterward. Has your jaw unclenched? Do you understand the problem better? Or are you pacing faster and composing an email that absolutely should not be sent until morning—if ever?
You’re sharing at a 10 when the relationship is at a 2
Sometimes it isn’t the complaint itself that makes a conversation uncomfortable. It’s the gap between what you’re disclosing and how well you know the person hearing it.
“You’re giving information and providing detail that’s at an intimacy level of 10 when the relationship is actually at an acquaintance level of 2,” Martin says. The coworker you’ve eaten lunch with twice might be up for hearing that your divorce has been difficult. They may not be ready for a scene-by-scene account of your most brutal argument.
That mismatch can leave the other person frozen, with no idea how to react or respond. Are they supposed to offer advice? Ask questions? Hug you beside the office microwave?
Sharing with a near-stranger can feel surprisingly safe, Martin says. Their opinion may carry fewer stakes than the reaction of someone you love. The problem is that disclosure can outpace the relationship: You’re revealing more intimate information much faster than the connection itself is deepening. Before going further, consider how this person has responded to smaller disclosures—and whether the relationship is ready for something bigger.
People have stopped asking how you are
Most people won’t announce that your venting has become too much—but there will be signs.
Friends who once asked how you were feeling may switch to safer questions: “What are you doing this weekend? How’s the house project? Have you watched that show?” If the conversation edges toward an emotional subject, they quickly guide it elsewhere.
You might also notice that someone who used to spend time with you one-on-one now prefers group plans. “People want to have buffers around these people so that they’re not cornered,” Martin says. Or your calls increasingly go unanswered—and when you do connect, the other person seems ready to hang up before you’ve said anything at all.
None of these signs proves that your venting is the reason. People get busy, distracted, and overwhelmed by their own lives. But if several relationships seem to be shifting in the same direction, it’s worth getting curious rather than defensive. Are people avoiding you—or a role they’ve come to expect they’ll have to play?
How to vent without turning a friend into a complaint department
You don’t need to stop venting, nor does every complaint need to become a model of emotionally evolved communication. Sometimes the unhinged version is exactly what needs to come out first. The trick, Cartwright says, is being clear about what you want from the exchange.
For example: “Can I complain for 10 minutes? I don’t need advice—I just need you to hear how irritating this was.” Or: “Can I tell you what happened and get your honest take?” As Cartwright puts it: “Do you have a minute? Because I need to vent.” That lets your friend know whether you’re looking for validation, perspective, or help deciding what to do.
The time limit is useful, too. Mahalec describes healthy venting as time-limited—not because frustration expires at minute 11, but because a time boundary gives the conversation an off-ramp. When you reach it, take a breather. You can always ask whether your friend has the energy to keep going.

‘They destroy, we build’: Gazans rebuild their homes out of mud and rubble
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Next to his destroyed home in Khan Younis, Fayez Abu Shamala, 76, a Palestinian academic and former mayor of Khan Younis, is building again.
Abu Shamala salvaged usable stones from the debris of destroyed buildings, collected and repaired them, and, with the help of his family, built a small house. Instead of cement, unavailable anywhere in Gaza, he used clay to hold the stones together.
He then fixed pieces of nylon over the walls to protect them from rain. He also recovered some windows and doors from the wreckage, modified them, and installed them in what is now his home.
“I am here on my land,” Abu Shamala said. “To my right is the house I built, and to my left is the house the Israeli army destroyed. They are the destroyers, and we are the builders.”
Abu Shamlah has slept in a mudhouse before, after he was displaced from his village in what is now the city of Ashkelon during the 1948 Nakba, when his family was forced from their land and lived for years in mud houses in the Gaza Strip. More than seven decades later, the cycle is being repeated across Gaza.
As Israel blocks the entry of cement, steel, and all conventional building materials, classifying them as “dual-use” items that could serve a military purpose, Abu Shamala and others across Gaza are constructing mud houses to brace for the cold and rainy season. By October 2025, UNOSAT satellite imagery found approximately 81 percent of all structures in the Gaza Strip had been damaged, with more than 123,000 destroyed outright. The UN estimates that the destruction generated 61 million tonnes of rubble. With large-scale reconstruction at a standstill, Palestinians are rebuilding with whatever they can salvage.
Alternatives to the alternatives
On August 15, the first two-story building in the Gaza Strip constructed entirely without banned building materials was unveiled. The building was constructed of steel rebar and aluminum on the inside and Jerusalem limestone on the outside. All the materials were extracted from the rubble.
The building, constructed by the Al-Rimal Company in Gaza City, will be used to run international organizations’ operations, including receiving and storing aid and overseeing its distribution across the Strip. Three engineers from the company planned and built the structure in collaboration with several professionals, technicians, and workers. It took them four months to complete.
“If it weren’t for the occupation, we would not have built this building,” said Younis Abu Mueilaq, one of the engineers who supervised the construction, meaning that the challenges imposed on Gaza ultimately forced the development of new and unprecedented approaches to rebuilding.
Al-Rimal Al-Taybeh is a partner of international organizations that operate warehouses across the Gaza Strip. As the war intensified and many of those warehouses were destroyed, the organizations began looking for alternatives once the situation became relatively calmer following the signing of the October 2025 ceasefire.
According to Abu Mueilaq, several alternative warehouses were established to replace those destroyed during the war, and as the company’s work with international organizations increased, an administrative building became necessary.
Israel continues to refuse to allow in the building materials needed for reconstruction, as well as the heavy machinery needed to remove the rubble, which has generated 61 million tonnes of debris — about as much as 15 Great Pyramids of Giza or 25 Eiffel Towers by volume, according to the UN. As a result, people in Gaza are turning to alternatives, some of which date back hundreds of years, such as mud houses, while others involve developing new methods that are expensive and beyond individuals’ means. Such projects are instead undertaken by companies and institutions, such as Al-Rimal Al-Taybeh, which constructed this building.
The building would ordinarily have been constructed with cement, Abu Mueilaq says, but since it remains unavailable due to Israel’s blockade, the team turned to construction metals recovered from destroyed buildings and modified them for reuse.
The external structure was mainly made of steel rebar fastened together with bolts. But when it came time to cover the structure with sheets of metal on the outside, as an alternative to cement, none was to be found.
“That was when we began looking for alternatives to the alternatives,” Abu Mueilaq said. “We started looking for whatever we could use. We found that there was a technique used in modern architecture in places such as Dubai, where the steel structure is covered with aluminum.”
Suitable aluminum was also unavailable in Gaza, either, so they eventually landed on another solution: Jerusalem limestone salvaged from destroyed buildings, cleaned and reused, to cover the structure. Each stone, five centimeters thick, was drilled at its four corners and fitted with a metal bracket to attach it to the steel structure.
“We placed one stone on top of another and secured them properly, and this beautiful structure emerged as a result of the hard work of the teams,” Abu Mueilaq said.
Once the exterior structure was resolved, the interior presented its own challenge.
Wood, cement, and suitable aluminum were all unavailable, but the team found aluminum used to manufacture kitchen cabinets — a material that had accumulated in warehouses because the other components needed to manufacture aluminum kitchens were unavailable. The aluminum was used to divide the building internally and create walls and partitions.
Abu Mueilaq says the project’s cost was extremely high, much like the cost of living in Gaza, he says, which increased many times over compared to before the genocide.
He also emphasizes that this experiment isn’t easily replicable. The materials used were recovered from within Gaza and cannot easily be salvaged or replaced.
“What we are using now cannot be used again later,” Abu Mueilaq explained.
The building, nevertheless, gave people something beyond shelter. “It gave people hope,” Abu Mueilaq said. “Hope that Gaza has the skilled workers, thinkers, and professionals capable of rebuilding their homeland if they are provided with the necessary resources.”
‘We are the builders’
Beyond the question of large-scale reconstruction, Palestinians have also resorted to ancient methods of building shelters that had been all but defunct for generations: using mud and clay to build houses.
Abu Shamala is one of them. The house he built from salvaged stones and clay is not large enough to accommodate his entire family, but it is a shelter. Still, it is a far cry away from what was once his family home of 500 square meters, made up of four stories that housed an extended family of over 20 people.
But Abu Shamala also worries about the approaching rainy season, since rain can dissolve the mud walls, and he cannot yet predict what will happen to the structure in such conditions.
“Obtaining clay is not straightforward either,” he explained. Khan Younis, where he lives, is divided into two areas: the eastern part, where clay can be located, and the western al-Mawasi area, which is sandy. The problem is that the clay-bearing eastern region is controlled by the Israeli military, beyond the so-called “Yellow Line” that demarcates the parts of Gaza divided between Israeli and Hamas control.
“Obtaining clay can sometimes come at the cost of lives,” Abu Shamala said. But despite the difficulties, he says building the house has given him a sense of movement toward stability, particularly after realizing that the Israeli occupation will not initiate or enable reconstruction and is instead increasing its restrictions on it.
“We are here, confronting the blockade and the aggression, trying to create life,” he said. “We are rebuilding our lives with our weak and limited resources, but we remain steadfast on our land.”
Abu Shamala says Israel accuses Palestinians of being destroyers, gesturing at the carnage surrounding him. “Here is a clear picture of who destroys and who builds. We build, and the enemy destroys.”
“This is the evidence of our love for our land,” he continued. “Of remaining steadfast on the land where we were born and raised, which gives back to us in equal measure to our affinity for it.”
He says he is part of a people that refuses to die and refuses to disappear.
“Despite the destruction, the bombing, the blockade, the deprivation of water and food, and the prevention of reconstruction, and despite all the crimes committed against us by the Israeli enemy, this is a people that builds its land with the barest of resources,” he said.
Tareq S. Hajjaj
Tareq S. Hajjaj is the Gaza Correspondent for Mondoweiss and a member of the Palestinian Writers Union. Follow him on Twitter/X at @Tareqshajjaj.

Türkiye's SCO membership perspective never means turning its back on West: President Erdogan

Türkiye's perspective of becoming a member of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) "never means turning its back on the West," President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Wednesday.
Speaking to reporters aboard the presidential plane while returning from the SCO Heads of State Summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, which he attended at the invitation of Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov, Erdogan said Ankara seeks to pursue a broad-based foreign policy.
"Our goal is to increase our own weight with a 360-degree vision," he said.
Erdogan said the Bishkek summit demonstrated Türkiye's determination to diversify its economic, political, and strategic options.
Türkiye has commercial and economic relations with SCO member states across a vast geography stretching from China and Central Asia to Russia and South Asia, he said.
Erdogan noted that Türkiye has made significant progress in its relations with the organization in recent years as a reflection of its multidimensional foreign policy.
"Türkiye is a country that can develop balanced relations with both the West and the East and deepen its ties accordingly," he said, adding that Ankara sees the possibility of advancing its relations with the SCO further.
Russia-Ukraine conflict
On the Russia-Ukraine war, Erdogan said both he and Russian President Vladimir Putin want the conflict to end in peace as soon as possible.
Erdogan said his meeting with Putin on the sidelines of the summit was "very productive" and held in a "very sincere atmosphere," with the two leaders discussing developments concerning the Russia-Ukraine war.
"We want a peace process between Russia and Ukraine to take place as soon as possible and for peace to prevail in the region," Erdogan said.
He said the war has produced no beneficial outcome for the region, the world or the parties involved, adding that Putin also wants the conflict to end.
"I told Mr. Putin that we are ready to do everything we can for peace. It is a fact that peace, not war, will win. We are ready to make every effort for this," he added.
Erdogan also stressed the importance of the security of civilian maritime transportation in the Black Sea, saying the fighting must not reach a point that threatens the safety of civilians and commercial activity.
He said Türkiye's concern extends beyond Turkish-flagged or Turkish-operated vessels to all civilian maritime transportation in the Black Sea.
"We need a mechanism that will permanently ensure the security of commercial maritime transportation in the Black Sea," Erdogan said.
He also warned that the grain crisis is re-emerging, particularly in Africa, and said it would be beneficial to take an initiative before the problem grows further.
F-35 program, indigenous KAAN fighter jet
Turning to defense issues, Erdogan said Türkiye is continuing talks on rejoining the F-35 fighter jet program.
He recalled that Türkiye was previously a partner in the program and had made significant contributions to it.
"We are continuing our talks on Türkiye's re-inclusion in the program. Once the processes in the US are completed, this issue will be behind us," he said.
At the same time, Erdogan stressed that Türkiye would continue developing its own defense capabilities.
"We are not giving up on KAAN or developing our own air defense systems. We are increasing Türkiye's options. This is the roadmap of a strong Türkiye," he said.
‘Mecca Defense Alliance established for stability, security in region’
On the Mecca Defense Alliance, Erdogan said the pact was established to promote stability and security in the region.
He described the first meeting of the alliance's strategic, political, and military committee in Istanbul as "very important," saying the foreign and defense ministers and chiefs of general staff of Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan came together to take the alliance's first concrete steps.
Erdogan said the meeting addressed the establishment and operationalization of a secretariat, as well as military and political issues.
Defense industry cooperation and operational military cooperation, including military training, standardization, and the sharing of information on military threats, capabilities, and capacities, were also discussed, he added.
Decisions were taken on the timing and implementation of those steps, Erdogan said.
"There are very few countries that openly oppose this alliance, but there are also countries that oppose it behind the scenes," he said. “The balance between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Türkiye makes it difficult for many actors to openly criticize this alliance.”
"This alliance was established for stability and security in our region. We will continue on our path together with our brothers, growing stronger," he added.
‘Greece must reverse wrong path’
Erdogan also called on Greece to reverse a "wrong path" and stop arming islands with demilitarized status.
He said Türkiye wants to proceed with Greece on the basis of good neighborly relations and has acted sincerely and constructively, but often did not see its goodwill reciprocated.
"Greece must now understand this: Türkiye has no designs on anyone's territory, but it will not allow anyone to violate its rights," Erdogan said.
He warned that disregarding and violating international agreements would benefit no one.
"Anyone who interprets Türkiye's calm and prudent approach as weakness is making a grave mistake," he said.
“Greece must reverse this wrong path and stop arming islands with demilitarized status. History is a very good guide for those who learn lessons from it.”
Erdogan said Türkiye would continue working for peace, security, and stability in the region.
‘Terror-Free Türkiye’ process
On the "Terror-Free Türkiye" initiative, Erdogan said Ankara sees the process as a matter of achieving its objectives rather than merely adhering to a timeline.
"Of course, as a state, we have our roadmap, plan, and schedule," he said.
Referring to the framework legislation linked to the process, Erdogan said its implementation requires the PKK to lay down its arms and dissolve.
"How the determinations and verifications will be made is clear. The process is moving forward step by step," he said.
Erdogan said Türkiye would not tolerate approaches that damage the nation's sense of brotherhood or risk reactivating fault lines created by terrorism in the past.
"We will strengthen the home front. With our differences, we will unite around the common denominator of Türkiye. We call this the Great Türkiye Consensus. We are moving forward knowing what we are doing," he added.
Syria, dissolution of SDF
On Syria, Erdogan said Türkiye wants the country to be united with all its components, stressing that such unity is important for sustainable development and capacity building.
Erdogan welcomed the announced decision on the dissolution of the SDF and its integration, saying Türkiye is following its implementation on the ground along with the Syrian side.
He praised Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa's handling of difficult processes and said Ankara is hopeful about both the integration process and the gains achieved by the Syrian people.
Erdogan said he believes the process would "open the door to a new era" not only for Türkiye and Syria but for the entire region.
"The chapter of terrorism must now close. The era of weapons and violence must now come to an end," he said.
Asked about Washington's recent emphasis on Syria's territorial integrity, Erdogan said Türkiye's position on the country has remained consistent.
"We are saying today what we said yesterday about Syria," he said.
Türkiye had long warned that Syria could not be allowed to become an arena for terrorist organizations and that instability there could spread across the region, Erdogan said.
"It means that America has now also become aware of the realities of Syria," he added.
Erdogan called on all neighboring and friendly countries to help with Syria's reconstruction.
He also stressed the need to counter provocations and prevent those seeking to undermine Syria's internal peace from gaining room to operate.
"The path to stability in Syria lies in clearing away the seeds of discord," he said.

What do we know about the fatal US bombing of a wedding in Iran’s Sirik?

What do we know about the fatal US bombing of a wedding in Iran’s Sirik?
A residential building and a telecommunications tower were struck overnight, as Iran and the US launched more strikes over the control of Strait of Hormuz.
Tehran, Iran – The city of Kuhestak, located in southern Iran’s Sirik County in Hormozgan province, close to the Strait of Hormuz, was the target of multiple overnight attacks by the United States military, with local sources and authorities saying a wedding ceremony was struck.
The Hormozgan governor’s office on Wednesday identified four victims as four-year-old Amir Ali Karimi, 16-year-old Mohammad Malahi, 43-year-old Kolsoum Malahi and 43-year-old Zarkhatoun Taheri. More than 60 others were wounded, some seriously.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4UN watchdog urges access to Iran nuclear sites over proliferation concerns
- list 2 of 4Iran says US bombed a wedding party in Sirik, killing at least four people
- list 3 of 4‘We had an ordinary life’: Iran fisherwoman navigates uncertainty of war
- list 4 of 4Iran, US exchange new attacks: Who was hit in latest strikes?
Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for US Central Command (CENTCOM), said they were aware of reports of civilian casualties “originated from Iranian state media”.
“The US military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC,” he said, in reference to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
But while the operational details behind the strikes remain unclear, numerous videos and images from the area, witness accounts and official reports indicate that multiple projectiles hit Kuhestak, some to deadly effect.
Footage showed that several projectiles struck a telecommunications tower located near the city’s shoreline and destroyed it, with some locals saying they believed drones were among the weapons used. Based on fragments found in Kuhestak, defence experts say it might be a variant of the AGM-84K SLAM-ER, which manufacturer Boeing describes as an advanced precision-guided, air-launched cruise missile with “surgical strike capability”.
Wednesday morning’s footage, taken from some distance from the telecom tower, shows at least one direct hit to the roof of the building where the wedding was taking place.
More videos, released by locals and state media, showed partial destruction and debris inside the building, and electricity going out in the area. Women’s and children’s slippers could be seen scattered around. Several other adjacent residential buildings also sustained damage.
A state television reporter said three US missiles were used in the attack, with one penetrating through the roof and creating a 1.5-metre (5-foot) hole in the ground.
A man identified as Ali Malahi, the owner of the targeted building where his daughter’s wedding was taking place, told state television that people inside were all civilians.
State TV footage from a hospital in the area showed several wounded children and their families receiving medical care.
A young local man wounded in the attack said he and others were heading towards the house when they heard jets flying above, and the bombs caused massive explosions while they were arriving.
“Many young children and women were horribly wounded,” he said from the hospital bed.
A woman with bloodied hands said in a video released by state-linked SNN that she was there at the scene and could confirm that people present at the scene were civilians.
“This house was by no means close to any military site,” she said, adding that it appeared the munitions were directly targeting the building.
The Iranian Red Crescent Society said the incident was thoroughly documented, as it released several images from the site of the attack and the children who were injured.
It wrote to the Office of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court, seeking legal action against the perpetrators of the “grave” attack.
Other prominent attacks on civilians
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the strikes in Kuhestak complete the “catalogue of atrocities against the nation of Iran” by the US.
“This cruelty cannot be separated from the chain of atrocities that preceded it in Minab, Lamerd, Qeshm and elsewhere nor from the strikes on military targets that were dressed in deceptive justifications,” spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei wrote on X.
“More dangerous than the bomb itself is the normalisation of bombing; and more dangerous than silence is the conversion of silence into legitimacy,” he said.
In Minab, also located in Hormozgan province, the deadliest strike of the war in terms of civilian casualties largely destroyed an elementary school packed with children on the first day of the war on February 28. The attack killed about 156 people, mostly schoolchildren, as well as teachers, parents and others.
Despite evidence that its Tomahawk missiles were used in the attack, the US military has refused to release findings from its investigation. CENTCOM commander Brad Cooper claimed the school was located “on an active IRGC cruise missile base”.
In the southern Fars province’s city of Lamerd, evidence and witness accounts pointed to a missile strike on a sports hall being used by a women’s volleyball team on the first day of the war, killing 21 people, including four children.
While CENTCOM denied responsibility and accused Iran, investigations by The New York Times, BBC and independent analysts concluded that a US Precision Strike Missile (PrSM) was responsible for the destruction.
The munition was designed to explode midair, scattering thousands of tungsten pellets that could claim casualties and deal damage to buildings and vehicles in a large area.
During over six months of war on Iran, the US and Israel have also struck critical infrastructure like oil and gas facilities, fuel depots, steel and petrochemical factories, airports, ports and bridges, as well as power installations, medical centres and water facilities.
More than 3,500 Iranians have been killed since the start of the war, including more than 50 during the 60-day truce amid renewed fighting in July, according to authorities.

Newly discovered ‘demon cave fish’ hid out in Alabama military installation for 40 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:57:07 UTC
19:57:07 KST

Some hills in northern Alabama are burial mounds from the Copena people who lived there 2,000 years ago. Some contain decommissioned nerve gas from the cold war. But one holds a portal to the underworld—a low-slung knoll in a restricted military installation leads to a cramped but sprawling limestone network called Bobcat Cave, where scientists have discovered a strange, eyeless creature they’ve dubbed the demon cave fish.
The cave isn’t exactly welcoming to human visitors. “You’re stooped to hands and knees, crawling, and depending on the water level, you could be in neck-deep,” says Matthew L. Niemiller, a cave biologist at the University of Alabama in Huntsville. But because the system is a stronghold for the endangered Alabama cave shrimp, monitoring teams have explored the cave nearly every month since the early 1990s.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Despite this scrutiny, the demon cave fish was discovered only recently and completely by chance. On a routine survey in February 2025, Niemiller slipped in the red Alabama mud and fell headlong into a deep pool of water—and found himself face-to-face with a creature he didn’t recognize. This fish had a humped back and a slightly duckbilled snout, and, unlike the slightly more colorful Southern cave fish already known to inhabit the system, it was so ghostly white it looked blue under their headlamps. “It’s a shock and kind of embarrassing, in a way,” that it escaped notice for so long, says Niemiller, lead author of a paper presenting the new species and genus in Scientific Reports.
Genetic analyses suggest the demon cave fish and the Southern cave fish aren’t closely related and made their way underground separately: it appears they lost their vision because of different mutations. The study authors say it’s surprising to see two cave fish species living in not just the same cave system but the same pools and chambers. Whereas other cohabitating cave fish are like neighbors, the demon and Southern cave fish are like roommates—if those roommates had been trapped together for millions of years and potentially snacked on each other’s children.
Niemiller and his team have named the new species Demogorgonichthys arcanus, a wink to the otherworldly creature that emerged in a secret federal lab in the Netflix series Stranger Things. The finding is a humbling reminder of how much biodiversity remains undocumented even in the best-explored caves, says Suzanne McGaugh, an ecologist and cave fish expert at the University of Minnesota, who wasn’t involved in the new study. “We owe a debt of gratitude to them for their discovery,” she says.

Russia Pushes Across Four Fronts but Fails to Break Through as Ukraine Counterattacks, ISW Says
