Xi's Cairo visit tests Egypt's ties with Washington
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:43:11 UTC
19:43:11 KST

Breadcrumb
Xi in Cairo: testing balance between Beijing and Washington
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi is holding expanded talks Wednesday, 2 Sep, at the Ittihadiya Palace with Chinese President Xi Jinping, who arrived in Cairo on Tuesday, 1 September, for an official visit, his first in 10 years.
The visit coincides with the 70th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between Cairo and Beijing.
The talks with Xi in Cairo come amid an announced focus on advancing the Egyptian-Chinese partnership.
According to the Egyptian presidency, the visit includes "following up on the implementation of the comprehensive strategic partnership agreement concluded between the two countries in 2014, as well as consultations on several regional and international issues of common interest."
Regional and international developments are set to feature on Xi's agenda in Cairo and in his meeting with Sisi, particularly Gaza, the Middle East, the Red Sea, and the Nile River.
The future of the international system and relations among countries in the Global South are also expected to be featured.
The timing of the visit is sensitive for Cairo, which is operating in a turbulent regional environment stretching from Israel's war on Gaza and its repercussions to Sudan and the Red Sea, as well as the continuing dispute with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam.
At the same time, Egypt is seeking to expand its international room for manoeuvre by strengthening its relations with China and other powers, without abandoning its strategic partnership with the United States.
Palestine
The Palestinian issue appears to be the most prominent regional file bringing the Egyptian and Chinese positions together, which will be reflected in Xi's talks in Cairo.
This comes as Egypt has a direct role in mediation and arrangements concerning the Gaza Strip, while China occupies a different position as a permanent member of the UN Security Council.
In an article translated into Arabic and published by Egypt's Al-Ahram newspaper on Tuesday on the occasion of the visit, Xi wrote that "both sides firmly support the just cause of the Palestinian people in restoring their legitimate rights and seek political solutions to hot-button issues and the achievement of peace and stability in the region."
Egyptian sources told The New Arab that Sisi and Xi will discuss developments in Gaza, the future of political and security arrangements in the Strip and reconstruction.
They will also discuss the repercussions of regional conflicts on maritime security and developments related to Iran and the Gulf.
The war in Sudan will also be discussed, as it is a crisis that intersects with the security of the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa, according to the sources.
Maritime stability is a direct interest for both countries.
Egypt is concerned with protecting the Suez Canal and its interests in the Red Sea, while China relies on the region as a major route for its trade with Europe.
Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam: A test of China's position
On the Nile and the Ethiopian Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, the issue most directly related to Egyptian national security, Sisi was keen, in an article published in Al-Ahram on Tuesday, to point to the Chinese position calling for the avoidance of unilateral measures.
He wrote that "Egypt highly appreciates China's position, which affirmed its recognition of the vital importance of the Nile River to Egypt as its main lifeline and renewed the importance of refraining from taking unilateral measures and strengthening cooperation in good faith to achieve mutual benefit and win-win cooperation."
The message takes on significance ahead of Xi's talks in Cairo because of China's close relations with Ethiopia.
This makes Beijing an important international party for Cairo in its efforts to establish the principle of not harming the water interests of downstream countries.
Cairo does not appear to be seeking an explicit Chinese alignment against Ethiopia as much as it seeks to strengthen the Chinese position, calling for negotiations, consensus and the rejection of imposing a fait accompli.
This position could provide Egypt with diplomatic leverage in any future move concerning the Nile waters.
Although Sudan does not appear to be a main theme of the visit, its geographic location makes it part of Egyptian and Chinese calculations regarding the Red Sea and Africa.
Egypt is concerned with preserving Sudan's unity and stability and preventing the repercussions of the war from reaching its borders and interests.
China, meanwhile, has economic and political interests in Sudan and the African continent.
Balancing Beijing and Washington
According to experts, Cairo has maintained its strategic relations with Washington in recent years while expanding its relations with Beijing, Moscow, Europe and other powers.
However, Xi's visit to Egypt allows Cairo to strengthen what Sisi calls "strategic balance" by developing deeper relations with a major international power.
It also allows Egypt to benefit from China's permanent membership of the UN Security Council and its economic and political weight.
In his article on Tuesday, Sisi wrote that Egypt had adhered to "a policy of strategic balance as a direction for Egyptian foreign policy at a time when waves of polarisation and competition are rising, affirming its independent foreign policy and calling for the international community to coordinate its efforts to overcome global challenges that have come to threaten the entire world."
Significance of Xi in Cairo
In the same article, Sisi stressed that Egypt and China had become "partners contributing together to strengthening the role of the Global South in the global system in a way that achieves greater justice and fairness for developing countries."
In this regard, the future of the international system is likely to be one of the issues raised during Xi's talks in Cairo.
The issue is important for Cairo because of its membership in the BRICS group, founded in 2006 by Brazil, Russia, India and China.
Egypt, the UAE, Iran, Ethiopia and Indonesia joined the group during 2024 and 2025.
Cairo is also engaged in various multilateral frameworks, while Beijing sees Egypt as a partner that can help expand Chinese cooperation with the Arab world and Africa.
In this regard, former Egyptian ambassador to Beijing Ali El-Hefny told The New Arab that the importance of the visit and Xi's talks in Cairo was not linked only to the strength of bilateral relations but also to the circumstances facing the region and the world.
He explained that there was a clear convergence between the Egyptian and Chinese visions regarding the importance of stability in the region.
El-Hefny added that the repercussions of wars and conflicts in the Middle East do not stop at the borders of the countries where they take place but extend to the global economy and the interests of international powers, including China.
In his view, Egyptian-Chinese relations can form an important basis for supporting stability.
He noted that the partnership between the two countries should not be limited to the economic sphere, but could be expanded to include technology, industry, investment, infrastructure and other sectors that serve development plans.
El-Hefny stressed that maintaining stability is the condition through which these ambitions can be achieved.
For his part, former Egyptian assistant foreign minister Mohamed Hegazy said the Chinese president's visit to Egypt carries political and economic importance, particularly amid growing international polarisation and rising regional tensions.
He said these circumstances create a need to expand areas of cooperation without becoming involved in specific alliances or blocs.
Hegazy told The New Arab that what distinguishes relations between Cairo and Beijing is their historical foundation, which has allowed them to continue and develop despite changing international circumstances.
He considered China's current rise in influence to be, in part, a return to a global position it had historically occupied.
He added that Egypt's geographic location, political weight and ties with the Arab world and Africa give it a particular ability to develop its partnership with China.
This means the partnership does not have to remain confined to the bilateral framework but can extend to Egypt's regional surroundings.
In his view, the challenge during the next phase is to turn seven decades of trust and understanding between the two countries into more influential practical partnerships.
Such partnerships can offer a more balanced model for cooperation among countries around the world.
Article translated from Arabic by Afrah Almatwari. To read the original, click here.

Kernel makes world's first sale of low-carbon sunflower oil at sustainability premium
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:42:11 EEST
19:42:11 KST

Kernel agroholding has signed the world’s first deal to sell sunflower oil with a reduced carbon footprint and verified climate impact, the company’s press service reported.
"Despite the war and constant pressure on our operations, we continue working on climate-resilient solutions in the agricultural sector. And this deal proves that we can not only implement the relevant practices in production, but also verify the results through calculations and turn them into commercial value," said Marta Trofimova, Kernel’s head of sustainability.
The buyer was a multinational corporation pursuing a global net-zero carbon strategy, which paid a premium above the market price for verified emissions reductions in the product’s production, the statement said.
The carbon footprint reduction is achieved at three stages: sunflower cultivation, supply chain tracking, and oil production.
The project is based on a system for precisely calculating a harvest’s carbon footprint at the level of individual fields, taking into account soil, weather conditions, crop rotation and cultivation technologies. This makes it possible to identify fields where sunflowers are grown with the lowest climate impact and to build low-carbon supply chains.
The company tracks the entire chain - from the fields with the lowest carbon footprint, through elevators, to the plant - and can confirm exactly which fields the product comes from and the volume of reduced greenhouse gas emissions associated with it.
Kernel’s processing plants use electricity from renewable sources, further reducing atmospheric emissions.
"The global market for low-carbon agricultural products is only just taking shape. The size of the climate premium is calculated based on the volume of verified emissions reductions and the market value of a tonne of carbon, so the price can reach $100 or more per tonne of CO2 equivalent," the statement said.
To further automate calculations, ensure compliance with international standards, and scale up its low-carbon offering, Kernel has begun cooperating with the international technology company Regrow, the statement said.
According to the company, this is the first case on the global agricultural market in which transparency and verified emissions reductions across the entire production chain have created real added value for a product.
Kernel agroholding is the world’s largest producer and exporter of sunflower oil, Ukraine’s largest grain exporter, an operator of an extensive network of logistics assets, and a leading producer of grain and oilseed crops in Ukraine. It is also one of the largest producers and sellers of bottled oil in Ukraine. The company grows agricultural products and sells them.
For the first nine months of fiscal year 2026 (starting July 1, 2025), Kernel’s net profit fell 5% to $208 million, revenue rose 0.4% to $3.092 billion, and EBITDA rose 1% to $403 million.

BIG’s suzhou museum of contemporary art opens to the public as a village of 12 pavilions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

10:37:51 UTC
19:37:51 KST

BIG’S FIRST COMPLETED ART MUSEUM OPENS TO THE PUBLIC
Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG), together with ARTS Group, VIA.inc, and SHUISHI, completes the Suzhou Museum of Contemporary Art, a 60,000-square-meter cultural complex on the shores of Jinji Lake in Suzhou, China. Now officially open to the public, the museum is BIG’s first completed art museum and brings together twelve interconnected pavilions beneath a ribbon-like roof. The project draws on the spatial logic of Suzhou’s historic gardens to create a porous network of galleries, gardens, paths, bridges, and public spaces between the city and the lake.
The museum arrives in Suzhou’s rapidly developing lake district as a new venue for contemporary art, design, and public programming. Its opening follows a series of preview exhibitions, including BIG’s Materialism, which remains on view (find designboom’s previous coverage here). The inaugural program of the museum also includes exhibitions spanning modern and contemporary art, technology-driven artistic practices, and exchanges between Eastern and Western artistic traditions.
all images courtesy of Suzhou MoCA
A MUSEUM ORGANIZED LIKE A CHINESE GARDEN
At the center of BIG’s architectural concept is the lang 廊, the covered corridor traditionally found in Chinese gardens. The architects reinterpret this element as a continuous circulation route connecting the twelve pavilions that compose the museum building. Visitors move through galleries and gathering spaces along a main path while smaller routes branch toward individual exhibitions and gardens.
Bridges and tunnels connect spaces above and below ground, allowing the museum to operate less like a sequence of enclosed rooms and more like a landscape of interconnected destinations. The organization also gives the institution flexibility as exhibitions and public programs change over time.
For Bjarke Ingels, the project responds directly to its position between Suzhou’s urban fabric and Jinji Lake. ‘By dissolving the museum into a Chinese garden of interconnected galleries, distributed across the site like pavilions in a park, the museum becomes a connection between the city and the lake, rather than an obstacle,’ he says. The underlying ambition of the proposal is one of urban porosity: visitors can move through sculpture gardens toward the waterfront while water and landscape extend between the buildings.
Suzhou Museum of Contemporary Art sits on the shores of Jinji Lake
CONTINUOUS ROOF LINKS 12 PAVILIONS ACROSS SUZHOU’S LANDSCAPE
From above, the looping roof of the museum creates a distinct figure across the site. BIG describes its geometry as recalling an infinity knot, while Catherine Huang, Partner at BIG, compares the aerial composition to traditional papercut patterns framing the gardens below. The roof also responds to the neighboring Ferris wheel, whose elevated visitors overlook the museum. As Ingels notes, this makes the roof surface effectively the building’s ‘fifth facade.’ The project therefore considers two very different experiences at once: a precise graphic composition viewed from above and a more fluid sequence of gardens, art, and architecture experienced at ground level.
‘The gardens begin to flow into one another, unfolding as sequences of spaces, views, art, and nature,’Huang says.‘A composition that appears precise from above’ becomes ‘an experience of exploration and discovery on the ground.’
The strongest idea behind the project lies in its attempt to resist the conventional museum as an isolated object. Spread across twelve pavilions and threaded together by a continuous roof and circulation network, the Suzhou Museum of Contemporary Art positions movement through the site as part of the architectural experience. Whether that ambition translates into a genuinely public connection between city and waterfront will depend on how the gardens, galleries, and open routes are used over time.
Among the exhibitions currently presented at Suzhou MoCA is Materialism, BIG’s exploration of the materials used across its architectural projects. The exhibition follows ten materials, from stone to recyclate, through large-scale mock-ups and models. Alongside Materialism, the museum opens with exhibitions dedicated to modern and contemporary art, including a Picasso exhibition and a large survey of contemporary Chinese art.

Six missing after vessel capsizes off South Korea's southeastern coast

2026-09-02

19:37:49 KST

At least six people were missing after a tugboat capsized off the southeastern coast of South Korea on Wednesday, officials said.
The TNS Catcher, a 286-tonne tugboat, capsized about 9 kilometres southeast of Oryukdo with eight crew members aboard.
The crew comprised six South Korean nationals and two Indonesian nationals. An Indonesian crew member was rescued by a nearby merchant vessel 20 minutes after the accident. He was not in life-threatening condition.
A second Korean crew member was found unconscious inside the capsized tugboat and transported to a hospital aboard a Coast Guard rescue vessel but later died.
The Coast Guard deployed 13 patrol and rescue vessels, aircraft and the Korea Coast Guard Special Rescue Unit. It also requested assistance from the Navy, other government vessels and private boats.
The Coast Guard said waves of 1 to 1.5 metres and strong currents were complicating the operation. Northwesterly winds were blowing at 4 to 6 metres per second.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung directed authorities to “mobilise all available resources for the search and rescue efforts.”
It said a cargo ship passing through the area rescued one crew member, while the second was found unconscious.
At least eight crew members were believed to be aboard the vessel when it capsized.

80-Year-Old Sen. Ed Markey Holds Off Younger Challenger in Democratic Primary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:37:42 UTC
19:37:42 KST

Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts won the Democratic primary race for his seat on Tuesday, fending off a challenge from the decades-younger Rep. Seth Moulton as he seeks another six-year term in the upper chamber.
Running on a progressive platform, Markey adds to a series of primary wins including Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, suggesting an appetite among Democratic primary voters for a shift away from the center.
Read More: Congress Is Headed for a Massive Turnover
Moulton’s campaign focused largely on affordable housing and health care. His efforts to position himself as a fresh voice in politics ultimately failed against Markey’s decades of experience.
With around 96% of the ballots counted early Wednesday, Markey had 64.9% of the vote to Moulton's 35.1%.
“Massachusetts needs a Senator who stands up and fights back, a Senator who never forgets who they are fighting for,” Markey told the crowd during his victory speech. “That has been the mission of my life, and it always will be.”
A ‘generational showdown’
Tuesday’s primary was considered by many to be a “generational showdown” between Markey, 80, and Moulton, 47.
During the campaign, Moulton contended that it was time for change in the state's political representation.
“Massachusetts has a choice: settle for the status quo, or demand better,” he wrote in a social media post Tuesday.
The young moderate rose in the polls earlier this year, narrowing the gap between himself and the two-term incumbent. But in the month or so leading up to Tuesday’s primary, polls showed that Markey had regained ground and was holding a comfortable double-digit lead.
This isn’t the first time Markey, who served in the House for nearly 37 years before winning a seat in the Senate in 2013, has held off a younger primary challenger. In his last reelection bid, the then-74-year-old Senator defeated then-Rep. Joseph Kennedy III, who is 34 years his junior, to advance to the November ballot.
Progressives notch another primary victory
Markey has built up a long progressive record over his years in Congress, co-sponsoring the Green New Deal alongside Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and championing left-wing positions on an array of issues. And he made that record—as well as his extensive experience—a focus of his campaign. Markey argued during the primary that Moulton’s stances on various issues don't align with those of their constituents in deep-blue Massachusetts, saying that “there’s only one progressive in this race” and that “we don’t just need a democratic majority in the Senate. We need a progressive majority.”
“It’s not about your age, it’s about the age of your ideas. And I am the youngest guy in this race when it comes to ideas,” Markey told POLITICO. “Democrats want a victory this November. But then they want, beginning next January … a progressive vision turned into reality on the floor of the House and Senate.”
Markey, a staunch and vocal supporter of transgender rights, criticized Moulton for comments he made about transgender athletes in the aftermath of the 2024 election. In an interview with The New York Times in 2024, Moulton said, “I have two little girls, I don’t want them getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete, but as a Democrat I’m supposed to be afraid to say that.”
Moulton has since apologized, saying during a debate last month, “If you’re in the trans community or you’re a trans kid feeling the weight of the Trump Administration and the Supreme Court, you matter.” The Congressman also told POLITICO over the weekend, “I never intended to hurt anybody with my comments,” but went on to say, “I absolutely do not apologize for starting a debate that we need to be willing to have in the Democratic Party.”
Markey is the latest of a number of progressives who have emerged victorious in recent races. Last month, Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, while other progressives earned the party’s nominations in key House races in the state. And Democratic socialists have scored wins in several high-profile contests in the past year, with Zohran Mamdani—who sent shockwaves through the Democratic establishment when he won the New York City mayoral race in November—perhaps most prominent among them.
Markey will next face the uncontested Republican nominee, John Deaton, a lawyer who previously unsuccessfully challenged Sen. Elizabeth Warren for her seat in Congress.
But Democrats are expected to keep the Senate seat in November: The Cook Political Report rates the race as “Solid Democrat,” ranking it among the seats it considers least likely to flip in the upcoming midterms.

EU is already advancing new sanctions against Russia - what is being proposed and will there be a change in approach
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:36:02 EEST
19:36:02 KST

EU is already advancing new sanctions against Russia - what is being proposed and will there be a change in approach
Kyiv • UNN
Kaja Kallas said that a proposal for sanctions against 1,600 entities in russia’s military-industrial complex is being advanced. The new restrictions may be adopted in the autumn.
The European Union has taken another step toward introducing new sanctions against Russia. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on September 2 that a new proposal for restrictions against 1,600 entities was advancing within the bloc, while not ruling out expanding the list, UNN writes.
New sanctions against the Russian Federation
The EU's High Representative, arriving at an informal meeting of the EU countries' foreign ministers, announced that an attack in Leipzig would be discussed.
"First of all, of course, everyone will discuss the attacks in Leipzig, and it is also obvious that this bears all the hallmarks of state terrorism. The question is, what do we do about it? We have already summoned the Russian ambassadors, as have many member states, and we will discuss what else we can do," Kallas said.
We are already advancing a list of 1,600 entities from Russia's military complex, and more may be added. Of course, this is not something we are deciding today, since this is an informal meeting. But we will certainly discuss it
Russian hybrid attacks are an "alarm bell" for countries that have so far been reluctant to impose deeper sanctions, she said.
According to Radio Free Europe's Europe editor Rikard Jozwiak on X on September 2, "EU member states have received a proposal to impose sanctions against another 1,600 individuals/organizations from the Russian Federation."
Meanwhile, Jozwiak noted, "only Slovakia is opposing the extension of the current blacklist (3,000+) for 12 months instead of the current 6."
What the new sanctions entail
In August, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said that the European Union intended to significantly expand sanctions against Russia in the coming months because of its war in Ukraine.
"EU sanctions have already cost Russia dearly, depriving its war machine of more than €1 trillion (US$1.16 trillion), and in the autumn I will propose the farthest-reaching sanctions lists since the beginning of the war," Kallas told Die Welt.
"Once adopted, the total number of sanctioned Russian entities will immediately increase by one-third. The pressure must continue to grow until Moscow ends its war," Kallas said.
At the time, she did not specify the timing or details of the new sanctions lists, but later EU diplomatic sources told Reuters that the European External Action Service (EEAS) would propose adding around 1,600 individuals and organizations based in Russia and focused on Moscow's military-industrial complex to the list.
They added that the new sanctions would include travel and transaction bans, as well as asset freezes. The EU has already listed nearly 3,000 individuals and companies.
The aim is to adopt the new sanctions in October, Reuters sources added.
What else is being proposed amid the attack in Leipzig
The foreign ministers of European countries will discuss adapting their approach to sanctions against the Russian economy at a meeting on September 2. This is happening as the EU seeks to maintain pressure on Moscow, Euractiv notes.
Although Germany's accusations that Russia was behind the attack on Leipzig airport this summer gave fresh political impetus to calls for sanctions, the real reason for reconsideration, the publication writes, "is the growing difficulty of reaching unanimous agreement on new sanctions."
The latest package of sanctions against the Russian Federation, it is noted, "turned into a fierce tug-of-war between Greece and other member states in July, as Athens sought to protect its profitable gas transportation sector."
The heated discussions showed some that the EU's method of gradually increasing pressure on Moscow through large-scale cross-sectoral sanctions packages is exhausting its potential, the publication points out.
Instead, according to Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braže, the EU is exploring a more fragmented, or "thematic," approach.
"Whenever we have an ecosystem ready for sanctions, such as Russian ballistic missiles or cryptocurrencies, as soon as we have it, let's simply impose sanctions. We need to be faster," Braže said.
"Last time, there were issues unrelated to sanctions that delayed [the package]," she said. Large packages can still be proposed to include "slower" issues, Braže added.
The Baltic minister said that Europe should respond to Russia's attack in Leipzig by reducing the presence of Russians in Europe, restricting tourist visas and tightening restrictions on embassies.
What is Ukraine's position
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha also took part in the informal meeting of the foreign ministers of the European Union member states in the "Gymnich" format on September 2.
Speaking to journalists before the event began, the Foreign Minister stressed the need for a joint and resolute European response to the intensification of Russian aggression, including hybrid attacks against European states.
"Europe may think that it is not at war with Russia, but Russia does not think so (...) Putin will escalate, Putin does not want to end this war, so we must act jointly and decisively," Sybiha said.
The minister said that he would brief his European colleagues on the situation on the battlefield, Russia's missile terror and Ukraine's proposals for intensifying peace efforts. He would also call for stronger support for Ukraine's air defense and increased pressure on Russia, in particular through new sanctions against its missile production capabilities.
"We are working to secure additional strong decisions on closing Ukraine's skies," Ukraine's Foreign Minister stressed.
Sybiha paid particular attention to Ukraine's preparations for the coming winter and the need for additional support for the energy system, including generators, transformers and other necessary equipment.
"We are counting on the support of our partners to get through this winter with concrete decisions and concrete support," the minister said.
Other issues included the use of frozen Russian assets, Ukraine's further progress on its path toward EU membership and increasing pressure on Russia by blocking the Black Sea, which poses threats to global food security.
Kallas, for her part, noted regarding Ukraine that "it is clear that we need to coordinate what else we can do in this situation, when Russia is escalating and is truly killing civilians and causing them as much harm as possible."
"The discussions [will be about] how we can actually increase pressure on Russia so that they stop this war," the EU's chief diplomat noted.

Tunisia: Final judicial avenue to overturn convictions in unjust ‘conspiracy’ case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:32:45 UTC
19:32:45 KST

Ahead of the final appeal hearing at Tunisia’s Court of Cassation on 3 September in the unjust “conspiracy case”, which is a chance to overturn the convictions of opposition figures jailed solely because of their peaceful political opposition, Sara Hashash, Deputy Regional Director for the Middle East and North Africa at Amnesty International said:
“Tunisia’s authorities must seize this opportunity to rectify a travesty of justice that has upturned the lives of 34 prominent opposition figures, human rights defenders and lawyers who were convicted on unfounded charges in a mass trial marred by due process violations. These defendants were targeted with politically motivated charges and should have never been imprisoned in the first place. Many of them have been languishing in jail with deteriorating health problems, with recent successive heatwaves further worsening detention conditions inside poorly ventilated cells.
It is time to put an end to this pattern of instrumentalizing the justice system to target dissent.
Sara Hashash, Amnesty International
“The authorities must overturn these unjust convictions and sentences and release all those arbitrarily detained in this case. It is time to put an end to this pattern of instrumentalizing the justice system to target dissent. Authorities must ensure that prison conditions across the country comply with international standards and that all detainees have regular access to their families, lawyers and adequate healthcare. “
Background
On 18 April 2025, following a mass trial based on unfounded charges and marred by a litany of fair trial rights violations, the Tunis Criminal Court of First Instance convicted 37 individuals, including prominent politicians, lawyers and human rights defenders, on spurious “State security” charges and sentenced them to terms of imprisonment ranging from four to 66 years.
On 27 November 2025, the Tunis Court of Appeal upheld the convictions of 34 defendants and imposed prison sentences ranging from five to 45 years, following proceedings marred by serious violations of fair-trial rights. Those imprisoned include Ayachi Hammami, Chaima Issa, Ahmed Nejib Chebbi, Jaouhar Ben Mbarek, Issam Chebbi, Ghazi Chaouachi, Ridha Belhaj, Khayam Turki and Abdelhamid Jelassi, Sahbi Atig and Said Ferjani. Several defendants have been arbitrarily detained since February 2023 solely for exercising their human rights.

ICAC sets integrity standards for government computers to fight misuse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:32:33 UTC
19:32:33 KST

ICAC sets integrity standards for government computers to fight misuse
Independent Commission Against Corruption unveils standards after revealing procedures for government computer systems had loopholes
Hong Kong’s Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) has unveiled standards for the use of government computer systems after uncovering loopholes, including requiring bureaus and departments to ensure compliance when requesting digital project funds.
Danny Woo Ying-ming, commissioner of the ICAC, said on Wednesday that an investigation had found that some procedures for government computer systems had loopholes that raised the risk of corruption.
“Once systems are abused, data is tampered with and proper procedures bypassed, not only will it incur corruption risks, but it can also damage the government’s integrity,” he said at a ceremony introducing the standards.
Woo said that as of July, all government bureaus and departments were mandated by the Digital Policy Office to assess whether their computer systems complied with the standards when requesting funds under the Capital Works Reserve Fund for administrative computer systems.
The integrity assurance standards cover 12 steps for internal work processes and focus on users, system administration and monitoring.
Requiring government organisations to assess their compliance with the standards was intended to prevent corruption-related risks, the ICAC said.
Such risks include unauthorised data access, ineffective due diligence, circumvention of rules and over-reliance on manual steps, such as checking and sampling, that could be prone to manipulation for corruption.

Families hold symbolic funerals for thousands missing in Nepal floods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:32:00 UTC
19:32:00 KST

Families in Nepal held symbolic funerals Wednesday for relatives still missing a week after deadly flash floods swept away villages and homes in the Himalayan region.
Emergency teams have recovered more than 1,100 bodies and nearly 5,000 people are missing after the gigantic wave of freezing water, rocks and debris triggered by a high-altitude glacial collapse roared down the China-Nepal border on Aug. 26.
After days of searching shelters and mortuaries, relatives of some of the missing lost hope and began conducting last rites, burning straw effigies in Hindu rituals.
"We had to do this to set his soul free, so that he is at peace and happy wherever he is," said Dolma Newar Tamang, flanked by her sobbing son, at a funeral for her husband.
He had been en route to China when the disaster struck.
"I saw the news and called him," she told Agence France-Presse (AFP). "I called repeatedly, but he never picked up."
A week on from the colossal disaster, Nepali rescuers are still seeking survivors, including by digging through packed sludge that has entombed multiple tunnels of hydropower plants.
So far, rescuers have recovered only bodies from tunnels, but teams were still digging, drilling and blasting through debris.
Nepal's Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said he still hoped some missing could be alive.
"Miracles do happen," he told AFP. "At this point, I do not want to completely give up hope."
There is growing anger at the scale of destruction to hit Nepal, a largely rural nation of 30 million people.
The country has contributed little to the greenhouse gas emissions driving global warming, but is among those suffering its consequences.
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah warned the catastrophe was "a serious indication" of the risks the Himalayan nation faces.
Scientists say the Himalayas, the world's highest mountain range, are warming rapidly as global temperatures rise, accelerating glacier melt.
Glaciers in the wider Himalayan and Hindu Kush ranges are a crucial water source for around 240 million people in the mountainous regions, as well as for another 1.65 billion people in the South Asian and Southeast Asian river valleys below.
"Climate change is a global contribution, and disaster response is also a global responsibility," Shah said in a social media post.
Kathmandu has warned reconstruction could cost billions of dollars.
Nepal, which marks a year this month since deadly mass protests over rampant corruption and a woeful economy overthrew the then government, has limited resources to respond to a disaster of this scale.
In an illustration of the scale of destruction, Chinese state media said road access to hard-hit Gyirong Port in Tibet had finally been restored on Wednesday after "days of round-the-clock repair work."
With mortuaries overflowing in Nepal, authorities have had to bury hundreds of unidentified bodies after DNA sampling.
Nepal said 1,114 bodies had been recovered by Wednesday, while 3,916 people remained missing.
China's state media reported 16 dead and 546 missing.
That takes the overall number of reported dead to 1,130, and 4,462 missing.
More than 800 foreigners from over 30 nations are among the missing: 583 in Nepal and 261 in China.
They include tourists who came to trek in the Himalayas, as well as Hindu pilgrims seeking spiritual peace at Tibet's sacred Mount Kailash.
At least 17 bodies have also been pulled from rivers downstream in India.
In China, foreign journalists are restricted from reporting in Tibet, and Chinese authorities have a tight grip on information sources in the region.
Tibetan advocacy groups in exile have questioned China's account of the disaster, but Beijing insists that the "release of information has been open, transparent and timely."

MOD allocates £50m to military medical upgrades
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:30:56 BST
19:30:56 KST

The Ministry of Defence has allocated up to £50 million over four years for battlefield medical equipment, blood products, treatments for severe bleeding and field hospital equipment as it seeks to rebuild Defence Medical Services capacity for larger-scale operations, the department has said.
The funding was set out in a written parliamentary answer to Conservative MP Stuart Anderson, who asked the Defence Secretary what capabilities were planned for the Defence Medical Services in terms of capacity and specialised medical care. Veterans and People Minister Calvin Bailey said the DMS supports Defence outputs across the Royal Navy, Army, Royal Air Force and Cyber and Specialist Operations Command, including NATO commitments, crisis response, strategic resilience and global competition.
Bailey said: “The Strategic Defence Review recognised the need to rebuild both medical capacity and capability within Defence to ensure our Armed Forces remain fighting fit in peacetime and are prepared to meet operational demands when at war.” He said the immediate priority was to make the best use of existing capability so that the Defence Medical Services could reliably provide the support required by the Armed Forces today.
The second priority is the modernisation of operational medical capability and the healthcare support needed to generate forces for deployment. Bailey said: “The second priority is to modernise operational medical capability and the healthcare support to force generation to meet the demands of contemporary warfare and evolving clinical practice. To accelerate modernisation, Defence has allocated up to £50 million through the Defence Investment Plan over four years, focused on delivering priority capability enhancements.”
Of that funding, £20 million has been allocated to Tactical Combat Casualty Care, providing kits for combat personnel based on the latest research into equipment intended to save lives on the battlefield. A further £10 million will be used to develop or procure dried blood products for use forward, while £10 million has been allocated to Tranexamic Acid, or TXA, to improve the treatment of severe blood loss. The remaining £10 million will go towards field hospital equipment intended to support combat operations at scale.
The MOD is also preparing for a longer-term expansion of military medical capacity. Bailey said: “The third priority is to prepare to expand medical capacity to deliver the Strategic Defence Review’s vision of enhanced warfighting readiness.”
According to the minister, rebuilding Defence medical capability will concentrate on four functions: “Medically preparing the Integrated Force; maximising deployable medical capability and capacity within available resources; managing scalable and adaptable Operational Patient Care Pathways from point of injury or illness to definitive care and rehabilitation in collaboration with allies and UK healthcare systems; [and] building on our world class military medical research to adapt medical advances to gain operational advantage.”

The World’s 50 Best Hotels 2026: 16 hotels in Europe feature on extended 50-100 list
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:30:23 UTC
19:30:23 KST

Ahead of The World’s 50 Best Hotels 2026 unveiling on 15 September, an extended ranking sees 16 properties in Europe included in the 50-100 list.
As the hospitality world counts down the days to see which properties make the cut for The World's 50 Best Hotels 2026 list, an extended ranking has revealed the hotels in 51st to 100th place.
Unveiled by 50 Best, the 51-100 list features hotels from 23 different territories and 40 cities, with 16 properties in Europe, including nine in Italy.
Determined by the votes of more than 800 anonymous experts, The World’s 50 Best Hotels ranking for 2026 will be unveiled in Paris on 15 September.
Asia leads the way, followed by Europe
In the 51-100 rundown, Asia tops the list with 20 hotels ranked. Japan alone has seven properties in the ranking, with Janu Tokyo at No.52, while other new entries in the capital include Park Hyatt Tokyo (No.53), The Okura (No.69) and Palace Hotel Tokyo (No.73).
Represented by 16 hotels, Europe’s entries on the extended list span both “newly opened properties and long-established favourites”, 50 Best said.
La Réserve Paris re-enters and tops the extended list at No.51, while France is home to three other properties, including new entries Ritz Paris at No.72 and Carlton Cannes (No.80).
The Maybourne Riviera, in Roquebrune-Cap-Martin, has also re-entered the list at No.93.
Of the European countries, Italy has the highest number of hotels included, with nine.
Il San Pietro di Positano (No.58) is Italy’s highest new entry, while Castiglion del Bosco in Montalcino (No.62), Orient Express La Minerva in Rome (No.66), Forestis Dolomites (No.68) in Brixen, and Villa Treville in Positano (No.91) all enter the list for the first time.
Splendido in Portofino comes in at No.60, followed by Borgo Santandrea in Amalfi at No.84 and Borgo Egnazia in Savelletri at No.88. Reschio in Lisciano Niccone was ranked at No.95.
Elsewhere in Europe, the UK has two hotels on the list: new entry Rosewood London (No.56) and Gleneagles (No.100) in Auchterarder, Scotland. In Türkiye, independently-owned Maçakızı in Bodrum was at No.76.
Meanwhile, North America had a total of nine hotels on the 51-100 ranking, while South America and Oceania had two each, and Africa one.
European hotels on the 51-100 list
Sixteen hotels in Europe were included on the extended list:

Europe vows to stay united as hybrid war activity surges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:29:23 UTC
19:29:23 KST

Europe and Canada have said they won't succumb to the growing number of hybrid attacks from Russia. The show of unity comes as Germany takes the unprecedented step of formally blaming to the Kremlin for a drone incident at Leipzig airport last month.
European foreign ministers have said they're ready to stand firm against a surge of Russian hybrid war attacks across the continent, rallying behind Germany after its decision to formally hold Russia responsible for a drone incident at Leipzig airport last month.
The show of unity came at a summit of EU foreign affairs ministers in Wicklow, Ireland, also attended by ministers from Ukraine, Canada, Switzerland and the United Kingdom.
The Leipzig airport incident on 4 August saw German authorities intercept a drone carrying military-grade explosives. Berlin has been unequivocal in attributing the incursion to the Kremlin.
"The means used – such as the drone configuration, components, explosives and detonation systems – are known to us from other hybrid operations by Russia," German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said on Tuesday, framing the attack as part of a "long series of destabilisation operations" against Europe.
In remarks condemning Russia's activities, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband referred to his country's experience of Russian attacks in recent years, such as the attempted chemical assassination of former Russian KGB operative Sergei Skripal in Salisbury.
"We stand in full solidarity with Germany and Ukraine," Miliband told journalists. "We know from the past from Russian attacks on our soil these attempts to divide us will not work, but this is a dangerous sign of attempt by Russia to divide us and to think they can send a chilling effect on European countries when it comes to their invasion of Ukraine."
Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys, meanwhile said Russia appears to be dialling up the volume of hybrid attacks it is launching.
"We see they are expanding and quadrupled attacks against us in the last year," he said. "Our goal is to show these activities won't intimidate us or stop us supporting Ukraine."
Also on the agenda at the informal so-called Gymnich meeting are proposals that the European Commission could reopen the question of using immobilised Russian sovereign assets to fund Ukraine, an idea being pushed by Sweden, Spain and Poland and the Netherlands.
Finnish Minister for Foreign Affairs Elina Valtonen said that "Europe needs to support Ukraine ahead of the winter".
"This is a good space and time to talk about the frozen assets," she said ahead of the summit. "We need to explore all options on the table."

Sweden convenes National Security Council after Berlin blames Russia for Leipzig drone incident
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:29:00 EEST
19:29:00 KST

Sweden convenes National Security Council after Berlin blames Russia for Leipzig drone incident
Sweden has held a meeting of its National Security Council in response to the German government's statement that Russia was involved in an incident in which a drone fitted with explosives was found at Leipzig airport.
Source: Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson on X (Twitter), as reported by European Pravda
Details: Kristersson announced that a meeting of the National Security Council, which was convened after Germany said Russia was responsible for the failed drone attack at Leipzig airport, had just concluded in Stockholm.
"At the meeting, the Swedish Military Intelligence and Security Service and the Security Service briefed the government on their assessment of the situation regarding the Russian hybrid threat to Sweden. The government believes the events in Leipzig should be regarded as part of Russia's increasingly active hybrid actions, which are characterised by growing recklessness and indifference," the Swedish prime minister said.
"The aim of Russia's actions is to undermine Europe's support for Ukraine, increase pressure on our societies, and sow division and fear. But Russia will not succeed," Kristersson added.
Background:
- On 1 September, Germany directly accused Russia of carrying out a hybrid attack at Leipzig airport in early August and announced measures in response, including the closure of the consulate general in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul summoned the Russian ambassador in connection with this.
- The EU and several member states also summoned Russian diplomats over the Leipzig incident.

Russian attack on Kyiv injures seven people

Russians attack Dnipro: six injured, food warehouses damaged
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:28:00 EEST
19:28:00 KST

Two killed and eight injured in Russian missile strike on Dnipro – photos
Two people were killed and eight others were injured in a Russian missile strike on Dnipro on 2 September. Updated reports indicate that eight people have sustained injuries.
Source: Oleksandr Hanzha, Head of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Military Administration; Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Prosecutor's Office
Update: Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Military Administration said that the number of those who sustained injuries in the Russian attack on Dnipro had risen to eight. Three people have been taken to hospital in a critical condition, and the rest are in a moderate condition.
The Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Prosecutor's Office said early reports indicate that the Russians carried out the strike using a Banderol missile drone.
Two people were killed and five injured in the attack. Damage was caused to warehouse facilities, cars and a building belonging to an educational institution.
The Prosecutor's Office has launched an investigation into a war crime under Article 438 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine.
Details: Before the clarification came from the Prosecutor's Office, Hanzha had reported that two people had been killed. He said a woman who had sustained serious injuries died in hospital, and rescue workers recovered the body of a man from under the rubble.
Hanzha also reported damage to food warehouses belonging to a retail chain. A fire broke out in the city following the strike.
Background: On the night of 24-25 August, Russian forces destroyed the Karavan shopping centre in Dnipro.

‘Fight for humanity’: Avoiding a climate catastrophe means acting now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:22:02 UTC
19:22:02 KST

‘Fight for humanity’: Avoiding a climate catastrophe means acting now
Record heat waves, deadly flooding and extreme weather reflect an ever-warming planet poised to soon breach safe temperature limits, according to a UN report released on Tuesday, but doubling down on climate action now could avoid a climate catastrophe.
Key points
- Rapid, collective and global action is vital to cap the temperature rise at 1.5°C
- Climate action can reverse current trend by slashing methane pollution, protecting land, forest and oceans and accelerating the phaseout of fossil fuels
- Every fraction of a degree will cost lives, destroy livelihoods, deepen inequality and push ecosystems closer to irreversible damage
The scorching heat in the northern hemisphere in recent months, raging wildfires and deadly floods are a warning of what lies ahead, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said.
He recalled that the historic 2015 Paris Agreement on climate change saw world leaders pledge to keep temperature rise to the 1.5°C limit above pre-industrial levels, which scientists say is critical to avoiding the worst climate devastation.
Indeed, the world is failing to keep that promise, according to the new report from the UN Environment Programme (UNEP)
“The fight for 1.5 degrees is the fight for humanity,” he said. “We are set to breach the 1.5°C limit within the next few years.”
‘Every fraction of a degree will cost lives’
There are no good outcomes if temperatures remain above 1.5°C consistently, warned UNEP chief Inger Andersen.
“Across the globe, extreme heatwaves are already proving that climate impacts will strike faster, hit harder, and last longer, costing more lives and causing deeper disruption,” she said.
“Now is the time we must double down on climate action. We can and must get on the right path. By cutting greenhouse gas emissions, strengthening resilience and adaptation and ensuring exceedance of 1.5°C is as small and short as possible.”
The UN chief agreed.
“Every fraction of a degree will cost lives, destroy livelihoods, deepen inequality and push ecosystems closer to irreversible damage,” the Secretary-General said. “Humanity is speeding past the limit to avoid climate catastrophe.”
‘Solutions are at hand’
However, swift climate action can bring the world back from the brink, Mr. Guterres said.
“We can still bring warming back below 1.5°C by the end of the century,” he said. “We must make the overshoot as small and short as possible, limiting how high temperatures rise and how long they remain above 1.5.”
That demands an “overshoot of ambition” through accelerating the phaseout of fossil fuels and the renewables revolution, slashing methane pollution and protecting land, forest and oceans, he said.
It also means governments must over-deliver on national climate plans, net zero commitments and beyond, and developed countries must triple adaptation finance and ensure it reaches those most at risk.
“The science is clear,” Mr. Guterres said. “The solutions are at hand, and the world has never been better equipped to deploy them. Now is the time to raise ambition and accelerate action.”
Highlights from the new report:
- Above 1.5°C, risks and impacts will intensify with every extra fraction of a degree and every year, including intensified extreme weather, ecosystem loss and submersion of small island developing States and low-lying coastal cities alongside severe damage to human health, food security, water supplies, nature, cities, infrastructure and economies
- The likelihood of crossing irreversible tipping points increases with the magnitude and duration of higher temperatures, including the destabilisation of major ice sheets and degradation of the Amazon rainforest
- Mitigation and adaptation must advance together, prioritising such interventions as nature-based cooling
- Net zero is a milestone towards net-negative in sustained reductions in greenhouse gas emissions
- Conditions for success include strong political will and multilateralism, effective policies, inclusive governance, and finance
- Countries with greater responsibility for climate change should act the fastest with the greatest ambition

Moscow vows to respond as Germany announces shutdown of Russian consulate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:21:52 UTC
19:21:52 KST

MOSCOW, September 2. /TASS/. The German government has decided to shut down Russia’s consulate general in Bonn from September 18 over an early August drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport, Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said.
Russian Ambassador to Germany Sergey Nechayev strongly rejected Berlin’s allegations of Moscow’s involvement in the incident as unfounded and absurd.
TASS has gathered the key details of the situation so far.
Russian embassy’s comment
- Staff of the Russian consulate in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin, along with their family members, are to leave Germany as part of measures taken by the country’s authorities following a drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport, the Russian embassy said in a comment.
- According to the diplomatic mission, "the German authorities blamed Russia for preparing an act of sabotage without providing any evidence or arguments."
- The embassy specified that Berlin had decided to shut down the Russian consulate in Bonn by September 18, 2026, and end the 2011 German-Russian intergovernmental agreement on cultural and information centers, effectively paving the way for the closure of the Russian House of Science and Culture in Berlin.
- Russian Ambassador to Germany Sergey Nechayev strongly rejected Berlin’s accusations of Moscow's involvement in the drone incident as groundless and absurd.
- He stressed that the hastily contrived act of provocation only served the interests of the Kiev regime, warmongers within the European political class and military industrialists interested in fomenting the Ukraine conflict.
- Nechayev pointed out that the measures announced by Germany amounted to an unprecedented escalation of tensions that would not remain without consequences.
Russian president’s statements
Germany’s new anti-Russian decisions, announced citing the drone incident at Leipzig Airport, are another "gross error" that harms the interests of the country’s own people, Russian President Vladimir Putin said.
- In his view, the decisions result from Germany’s domestic political situation, particularly the difficulties facing Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Russian Foreign Ministry’s reaction
- Russia will respond to Germany’s move to shut down the Bonn consulate "as it sees fit," and the process will not take long, Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Grushko said.
- He noted that Germany had chosen a path of escalation "that excludes nothing on the diplomatic track."
- Germany’s actions are set to literally erode all positive aspects of bilateral relations that took decades to build, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said.
- Germany opted to escalate tensions with Russia under a completely far-fetched pretext as Berlin has no evidence to support its accusations against Moscow, Zakharova pointed out.
- She emphasized that Germany would receive an appropriate response to its decision to close the Russian House in Berlin and the Russian consulate general in Bonn.
Reaction in Russia
- Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev described the leaders of European countries as sponsors of the Kiev regime’s terrorism amid allegations of Moscow’s involvement in the attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport.
- The closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn and the expulsion of Russian diplomats "will only speed up the decay of Russia-Germany relations," Leonid Slutsky, head of the State Duma (lower house of parliament) Committee on International Affairs and leader of the Liberal Democratic Party, told TASS.
- Igor Chaika, head of Rossotrudnichestvo, Russia's government agency for international cultural cooperation and public diplomacy, said he would not be surprised if the Moscow branch of Germany’s Goethe-Institut cultural organization were closed in a tit-for-tat response.
Drone incident
- A drone loaded with an explosive device was discovered on the tarmac at Leipzig/Halle Airport near a Ukrainian Antonov transport aircraft on the evening of August 4.
- The same night, another drone crashed into a DHL cargo plane.
- Ten days later, investigators found a third drone, along with traces of a powerful explosive, presumably about 50 grams of hexogen.
- German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt described the incident as "a scenario for a hybrid attack," saying that it could have been orchestrated by "foreign powers."
- On September 2, Germany will raise the incident for discussion at a NATO Council meeting, the Bild newspaper reported, citing government sources.

The Skelya Regiment has officially come under the operational command of the Azov Corps
Kyiv • UNN
The 425th Skelya Regiment has officially been placed under the operational command of the 1st Corps of the National Guard of Ukraine, Azov. It is noted that Skelya units have already carried out combat missions.
The 425th Separate Assault Regiment "Skelya" of the Ukrainian Armed Forces’ Ground Forces has officially come under the operational command of the 1st "Azov" Corps of the National Guard of Ukraine. The corps’ press service reported this, according to UNN.
Details
"Azov" noted that during August, several of "Skelya's" battalions, together with the regiment’s command, were redeployed to the area of responsibility of the 1st NGU Corps and had already completed their assigned combat missions to clear infiltrated enemy forces from the brigades’ defensive lines.
The "Azov" Corps will do everything possible to pass on its experience to the command and soldiers of "Skelya," as well as our values and principles, which will help the regiment continue to effectively carry out its assigned tasks while preserving the lives and health of its personnel
Additionally
The State Bureau of Investigation reported that two servicemen of the "Skelya" regiment had been notified of suspicion of cruel treatment of their comrades.
The commander of the 425th Separate Assault Regiment "Skelya," Lieutenant Colonel Yurii Harkavyi, was removed from his duties for the duration of the investigation.
UNN also reported that President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed the detention of the former commander of the 155th Brigade and other military personnel - 10 people in total - in the case concerning the killing of two residents of the village of Kalynivka in the Kyiv region. Before that, UNN confirmed with the Office of the Prosecutor General that the commander of the 155th Brigade, Stanislav Luchanov, had been detained.
We remind you
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy emphasized the need to transform the assault forces, noting that there would be changes at the level of assault forces’ command.

Live Updates: Iran war ramps back up as Tehran accuses U.S. of bombing wedding party, attacks Gulf states
What to know about the Iran war today:
- Iranian officials said Wednesday that a U.S. strike hit a wedding party in the country's south, claiming more than 50 people were killed or wounded as fighting in the Middle East war ramps back up. A U.S. military spokesman said Central Command was looking into the reports, and that the "U.S. military never targets civilians."
- Iran targeted U.S. allies Jordan, the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait with missiles and drones overnight in retaliation for the latest round of American airstrikes, which the U.S. military said struck Iranian military targets.
- President Trump downplayed the likelihood of a peace deal on Tuesday and renewed his call on Iranians to "rise up" against their leaders.
Videos show aftermath of alleged U.S. strike on Iran wedding party
Videos from southern Iran show the aftermath of what Iranian officials claim was a deadly U.S. strike that hit a wedding party at a home.
Iranian authorities said the strike killed at least four people and wounded dozens more. A spokesman for U.S. Central Command said the military was looking into the allegations and that the U.S. doesn't target civilians.
On Wednesday morning, the Iranian Red Crescent shared a video apparently filmed from above after daybreak, showing a hole in the roof of a house at the wedding site, with wreckage and rubble strewn across nearby alleyways.
In a separate video carried by state media, the father of the bride, Ali Mallahi, called it "a very saddening incident."
"I really don't know what to say," he said. "Thank God the casualties were not higher."
Other footage carried by Iranian media showed wounded children lying in hospital beds.
One man, apparently suffering from a head injury and lying in a hospital bed, said he was on his way to the wedding when he heard fighter jets overhead.
"As we arrived there, an explosion happened. It was really powerful, so powerful that even before I arrived there, pieces and debris from the building smashed into my head and face and I passed out," the unnamed man said in a video carried by local media.
"Lots of children and women were horribly injured. All the people were ordinary people," he added.
CBS/AFP
Trump floats renaming Strait of Hormuz as Trump Strait
President Trump suggested renaming the Strait of Hormuz after himself Wednesday.
"Now that we have it under U.S.A. control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT??? Like America itself, it would be 'hotter' than ever before!" Mr. Trump said on his Truth Social platform.
The key waterway has been at the center of renewed hostilities between the U.S. and Iran. The flare-up was sparked Sunday when American forces struck what a military spokesman said was Iran's Revolutionary Guard preparing to place more sea mines in the strait.
Last month, Mr. Trump vowed to declare the waterway a U.S. territory.
U.S. military looking into reports of deadly strike on Iran wedding party
U.S. Central Command is now looking into reports that a wedding party was hit during Tuesday's strikes on Iran, a spokesman said in an updated statement Wednesday.
"We're aware of the reports, which originated from Iranian state media, and we are looking into them. The U.S. military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC," CENTCOM spokesman Navy Capt. Tim Hawkins said in the updated statement, referring to Iran's Revolutionary Guard.
An earlier statement from Hawkins didn't say CENTCOM was looking into the reports.
Iranian state TV said at least four people were killed at the wedding party.
Iran arrests 11 foreign nationals suspected of fuel smuggling, state TV reports
Iranian authorities have arrested 11 foreign nationals on suspicion of attempting to smuggle fuel out of the country, state television reported Wednesday.
The arrests in the southern part of the country come as Iran faces difficulties importing enough fuel to meet demand as the U.S. maintains a naval blockade of Iranian ports.
State television didn't report the suspects' nationalities.
It said border guards acted on intelligence reports of smuggling attempts using a tugboat.
During a search of the boat, the guards found 382,000 liters, or 99,320 gallons, of diesel fuel, it added.
Iranian authorities have for years sought to curb widespread fuel smuggling, particularly in the south, where it has contributed to local shortages.
More recently, Washington imposed its blockade of Iranian ports in retaliation for Tehran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
On Tuesday, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf called on citizens to curb gas consumption. Long lines have formed at filling stations in Tehran in recent days.

USS Abraham Lincoln docks in Thailand after more than 9 months at sea
The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier docked at a port in eastern Thailand on Wednesday after its grueling deployment in the Middle East that kept the ship at sea for more than 250 days.
Associated Press journalists watched the Lincoln, which is carrying about 5,000 service members, as it made its way into the Laem Chabang port in Chonburi province shortly after the destroyer USS Frank E. Petersen Jr. sailed past the area.
The Lincoln has been supporting the U.S. war against Iran. Its deployment included a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea. Concerns have grown about the Lincoln's lengthy deployment following reports of deteriorating mental health among the crew and shortages of supplies including food and hygiene products.
2 killed in Monday attack on Saudi oil tanker in Strait of Hormuz, shipping firm says
Two Filipino sailors were killed in an attack on an oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, Saudi Arabia's national shipping company Bahri said Wednesday.
"Bahri confirms that its vessel SIDR was involved in a security incident while transiting the Strait of Hormuz" on Monday night, the carrier said on social media, confirming "the loss of its two Filipino seafarers as a result" of the attack.
Saudi Arabia condemned the attack and other strikes carried out by Iran against Middle Eastern countries in a statement from its Foreign Affairs Ministry.
"The Kingdom calls on all parties to de-escalate, halt the escalation, respect international law, and return to negotiations and peaceful solutions," the ministry said.
CBS/AFP
Iran says 2 oil tankers on fire after hitting mines in Strait of Hormuz
Iran's Revolutionary Guard said Wednesday that two oil tankers caught fire after striking mines while transiting the Strait of Hormuz outside a route designated by Iranian forces.
In a statement, the Guard said the oil tankers sought "at the urging of the U.S. military to transit via an illegal route" in the strait before "striking mines and exploding," adding that they "are currently on fire."
Kuwait says residential fire sparked by "criminal Iranian aggression" brought under control
Fire crews managed to bring a blaze in a residential complex that was caused by an Iranian attack under control early Wednesday in Kuwait City, the Persian Gulf country's national fire brigade said.
The fire broke out in the complex in Kuwait's capital after it was hit by "a hostile drone as part of the criminal Iranian aggression," Kuwait Fire Force spokesman Brigadier General Mohammed Al-Gharib said in a statement quoted by the country's Al-Anba newspaper.
Al-Gharib said teams from the Al-Hilali and Al-Madina Fire Stations immediately tackled the fire and the operation was completed and the fire brought under control. He said there were no casualties and only limited material damage.
Iranian state TV says 4 killed by U.S. strike on wedding party in country's south
Iran's IRIB state television network reported Wednesday that a wedding celebration in the southern province of Hormozgan was struck by three missiles, killing at least four people and leaving dozens more wounded.
The Iranian foreign ministry earlier said a U.S. strike hit the party in a private home in southern Hormozgan province's Sirik district, killing and wounding some 50 people.
The state TV report put the total number of casualties at just under 70, with six people said to be in critical condition.
IRIB interviewed a man identified as Mr. Malahi, a local fisherman who said the wedding was for his daughter.
The IRIB reporter said one missile crashed through the roof of the room where the party was underway, leaving a roughly 5-foot crater in the floor, while another struck a palm tree in the courtyard before destroying a wall of the home.
CENTCOM says U.S. military "never targets civilians" amid reports of missiles hitting wedding
The U.S. military did not immediately confirm or deny reports that an American airstrike hit a wedding party in southern Iran on Tuesday evening.
"We're aware of the reports, which originated from Iranian state media," U.S. Central Command spokesman Capt. Tim Hawkins told CBS News.
"The U.S. military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC," he added, referring to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
The Associated Press and the New York Times first cited CENTCOM officials with the same statement.
Iranian state TV said the strike killed at least four people attending a wedding celebration in a home in the southern Hormozgan province.
Iran claims to have targeted at least 7 bases used by U.S. across Mideast
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and its central military command, in a series of statements posted overnight, claimed to have targeted at least seven military bases across the region where U.S. forces are or have been based.
The bases mentioned by the IRGC and the military include Camp Tabrin and Prince Hassan Base in Jordan. The IRGC claimed to have killed multiple U.S. personnel in a ballistic missile strike on Camp Tabrin, but U.S. Central Command dismissed that claim, and the camp is not a U.S. base, as the IRGC suggested.
The U.S. military does not maintain any bases inside Jordan. There are several facilities in the kingdom where Jordan's military hosts U.S. forces, including the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, where three U.S. soldiers were killed in an Iranian missile strike in July, and which has been targeted again this week, and the Prince Hassan Air Base.
Iran's armed forces also claimed attacks overnight on the sprawling bases in Erbil, northern Iraq, Ali Al Salem in Kuwait, the vital U.S. Naval Base in Bahrain and the Al Dhafra and Al Minhad bases in the United Arab Emirates.
There was no confirmation of Iranian weapons impacting any of the bases by the U.S. military, and both Bahrain and Jordan said the missiles and drones were either intercepted or landed without causing any damage.
Iran foreign minister says 50 people killed or wounded in U.S. strike that hit wedding party in home
Iran's foreign ministry accused the U.S. of killing or wounding more than 50 people with an airstrike that hit a wedding party in a private home on Tuesday evening in the country's south.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said in a post on X that the home in Kuhestak, in the southern Hormozgan province's Sirik district, "was brutally attacked tonight while families were celebrating a wedding. More than 50 innocent men, women and children were martyred or wounded."
Baqaei referred to the purported strike as the latest in a "chain of atrocities" that he said included the strike on a school in Minab early in the war that killed dozens of children. The United States was "likely" responsible for the deadly attack on the school, but did not intentionally target the facility and may have hit it in error, possibly due to the use of dated intelligence which wrongly identified the area as still part of an Iranian military installation, a person briefed on the preliminary intelligence told CBS News in March.
There was no immediate comment from U.S. officials on the allegation of a wedding party being hit by an American strike Tuesday in southern Iran.
"More dangerous than the bomb itself is the normalization of bombing; and more dangerous than silence is the conversion of silence into legitimacy. Iran will respond to these savage crimes with firmness," said Baqaei, warning that "those who remain silent today will not be immune to its consequences tomorrow. Turning a blind eye to injustice does not contain it; it only emboldens the perpetrators."
Brent crude oil trading around $95 a barrel as rekindled war drives prices up 40% on the year
Oil prices were still up early Wednesday after Iran and the U.S. traded another volley of airstrikes. The return to direct hostilities this week could dim market hopes that the war might have been close to wrapping up.
International benchmark Brent crude oil traded just below $96 a barrel for November deliveries on Tuesday night, but dropped slightly to sell for around $95 early Wednesday morning. U.S. staple crude West Texas Intermediate was trading at over $90 a barrel.
Both benchmark crude prices have risen between 1% and 2% per day since fighting resumed over the weekend, putting them each about 40% higher compared to a year ago, before the Iran war severely limited tanker traffic through the vital Strait of Hormuz.
Trump urges Iranians to "rise up and fight"
In a social media post defending the U.S. position in the Iran war, President Trump asked Tuesday, "When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?"
Mr. Trump said in the Truth Social post that the Iranian regime is "just playing out the inevitable," with its "economy totally collapsing," and said: "I couldn't care less if they sign a worthless, to them, agreement."
Mr. Trump's call for the Iranian people to "rise up" echoed his message hours after the war began in late February, when he urged Iranians to "take over your government." He also encouraged Iranian protesters to take to the streets before the war began.
Later, however, as a war he initially said would take a few weeks stretched on for months, Mr. Trump backed away from calling for the Iranian regime's ouster, saying he "never cared about regime change" and considered the deaths of top Iranian officials to be a kind of regime change.
He has also, at various times, sought to negotiate a peace deal with the regime, calling what he has portrayed as the country's new leadership "very rational" in June.
Latest round of U.S. strikes on Iran concluded, CENTCOM says
The U.S. military's Central Command said Tuesday evening that the latest round of strikes on Iran was complete.
"U.S. forces struck Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets including air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities, and communications sites," CENTCOM said in a statement shared on social media.
Jordan says it was targeted by Iranian missiles, Bahrain by Iranian drones
Jordan's military said early Wednesday that the kingdom was "subjected … to a missile attack originating from Iranian territory," marking the second apparent attack in recent days.
The Jordanian armed forces said 13 ballistic missiles were detected, of which 10 were intercepted and three fell in remote areas. No injuries or deaths were reported.
Iranian state media claimed U.S. forces were killed in the strike on Jordan, but a U.S. official told CBS News that was not true.
The strikes on Jordan — a key U.S. ally that hosts American forces — came after Iran announced it had fired missiles and drones in response to U.S. airstrikes on Tuesday.
Iran's armed forces also targeted a military base in Bahrain with attack drones, Iran's semi-official Fars and Tasnim news agencies said early Wednesday.
Bahrain's state news agency later confirmed that Iranian drones had been intercepted.
Trump waves off idea of reaching deal with Iran, warns "if they retaliate, they'll be hit much harder"
President Trump warned Iran against retaliating against the U.S. for the latest American strikes on Tuesday.
"If they retaliate, they'll be hit much harder. And if they do it again, they'll be no longer," the president told Fox News' Trey Yingst.
Iran said earlier Tuesday that it was responding to the new U.S. strikes with drone and missile attacks targeting U.S. forces in the region.
Asked if he was interested in a deal to end the war with Iran, which the Trump administration has sought on and off for months, the president said: "I think an agreement with them isn't worth the paper it's written on. We gave them a lot of chances."

Explosion occurs in Moldova near border with Ukraine, possibly caused by drone
Moldova has launched an investigation into the explosion of an unidentified object near the village of Crocmaz on the border with Ukraine. A drone may have caused the explosion.
Source: European Pravda, citing NewsMaker
Quote: "Specialised units have been dispatched to the scene. They will carry out all necessary measures and establish the circumstances of the incident."
Details: At around 02:30 on 2 September, Moldovan border guards near the village of Tudora heard a sound resembling a missile flying overhead. At 02:38, a powerful explosion occurred, which was also heard by a nearby patrol.
The Ukrainian side reported that an air-raid warning was in effect in Odesa Oblast at the time due to Russian attacks.
Moldovan radars did not detect any violations of the country's airspace, and initial patrols of the area failed to locate the site of the explosion.
Border guards later received information from a local resident who said he had heard a loud explosion on Moldovan territory while travelling between villages, prompting a search of the area.
At around 07:00, a scorched patch of ground and pieces of metal and plastic were discovered on the outskirts of Crocmaz, 6 km from the Ukrainian border.
People who hear sounds resembling a missile or drone flying overhead, or explosions, are advised to take shelter inside a building and not to approach any suspicious wreckage they may find.
Crocmaz is located near the Maiaky-Udobne-Palanca border crossing, through which virtually the only currently available transit road between the northern and southern parts of Odesa Oblast runs.
Background:
- Russia has recently carried out strikes on several border crossings between Ukraine and Moldova and Romania. On the night of 31 August-1 September, Russian Shahed drones attacked the Orlivka international ferry crossing on the Ukrainian-Romanian border, forcing it to suspend operations.
- Earlier, the Vynohradivka road border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova came under attack. It has since resumed operations.
