The Ministry of Defence has pushed back its target for expanding the UK’s cadet forces by 30% from 2030 to 2035, while confirming that the funding required to support the planned increase has yet to be finalised, the department has said.
The change was disclosed in a written parliamentary answer to Conservative MP Stuart Anderson, who asked the Defence Secretary what target had been set for the size of the cadet forces by 2030 and what funding had been allocated to achieve it.
Veterans and People Minister Calvin Bailey said the original target came from the Strategic Defence Review published in June 2025. He said: “The Strategic Defence Review, published in June 2025, recommended that MOD should expand in-school and community-based Cadet Forces across the country by 30% by 2030. This timeline has recently been re-set in the Defence Investment Plan to 2035 as one of the measures required to increase the rate of Armed Forces transformation.”
The MOD currently supports just over 137,000 cadets alongside around 28,000 adult volunteers. Bailey said achieving the planned 30% expansion would mean recruiting around 40,000 additional cadets, taking the overall number to roughly 177,000, while also requiring a substantial increase in the number of adults supporting cadet units.
He said: “There are currently just over 137,000 cadets supported by 28,000 adult volunteers. An increase of 30% in cadet numbers equates to an additional 40,000 cadets, an expansion that would also require approximately 8,000 more adult volunteers. Details of the funding necessary to support this level of growth are yet to be finalised.”
The department is therefore working towards an expansion of both cadet numbers and the volunteer workforce needed to support them, but has not yet set out the final financial requirement for delivering the programme. On the figures provided by the minister, the adult volunteer population would need to rise from around 28,000 to approximately 36,000 if the planned increase is delivered.
Bailey said work was already underway on how the expansion would be carried out. “Work is currently underway to set the foundations for sustainable growth and to determine how the 30% increase in cadet numbers will be delivered.”
The MOD is also preparing a new Cadet Action Plan, which Bailey said would be announced in October during the first National Cadets Week. The plan will cover both cadets and the adults who support them, including recruitment, retention and the resources available to individual units.
Bailey said: “And we are developing a new Cadet Action Plan, to be announced in October during the first National Cadets Week. The Plan will focus on modernising the cadet experience, providing an attractive offer to retain and recruit adult volunteers, and ensuring that cadets and volunteers have the right resources and support.”

====================================================================================================

For fibromyalgia, gentle and enjoyable exercise seems to works better than pushing through pain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:00:46 UTC
19:00:46 KST

A tailored, low-intensity exercise program provides evidence of lasting relief and improved quality of life for people with fibromyalgia. Brain scans indicate that these benefits are linked to changes in the cerebellum, a brain region involved in movement and pain processing. The research was published in Scientific Reports.
Fibromyalgia is a chronic disorder characterized by widespread pain, fatigue, poor sleep, and a nervous system that is overly sensitive to physical sensations. It often severely impacts a person’s daily life and functional independence. Adapted physical activity involves physical exercises customized to an individual’s specific capabilities, needs, and health limitations.
“When I came to this chronic pain center in 2015, after working in supportive and palliative care, sports medicine, and emergency medicine, I really did not understand this disease,” lead author Stéphanie Ranque-Garnier, a pain medicine physician at Timone Hospital’s Pain Assessment and Treatment Centre in Marseille, France, told PsyPost.
“I often heard that it was ‘not a real disease’ because it was not dangerous in terms of survival, and that people with fibromyalgia ‘would not heal,'” she continued. “This seemed very paradoxical to me.”
A 2019 review gathered earlier clinical trials to show that combining different types of exercise can help people manage fibromyalgia. Additionally, a 2020 review explains the biology behind why working out can provide both immediate and long-term pain relief.
Despite exercise being a recommended treatment, many patients with fibromyalgia remain sedentary because typical workouts tend to trigger symptom flare-ups. Standard exercise guidelines can be vague, leaving patients unsure of how often, how long, or how intensely they should be active.
“In my clinical practice, I was struck by how difficult it was for many patients, especially with fibromyalgia, to become physically active, even when they knew that physical activity could be beneficial,” Ranque-Garnier noted. “I realized that simply telling patients to ‘exercise more’ was not only insufficient, but could even be counterproductive.”
For the current study, the authors wanted to see if a highly structured, supervised, and well-tolerated exercise routine could bring sustained relief. They also sought to understand the brain mechanisms involved by using neuroimaging.
The research, led by Ranque-Garnier and her colleagues, involved 79 adults with moderate to severe fibromyalgia. The scientists randomly assigned the participants into two groups. Thirty-nine patients received the supervised adapted physical activity program alongside standard care, while 40 patients received only standard care. The researchers followed both groups for a total of 12 months.
The exercise intervention lasted for six months and consisted of three two-hour sessions per week. These sessions included a mix of pool and land-based activities kept at a very low intensity. The exercises were broken up into small bursts based on each person’s tolerance limits to avoid exacerbating their pain.
“The activity had to be adapted not only to their physical capacity and symptoms, but also, and importantly, to their tastes,” Ranque-Garnier said. “Motivation cannot come from cycling like a laboratory rat, especially if you do not like cycling!”
The research team used questionnaires to measure the patients’ quality of life, pain levels, sleep quality, and fatigue. They also used pedometers to track daily steps and conducted aerobic fitness tests. A subset of 33 patients underwent positron emission tomography, or PET, scans to track changes in brain metabolism.
The findings showed that quality of life improved for the exercise group. At the six-month mark, the exercise group showed a 14.5 percent better score on a standardized fibromyalgia impact questionnaire compared to the standard care group. Patients in the exercise program reported less average pain, better sleep, and greater flexibility. They also reported immediate symptom relief after individual sessions.
The team carefully monitored this immediate impact. “Our simplest tool for knowing whether a session was appropriate was the patient’s own evaluation before and after the session,” Ranque-Garnier explained. “The session should leave the patient at least as well as, and ideally better than, before — in terms of pain, mood, fatigue, and concentration.”
The exercise group also became more active outside the program. At three months, they added an average of 1,619 daily steps to their baseline of about 4,185 steps, while the standard care group experienced a slight decrease in their daily steps.
These physical and emotional benefits occurred even though the patients did not show improvements in maximum aerobic capacity. This suggests that people with fibromyalgia do not need to endure high-intensity, exhaustion-inducing workouts to experience real health benefits.
“The main message is that physical activity is a major therapeutic approach in fibromyalgia, but more is not better,” Ranque-Garnier told PsyPost. “Quality of life and fibromyalgia symptoms improved even though we did not observe a major improvement in the shuttle walking test.”
In fact, focusing on performance can backfire. “Some patients in the control group became physically more active but experienced worsening symptoms and eventually abandoned their activity because they had pushed themselves too hard,” she noted. “We think that some had been motivated by the title of the study and applied the familiar ‘no pain, no gain’ principle.”
This led to a crucial realization for the research team. “In fibromyalgia, an activity that is physically possible is not necessarily an activity that is therapeutically appropriate,” Ranque-Garnier added.
The brain scans indicated an increase in metabolism in the right cerebellum of the exercise group. The cerebellum is a structure located at the back of the brain that traditionally helps coordinate movement, but it also plays a role in regulating pain and emotion. This metabolic increase was directly correlated with the patients’ increased daily step counts.
“The increase in cerebellar metabolism after six months of the program is particularly interesting in this regard and raises the possibility of changes in neural networks involved in cognitive, movement, and pain processing,” Ranque-Garnier said.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2017, which similarly found that lighter forms of physical activity improve quality of life and reduce pain. The 2017 study evaluated natural daily activity levels across healthy adults rather than a structured low-intensity exercise intervention in fibromyalgia patients.
The results also parallel a 2023 study covered by PsyPost, which found that physical activity provides pain-relieving benefits. However, that previous research evaluated experimental pain tolerance in the general population rather than clinical pain reduction and quality of life in fibromyalgia patients following a structured exercise intervention.
Additionally, the current results echo research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found that structured exercise improved sleep and modulated cerebellar brain activity. That 2024 work examined brain functional connectivity in older adults with insomnia rather than cerebellar metabolism in fibromyalgia patients.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The patients in this study were recruited from a specialized pain center and had already participated in therapeutic education workshops. This specific background means they might have been more motivated and ready to adopt new habits than the average person with fibromyalgia.
“Our study does not mean that any form of exercise will improve fibromyalgia, nor that patients should simply push through their pain,” Ranque-Garnier cautioned. She emphasized that the intervention was closely supervised by professionals specifically trained to adapt exercises for chronic pain.
The brain imaging findings are based on a small subset of the total participants. The researchers note that these mechanistic conclusions should be interpreted cautiously until they are confirmed in larger groups.
“The neuroimaging findings should also be considered as mechanistic clues rather than proof of causality,” Ranque-Garnier said. “We therefore cannot conclude that we have identified a single brain mechanism or a universal exercise prescription for fibromyalgia.”
Spontaneous physical activity in the control group could not be fully controlled, and wearing a pedometer might have influenced the behavior of the participants.
Looking ahead, the team hopes to identify predictive factors that lead to long-term remission in chronic pain. The ultimate goal is to help patients regain confidence in their bodies and become more active in their everyday lives.
“One of the most beautiful things I hear from patients in remission is: ‘I stopped passively enduring my symptoms and started being active with the resources I have,'” Ranque-Garnier said.
The study, “Efficacy and mechanism of supervised adapted physical activity on quality of life for patients with fibromyalgia: single-center, prospective, randomised clinical and neuroimaging study,” was authored by Stéphanie Ranque, Jérôme Laurin, Marius George Linguraru, Zhifan Jiang, Anderson Loundou, Laurent Boyer, Régis Guieu, José Boucraut, Caroline Sault, Jeremy Simon, Fanny Barthelemy, Anne Donnet, and Eric Guedj.

DLR Group on translating urban density into intimate neighborhoods in the middle east
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:00:24 UTC
19:00:24 KST

SHAPING MIDDLE EASTERN URBANISM FROM MASTERPLAN TO MICRO-MOMENT
‘When you have the same types of buildings and spaces replicated everywhere, you lose any sense of place,’ states Henrique Dias, Middle East Hospitality & Mixed-Use Director at DLR Group, in an interview with designboom. Across the Middle East, cities are building at an unprecedented speed and monumental scale. As sprawling block footprints and towering verticality dominate the landscape, urban density is often viewed as an environmental and psychological challenge. In our conversation with DLR Group, it becomes clear that the key challenge of modern urbanism is not high density itself, but how that density is designed, experienced, and rooted in place. Key decisions about scale, walkability, and sensory environment determine how millions of people experience life for generations.
‘Density isn’t the problem — repetitive, overwhelming design is. In our design process, we create spaces that allow users to connect with the environment and navigate a complex plan while recognizing that every location and design is distinct,’ continues Dias. ‘From a landscape perspective at the ground level, it’s about creating distinct moments within dense environments, giving people choices, whether for gathering, socializing, or finding quiet spaces. It comes down to sensory richness and variety rather than repetition,’ adds Stefan du Toit, Design Director, Landscape. For DLR Group’s work in the Middle East, that philosophy plays out differently depending on terrain, climate, and cultural context, from mountain masterplans in Makkah to heritage-driven interiors in Abha.
DLR Group creates for human scale by integrating porosity and organic flow into what otherwise might be one large mixed-use block | all images courtesy of DLR Group
HOW DLR GROUP BRINGS SPATIAL CALM TO DENSE URBAN ENVIRONMENTS
By shifting the lens from megaproject massing to human-scale perception, DLR Group’s multidisciplinary team aligns master planning, architecture, landscape, and interior design to translate massive urban footprints into legible, approachable, and deeply authentic communities. Humans require environments that feel intuitive, welcoming, and responsive to maintain a sense of emotional security. When developments become overly uniform or monumental, individuals lose their bearings and lack a clear pathway to connect with the surrounding space.
‘Architecture can sometimes suffer from designer ego, where architects try to scream louder than one another with flashy, contextless sculptures,’ reflects Dias. ‘There is no room for architectural ego in designing for the greater good of the project and end user. The design must be humble, meaningful, and aligned with the user experience while meeting client expectations.’ To counter this alienation, DLR Group prioritizes spatial clarity and cognitive ease over visual spectacle, embedding tactile materials, balanced spatial hierarchies, and central civic anchors to foster daily social encounters and a genuine resonance with nature.
rooted in Makkah’s spiritual and natural identity, MAAD’s mixed-use masterplan is designed to balance seasonal pilgrim flows with permanent urban livability
DECONSTRUCTING SCALE AT FOR SENSORY-RICH AND WALKABLE COMMUNITIES
A human-scale experience is primarily won or lost at the horizontal surface where people actually stand and move. Rather than allowing high-rise structures to plunge abruptly into hard paving, landscape architecture acts as a vital calibration tool, stepping down massive architectural volumes into digestible foregrounds.
‘We view landscape as an interface between the scale of architecture and the human scale,’ explains Stefan du Toit, Design Director, Landscape. ‘Instead of creating an abrupt transition between a high-rise building and the ground level, we step it down using curated topography and layered experiences. As a user approaches a building, we break down that mass using plants, shade structures, and artistic features. Working hand-in-hand with architects allows us to introduce new amenities at multiple vertical levels, breaking the sheer scale into digestible human experiences.’
EMAAR – The Heights in Dubai, UAE, breaks down a large development into places that feel local, walkable, and centered around family life
In hot, arid climates, outdoor spaces are often abandoned unless thermal comfort and sensory engagement are actively designed. Whether people choose to walk depends on more than basic street proportions, as a route is walked when it is continuously shaded, comfortable underfoot, and rewarding to move along. This first-principles approach to walkability is vividly illustrated at EMAAR – The Heights in Dubai, a vast 750-hectare masterplan where DLR Group translates thoughtful master planning into everyday family living. Rather than allowing the development’s scale to overwhelm residents, the plan organizes over 7,500 homes into an array of intimate neighborhood clusters, each anchored by a central Wellness Club directly sited amid a polycentric open space network spanning 1.9 million square meters. Curvilinear villa layouts, green noise-filtering buffers, neighborhood pockets for dwell or play, and shaded pedestrian routes work alongside continuous blue/green systems to maintain neighborhood intimacy at scale and make wellness feel tangible.
SUMOU in Al Khobar is organized as a live-work-play ecosystem, reducing the need for long-distance movement
Similarly, in mixed-use developments like SUMOU in Al Khobar and LIWAN Najd in Riyadh, DLR Group weaves continuous pedestrian networks and central car-free wadis using tree canopies, vegetated groundcover, water features, and lighter paving surfaces to lower radiant temperatures. To balance density with daily well-being, the team structures these developments around central civic nodes such as schools, mosques, workplaces, and retail destinations, wrapping residential clusters around them so essential daily life sits within a comfortable walk. Elevated green terraces, subtle level changes, and shifting planting densities create a natural gradient between active public plazas and tranquil home environments. By sequencing shade, seating, and framed views, distance across both developments is measured in spatial experience rather than physical exertion, creating places where people naturally want to slow down and linger.
‘In this climate, streets must be both functional and beautiful. We have to push back against the obsolete thinking that it’s simply too hot to walk here,’ notes Shawn Meyers, Middle East Master Planning Director at DLR Group. ‘If people have a tree canopy, a place to rest, or a reason to linger, they’re willing to walk further and engage more fully with their neighborhood — and, more importantly, with their neighbors,’ adds du Toit.
conceived as a car-free, green pedestrian spine, LIWAN Najd in Riyadh’s Granada District connects hospitality, housing, commerce, worship, and community life
TERRAIN, CULTURAL ROOTS, AND REGIONAL AUTHENTICITY
Modulating the monumental scale also demands deference to terrain and local context. At MAAD in Makkah, a mixed-use masterplan designed to balance seasonal pilgrim flows with permanent urban livability, DLR Group used the site’s steep mountainous terrain as an organizing framework rather than flattening the landscape. By concentrating high-density development at lower elevations and tapering massing as the topography rises, built forms merge naturally into the mountain through stepped terraces and landscape-led transitions.
Where developments touch deeply personal or spiritual journeys, architecture must yield to quiet humility. ‘For destinations such as Makkah, the interior design is never intended to become the focal point of the experience — it exists to support the journey taking place within the guest,’ explains Vaida Buchrotaite, Middle East Director of Interior Design at DLR Group. ‘As the architecture merges into the mountains, the interiors continue that story through restrained materiality, gentle spatial layering, and carefully choreographed arrival sequences that encourage moments of reflection and calm.’
natural features such as the surrounding mountains and wadis define movement, density, and urban form
forms, textures, patterns, materials are an extension of the physical terrain and create a continuum of the land’s cultural significance
A similar sensitivity defines how regional heritage is expressed across DLR Group’s projects. At The Point in Abha, traditional Al-Qatt Al-Asiri wall art is not applied as superficial decoration, but distilled into custom textiles, geometric textures, and warm, mineral-toned palettes. Rather than recreating historical styles, the design team abstracts regional patterns and local crafts into modern, bold lifestyle destinations that feel authentic, warm, and deeply rooted in place.
‘We celebrate local culture by infusing our interiors with subtle echoes of regional patterns, craftsmanship, textures, and art rather than applying them literally,’ continues Buchrotaite. ‘These references are paired with contemporary styling, refined detailing, and sometimes even bespoke patterns developed specifically for each project.’
The Point is a vibrant mixed-use development situated in southwestern Saudi Arabia, within the Asir Region, which is well known for its cultural heritage and natural landscapes
THE INTEGRATED STUDIO WORKFLOW
Ensuring that a macro-scale urban vision successfully translates into micro-level sensory touchpoints requires breaking down traditional design silos. ‘For us, integrated design is an active, iterative workflow rather than a passive collaboration,’ notes Shawn Meyers, Middle East Master Planning Director at DLR Group. ‘We can achieve far greater value when the master planners, architects, landscape architects, and interior designers shape the vision together from day one, rather than working in a sequential hand-off.’
By embedding this holistic workflow across every phase, DLR Group proves that even the most ambitious megaprojects can be crafted as intimate, legible spaces where human experience remains the ultimate priority. ‘Bringing all key decision-makers together at project inception creates alignment around a common vision from the outset,’ adds Buchrotaite. ‘Maintaining open dialogue and actively inviting input from every discipline throughout the design process leads to stronger decisions, a more cohesive outcome, and a more collaborative experience for both the team and the client.’
all food and beverage patios and terraces have a clear line of sight toward the central entertainment space

brand: DLR Group

 interviewees: Shawn Meyers (Middle East Master Planning Director),  Vaida Buchrotaite (Middle East Director of Interior Design), Henrique Dias (Middle East Hospitality & Mixed-Use Director) and Stefan du Toit (Design Director, Landscape)

Thames Water, I refuse to pay the sewage charge in my bill while you pollute Britain’s rivers and coastlines | Jenny Jones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:00:21 UTC
19:00:21 KST

I can’t even remember when I decided to stop paying the sewage element of my Thames Water bill. It might have been after reading this headline from the Guardian in July 2025: “Serious pollution incidents by English water companies rose 60% last year,” with the subheading: “Environment Agency records 75 serious incidents among total of 2,800, with Thames Water being worst offender.”
Living in London means that my supplier is Thames Water, which makes a profit out of pollution. I decided that if the government wouldn’t act, I could at least do my part and not pay for this travesty.
The case for not paying these outrageous charges is clear. The water companies are not fulfilling their duties and instead they are discharging raw sewage into our waterways and lives. Beyond that, they have brought in hosepipe bans, despite last winter being one of the wettest on record, because they haven’t built enough reservoirs to store water for use in the summer.
They ask us to use water wisely, and send us advice on how to cut our usage, and to consider dynamic pricing, while at the same time failing to fix the leaks that lose about a fifth of all public supply in England and Wales. My final gripe is that a huge chunk of my bill doesn’t even get spent on fixing these problems; instead it is spent on interest payments for debts that enable Thames Water to pay shareholders billions of pounds.
Nothing will change until these companies go officially bankrupt and the quickest way of ensuring that happens is if people stop paying their bills. A few decades ago millions of people did exactly that with the poll tax and the government backed down. (I was taken to court over that.) So why not use the same nonpayment tactic to end water privatisation? Even a few million of us delaying the payment of our bills by several months would threaten the viability of these water companies.
As a Thames Water bill-payer, I felt that it was hypocritical of me to be constantly campaigning on the issue and then meekly paying up. As a Green party member since 1988, and green-minded since my teens, it just seemed wrong not to take a stand.
When I decided I had to do more than just speak out, I wrote to Thames Water and explained that I was very happy to pay the proportion of the bill related to their supplying me with water, but not to the proportion for their dealing with sewage. They wrote back saying that they don’t work out the proportions like that between water and sewage. And followed it up with a threatening letter and a vastly increased bill with penalty charges.
Of course the real solution to this problem would be nationalising these companies. Public opinion is firmly in favour of renationalisation, yet the government keeps trotting out a fictitious number of £100bn as the cost of taking companies over. That figure is bogus because it includes the companies’ debt as part of its value. Many argue that the nationalisation cost is actually far lower, possibly even zero.
The government has also talked about “public control”, which is of course not public ownership, but would allow oversight of how companies are run and the ability to impose penalty charges. But if laws and oversight worked, we wouldn’t be in this mess.
We aren’t holding the bosses to account for their failures. We aren’t prosecuting them, finding them guilty of illegal dumping of effluent. No need to send them to our overcrowded prisons. They can be sentenced to community service of 20 hours a week cleaning up the filth they’ve allowed into in our streams and rivers and on our seashore.
None of this is new. We’ve had a Labour government for more than two years, but nothing has really changed and the bills are getting bigger while our precious chalk streams are dying, river ecosystems are collapsing and swimmers are being made ill by sewage floating near beaches.
I will continue my own protest. The letters are unpleasant, and there has been mention of bailiffs, so I don’t recommend anyone else going into this lightly. I will calmly read all the threatening letters and await the court case against me. Despite having a seat in the House of Lords, I don’t have a lot of assets but, win or lose in court, by taking on Thames Water I know I can only win in terms of my own self-respect.
I have drawn a line in the sand. And I hope to win this particular battle.
- 
  Jenny Jones is a Green party peer

The deportation of Milo Yiannopoulos signals a rupture within Maga | Moira Donegan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:00:21 UTC
19:00:21 KST

It’s been a long, slow decline for Milo Yiannopoulos. From the vantage point of 2026, it’s easy to forget that he was once a big deal.
The British-born far-right provocateur, who was arrested by ICE in Louisiana and deported from the US this week, was among the first media figures to ride the “gamergate” controversy and ensuing rightwing populist wave that brought Donald Trump to office in 2016. An editor of the then ascendant Breitbart News from 2014 to 2017, Yiannopoulous was an early adopter of the media strategy of algorithm-optimized outrage bait, trawling the internet and consulting a large network of well-placed sources in search of stories he could use to fan the flames of online culture war discourses. He would write a story mocking a feminist, or fire off a tweet saying something racist about Muslims, and the ensuing firestorm of controversy would result in online arguments, media coverage, and his own promptly and decisively rising star. Rinse, repeat.
Back then, at the start of the Trump era, Yiannopoulous was something of a novelty. Rightwing provocation peddlers had not previously come in his millennial, digitally savvy mold; few others had adopted a fey, gregarious kind of gay male humor for the increasingly theatrical right. But soon, Yiannopoulous was overrun with competitors. The rightwing influencer field became crowded, then saturated. He has spent the past few years at the fringe of the fringe, working for and hobnobbing with a hodgepodge of odious figures who aim to critique Donald Trump from the right, such as the former congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene, the white nationalist streamer Nick Fuentes, and the antisemitic rapper who now goes by Ye. In a particularly pathetic bid for relevance, he once declared himself “ex-gay” and set about promoting conversion therapy.
His downfall had been a long time coming. Yiannopoulous, often willing to say in vulgar terms what many parts of the American right were only willing to allude to in polite ones, often found himself overstepping. He was banned from Twitter, then from Facebook; he was banned from Australia. In 2017, he resigned from Breitbart and lost a book deal with Simon and Schuster after comments resurfaced in which he claimed that sexual abuse of children by adults could be consensual and “hugely positive experiences”. Yiannopoulous’s comments, which he later apologized for, are not so far out of line from what some on the far right have said about child marriage, or the need to encourage childbirth among teen girls. But Yiannopoulous was talking about boys, not girls, and by then the Maga movement he had helped to galvanize no longer needed him. There were already plenty of Milo imitators, eager to see a rival deposed and ready to fill his grotesque niche.
Several of those imitators are now claiming victory, declaring themselves responsible for Yiannopoulous’s recent deportation. Laura Loomer, a far-right influencer, provocateur and conspiracist in Yiannopoulous’s mold, who has become a confidante of Donald Trump, quickly claimed to have orchestrated Yiannopoulous’s arrest. “I reported him to ICE and the FBI,” Loomer posted. “I told you all that Milo was an illegal alien.” As Anna Merlan of Mother Jones reported, two other far-right influencers – who, unlike Yiannopoulous, are still in good standing with the Maga regime – also claimed to have advance knowledge of the DHS’s plans to remove and deport their enemy: Raheem Kassam, a onetime Breitbart UK editor and current Washington DC restaurateur, and Benny Johnson, a Maga-aligned writer and social media personality. There’s reason to take at least Loomer seriously: last year, Trump fired several high-ranking national security officials after their names appeared on a list of alleged enemies that Loomer presented to him in the Oval Office. If these figures’ boasts are true, this would mean, at best, that at least some figures within the DHS are leaking information about what are supposed to be confidential proceedings to online grifters and grievance peddlers, so that those influencers can get in a bit of satisfying mockery online. At worst, it would mean that the country’s massive federal security apparatus is being deployed to settle internet feuds among crackpot influencers.
There’s always a bit of schadenfreude to witnessing these incidents, watching the Trump camp dissolve into infighting and treachery, and seeing the amorality, bigotry or cynical opportunism of those who once sided with Trump be punished with a blow to something those actors actually care about: their own status and careers. By now, there have been so many purges and abrupt reversals of fortune for the once-ascendant members of the Maga coalition that it is hardly worth enumerating them all: Trump, it turns out, has done his purging more frequently and unexpectedly, less a single Night of the Long Knives and more a recurring series of Afternoons of the Mean Tweets.
But Yiannoupoulous’s downfall is more than just another case of the Maga revolution eating its children. His abrupt arrest and deportation seems, instead, like the product of a bigger rupture within the Trump movement, wherein the isolationist, anti-Zionist, and increasingly antisemitic faction is in revolt against Trump and the neoconservative, expansionist and pro-Israel and pro-military adventurism wing that persuaded him to go to war with Iran. As the unpopular, unwinnable war drags on, sending prices soaring and making it seem more likely that irate voters will look to punish the Republicans in the November midterms, fingers are pointing within the Maga coalition, as major players look to dilute their own responsibility and find someone else to blame. Milo’s deportation might be just one instance in the much uglier fight to come as these figures seek to throw one another under the bus. If they were honorable people, after all, they wouldn’t be in the Trump camp in the first place.
Those of us hoping for a sizable Democratic victory might understandably welcome this outcome. Let them fight; let them tear each other to pieces; let them destroy themselves, and nothing of value will be lost. But there is something gruesome, too, about seeing the government deployed this way. It is humiliating to be ruled over by such people – conspiracists and bigots and idiots, people without virtue or competence or even dignity to match their power. They’re all going to suffer in the ugly infighting that’s coming. But we’re all suffering, too.
- 
  Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

Walmart’s Sam’s Club accelerates expansion in China as membership passes 10.7 million
Company to open 13 new stores this year, bringing total to 76, as value prices and exclusive goods prove to be a winning formula
US membership-only retailer Sam’s Club has sped up its expansion in China this year, with the launch of its sixth Beijing location on Monday drawing long queues of eager shoppers.
The Walmart-owned warehouse retailer has found a winning formula in China, with its value pricing and exclusive goods attracting middle-class consumers even as some foreign brands shut down stores or pull out of the country.
Sam’s Club said last month that it had 10.7 million paid members in China as of June. Its total annual membership revenue could hit 3 billion yuan (US$450 million) this year, with its basic and premium memberships priced at 260 yuan and 680 yuan a year, respectively.
“The appeal of Sam’s Club is the breadth and quality of goods offered along with wholesale pricing,” said Cathy Chao, senior director of Asia-Pacific corporate ratings at Fitch Ratings. “Many goods are unique and cannot be found through alternate channels, and consumers hold a general impression of consistently high-quality goods at a reasonable price, which can justify the membership pricing.”
In addition, the membership model encouraged frequent visits by consumers seeking to maximise the value of the annual fee, Chao added.
The company said that it planned to open 13 new Sam’s Club stores nationwide this year, including in several lower-tier cities, bringing the total to 76.

A woman in China, suffering from severe scoliosis, has gone viral after accusations that she is “making money by doing nothing” surfaced.
This scrutiny followed the revelation that her boyfriend, Yan Ruize, worked gruelling food-delivery shifts to fund her much-needed surgery.
He Ling, 23, hails from southwest China’s Sichuan province and was diagnosed with congenital scoliosis – a sideways curvature of the spine – at five years old. Now, at just 1.35 metres tall and weighing 31.5kg, she requires surgery estimated to cost around 300,000 yuan (US$45,000).
After completing secondary school, He worked in a mobile phone parts factory, where she met Yan in 2021. Subsequently, she trained as a manicurist and began running a stall at a night market.
When the factory where Yan was employed shut down, the couple initially depended on He’s income. In 2024, Yan became a food delivery rider, often working up to 14 hours a day to gather funds for her operation.
Recently, a social media creator filmed their story, which went viral, garnering over 18 million views and significant public support. As reported by Fengmian News, online fundraising efforts approached 100,000 yuan, bringing He closer to her surgery goals.

The Hidden Value of Back-to-School Shopping
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:00:02 UTC
19:00:02 KST

One of my first school memories comes from the first day of first grade, when my German mother dropped me off with a blue paper cone stuffed with fresh school supplies and a brand-new, boxy green backpack. Peering into the cone, inside at a Staedtler eraser and a pack of gummy bears, I felt like an alien about to make first contact with my classmates at Blessed Sacrament in Johnson City, N.Y.
Even without a Trapper Keeper, I blended in.
Americans were agog over back-to-school shopping then, as they are now. This year, the average family is projected to spend $489 per child on stationery, devices, clothing, shoes, and the latest technology for packing organic strawberries.
It's easy to dismiss our collective consumer ritual as another marketing season. Yes, it was invented by department stores selling school uniforms in the 1800s, and then turbocharged with seasonal catalogs and sales by retailers like Montgomery Ward and Sears in the century that followed. And it is a sort of pre-Halloween ritual in which we all foist new costumes on our children.
But all those new backpacks, sneakers, pencil cases, and lunch boxes do something else. They help turn our children back into students.
For two glorious summer months, we released our children from the routines and identities of school. They've spent a culturally sanctioned rumspringa at pools, beaches, and camps, in the woods, or on a Nintendo. Then, almost overnight, we thrust them back into desks, routines, homework, and a social world that is often new and uncertain.
A handful of new pencils can help.
Others are more aspirational. A set of cleats doesn't make you a soccer player, and a graphing calculator doesn't teach you calculus. But these objects signal the roles we are stepping into—to the people around us and to ourselves. Possessions can help us become someone new.
That's why transitions are so often linked to new possessions. We wear funny hats and robes when we graduate from college. Wedding rings, dresses, and tuxedos mark our transition from singlehood to married life. We furnish nurseries before our babies arrive. A suit, scrubs, or a desk can make a new professional identity feel real.
Possessions can be the bridges we need to new identities before we feel entirely comfortable inhabiting them. Having a first child is a psychedelic experience. You're handed a fragile infant and sent off to do your best. A first-year medical student is a long way from being a physician. Possessions associated with these roles help cement identities as we grow into them.
Our children often face no less dramatic transitions.
My son, who was just a giant in the familiar melee of daycare, will become a kindergartner this week in an enormous building filled with children much bigger than him. Your sixth grader is becoming a middle schooler. Or your ninth grader is starting high school. They may not yet know what role we and their peers expect them to play.
Practically, their old backpack works. And, yes, buying what you already own is expensive and wasteful. A replacement will not kindle new friendships and a sudden capacity for algebra. Teaching our children about waste and having enough are important lessons.
But the mistake is assuming that we buy possessions purely for function. An old backpack can still carry books. Shoes that fit in June may miraculously survive until September. They may also carry an old identity. To a child, they may feel like a younger self.
A transition doesn't require us to replace everything. One or two new possessions may be enough to construct the new identity. A new ring is enough for many married couples.
A new backpack, sneakers, pencil case, lunchbox, or graphing calculator is a prop for this new identity. It tells classmates and teachers, “I belong.” More importantly, it can help our children say this to themselves.

Press review: NATO excludes Russia from drone probes as Japan pursues remilitarization
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

MOSCOW, September 2. /TASS/. NATO excludes Russia from probes into drone incidents, and the top two US negotiators seem more focused on Iran and domestic issues than on Ukraine. Meanwhile, Japan’s remilitarization drive raises concerns in Russia, China and North Korea. These stories topped Wednesday's newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: NATO squeezing Russia out of drone probes
The North Atlantic Alliance has not approached Russia with proposals to jointly investigate drone crashes, Vladislav Maslennikov, director of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s Department of European Affairs, told Izvestia. Nor does the bloc make use of emergency communication channels through the Russian embassy in Belgium, he added. Germany has accused Russia of involvement in the drone incident at Leipzig Airport. In May, Romania blamed Moscow for the shooting down of a drone in the city of Galati. Experts say that NATO allies refuse to conduct a joint investigation with Moscow because of the risks of uncovering a Ukrainian trace.
Natalya Yeryomina, a professor at St. Petersburg State University, told Izvestia in an interview that NATO’s refusal to conduct a joint investigation with Russia is linked to concerns about exposing Ukraine's role. Otherwise, it will become clear that the incidents are related to Kiev's actions, and the West does not want to make it responsible.
Drone crashes in Romania, Poland and Germany are used to justify increased military spending. In parallel, the bloc is boosting its presence in Eastern Europe. Thus, in September 2025, it launched Operation Eastern Sentry with a view to integrating radars, anti-aircraft missile systems and aircraft of NATO allies into a single network spanning from the Barents Sea to the Black Sea. The North Atlantic Alliance has stationed nine multinational combat groups in Bulgaria, Britain, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Slovakia, Finland, and Estonia. NATO air patrol missions are conducted in the Baltics and in the Balkans. On August 1, Spain deployed a tactical air detachment including three NH-90 helicopters designed to combat drones at low altitude to Romania as part of NATO’s enhanced Air Policing mission.
The bloc will continue to gradually reinforce its groups in the region, Yeryomina believes. In her opinion, it could increase personnel and counter-drone means. Germany will be the main donor, which has already announced plans to boost the number of its Bundeswehr troops to 460,000. At the same time, a radical buildup of NATO forces in Eastern Europe should not be expected amid a lack of consensus, political analyst Denis Denisov maintained.
The lack of NATO proposals to investigate drone incidents shows that the alliance is unwilling to find out the true cause behind them. And they provide an opportunity to justify the need for increased military spending. A joint investigation with Russia may reveal Ukraine's role, which is definitely not part of Brussels' plans.
Vedomosti: Witkoff, Kushner focused on Iran, domestic issues instead of Ukraine
A recent visit to Moscow by CIA Director John Ratcliffe prompted questions about where US special envoy Steve Witkoff and the US leader’s son-in-law Jared Kusher, the two top US negotiators on Ukraine who were expected to visit Moscow and Kiev late last month, have disappeared. The Hill, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ), The Washington Post and Axios mentioned three major issues that could divert Kushner and Witkoff from resolving the Ukraine conflict, namely their personal financial interests, domestic US issues and Iran.
It’s not only about their preoccupation with Iran or any other track but rather the fact that the US is currently pursuing the goal of securing concessions from Russia so Moscow can agree to conditions being sought by European warmongers and Kiev, Dmitry Suslov, Deputy Director of the Center for Comprehensive European and International Studies at the Higher School of Economics, told Vedomosti. Witkoff and Kushner could return to work only when the US administration understands how things really stand with Russia winning on the battlefield, he explained. "Maybe, after the winter. Meanwhile, the positions of such hawks as Secretary of State Marco Rubio and CIA Director John Ratcliffe are strong in [US President Donald] Trump’s administration," the expert said. Besides, he continued, Washington has been unable to exert pressure on either Kiev or Europe.
Witkoff last commented on the Ukraine conflict after Moscow released ex-US marine Robert Gilman in mid-August as he thanked the Russian side for its assistance in that matter. Both Witkoff and Kushner spoke with Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky in late July.
Now that the United States has realized that it has failed to persuade Kiev to accept conditions negotiated with Moscow, it is trying to pressure Moscow into considering terms agreed with Kiev, Andrey Kortunov, an expert at the Valdai International Discussion Club, said. It is for this reason, he stressed, that Witkoff and Kushner have yet to visit Russia. At first, they apparently seek to establish contact with Zelensky, making him more cooperative. But such an approach looks dubious because Kiev may put forward only unrealistic proposals. Another problem is Witkoff and Kushner’s administrative weakness compared with Rubio, for there are no major government institutions behind them, Kortunov noted. The whole thing can involve the course of the negotiating process or the Russian side’s intention to keep that at a level that is appropriate to the negotiators’ status, diplomats told Vedomosti.
Kommersant: Japan’s remilitarization course raises concerns in Russia
The Russian Foreign Ministry has warned Japan about potential negative implications of Tokyo’s recent policy course in the military sphere. Among other issues, Moscow is concerned about Japan’s upcoming joint exercises with the United States and Australia in areas near the Russian border which may see the deployment of the latest US Typhon missile system. Russia slammed the drills as provocative and unacceptable as it threatened Japan with "compensatory countermeasures." Meanwhile, Japan is seeking a record defense budget, citing alleged Russian threats.
"Japan is obviously seeking to draw conclusions from the wars raging in Iran and Ukraine, especially given North Korea which is directly watching the Ukraine hostilities and China which has actively supplied equipment and drones to both Moscow and Kiev could be its most likely enemies," Ilya Kramnik, research fellow with the Center for Strategic Planning at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of World Economy and International Relations, told Kommersant. "Amid tensions with Russia, Japan apparently finds it necessary to prepare for potential hostilities in this direction as well, given the enemy will have combat experience from which Tokyo is absent," he added.
Hence, he said, it is giving priority to drone systems, bolstering air defenses and anti-aircraft systems and deploying attack drones. "And Japan will likely develop skills in the aforementioned spheres in close cooperation with the United States which is actually facing the same problems, albeit on a larger scale," the expert maintained.
For obvious reasons, the measures to increase its military capabilities taken by Japan in the past few years raise concerns not only in Russia but also in China and North Korea. Last week, Zhang Xiaogang, a spokesperson for the Ministry of National Defense of China, said that Japan’s remilitarization course and other "dangerous trends" look like war preparations by "militarist Japan" ahead of and during WWII. And the sister of the North Korean leader, Kim Yo Jong, warned that Pyongyang will weigh "additional military options" in response to Japan’s remilitarization.
Izvestia: EEF discussing digital assets, neural networks and social issues
The central theme of the 11th Eastern Economic Forum (EEF), taking place in Vladivostok on September 1-4, is titled "The Far East: Development for the Benefit of People." This year, the forum no longer discusses investments only, with its focus being on housing, personnel, cities, infrastructure and a search for new funding for the region.
The interest in cooperation with Russia remains, said Deputy Prime Minister and Presidential Envoy to the Far Eastern Federal District Yuri Trutnev. Delegates from 80 countries are attending the 2026 EEF, compared to 75 a year earlier. The program includes business dialogues with China, India, the UAE, Mongolia, Vietnam, and ASEAN.
Over the years, the EEF has become a major instrument for attracting capital to the Far East and strengthening Russia's ties with partners in the Asia-Pacific, Natalya Milchakova, a leading analyst at Freedom Global, told Izvestia. According to her, this is how the forum differs, for example, from the SPIEF, with its focus being on Far Eastern projects and Asian investors. In 2025, 358 agreements, contracts and other documents worth 6.6 trillion rubles ($76 billion) were signed at the venue. And the figure may increase by another 5% to 8% in 2026, the expert believes.
At the same time, the investment landscape is also changing. The theme of the latest edition of the EEF suggests a greater focus on projects that directly affect the quality of life, Milchakova emphasized. Along with steelmaking, energy, food and logistics industries that are traditional for the Far Eastern Federal District, the expert expects new initiatives in robotics and AI.
And the forum itself has stopped being merely a showcase for the Far East, Yaroslav Kabakov, Director of Strategy at Finam, argued. According to him, Russia is now simultaneously trying to attract private capital to the region, reorient its foreign trade to Asia and find new sources of growth. At the same time, not the number of signed documents, but how many projects will eventually move into the construction and production stage serves as the success rate.
This becomes particularly important as Russia diversifies its foreign economic relations, Yulia Kovalenko, Deputy Head of the Higher School of Economics of Moscow at Plekhanov Russian University of Economics, maintained. According to her, against the backdrop of the sanctions, the role of European partners has decreased, while countries in Asia and the Pacific region are playing a more active role in Russian investment projects. Therefore, not only attracting foreign capital, but also assisting Russian producers in entering international markets becomes an important task of the EEF, she concluded.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Experts weigh in on oil volumes lost because of Hormuz
According to Bloomberg, in August, Saudi Arabia's oil exports fell to their lowest since the turn of the century, as by August 23, daily Saudi oil supplies to the global market averaged 3.2 million barrels per day. Simultaneously, supplies from Iran dropped to a near-record low of 260,000 barrels per day.
Meanwhile, the US Department of Energy claimed that traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is growing and that oil and petroleum exports from the Persian Gulf had rebounded to 15-16 million bpd, or 75% of the pre-crisis level. The DOE takes into account oil volumes bypassing the Hormuz Strait, a route that is available to Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Iraq.
Russian National Energy Security Fund head Konstantin Simonov told Rossiyskaya Gazeta that the United States is a stakeholder that would benefit from the Hormuz situation not appearing critical. Therefore, calculations by Kpler and Bloomberg, based on tanker tracking data, look more credible to the expert.
According to DA Consulting CEO Daniil Tyun, the actual oil deficit currently amounts to roughly 2 million barrels. The International Energy Agency (IEA) put the Q3 deficit at 1.8 million bpd in its August report. The significant reserves held by oil importers significantly affect the situation, Simonov said: instead of putting the market for "free" oil volumes at higher prices, they used their oil reserves and have not yet felt the full impact from the Hormuz crisis.
Tyun agrees that the physical oil shortage is much larger than one might expect by looking at how much a barrel costs. It is partially offset by strategic and commercial reserves, bypass pipelines, alternative routes, US exports, Russian supplies and perhaps some flows that are not immediately detected by standard monitoring systems, he said. And oil stockpiles are declining. Simultaneously, high oil prices are putting pressure on demand globally. But the market has adjusted to a closed Hormuz much better than expected in the spring.

Pangram Has Emerged as the Gold Standard of AI Detection. Should You Trust It?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Pangram is an AI startup with 24 employees, headquartered above a Popeyes in Brooklyn. It has raised $13 million to date—about 0.0072 percent of what OpenAI has—and was virtually unknown until earlier this year. But if Pangram is to be believed, it’s the one force standing in the way of a full machine takeover of the written word.
Pangram promises to detect how much AI was involved in the generation of any given text, and it does so as a best-guess percentage (using AI, of course). In January, speculation swirled on Reddit and YouTube that the author Mia Ballard may have used AI to write Shy Girl, a self-published novel picked up for traditional publication by Hachette. Although Ballard denied it, Pangram’s CEO posted on X that the book was 78 percent AI-generated. Hachette later canceled the release.
A barrage of similar accusations followed. The New York Times was called out for running an AI-generated installment of its Modern Love column. Pangram score: 100 percent. Then came a winner of the Commonwealth Short Story Prize (100 percent), the novel Daggermouth (60 percent), and a thriller titled Call Me, I’ll Hide the Body that had sold for $2.4 million (97 percent). In late July, Substack announced it was integrating Pangram into its platform so readers could quickly determine possible AI use.
Not all writers see this as a good thing. “There is such distaste and anger at the AI detection software,” says Jane Friedman, an author and publishing expert. “There’s this feeling like they are just as evil, if not more evil, than the AI companies themselves.” Outside of publishing and higher education, Pangram isn’t a household name, but I suspect it’s about to be; the demand to distinguish LLM churn from human writing grows with each passing day. The question to ask now is: How much can the company be trusted?
Max Spero, Pangram’s 30-year-old cofounder and CEO, dials into our Google Meet from his phone, takeout box in one hand and skyscrapers in the background. He’s wearing a beige T-shirt and has short dark hair, a boyish expression, and a wide smile. He says he’s rushing home with lunch and will call back. Ten minutes later, Spero reappears inside his Brooklyn apartment. He’s been on hiring calls all morning, he says. In July, Pangram raised $9 million and announced the launch of its newest model, Pangram 4. The company’s website lists six new job openings, which would increase headcount by 25 percent.
I ask Spero about growing up in California, a softball question that makes him visibly uncomfortable. Discussing the nuances of Pangram’s tech comes more naturally to him than answering personal queries—or speaking to the company’s involvement in literary scandals. Spero takes a bite of his meal and says he was raised in the Los Angeles suburb of La Crescenta. He loved programming and joined his school’s robotics team. As an undergrad at Stanford, he met Bradley Emi, his eventual Pangram cofounder. (My several emailed requests to interview Emi were ignored by the company’s comms team.) After school, Spero went to Google, where he worked on FLoC, a technology designed to replace third-party cookies by grouping Chrome users by interests. (Google killed off FLoC in 2022 after the product was met with privacy concerns.) Spero later worked for the autonomous car company Nuro, while Emi made his way through Tesla and AI biotech company Absci. After ChatGPT launched in 2022, the duo saw a business opportunity to confront a future filled with AI content. In 2023, they founded Checkfor.ai, then renamed the company Pangram a year later. By then, at least a dozen other companies were crowding the detection space, including Originality.ai, GPTZero, and Turnitin; Pangram performed well in some early, independent testing and emerged as a front-runner.
As our interview progresses, Spero’s responses seem sticky, stopping and starting, and not just because he’s eating. I ask about his hiring ethos. Spero murmurs “hmm” before turning away without apology to microwave his food. Fifteen long seconds pass in silence. He finally faces me again and says, “The average person is at Pangram because they care about the mission.”
To detect AI, Pangram uses a method called “synthetic mirroring” by which it takes human writing and has LLMs generate a close match. This teaches its model how AI writes. Pangram also uses “hard negative mining,” searching datasets for false positives that it can synthetically mirror and use to augment its training set—using mistakes to retrain the machine. “All of our datasets are properly licensed, which I think is kind of rare in the AI world today,” Spero says, though that’s partly because Pangram’s product is far less data-hungry than ChatGPT or Claude. “I don’t want to completely throw the AI companies under the bus,” he adds, “but I think they’ve lost a lot of trust, especially in the world of creatives.” Today, Pangram caters to several industries, including education, the legal field, and recruitment, but creative writing constitutes the largest segment of the training text.
The Shy Girl story put Pangram on the map. Spero had already been calling out suspected AI writing from his social accounts, so it wasn’t a surprise when, in January, he was tagged in a Reddit post and subsequently sent a PDF of Ballard’s manuscript. “I put it in [Pangram], I posted it, and then later The New York Times asked me for comment,” he says. “I think people overstate the importance of Pangram in the Shy Girl story.” Except that wasn’t exactly how it happened. Like a game of AI-scandal telephone, it was a Pangram account executive who discussed the story with a publishing industry analyst who, in turn, brought it to the Times.
Another twist: Critics of Pangram, including the investigative project The Drey Dossier, pointed out that Spero’s copy of the manuscript came from a pirating website. When I ask Spero about this, he says, “Yeah. And, like, yeah … it is what it is. I hadn’t looked too closely. I didn’t go read the whole PDF. I just put it straight into Pangram.”
Pangram hasn’t exactly shied away from controversy since then. After the Commonwealth Short Story Prize winner returned a high Pangram score, the company analyzed every winner since 2012, calling out three more potential AI uses. Still, Spero downplays Pangram’s impact, particularly on axed book deals. “Basically, with every book deal, to my knowledge, it hasn’t really been about the Pangram score,” he says. “That is a part of it, but if you talk to anyone involved, it is only a small, small part of the bigger picture.”
We move on to Pangram’s Substack integration. “People shouldn’t be afraid about disclosing this because your work should stand on its own as quality and something that people want to read, regardless of … ” Spero trails off. “Well, how do I want to put that?” He pauses. “I think I … oh, I know what I said the other day.” He gains confidence and his voice speeds up. “If the value of your work is dependent on deceiving the end user into thinking it wasn’t written by AI, then”—he hesitates again—“that’s going to be a problem.” (Later, I realize his intonation changed because he was quoting his own post on X.)
Substack would not confirm any specifics of its Pangram partnership structure or whether Substack pays the company per scan. “Substack’s philosophy is not anti-AI,” a representative tells me. “We simply believe you should know what you’re consuming.” Some authors are wary. There’s a sense, one tells me, that an entire career can be destroyed with the click of a button.
Book publishing, a notoriously slow industry, has been particularly slow to reckon with AI. Still, the reality is that AI is used by a growing subset of authors, publishers, and agents. Last year, Gotham Ghostwriters polled 1,481 working writers and found that 61 percent use AI tools, with 7 percent saying they’ve published AI-generated text. When Tuhin Chakrabarty, an assistant professor of computer science at Stony Brook University, used Pangram earlier this year to analyze 14,419 self-published novels, he found that nearly 20 percent had substantial AI-detection scores. His working paper has been widely cited, and that data was the original source for the Daggermouth accusations.
I reached out to the Big Five publishers to ask if they use AI detection. Simon & Schuster and HarperCollins declined to comment; Hachette and Macmillan did not respond. A spokesperson from Penguin Random House confirmed that its editors may use approved AI-detection tools “as one additional means of identifying potential AI-generated content,” but that such tools are “not determinative and are only one component of a broader editorial process.” Some agents are using detection too—and for every public execution of a book deal, others are being quietly killed offstage. “Normally, agents say nothing,” Friedman says.
I wanted Chakrabarty’s perspective. He first heard about Pangram from one of Spero’s posts in late 2024. After he signed up, Spero sent him API credits. The two have since become “close friends,” Chakrabarty tells me, and Pangram has continued to supply Chakrabarty with credits to support his research. Chakrabarty posts Pangram results on social media and regularly defends the company. He says he has met with publishers to talk about detection in the wake of AI scandals. “Pangram should not be the de facto judgment,” he says. “But I think your own discretion coupled with Pangram’s judgment cannot be wrong.”
Chakrabarty is also in a relationship with Todd Shuster, the co-CEO of Aevitas, a top New York literary agency. Chakrabarty encouraged Shuster to meet with Pangram. “It was instantly a very helpful tool,” Shuster tells me. “Right away, we started having to have difficult conversations [with authors] because Pangram was showing their works to be anything from 50 percent AI-written to 95 percent.” Shuster now uses Pangram to analyze manuscripts and book proposals. He also consults for Pangram, a role that includes making introductions between Pangram and publishers. When authors are confronted, Shuster says some are defensive or seem to fib, while others are honest about their AI use. Shuster says he has asked authors to rewrite work with their own voice and ideas.
Critics point to two major issues with Pangram: the damage done by false positives and the potential bias built into its machine learning. “I don’t think [AI detectors] work,” says Sam Illingworth, a professor of critical AI literacy at Edinburgh Napier University. “I think that detectors are prejudiced against certain people.” One study showed that detectors were more likely to identify work by non-native English writers as AI-generated, and neurodiverse writers have also claimed that their writing patterns are disproportionately flagged. (That study predated Pangram, and Spero points to internal research countering it.) The three novels mentioned earlier—Shy Girl, Daggermouth, and Call Me, easily publishing’s biggest AI-detection scandals—were all written by writers of color. (I reached out to these authors; two didn’t respond and one declined to comment, citing legal concerns.) “As an African American agent, I do think we really need to pay attention to some of the inequities within the industry,” says Regina Brooks, the president of the Association of American Literary Agents. Whose work gets scanned, and who gets publicly accused, is after all an inherently human process—and therefore vulnerable to bias.
In some cases where writers have claimed that their work was wrongfully flagged as AI-generated, Spero has offered a cash reward if they can prove they wrote it themselves. “I’ve offered the bounty in cases where I’m almost certain the person is lying,” he says. “Or, if they’re not lying, then it’s very valuable for us to know.” So far, he says, nobody has taken him up on it.
“Of course, you can fool Pangram,” Chakrabarty says. Some writers have tweaked text or written like AI to elicit false results. A new working paper from Notre Dame, titled “Why AI Detection Fails for Academic Integrity,” notes that Pangram’s 3.2 model flagged light AI editing on academic abstracts as AI writing 64 to 80 percent of the time. However, after putting AI-generated text through a humanizer—a tool that makes AI work seem more human—Pangram caught AI writing less than 4 percent of the time.
Pangram does disclose that its tool performs worse on shorter blocks of text, particularly anything under 100 words. This is a complication, considering that Pangram’s free service offers a limited number of credits per day, totaling about 2,000 words. The median input is 350 words. The company also concedes that an identical passage can get different verdicts depending on whether it’s scanned alone or within a larger context—which is exactly what might happen if a short excerpt is copy and pasted from a novel.
All told, Pangram claims false positives only happen 0.0041 percent of the time with its new model (an improvement over a previously reported rate of 0.01 percent). If anything, Spero says, Pangram is conservative. If text falls on the borderline, the tool errs on the side of declaring it human-written. “This is an intentional choice that we made,” Spero says. It’s partly responsible for the low false-positive rate—and means AI-generated work is more likely to slip under the radar. By Pangram’s measure, human essays that are heavily rewritten by AI are still detected as human-written 41.37 percent of the time.
During our interview, Spero pulls up several social posts to illuminate points he wants to make, pasting them in our chat with such rapid speed that I wonder if he has his own AI system running in the background.
According to Rod Breslau, a journalist and former Pangram contractor, Spero is “personally online all day. He is going to reply to your tweet; he is going to reply to your post on Reddit. He’ll probably reply to your post on LinkedIn.” Breslau first approached Spero at the beginning of the year, offering his services as an “attack dog.” He was sick of seeing AI content flood social media. Breslau’s contract work for Pangram included consulting on its social media strategy and securing interviews for Spero, but he also scrolled the internet with the Pangram extension, publicly calling out suspected AI users. “I wanted to take a harsher approach because I thought that people were getting off too easy,” Breslau says.
Pangram parted ways with Breslau in part because it changed strategies—the company now predicts that AI use will become more accepted. Spero seems to have lost interest in chasing down just anyone who uses AI, but he’ll be vocal, he says, in cases where writers are being “deceptive.” He adds that Pangram will soon be able to flag instances where AI was used even for light editing. “That’s the road map,” Spero says. “Higher granularity, better detail, provide more information to the end users.” As far as I can tell, Pangram ultimately wants to be the go-to arbiter of originality for every sector: publishers, schools, and everyone else.
For now, Spero’s small team includes former educators and one former publishing professional. (A Pangram spokesperson also notes that a researcher has a degree in English literature.) There have been hints of defamation suits brewing from accused authors but, when asked about any lawsuits, Spero says, “I don’t believe anything has come to pass.” He plans to continue publishing technical reports on Pangram’s models and training. “Everybody else is sort of this black box, so I think our strategy here is really just build trust through transparency, be as open as possible, and engage with the community online as much as possible.”
As our conversation wraps, I reflect on the fact that Spero has come across as less than 100 percent engaged. Cagey, even. He roamed around his apartment throughout the interview. He took his laptop to sit near his living room, then to a window with a clutter of houseplants, then a different corner of his kitchen. At several points, his face floated halfway out of frame. He slipped on his headphones, then took them off again. At one point, while discussing model training, he gently burped.
I hadn’t expected this. Was he just busy and tired? Did he not take me seriously? Had the deluge of media coverage rendered interviews rote—or annoying? In the end, I could make assumptions, but there’s only so much anyone can ascertain from an hourlong interaction. Pangram aims to take all the nuances, variables, and unknowns from a piece of communication and return a number. Humans, of course, are far more ambiguous than all that.

Astrotourism: Two resorts in Saudi Arabia are the first to receive DarkSky certification
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:56:32 UTC
18:56:32 KST

Looking for a stargazing escape? Desert Rock Resort and Nujuma, a Ritz-Carlton Reserve in Saudi Arabia have earned DarkSky’s Approved Lodgings & Resorts certification.
Can’t wait until 2027’s “eclipse of the century” for your next celestial adventure? DarkSky International has given its seal of approval to two resorts in Saudi Arabia which offer guests the perfect vantage point to gaze into the night skies.
DarkSky, which champions efforts to tackle light pollution while promoting responsible outdoor lighting that is “beautiful, healthy and functional”, kickstarted its Approved Lodgings & Resorts certification programme in August.
Based on a set criteria, the certification process assessed factors, including whether a facility is located in a region with an exceptional dark sky resource, as well as understood sensitive nighttime resources and means to reduce the impact of light.
Two resorts in Saudi Arabia are among the first to receive the accolade, including Nujuma, a Ritz-Carlton Reserve and the expansive 30,000 square-metre Desert Rock Resort.
Nujuma, encircled by the isles of Saudi’s turquoise Red Sea, takes its name from the Arabic word for “stars” and offers guests a beachfront escape, private villas with wall-to-wall windows with panoramic views of the starlit-filled sky come sundown.
The hotel has its very own resident astronomy expert who leads guests on guided stargazing tours, inviting them to look up and learn about the local significance of the stars.
Meanwhile, recognised for the quality of its night sky, outdoor lighting practices and providing educational outreach, Desert Rock’s 54 villas and 10 suites are embedded within the mountains or suspended from rocky pinnacles in the heart of the Kingdom’s Hijaz Mountains, where, according to the resort, “the landscape continues long after sunset”.
A 20-minute drive away from Red Sea International Airport, the resort’s residences each feature their own private pool alongside sweeping views of the valley.
At sundown, the Astronomy Centre allows guests to observe planets, constellations, meteor showers and other celestial wonders visible from the resort’s vantage point, using powerful telescopes.
The hour-long Arabian Astronomy Observation experience blends science and Saudi culture to explore the dark skies.
Desert Rock also encourages guests to venture out on night hikes, including via its Luna Trail, which offers an ideal route for stargazing in the desert landscape.
The Al’Ayali Albeidh Lunar Nights experience is led by an astronomy expert, where the moon and stars are the focal point of discussions about their cultural significance as well as historic role in navigation and calendaring.
All these efforts are made as part of prioritising protecting the night sky. Desert Rock limits its use of unnecessary artificial light, helping to create optimal stargazing conditions, while maintaining the natural light-dark cycle for local wildlife.

The City of Copenhagen is ready to send more displaced Ukrainians to Jutland after five Jutland mayors opposed the government’s bill to halt immigration from 14 Ukrainian regions in Jyllands-Posten.
Andreas Keil, Social Democrats, Mayor of Employment, Integration, and Business, wrote this in a letter to the mayors.
“If you have the opportunity to receive a number of displaced Ukrainians, it will be a great help to Copenhagen,” he wrote in the letter.
He further writes that it will simultaneously be a concrete contribution to the redistribution among municipalities that Minister for Immigration and Integration Morten Bødskov (Social Democrats as well) has previously requested.
“I understand it to mean that the five Jutland municipalities would like more settlement, labor, and have more opportunities to accommodate the newcomers, while we, conversely, in Copenhagen are challenged to find accommodation for more than the 3,800 Ukrainians we already accommodate now,” he stated.
The letter has been sent to the mayors of Hjørring, Lemvig, Vesthimmerland, Skive, and Brønderslev Municipality, respectively.

Para shot putter Alipour targets fifth gold of his sporting career

Para shot putter Alipour targets fifth gold of his sporting career
TEHRAN - Iranian para-athletics star Amirhossein Alipour is determined to add another gold medal to his impressive collection at the 2026 Asian Para Games in Nagoya, as he looks to strengthen his path toward qualification for the next Paralympic Games.
Alipour, an F11 shot putter, has already claimed four gold medals at major world and Asian competitions and is now preparing for his second appearance at the Asian Para Games.
Speaking about his preparations for Nagoya, Alipour said he began his training program after competing at the World Championships in India. He has continued his preparations both through national training camps and independently.
“So far, I have reached around 70 to 80 percent of my ideal fitness level,” Alipour said. “With the training program I will follow until our departure for Japan, I expect to reach 90 to 100 percent readiness.”
The Iranian thrower made his Asian Para Games debut at Hangzhou 2022, where he won the gold medal at just 19 years of age. He was one of the youngest members of Iran’s delegation at the event.
“That was my first experience at the Asian Para Games and winning the gold medal at such a young age was very special and memorable for me,” Alipour said. “I am determined to repeat that achievement in Nagoya.”
For Alipour, gold is more than just another medal. The 2026 Asian Para Games represent an important step in his campaign to secure qualification for the next Paralympic Games.
“I believe every athlete goes into a major competition aiming for gold. No athlete competes hoping to win anything other than the best medal,” he said. “I am going to the Asian Para Games with the same goal—to defend my title from the previous edition.”
Alipour has enjoyed a remarkable run of success on the international stage. According to the Iranian thrower, every major competition he has entered has ended with him standing on top of the podium.
“I have won gold at the Asian Games in Hangzhou, the World Championships in Japan, the 2024 Paris Paralympics and the World Championships,” he said. “With four world and Asian gold medals already, I am now preparing to win my fifth. This gold is particularly important because the Asian Para Games are one of the significant events in the qualification process for the Paralympics.”
His immediate focus, however, remains Nagoya, where he hopes to make another statement with a fifth major gold medal.
“I want to go to the qualification events with the Nagoya gold behind me and then fight for another Paralympic title,” Alipour said.
