How the SCO chips away at US power without an alliance system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:30:06 UTC
17:30:06 KST

How the SCO chips away at US power without an alliance system
The SCO’s significance is practical: it gives those who do not want their future defined in Washington a forum to coordinate and hedge
The timing is important. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine remains unresolved, while the war between Iran and the US has turned the Persian Gulf into another theatre of strategic competition, with energy markets again exposed to disruption around the Strait of Hormuz. The SCO now brings together China, Russia, India, Iran, Pakistan, most of the Central Asian republics and Belarus, alongside partners including Turkey and multiple Gulf states.
Its 10 full members represent more than 3.4 billion people and roughly a quarter of global GDP. However, its growing importance is not simply a matter of size.
Calling the SCO an anti-American alliance is a mistake. Its members have different interests. India and China remain strategic competitors; India and Pakistan have long-standing tensions; and Central Asian governments want room to manoeuvre between Moscow, Beijing, Ankara, Brussels and Washington. Turkey remains a North Atlantic Treaty Organization (Nato) member while pursuing a larger Eurasian role.

'It’s not 19th century': Kerala CM Satheesan slams cleric over 'women should stay home' remark
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:30:05 UTC
17:30:05 KST

Satheesan’s remarks came amid mounting criticism of Aboobacker over his comments defending restrictions issued by the Kanthapuram faction of the Samastha Kerala Jamiyyathul Ulama on women’s participation in religious events.
NEW DELHI: Kerala chief minister VD Satheesan on Wednesday rejected Sunni cleric and Grand Mufti of India Kanthapuram AP Aboobacker Musliyar’s call for restrictions on women’s participation in public life. He said women must join the mainstream, asserting that such views have no place in a developing Kerala.Speaking to reporters, Satheesan said the state government did not agree with Aboobacker’s position that women should remain at home, adding that even Islam did not require women to be confined to domestic life."We don't agree with his statement that women should stay home. It's not a suitable stand in our developing Keralam. It's not the 19th century that one should make such statements. Even Islam doesn't say that. Women should not stay home, but join the mainstream. That is our stand," he said.Satheesan’s remarks came amid mounting criticism of Aboobacker over his comments defending restrictions issued by the Kanthapuram faction of the Samastha Kerala Jamiyyathul Ulama on women’s participation in religious events.Labour minister Bindu Krishna also criticised the cleric, saying such remarks undermined women’s constitutional rights and sought to push them "centuries back".
"Constitution of India assures equal rights to women and men, irrespective of sex. The people have the right to live a free and liberal life. And also, these types of statements push women centuries back. So, we can't accept such statements. Our women are free to move. They are best rulers. Our girls are always coming through this society, and we can't accept such statements," Krishna told ANI.The controversy followed remarks made by Aboobacker at the Hubbul Rasul Conference in Kochi, where he defended recent directives issued by the Kanthapuram faction of Samastha to local Mahalls on women’s participation in religious celebrations.A circular issued by the organisation directed Madrasas not to allow women to be present among unrelated men at religious events. It also advised against displaying young women on public stages and having them participate in road processions alongside unrelated men.
Defending the directives, Aboobacker said women should remain within the home and invoked the Quran to support his position."Women should remain confined within their homes. They should not enter the public sphere. The Holy Quran says so," Aboobacker said, while defending the purdah system as a practice intended to protect women’s dignity.He argued that allowing women into public spaces without restrictions could result in "great destruction", insisting that the measures were intended to honour and protect women rather than diminish them.Aboobacker also said Islam had granted women property and inheritance rights centuries ago to improve their status without requiring them to leave domestic life. He maintained that he was not concerned by opposition or political criticism and said no one could silence him or force him to change Islamic doctrines.

Azerbaijani authorities evacuated 5,000 people after a fire triggered explosions at an ammunition depot overnight from Tuesday to Wednesday, officials said, adding that there were no casualties.
The blaze broke out at a depot near Nizami village in the western Goranboy district, the emergency situations, defence and interior ministries said in a joint statement.
Emergency and defence ministry personnel, working with police and local authorities, launched an operation and brought the situation under control, they added.
People living nearby were evacuated as a safety precaution, the statement added.
Residents of Nizami and the neighbouring village of Khoylu were moved to nearby areas, Goranboy deputy chief executive Seymur Nazarov told journalists.
"The total number of evacuees is 5,000," said Nazarov, who heads the district's emergency commission.
He said the fire was still burning and sporadic explosions could still be heard, but that efforts were under way to prevent the blaze from spreading and to extinguish it.
No homes had been damaged and no deaths, injuries or serious losses had been recorded, he added.
Security measures were in force at the entrances and exits of both villages, while evacuees were being accommodated in safe conditions, Nazarov said.

Ed Markey wins: Key takeaways from Massachusetts primary election results
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:27:35 UTC
17:27:35 KST

Ed Markey wins: Key takeaways from Massachusetts primary election results
Markey secures the Democratic nomination as Massachusetts voters back several of the state’s long-serving lawmakers.
Veteran Democrats defeated younger challengers in Massachusetts’s primary elections on Tuesday, with Senator Ed Markey beating Representative Seth Moulton for the Democratic nomination.
Long-serving representatives Stephen Lynch and Richard Neal also won their races.
Recommended Stories
list of 1 itemend of list
Here are five key takeaways from the Massachusetts primary election results.
Veteran Democrats survive challenges from younger rivals
Several of Massachusetts’s longest-serving Democrats survived challenges in Tuesday’s primaries.
Senator Ed Markey, 80, defeated 47-year-old Representative Seth Moulton to secure the Democratic nomination.
Similar challenges also failed in the House. Representative Stephen Lynch, 71, who has held his seat since 2001, defeated 39-year-old progressive lawyer Patrick Roath in the 8th Congressional District.
In the 1st District, 77-year-old Representative Richard Neal, first elected to Congress in 1988, defeated 39-year-old public school teacher Jeromie Whalen.
All three will now advance to November, with Democrats heavily favoured in Massachusetts.
Markey wins the progressive argument despite his age
Moulton campaigned on the need for a new generation of political leadership, but Markey’s age did not appear to work against him.
Markey, 33 years older than Moulton, ran as the more progressive candidate, with backing from prominent figures on the Democratic left, including Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and independent Senator Bernie Sanders.
Markey also had the backing of Senator Elizabeth Warren and other members of the state’s congressional delegation, while no member of the delegation endorsed Moulton.
Moulton, a Marine veteran who ran as the more moderate alternative, instead received support from groups including VoteVets and New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill.
Markey also repeatedly attacked Moulton over his comments questioning transgender girls’ participation in girls’ sports. Moulton later apologised and said he supported the transgender community, but Markey continued to raise the issue during the campaign.
“If you’re in the trans community or you’re a trans kid feeling the weight of the Trump administration and the Supreme Court, you matter,” Moulton said during an August debate. “You’re valued, and I will always have your back.”
However, the opposite dynamic played out in the 8th District, where the younger Roath — unsuccessfully — challenged Lynch from the left.
The results showed that age and ideology did not necessarily go hand in hand in Massachusetts.
“Generational change isn’t about compromising, to do the small things better,” Markey said Tuesday. “It’s about fighting to do the big things best.”
In a concession speech, Moulton said he would now support Markey.
“Challenging the establishment and calling for a new generation of leadership isn’t easy. But it is necessary,” Moulton told supporters. “We started conversations that needed to happen.”
Progressive challengers make gains but fall short
While younger challengers failed to defeat the state’s veteran Democrats, some still mounted competitive campaigns.
Roath raised about $1.3m compared with roughly $910,000 for Lynch, despite taking on a congressman who has represented the area for more than two decades.
He also significantly narrowed the gap during the campaign. Lynch led Roath by 26 points in a February poll, but by the final stretch of the campaign, his lead had narrowed to seven points.
But Roath ultimately fell short against Lynch.
Whalen also challenged Neal from the left in the 1st District, campaigning on progressive policies including Medicare for All, but fell short against the veteran congressman.
Massachusetts bucks the national trend
The Massachusetts results differed from several Democratic primaries elsewhere in the country, where younger progressive candidates have defeated long-serving politicians.
In Connecticut last month, former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin defeated Representative John Larson, 78, who had served in Congress for nearly three decades.
In June, 29-year-old Democratic socialist Melat Kiros defeated Representative Diana DeGette, who had represented her Colorado district for nearly 30 years.
That came a week after two Democratic members of Congress were defeated by left-wing challengers in New York, including five-term Representative Adriano Espaillat.
In Massachusetts, all three major challenges to long-serving lawmakers failed.
But the results were not necessarily a rejection of progressive politics. Markey himself ran from the party’s progressive wing, while Lynch and Neal faced younger candidates running to their left.
Instead, the common factor was the strength of long-serving politicians, regardless of whether their challengers came from the centre or the left.
Biden-backed Dan Koh wins primary for open House seat
Former Biden White House aide Koh won the Democratic primary for Massachusetts’s 6th Congressional District, the seat being vacated by Seth Moulton as he ran for Senate.
Koh stood out in the five-way race for openly embracing the former Biden administration. He was endorsed by former President Joe Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris, as well as former Labor Secretary and Boston Mayor Marty Walsh.
Koh will now head into November as the favourite to win the heavily Democratic district.
Democratic primaries may have decided the races
In heavily Democratic Massachusetts, the primaries may prove to be the biggest electoral hurdle, with Democratic winners heavily favoured to prevail in November’s general election.
Markey will face Republican John Deaton, who ran unopposed in his primary on Tuesday. Deaton previously ran for the Senate against Elizabeth Warren in 2024, losing by about 20 percentage points.
The Democratic nominees in several House districts will also head into November as heavy favourites, meaning Tuesday’s results could in effect determine much of the state’s congressional delegation for the next term.

Which EU countries have the most paid online subscriptions?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:27:24 UTC
17:27:24 KST

Nearly one in three Europeans paid for online subscriptions in 2025 according to data from Eurostat, but the continent is deeply split on its digital budget. Subscription services are particularly popular in northern and western households, while parts of Eastern Europe lag far behind.
From binge-watching weekend drama series on Netflix or streaming live football matches on DAZN, nearly one in three people across the European Union now pay a recurring monthly fee just to watch films, series, or live sports online.
New data released by Eurostat shows that 32.7% of internet users across the bloc held a paid streaming subscription in 2025.
But how much Europeans actually open their wallets for digital content varies dramatically depending on the country they call home.
When breaking down the numbers by member state, a stark geographical split emerges: Ireland and Denmark lead the rankings by a wide margin, with 63.9% and 61.1% of internet users respectively paying for video and sports services such as Amazon Prime and Disney+, closely followed by the Netherlands at 59.2%.
At the other end of the spectrum, willingness to pay for streaming services drops significantly.
Bulgaria recorded the lowest adoption rate in the European Union at just 9.3%, followed by Slovenia (13.7%), Latvia (16.7%), and Lithuania (17.4%), creating a massive digital divide across the continent.
Beyond audiovisual entertainment, the data reveals clear differences in the popularity of alternative subscription sectors.
Audio platforms covering music streaming and podcasts on apps like YouTube Premium and Spotify count 23.0% of EU internet users as paying subscribers.
Traditional reads such as online news websites, digital newspapers, and magazines lag far behind at 7.2%, while interactive cloud gaming subscriptions like Xbox Game Pass trail at the bottom with 6.1%.
As digital services continue to anchor modern household routines, these figures highlight a deeply fragmented digital landscape across Europe.
Subscription services hit with lawsuits
Despite their apparent popularity in certain countries, subscription services in the EU have also come under fire from customers in recent months.
A Dutch consumer group is suing Netflix over its subscription price increases of up to 75% since 2017. It put the potential damages at up to €673 million.
It follows similar cases elsewhere in Europe, such as a court in Rome ruling in April that Netflix's price increases in Italy were illegal. The streaming platform is appealing against the decision.
Various courts in Germany have also ruled in favour of consumers in parallel legal battles, while another in Spain is still ongoing and another in Austria concluded in an out-of-court settlement on compensation.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

"On September 1, 2026, operators of the Active Action Department and the Unmanned Systems Department of the GUR of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, as part of a joint deepstrike operation with the Defense Forces of Ukraine, hit the Novatek-Ust-Luga complex in the Leningrad region of Russia," the defense intelligence service reported.
"As a result of the operation, key elements of the oil refining installation and technological equipment were hit, and a large-scale fire broke out at the plant," the press service added.
A record wave of Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries triggered renewed fuel shortages across Russia. Crude processing fell to near its lowest level in more than two decades, while motorists faced growing gasoline shortages and queues.
According to Bloomberg, fuel availability had improved during a slowdown in Ukrainian attacks in the second half of July. The recovery was short-lived, however, as Ukrainian forces struck refineries at least 21 times in August, which was the highest monthly number recorded up to that point.
Consequently, Russia processed an average of just over 3.8 million barrels of crude per day in August, down from the 5.3 million to 5.5 million barrels typically processed daily during the higher-demand summer period. Gasoline output fell by nearly 20% year-on-year during the first three weeks of August, while diesel production dropped by more than 23% over the same period.

Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine’s state railway operator, said there had been no strikes on railway infrastructure in central Kyiv.
The latest strike came after Russian attacks overnight and earlier Wednesday morning had already caused fires and damage across the Kyiv region.
In Kyiv’s Holosiivskyi district, debris from a Russian drone fell in an open area and caused a fire, Klitschko said. The same district was targeted during the previous evening’s attack, when falling debris also caused a fire in an open area. A private house in Kyiv’s Solomianskyi district was also set on fire.
Two people were wounded in the morning attack in the Kyiv region, according to Regional Military Administration head Tymur Tkachenko.
What changed in Russia’s drone war in Ukraine?
Since Thursday, Kyiv has been living under a constant drone siege.
Russia began shifting its long-range drone tactics in Ukraine on Thursday, Aug. 27 – the large swarms once or twice a week that Kyiv residents had become accustomed to have been replaced by near-continuous waves across Ukrainian airspace
As of Tuesday, Sept. 1, there has been no let-up in the strategy, with explosions ringing consistently over Kyiv and other cities, paralyzing businesses nationwide as some major chains were increasingly targeted.
The good news is that the overall number launched stayed relatively consistent and Ukraine’s interception rates remain high – but the bad news is that Russia can likely keep it up for some time.
No major spikes within the same timeframe – but not enough data on daytime launches.
The overall number of drones launched likely increased – though those recorded overnight stayed relatively consistent.
Based on the Ukrainian Air Force’s daily morning briefing, Russia launched an average of around 188 drones per night (6 p.m.-8 a.m.) between Aug. 27-31.
For comparison, the average in July recorded in the same 6 p.m.-8 a.m. window was close to 160 per day, with the lowest on July 21 (58 launched) and the highest on July 2 (496 launched).
The air force did not provide clear data on drones launched and intercepted outside the 6 p.m.-8 a.m. window, though its warnings over the past week suggest they range in the dozens per day.
For context, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense said Russia launched 8,653 drones in July – a few thousand more than the 4,955 Kyiv Post calculated based on the air force’s morning briefings.
Recent months also saw a drastic drop in total numbers launched in a single swarm, with Moscow launching a record swarm of over 1,500 drones within 24 hours in May, an attack that coincided with a renewed peace push from Washington and a reiterated hardline stance from Moscow at the time.
The largest number of drones launched in a single attack was on Sept. 7, 2025, when Russia launched 805 drones overnight in an attack that killed at least four civilians.
The known numbers suggest that unless Ukraine could hit Russia’s drone production, Moscow is likely able to sustain the number of launches.

Homemade Rockets Reportedly Hit One of Germany's Largest Power Plants in Sabotage Attempt
German authorities reported an attempt to attack energy infrastructure after discovering homemade explosive and incendiary devices near an electrical substation in Turnow-Preilack, located near the Jänschwalde lignite-fired power plant in Brandenburg.
The German newspaper Märkische Allgemeine Zeitung reported on September 1, obtaining a photograph showing what appeared to be an improvised device resembles a small homemade model rocket at the site.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Several improvised devices were found near the site in the Spree-Neisse district, and bomb disposal specialists were deployed to neutralize them.
The targeted substation distributes electricity generated by the 2,000-megawatt Jänschwalde facility—Germany's fourth-largest power station, which includes one 500-megawatt unit kept in reserve.
The plant supplies power to several million households and provides district heating to the city of Cottbus, with the affected substation situated about 5 kilometers away from the main facility.
German media indicated the apparent goal of the action was reportedly to cause a large-scale power outage linked to the nearby coal plant. Police noted that potential damage to a power line was recorded around 8 a.m., though initial reports confirmed no major blackouts occurred.
Brandenburg Prime Minister Dietmar Woidke referred to the event as a "trial attack." He stated, "The alarmingly high frequency of such incidents shows that we must decisively protect our infrastructure."
Woidke added that emergency services and personnel at the substation and power station prevented worse outcomes through timely actions, noting that no injuries were reported.
The event follows a series of sabotage incidents recorded across several European nations since early August. On August 4, an attack attempt targeting a Ukrainian An-124 cargo aircraft occurred at Leipzig airport using multiple drones, one of which struck a DHL company plane, though none detonated.
Earlier, a deliberate arson attack on a cable bridge connected to the Lichterfelde power station in Berlin damaged five high-voltage and ten medium-voltage power lines, leaving over 35,000 households and nearly 2,000 businesses without electricity and central heating across four districts.
A far-left extremist group known as Vulkangruppe claimed responsibility for the sabotage, prompting law enforcement to open a formal investigation while emergency crews worked to deploy temporary mobile infrastructure and restore full power to the affected areas.

OMA’s taipei housing renewal lets residents shape an alternative to the standard tower
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:25:35 UTC
17:25:35 KST

RESIDENTS COMMISSION OMA TO RETHINK URBAN RENEWAL IN TAIPEI
The residents of Taipei’s Songshan Yulin Yuan Community appoint OMA to redevelop their aging housing block, proposing an alternative to the standardized residential towers often produced through conventional, sales-led urban renewal. Set within a 1960s planned neighborhood in Taipei, the project asks whether increasing density can preserve some of the spatial habits, greenery, and sense of collective life that residents already value.
The commission arrives at a significant moment for Taipei’s housing stock. More than 70 percent of the city’s housing is now over 30 years old, while many buildings constructed before 1974 do not meet contemporary seismic standards. Taiwan’s Disaster-Prevention Urban Renewal policy, introduced in 2024, offers floor-area-ratio bonuses to encourage the reconstruction of vulnerable structures. The Songshan project responds to these conditions by placing residents themselves at the center of the renewal process. OMA says its proposal grows out of conversations with the existing community. The main challenge of the project is to determine which qualities of the neighborhood should survive the transition.
‘Rather than being commissioned by a developer, we were appointed directly by residents to redevelop their 1960s housing. The neighborhood is characterized by relatively low density, interconnected buildings, and abundant greenery. Through extensive conversations with residents, we learned that these qualities are precisely what they value and want to preserve. Our proposal therefore reinterprets the spatial and social qualities of the existing neighborhood to create a contemporary model of collective living. The aim is to retain a sense of community while accommodating future needs. I believe successful urban transformations grow out of the existing context and aspirations of the community.’ David Gianotten, OMA Managing Partner, tells designboom.
renderings by Stefania Trozzi, Diego Iacono, Nevena Ivanovic, courtesy of OMA
FOUR INTERLOCKING SLABS REPLACE THE AGING WALK-UPS
The architects at OMA transform the existing block into two 24-story residential towers composed of four interlocking vertical slabs. The massing steps and shifts across the site, breaking down the scale of the new development while creating openings between its different volumes. The configuration maximizes north-south facades and introduces vertical openings intended to bring daylight and natural ventilation deeper into the apartments. It also responds to a residential typology found in the original neighborhood, which OMA describes as a ‘front and rear balcony’ arrangement.
Living rooms and balconies face outward, while a central living zone connects to a rear service layer containing kitchens, bathrooms, and utilities. In this way, the project translates an existing domestic pattern into a larger and denser residential structure rather than abandoning it entirely. ‘Songshan Yulin Yuan is part of a 1960s planned neighborhood defined by low density, interconnected building types, and abundant greenery,’says David Gianotten. ‘Through close engagement with residents, we understood that these are qualities that the community wish to retain in the renewed housing.’
the two towers are composed as distinct volumes with stepped and shifted massing
PUBLIC PLATFORMS EXTEND DAILY LIFE INTO THE TOWERS
The spaces between and around the residential slabs become an important part of OMA’s strategy. A network of shared amenities extends through the project at different levels, creating connections between the towers and the surrounding neighborhood. On the second floor, a semi-open platform sits within the surrounding tree canopy and connects with nearby community parks. The space accommodates sports and leisure activities, while the ground floor opens toward nearby schools and the walking track of the park. Here, a receding facade frames the lobby and retail spaces to strengthen the relationship between the new development and its immediate surroundings.
Below ground, a community living room provides quieter leisure spaces. An atrium brings daylight into this lower level while maintaining visual connections between different parts of the building. Rooftop sky gardens occupy the tops of the lower slabs, offering views across Taipei. Together, these shared spaces are intended to form a continuous network for everyday life, extending beyond the individual apartment and into the wider neighborhood.
the proposed towers stand within Taipei’s dense residential landscape
CAN DENSITY PRESERVE A SENSE OF NEIGHBORHOOD?
The Songshan Urban Renewal Residence proposes a different way of thinking about the relationship between density and residential quality. Its architectural argument lies less in rejecting tall buildings altogether than in questioning whether renewal must inevitably produce isolated, repetitive towers. ‘Our aim is to increase density while preserving residential quality through the reorganization of massing, openings, and public spaces, fostering a sense of neighborhood character and domesticity rarely seen in recent renewal projects,’explains Chiaju Lin, OMA Project Director in Taiwan.
The project remains at the schematic design stage, but its commission reflects the active role residents have taken in the redevelopment of their community. The Songshan Yulin Yuan Community selected OMA to rethink their existing housing, drawing attention to the qualities residents hope to retain, including greenery, connected buildings, and familiar patterns of daily life. OMA responds through stepped slabs, balconies, shared platforms, gardens, and communal spaces. While the project is still in its early stages, it presents an approach to urban renewal in which residents take part in shaping the housing that will replace their existing homes.
the redevelopment introduces new housing into Taipei’s existing urban fabric
a shared platform at the base of the towers introduces leisure spaces
OMA’s facade combines deeply recessed windows with balconies and planted outdoor spaces
the two residential towers rise above a landscaped ground level, supported by angled structural elements

His brother died abroad. His boss kept asking when he would return to work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:24:30 UTC
17:24:30 KST

A Thai employee has resigned from his job after what he described as an insensitive response from his manager while he was arranging the return of his younger brother’s body from abroad and preparing for the funeral.
Somsak Butsri shared the story in a Facebook post that quickly went viral.
His brother, a well-known travel YouTuber known as Hlun Solo with millions of followers on social media, died while traveling in Georgia.
In the days that followed, Butsri said he followed company procedures and submitted a written leave request, while also discussing privately how long he would be away.
At the same time, he was coordinating with multiple agencies, handling documents, contacting the embassy and arranging the travel needed to bring his brother’s body home.
He said the process continued late into the night and left him with very little sleep.
According to his post, during that period his manager repeatedly questioned whether his absence was necessary, whether he needed to be physically present, whether the situation was urgent enough to justify leave and whether he could return to work sooner.
Two days after his brother’s body arrived in Thailand, while the family was still holding funeral ceremonies, Butsri received another phone call asking when he would return to work.
He said there were no urgent tasks requiring his presence at the time.
Butsri stressed that he was not asking for special treatment, but for basic judgment and respect.
He said the comments he received reflected a mindset that failed to recognize the human reality of losing a family member.
After the ceremonies ended, he decided to resign.
He returned to the office on Aug. 18 to complete his responsibilities through the end of the month and ensure a proper handover.
On Aug. 23, his birthday, he told his mother and grandmother that he could no longer continue working in an environment shaped by that attitude.
He said he worried they would be anxious because he still needed to contribute to the household income, but their reaction reassured him and allowed him to take a break without overthinking the decision.
Butsri also said he had prepared financially, maintaining an emergency fund that could cover one to two years without work or potentially be used to start a small business.
For now, he said, he has not decided what he will do next because many matters related to his brother remain unresolved.
He also made clear that he did not blame everyone at the company, saying he was sorry to leave supportive colleagues and emphasizing that his decision was not about them.
He ended his post by arguing that leadership should be measured not only by business results, but also by maturity, judgment and respect for people, especially when someone is dealing with one of the hardest moments of their life.

Yandex’s AI assistant could gain expanded permissions on mobile devices, including access to banking apps
Russia’s Digital Development Ministry is weighing new rules for preinstalling Russian services on smartphones, tablets, and other devices, a move that could give Alice AI, the assistant developed by Yandex, expanded permissions on users’ devices.
Alice AI could also gain access to banking apps and other applications that collect sensitive data and store it on their own servers, a source told the Russian business daily Kommersant. The source did not specify what kind of data would be involved.
If the new rules take effect, the source said, Yandex’s AI assistant could become a service “with access rights to user data far greater than any preinstalled app on the list.”
The outlet’s sources stressed that the initiative directly targets similar foreign smart assistants and AI models operating in Russia.
The Digital Development Ministry published a draft resolution for public discussion in early August that would update the existing preinstallation rules, referring to an AI assistant “with access to system functions, applications, notifications, authorization, and hardware capabilities.” The ministry has since pulled the document from its website for revision.
The Digital Development Ministry told Kommersant that the proposed changes “are at the discussion stage with the industry.” Yandex had not responded to a request for comment by the time of publication.
Russia has required the preinstallation of Russian software on smartphones, computers, and other electronics since 2021. Alice AI is on the government’s list of mandatory preinstalled apps for 2027.

Fewer foreign-language residents in Finland rely on welfare benefits
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:20:57 EEST
17:20:57 KST

A smaller share of Finland’s growing foreign-language population receives basic social assistance and unemployment benefits than a decade ago, according to figures released by the Social Insurance Institution of Finland, Kela, on Wednesday.
Kela data shows that the number of people whose registered mother tongue is not Finnish, Swedish or Sámi rose by more than 70 per cent between 2017 and 2025, from 373,000 to 646,000.
Despite that rise, the proportion receiving several forms of income support fell over the same period.
In 2017, 23 per cent of foreign-language adults received basic social assistance. By 2025, the figure had fallen to 18 per cent. The share receiving labour market subsidy dropped from 24 per cent to 16 per cent.
“The foreign-language population in Finland is larger than before, so their share of Kela benefit recipients has also increased. The development reflects the change in the population structure,” Kela research manager Signe Jauhiainen said in the agency’s release.
The number of foreign-language social assistance recipients still increased as the population grew. Kela recorded 110,000 recipients in 2017 and 137,000 in 2025. Last year’s total included 92,000 adults and 45,000 children.
Jauhiainen said much of the increase in recipient numbers came from Ukrainian speakers after 2023. Ukrainians living in Finland under temporary protection did not qualify for labour market subsidy.
Kela paid €408 million in basic social assistance to foreign-language recipients in 2025, representing 41 per cent of total spending on the benefit. In 2017, the corresponding amount was €172 million, or 24 per cent.
Foreign-language recipients received €597 million in labour market subsidy in 2025, accounting for one-third of total payments under the scheme.
Labour market subsidy and the basic unemployment allowance were replaced by Finland’s new general benefit on 1 May 2026.
Kela paid about €9.2 billion through nine main income-support benefits in 2025. Foreign-language recipients received around €1.8 billion, or 20 per cent. In 2017, they received 15 per cent of €8.6 billion paid through the same benefits.
Kela said the figures differ between benefit categories. Foreign-language recipients accounted for more than 40 per cent of basic social assistance spending in 2025 but less than 5 per cent of national pension payments.
General housing allowance followed a similar trend in recipient rates. Some 26 per cent of foreign-language adults received the benefit in 2017, compared with 18 per cent in 2025.
Their share of housing allowance spending moved in the opposite direction, rising from 19 per cent to 27 per cent. Kela linked part of the change to Ukrainians entering the Finnish social security system and changes to housing support rules.
Students moved from general housing allowance to the student housing supplement in 2025. Owner-occupiers also lost eligibility for general housing allowance during the year, changing the composition of recipients.
Kela said the declining use of unemployment and social assistance among the foreign-language population indicates that a larger share of the group is working or studying.

The water supply network has also suffered disruption, with 40 schemes currently affected. Hamirpur accounts for 23 of the disrupted schemes, while Shimla has reported 17.
NEW DELHI: Monsoon rains have claimed 259 lives and caused damage worth more than Rs 1,200 crore across Himachal Pradesh in just 64 days, according to State Emergency Operations Centre (SEOC) data. Meanwhile, the latest spell of rain has severely affected connectivity, with 150 roads currently blocked across Himachal Pradesh.Mandi has reported the highest number of closures at 78, followed by Shimla with 30. Fresh rainfall has also disrupted power and water supplies across the hill state.Essential services have also been hit. As many as 374 distribution transformer regions (DTRs) are out of service, affecting power supply across several districts. Mandi has recorded 128 affected DTRs, followed by Shimla with 84 and Kullu with 81.The water supply network has also suffered disruption, with 40 schemes currently affected. Hamirpur accounts for 23 of the disrupted schemes, while Shimla has reported 17.The mounting disruptions come against the backdrop of a deadly monsoon season that has claimed 259 lives between June 30 and September 1. Of the total fatalities, 106 were caused by rain and disaster-related incidents, including 18 deaths in landslides and 13 due to drowning.
Another 153 people died in road accidents during the period.Lahaul and Spiti, the high-altitude tribal district, recorded 15 deaths linked to monsoon-related disasters.The rains have also inflicted extensive damage on public and private infrastructure, with the cumulative losses estimated at Rs 1,202.64 crore. The Public Works Department bore the biggest share of the damage at more than Rs 914 crore, while the Jal Shakti Vibhag reported losses exceeding Rs 258 crore.
The disaster has completely damaged 460 houses and resulted in the deaths of 460 animals, the SEOC data showed.State government departments and field agencies are now carrying out restoration operations in affected districts, working to reopen blocked roads and restore power and water supply.With the monsoon continuing to disrupt normal life, the latest figures underline the scale of the crisis facing Himachal Pradesh, where hundreds of lives have been lost and critical infrastructure has suffered extensive damage in just over two months.

Germany successfully tests Israeli ballistic missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:14:24 UTC
17:14:24 KST

Breadcrumb
Germany successfully tests Israeli ballistic missile, officials say
Germany successfully tested an Israeli ballistic missile in the North Atlantic overnight, military officials said on Wednesday, as Western powers scramble to acquire long-range weapons to counter what they see as an increased threat from Russia.
The test of what officials said was a LORA missile built by Israel Aerospace Industries came hours after Berlin publicly blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month and ordered measures in response.
Germany does not currently have ballistic missiles, which fly at much higher speeds than the cruise missiles in its arsenal. The Israeli-built system has a range of up to 500 km (310 miles), Germany's defence ministry said.
Berlin is engaged in a number of multinational collaborations aimed at developing long-range missiles, and also looking at options to buy such weapons.
Navy chief Jan Christian Kaack said the test was a success.
"Our units can successfully deploy the system, and its potential range exceeds anything we have seen before," he said in a statement. "In terms of protecting Germany and our allies, this test marks a new chapter in deterrence and maritime defence readiness."
Germany is also working on an upgraded version of its Taurus cruise missile, currently its only weapon with a range of several hundred kilometres, with production scheduled to start in 2029.
The upgraded Taurus NEO missile will feature an extended range, improved shielding against interference, and advancements in navigation and seeker head technology, according to a budget document.
German forces have about 600 Taurus missiles with an official range of more than 500 km (310 miles) in their inventories, that can be launched from fighter jets such as the Tornado, the F-15 or the F-18.
The weapon, built by European defence company MBDA, is designed to destroy targets behind enemy lines such as command bunkers, ammunition and fuel dumps, airfields and bridges.

Across China: Gen-Z artists breath new life into China's naive art
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:14:12 CST
17:14:12 KST

A docent introduces an artwork to visitors during a farmer painting exhibition at the Xinhua News Agency Art Museum in Beijing, capital of China, Aug. 25, 2026. (Xinhua/Wang Jingqiang)
BEIJING, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- In a gallery of golden wheat fields on canvas, Wang Yaoyao in a pale pink qipao is a quiet contrast. The academically trained painter now embraces the unruliness of farmer painting -- a typical Chinese naive art.
At the exhibition hall in the financial hub of Beijing, under Wang's brush, a traditional paper-cutting-style piglet leaps onto a palette, and dives deep into a kaleidoscope of vibrant colors.
"Creating farmer paintings is about pursuing freedom," said the young artist, who studied traditional Chinese painting before joining a district-level workshop in northwest China's Xi'an city in 2021.
Emerging in Huxian County, now Huyi District of Xi'an, in 1958, farmer painting was but villagers' simple strokes on paper during slack farming seasons, before it gained a national audience, like the Chinese version of the legend of Grandma Moses.
At first sight, Wang was captivated by the art's bold use of color and exaggerated, uninhibited forms. A leaf can be blue or red, she said, and creativity can fly free of any conventional rules.
"Take the painting 'Endless Corn Cobs,' for example. The corn, a symbol of a bumper harvest, is depicted as huge as the locomotive carrying it. The artist's yearning for a good harvest is vividly expressed," Wang said. "I really love this kind of free expression."
For Wang, this sense of freedom represents a shared connection among farmer painters across generations, nourishing renewed vitality for their artistic spirits and works.
"Many young people are drawn to farmer painting because of its unconventional styles and the creativity of earlier generations of artists. They come together to learn and carry on the tradition of Huxian farmer painting," she said.
That tradition is never a one-way inheritance.
One of the artists Wang admires most is an 83-year-old painter, who still goes to the studio every day to paint. His style retains the simplicity characteristic of the 1970s and 1980s, while he also makes an effort to learn new approaches to composition from younger artists.
"While he learns from us, we also learn from him," Wang said.
Today's farmer paintings are no longer confined to traditional depictions of rural life.
High-speed trains racing across the landscape, electric vehicles on the roads, mechanized irrigation systems, and major industrial equipment have all entered the artists' field of vision as elements of contemporary China.
"China-Europe Railway Express: The Steel Camel Caravan" is one of Wang's latest creations. In her painting, the locomotive that once carried enormous corn has been transformed into the China-Europe freight trains carrying Chinese new energy vehicles from Xi'an to distant markets.
"The rapid development of our hometown is an inexhaustible source of inspiration, and it has also brought more visions of the future into our works," said the artist.
The paintings, in turn, are giving back to the land where their creators took root.
In Huyi, many farmer painters have turned their backyards into studios and galleries. Chinese and overseas visitors come to appreciate and purchase paintings and experience the creative process, bringing tangible income to the artists.
There are now more than 2,300 farmer painting artists in Huyi, with nearly 10,000 works having been exhibited in 88 countries and regions.
From Aug. 25 to Sept. 3, an exhibition of such paintings is being held at the Xinhua News Agency Art Museum in downtown Beijing, showcasing 120 selected works by 53 farmers from Huyi.
Huyi's stories resonated with China's push to advance all-round rural revitalization. The outline of China's 15th Five-Year Plan（2026-2030）calls for protecting and passing on rural cultural heritage to promote and develop rural culture.
"Each painting is both a vivid record of changes in rural society and a lively artistic testimony to the evolving face of China's urban and rural areas," said Wang Wenji, director of the Huyi District Farmer Painting Museum.
Huxian farmer painting represents an aesthetic tradition that has grown up from the soil, said Ma Fenghui, vice chairman of the China Artists Association.
Grandma Moses is merely a legend, yet art was her life's calling. For Wang Yaoyao, similar silhouettes at Huyi inspired her to imagine whether she, too, will still be holding a paintbrush in her 80s.
"We are using our brushes to record the changes brought about by rural revitalization, while extending our artistic vision beyond the fields and villages to a much broader world," Wang said. ■

Russian hybrid attacks across Europe bear “all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism”, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Wednesday, as the bloc considers further measures against Moscow.
Speaking ahead of an informal meeting of EU foreign ministers in Ireland, Kallas said several member states had summoned Russian ambassadors over the alleged attacks.
She said the EU already has 1,600 listings targeting Russia’s military-industrial complex in the pipeline, with more potentially to be added.
Kallas stressed, however, that no formal decisions would be taken at the informal meeting.
Referring to an alleged Russian drone attack at Germany’s Leipzig Airport in August, Kallas said Berlin’s response had sent “a very strong signal”. She added that German officials were grateful for support expressed by other EU member states.
“I think this is the unified response that we need to take,” Kallas said.
EU pressure on Russia
Kallas said the attacks should serve as “wake-up calls” for countries that have so far taken a less forceful position towards Moscow.
Ukraine will also join part of the discussions, which will focus on coordinating further measures to increase pressure on Russia amid what Kallas described as intensified attacks on civilians.
Ministers will also discuss how to make EU foreign policy more effective, particularly given the bloc’s unanimity requirement, she said.
“In this geopolitical context, we have to be more agile, and we have to really be able to react to situations that are upcoming,” Kallas said.
The agenda will also cover the protection of critical infrastructure, including the use of underwater drones and lessons learned from Ukraine’s technological innovations.
Regarding the Middle East, ministers will discuss freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, potential cooperation with a Saudi-led multinational initiative, and developments in the occupied West Bank.

Urgent needs persist three weeks after earthquake in Colombia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:12:01 UTC
17:12:01 KST

Three weeks after the 7.4-magnitude earthquake that struck western Colombia on 10 August, the initial phase of the emergency has ended, but thousands of people are still facing difficulties accessing medical care, mental health support, food, and materials to rebuild their homes.
Although the earthquake severely affected cities such as Cali and Pereira, the most critical gaps remain in areas that have long faced poverty, barriers to healthcare, and the presence of armed groups. In parts of Quibdó and Medio Baudó in Chocó, as well as Buenaventura in Valle del Cauca, where conditions were already precarious before the disaster, the earthquake has further exacerbated existing needs.
Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) sent assessment and response teams to Valle del Cauca, Chocó, and Risaralda, prioritising areas where needs remain greatest and where the response has been more limited.
“Unlike other emergencies, the effects of the earthquake in Colombia were not concentrated in one place,” says Siham Hajaj, MSF head of mission in Colombia. “The impact was felt across territories that may seem close to one another but are separated by rivers and mountains, which has made the response more difficult. We have also seen significant differences between areas with a stronger institutional presence and others that have historically been neglected, including Indigenous and Afro-Colombian communities.”
MSF has sent teams to the departments of Valle del Cauca, Chocó, and Risaralda, and, after conducting assessments in about ten municipalities. We’ve begun mobile clinics in Buenaventura (Valle del Cauca), as well as in Quibdó and Medio Baudó (Chocó), where greater barriers to accessing healthcare and lower response coverage were identified.
“In these territories, many communities are facing a double or even triple burden,” says Hajaj. “In addition to the effects of the earthquake, they are living in contexts marked by armed conflict, structural limitations in health services, and, in some cases, new climate-related events.”
In the municipality of Medio Baudó, Indigenous communities also faced flooding caused by the sudden rise of the Baudó River just two days after the earthquake, further worsening living conditions.
Health impacts
MSF teams have identified mental health needs as one of the main consequences of the disaster. Three weeks after the earthquake, common reactions include anxiety, acute stress, hypervigilance, insomnia, and a persistent fear of possible aftershocks and uncertainty about the future.
Blanca Lucila, an Embera1 woman from Medio Baudó in Chocó, said she was left deeply shaken. “In my community, three houses collapsed completely and the others were left leaning,” she says. “My head feels out of control; I get up and feel like I’m falling. People say something is going to happen, and we are all staying inside out of fear, waiting to see what will happen.”
My head feels out of control; I get up and feel like I’m falling.
In addition to healthcare, many families continue to need support to repair their homes and access food. In Buenaventura, Sebastián Cundumí returned from fishing to find his house destroyed. “The houses are devastated,” he says. “From the outside, some still look like they are standing, but when you go inside, there is nothing. We need materials to rebuild our homes.” 
Luz Hernecia Rojas, Sebastián Cundumí’s neighbour, saw his house collapse. “Now I’m sleeping in the living room of my daughter’s house, which was also affected, so when it rains, we all get soaked,” says Rojas.
MSF’s response
In Quibdó, Chocó, during the first days of the response, MSF teams focused their efforts on urban areas, including the Municipal Coliseum shelter and the neighbourhoods of Medrano, Las Palmas, Poblado, and Zona Minera. Over eight days, teams carried out more than 700 consultations, including 480 general medical consultations and nearly 60 individual mental health consultations. They also held 15 group psychoeducation sessions with more than 200 participants.
We have also worked in coordination with local institutions, such as ESE Ismael Roldán and the Colombian Family Welfare Institute (ICBF), on vaccination activities, nutrition support, and access to safe water.
Following this initial phase, we expanded our response to rural communities in the department, where significant needs persist and access constraints continue to hinder humanitarian assistance. In Medio Baudó, the team carried out more than 140 medical consultations in three days.
In Buenaventura, Valle del Cauca, the team continues to run mobile clinics in some of the city’s most vulnerable neighbourhoods, where residents had not received medical care after the earthquake. We have conducted activities in the Alberto Lleras, Palo Seco, La Carmelita, Pampa Linda, Santafé, and Unión de Vivienda neighbourhoods.
Throughout Buenaventura, MSF’s response includes a strong mental health and psychosocial support component. In the Alberto Lleras neighbourhood, for example, the team is setting up the “safe spaces” initiative, with recreational activities for children, mental health support, and health promotion activities.
In Buenaventura, the team has carried out nearly 800 consultations, including 600 general medical consultations and 84 individual mental health consultations. The team has also held 59 group sessions, reaching 750 people.
“This emergency has laid bare the inequalities that already existed before the earthquake,” says Hajaj. “One of the priorities now must be to ensure that the most isolated communities receive care.”

Congo’s Ebola outbreak kills more than 3,000, government figures show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:06:20 UTC
17:06:20 KST

Congo’s Ebola outbreak kills more than 3,000, government figures show
DAKAR – The number of deaths in the Democratic Republic of Congo’s Ebola outbreak has surpassed 3,000, government data showed on Sept 2, as the country’s worst epidemic continues to spread across its north-east.
The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, became the largest and deadliest in Congo’s history after surpassing the 2018-2020 epidemic.
It is now second only to the 2014-2016 West African outbreak, which infected more than 28,600 people and killed over 11,000 across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
Government figures showed the death toll had risen to 3,007, while confirmed cases reached 6,186.
The outbreak was formally declared in Ituri province on May 15, though some health officials and experts say it may have started as early as January.
It has since spread to six provinces, despite efforts by the Congolese authorities, the World Health Organization (WHO) and aid groups to contain it.
Health experts say weak surveillance systems, insecurity and community resistance have hampered efforts to identify and treat patients early.
The WHO estimates that 60 per cent of deaths happened outside treatment centres, highlighting the challenges of detecting cases before patients succumbed to the disease.
Bundibugyo has no approved vaccines or treatments, but several vaccines are under development, including candidates from the University of Oxford and the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative.
The Congolese authorities recently began vaccinating frontline health workers with Merck’s Ervebo vaccine, which is licensed against the Zaire species of Ebola and is believed to offer some cross-protection against Bundibugyo. REUTERS

GE Aerospace wins Korean Navy destroyer engine deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:02:57 UTC
17:02:57 KST

- South Korea's Navy selected GE Aerospace to supply 12 LM2500+G4 gas turbines for six KDDX destroyers.
- GE's Korean partner Hanwha Aerospace will manufacture and assemble engine components locally, while NRTEC builds the lightweight composite enclosure in Busan.
South Korea’s Navy has selected GE Aerospace to supply gas turbine engines for its next-generation KDDX destroyer program, with GE Marine set to deliver 12 LM2500+G4 engines to power six ships, the company said.
Each destroyer will carry two LM2500+G4 engines, integrated into a full electric propulsion configuration. GE Aerospace said the setup is intended to support the KDDX’s power demands as the first ship in Korean Navy history built with stealth-integrated radar and armed with anti-aircraft and land-attack missiles.
“The transition to full electric propulsion is a step toward the next generation of naval power,” said Asha Belarski, Vice President and General Manager of GE Aerospace’s Marine Engines and Systems. “We are honored to be a part of this project incorporating the latest advancements in shipbuilding. The selection of GE Aerospace’s LM2500+G4 technology strengthens our strong collaborations in Korea and demonstrates our commitment to local manufacturing.”
Each engine will be housed in a new lightweight composite enclosure, replacing the steel enclosure used on earlier LM2500 installations. GE Aerospace said the composite version cuts weight by more than 2,500 kilograms (5,512 pounds) while keeping the same footprint as the base LM2500 gas turbine. The company said the new enclosure also runs 60 percent quieter and reduces wall temperatures by 25 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit (14 to 28 degrees Celsius) compared with the steel version.
The Republic of Korea Navy has procured 163 GE Aerospace marine gas turbines across 95 ships to date. Under the KDDX program, GE’s longstanding Korean manufacturing partner, Hanwha Aerospace, will produce engine components and handle assembly, testing and in-country service support. The lightweight composite enclosure will be manufactured separately in Busan by NRTEC.
The LM2500+G4 entered service in 2012 and currently powers FREMM frigates operated by Italy, France, Egypt and Morocco. The U.S. Navy has also selected the engine for its Constellation-class frigate program, designated FFG-62, and more recently chose the LM2500+G4 to power the land-based test site supporting design work on its future DDG(X) destroyer class.

What a new Black Sea grain crisis means for the Middle East
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:00:27 UTC
17:00:27 KST

Breadcrumb
What a new Black Sea grain crisis means for the Middle East
Ukrainian drones struck Russian cargo ships carrying stolen Ukrainian grain in the Sea of Azov in April.
Since then, drone attacks by both sides have intensified in the Black Sea region, continuing throughout the summer months.
"For Ukraine, targeting Russia’s oil revenues - and particularly the so-called shadow fleet that enables Moscow to circumvent sanctions - is an important part of increasing the economic cost of the war and degrading Russia’s ability to finance and sustain its military operations," Dr Yevgeniya Gaber, a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Turkey Program, told The New Arab.
In August, two Turkish-owned civilian ships, the Yaşar and the Nadezhda, were struck by drones after departing from the Russian port of Novorossiysk. In response, Turkey’s Foreign Ministry called for the safe passage of commercial shipping through the Black Sea.
“Russia has fewer sea drones, but it is using both planes and drones to track the Ukrainian navy. For Russia, the Black Sea is now mainly used to strike southern Ukraine and protect their own commercial shipping, since their fleet is now hidden in ports,” Clément Molin, an open-source analyst following the Ukraine conflict, told The New Arab.
“Ukraine’s UAVs are being constantly used to track Russian ships, and more than 200 commercial ships have been targeted, mainly from [Russia’s] ghost fleet,” he said. “Ukraine has barely any navy but managed to create a new dimension of the war at sea with drones.”
No ceasefire in sight
On 13 August, Ukrainian drones hit the Russian port facility of Novorossiysk, damaging two grain export terminals. It wasn’t long before Russia carried out a wave of strikes in Ukraine’s Odesa Oblast, hitting food storage infrastructure.
“Russian forces have targeted Ukrainian ports, grain terminals, silos and export infrastructure throughout the war. What has changed is the scale and intensity of the pressure, including more attacks on civilian commercial vessels, warehouses and food-related infrastructure,” Gaber said.
“The consequences are particularly serious for agricultural exports and, therefore, for food security well beyond Ukraine. Between 1 and 26 August, Ukraine exported only 822,000 tonnes of grain - around 21 percent of what it could normally have exported with functioning logistics," she added.
"Total agricultural exports, including grain, oilseeds, oils and meals, amounted to approximately 1.4 million tonnes, only around one-third of Ukraine’s potential export capacity during this period, according to the Ukrainian government."
On 27 August, The Wall Street Journal reported that wheat prices had reached a three-year high as the Black Sea fighting disrupted grain exports, with Odesa and Novorossiysk losing export capacity.
In late August, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Russia was not ready for a ceasefire on grain shipments in the Black Sea. Moscow reportedly sought to include an end to attacks on Russian energy infrastructure in the agreement.
The Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure have been a key way for Kyiv to bring the war back home to Russia after four and a half years of the full-scale invasion.
“The problem is not limited to attacks on ships themselves. Russia is targeting the infrastructure that makes maritime trade possible: ports, grain silos, warehouses, railway connections and other logistical nodes,” Gaber told The New Arab.
“In July alone, Russia carried out 67 attacks on Ukrainian seaport infrastructure, 35 attacks on civilian vessels in ports, and 22 attacks on vessels operating through the Ukrainian maritime corridor.”
The attacks come as both Russia and Ukraine are in peak harvest season, and the grain will go to waste unless it is exported soon. Major commercial shipping firms are suspending operations due to the threat of drones in the Black Sea.
“This creates longer-term economic damage as well. Ukrainian farmers lose revenue from exports and face higher logistical costs, reducing the capital available to invest in the next planting season,” Gaber said.
Diplomatic tensions
The Turkish Foreign Ministry warned that the attacks could have “multifaceted negative repercussions”, including for food security.
“We therefore reiterate our call to all relevant actors, particularly the warring parties, to urgently implement concrete measures to ensure the safety of navigation in the Black Sea.”
The collapse of the Black Sea Grain Initiative, which Turkey had helped facilitate, effectively ended in the summer of 2023. However, Ukraine and Russia were still able to ship their agricultural products to the international market by staying close to the coastlines.
To mitigate any diplomatic blowback, Scott Lucas, Professor of International Politics at University College Dublin’s Clinton Institute, told The New Arab that Ukraine could signal that “we don’t want to be in this situation…of having to counter-attack against the Russian vessels in the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. The Russians put us in this situation”.
The politics surrounding grain shipments from the Black Sea to the Middle East have become an increasingly sensitive issue. The Ukrainian Foreign Ministry noted that stolen grain exported by Russia was reaching Turkey, Egypt, and Algeria.
In April, Ukraine and Israel exchanged accusations over a Russian shadow fleet vessel that arrived in Israel carrying grain from the occupied Ukrainian territories.
“Diplomatically, Ukraine has limited means to stop these attacks as long as Russia is unwilling to respond to calls for de-escalation. Kyiv has repeatedly called for a ceasefire and negotiations to end the war, while Moscow has continued to intensify attacks on critical infrastructure," Gaber said.
"This is why Ukraine argues that diplomacy has to be backed by greater economic, political and military pressure on Russia. Middle Eastern countries also have an interest in making this message clear.”
Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports and commercial shipping are not simply a bilateral Russian-Ukrainian issue, she said, as they directly affect the reliability and cost of food imports and therefore regional food security.
Syria and Egypt's food security
Over 90 percent of Ukraine’s agricultural exports are shipped through seaports, with countries in the Middle East especially vulnerable to prolonged disruptions in the global food supplies. Many have taken steps to mitigate these risks. In the spring, for example, Egypt reached a deal to receive grain shipments from Russia.
“In the case of Egypt, [it depends on] how much backstop they have from the Gulf States. Do they have alternative sources for supply?” Lucas told The New Arab.
Roughly 80 percent of Egypt’s wheat imports came from Black Sea ports in the first half of 2026.
The Emirati company Al Dahra Agriculture Trading and Egypt’s General Authority for Supply Commodities recently signed a five-year, $500 million wheat supply agreement. Egypt’s government has also imposed price controls on unsubsidised bread since March. In mid-August, Egypt expanded a cash subsidy scheme to cover more food items.
“Anytime you get a disruption to grain supplies, especially in countries that are already in a tenuous economic situation, you have to run it on a case-by-case basis on how well these countries prepared for such a shock. 2010 is a reminder of what can happen quickly,” Lucas added.
A poor harvest and high food prices in 2010 contributed to the uprising against the former regime of Bashar Al-Assad in Syria, which lasted nearly 14 years.
“A lot of countries don’t want Syria to fail,” Lucas said, explaining that Syria could likely rely on Turkish and US assistance since the Trump Administration is interested in maintaining Syrian stability.
Likewise, Ukraine has sought to build up its own avenues of cooperation with the new Syrian government.
“During President Zelensky’s visit to Damascus in April, food security was one of the issues discussed with President Ahmed al-Sharaa, alongside broader security and trade cooperation. Ukraine has offered to support Syria through initiatives such as Grain from Ukraine,” Gaber told The New Arab.
Syria has made progress in increasing its own domestic production of wheat. Benjamin Fève, a Senior Consultant at Karam Shaar Advisory Limited, told The New Arab that for now, Syria’s food supply was relatively safe.
“Syria had a very successful harvest. Its strategic reserves have been replenished, and Syria will be much less dependent on imports. Even if the food supplies are secure in the short term, in the medium and long term, they are not, given the huge variability in harvests and wheat production overall,” he said.
“In order to make Arabic flat bread, a staple food in Syria, you need 80 percent of soft wheat and 20 percent of hard wheat,” Fève added.
“Syria exports its surplus of hard wheat at a premium and imports less expensive soft wheat. Depending on where Syria sources its soft wheat, disruptions could cause food insecurity.”
Restarting negotiations
Changing weather patterns, conflicts, and high fuel prices are still significant concerns and could affect the food security of tens of millions of people dependent on the international grain trade. Still, the possibility of talks or a new Black Sea Grain Initiative between Russia and Ukraine appears distant.
“While Ukraine is offering additional grain supplies to countries that need them, Russia is attacking the ports, storage facilities and logistical infrastructure required to produce, store and export that grain,” Gaber told The New Arab.
The risk for the countries in the Mediterranean region and beyond remains present as long as the conflict shuts down the grain transits through the Black Sea.
“For Ukraine to play a stabilising role in food security across the Middle East and Africa, it first needs to be able to maintain production and secure access to the Black Sea. At present, Russia remains the principal obstacle to both," Gaber added.
Lucas noted that Ukraine has to find a way to get Russia to the negotiating table. “That hand was played very well by the Turks in supporting Ukraine in 2022. Can you do the same thing here?”
But while Ukraine has indicated that it wants to negotiate, Russia continues to pursue maximum demands.
The United States and the international community would have to put more pressure on Russia to reach an agreement. “If you can get that type of political strategy, you can put the onus on the Russians,” Lucas said.
Christopher Solomon is a Middle East analyst, researcher, editor, and writer based in the Washington, DC area. He is the author of the book In Search of Greater Syria (Bloomsbury)

The Verkhovna Rada is testing voting by MPs in a shelter

Members of Parliament began testing the voting system in the shelter of the Verkhovna Rada, reports UNN.
Details
Dear colleagues, an air raid alert has been declared in Kyiv. I ask everyone to proceed to safe places in accordance with the shelter plans posted at your seats. The plenary session will resume 15 minutes after the end of the air raid alert. I also ask those who wish to try the new system in the shelters
On Tuesday, September 1, Stefanchuk reported on his Facebook page that "together with the head and employees of the Secretariat of the Verkhovna Rada, we presented parliamentary journalists with an IT solution that will ensure the continuity of the plenary process even under such conditions."
Mobile workstations for all members of Parliament have already been set up in the shelter of the Parliament building. A backup system for electronic voting using personal mobile devices has been developed, and MPs will test it this week. Work on it began at the start of the full-scale invasion, without any expenditure of budget funds. This voting format will be used only during prolonged air raid alerts. In other cases, the Verkhovna Rada will work as usual in the session hall. Russian attacks must not paralyze Ukrainian state institutions. Parliament must remain capable of making decisions on which the country's defense, economy, and stable operation depend
MP Yaroslav Zhelezniak showed what voting in the shelter looks like.
Reminder
Due to the persistent air raid alerts in the capital, the Secretariat of the Verkhovna Rada is working on measures to ensure the uninterrupted operation of Parliament. In particular, there is an idea to vote through an app, but a final decision has not yet been made.

BP has appointed a new chair after a months-long search triggered by the controversial ousting of Albert Manifold, seeking to draw a line under years of boardroom turmoil at the UK oil and gas company.
Ian Tyler, who has served as the interim chair and has sat on the BP board as a non-executive director since April 2025, will assume the role on a permanent basis immediately.
His appointment comes after Manifold’s shock removal in late May after only eight months in the role, with BP citing “serious concerns” about his tenure.
Amanda Blanc, BP’s senior independent director who led the search for a new chair and also runs the insurer Aviva as chief executive, announced on Wednesday she would stand down at next year’s annual meeting.
She was criticised after Manifold’s short tenure as chair, because she had led the process that led to his appointment to replace Helge Lund. When Manifold left, Blanc said he had helped drive BP’s transformation but there had been “governance oversight and conduct issues” which the board deemed unacceptable.
Reports claimed senior colleagues had felt belittled by Manifold. He was also accused of aggressive behaviour and acting as if he had been an executive rather than a chair. Manifold responded by accusing the company of firing him without warning and disputed reports about his conduct.
Blanc came under fire after praising Manifold for his “relentless focus on performance which is well suited to BP’s needs” when he was appointed chair last July, after what she described as a “rigorous and comprehensive global search”.
Tyler is a former chief executive of the construction company Balfour Beatty. He chairs the builders merchants Grafton Group and is a senior independent director of the mining company Anglo American. In the past he chaired Cairn Energy and the housebuilder Vistry Group and served as a non-executive director of the defence contractor BAE Systems.
He is tasked with overseeing a shift in BP’s strategy to refocus on fossil fuel extraction and ditch renewable energy investments. The company’s chief executive, Meg O’Neill, urged Andy Burnham last month to make use of the UK’s oil and gas resources even though BP wants to sell its North Sea business.
O’Neill took the helm in April, the company’s third chief executive in less than five years. Bernard Looney, who had set a green strategy, resigned three years ago after admitting that he had failed to fully detail relationships with colleagues.
He was succeeded by Murray Auchincloss, who was ousted last December. BP came under pressure to improve its performance from the New York hedge fund Elliott Investment Management, which took a stake in the company last year.
Blanc said Tyler brought “significant experience providing challenge and support to executive teams, while maintaining strong governance and oversight on behalf of shareholders”.
Tyler said: “I will lead the board’s evolution, ensuring we have the depth, experience and capabilities needed to support the company’s strategic priorities and long-term value creation. I am committed to establishing regular and transparent engagement with our shareholders.”
He said he had asked Blanc to stay, but she believed that after four years it was an appropriate time for her to leave with a new chair in place.
Mark van Baal, the chief executive of the Dutch green activist shareholder group Follow This, said: “Many investors will ask if the new chair is able to fix BP’s broken governance.”
He said BP’s last annual meeting in April showed it was “completely out of touch with its shareholders” after protest votes against several resolutions, including an 18% vote against the re-election of Manifold as chair. More than half of the shareholders opposed BP’s plans to scrap its existing climate reporting.
“Having been on the board since 2025, Tyler is jointly responsible for BP’s governance problems,” he said. “We’re keen to learn what lessons he takes away from the triple shareholder rebellion in 2026, and how he aims to fix BP’s broken governance.”

FT: Russia secretly helped Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02

16:58:51 KST

Russia has secretly been helping Iran develop advanced supersonic cruise missiles since 2023 under a program code-named C430L, the Financial Times reports.
The program continued even after the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran, according to an FT investigation based on leaked Russian correspondence, travel records, and an analysis of military patents.
The program’s main goal, the journalists say, was to help Iran develop a ramjet engine capable of sustaining cruise missile flight at several times the speed of sound.
Rosoboronexport ran the program on the Russian side, coordinating the project with NPO Mashinostroyeniya and bringing in leading Russian missile designers to work on C430L.
Missile weapons experts say the technology being developed is intended for anti-ship missiles and weapons capable of striking ground targets. “This is the transfer of a highly strategically sensitive military technology from Russia that the Iranians have wanted to acquire for decades,” said Fabian Hinz, a senior analyst at the British organization Conflict Armament Research. “A program like this would require political clearance from the very top in Russia.”
Iran has already built the ramjet engine and conducted flight tests, the FT reports, though there is so far no evidence that the supersonic cruise missile developed with Russian assistance has entered service.
In June 2024, Vladimir Putin threatened, at a meeting with representatives of international news agencies, that Moscow would supply “similar weapons” to regions of the world “where strikes will be carried out on sensitive facilities of those countries that do this to Russia” in response to strikes on Russian territory with Western weapons, the FT reports. The C430L program was already underway at the time, according to the outlet.
