Xi calls on SCO to work toward more just global governance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:58:46 UTC
16:58:46 KST

Xi made the remarks in his speech at the "SCO Plus" meeting in the Kyrgyz capital of Bishkek.
"The meeting today focuses on strengthening the role of the United Nations and building a multipolar world, and it demonstrates SCO's commitment to reforming and improving global governance as required by our times," Xi said.
"Currently, major changes unseen in a century are accelerating across the globe. Hegemonism, unilateralism and protectionism are resurging against historical trends. Nevertheless, the overwhelming majority of the world do not condone power politics, conflict and confrontation, or isolation and backwardness," he added.
What they want instead, Xi said, is to hold a place on the world stage through national development and international cooperation.
Xi noted that in recent years, the rise of the Global South is driving a profound shift in the international balance of power, adding that the trend toward a multipolar world is irreversible.
"What kind of multipolarity does the world need? How are countries going to take part in and promote it? The international community should build consensus and make the right choice that can stand the test of practice and history," Xi said.
Noting that as a responsible major country, China advocates for an equal and orderly multipolar world, Xi said sovereign equality and mutual respect are fundamental principles; balance, order and the rule of law are inherent requirements; multilateralism, dialogue and consultation are essential pathways; mutual benefit, win-win and inclusiveness are the way forward for development.
"We should ensure equal rights, equal opportunities and equal rules for all countries, regardless of their size, strength and wealth," Xi said, adding that "as an important part of a multipolar world and a key driving force behind it, the Global South countries ought to have greater representation and voice in international affairs."
He called on various parties to promote the common values of humanity, reject double standards, exceptionalism, foreign interference, bullying and the law of the jungle, and advance the rule of law in international relations.
"Major countries in particular should take the lead in observing international norms and honoring the rule of law, and work together to tackle global challenges," he added.
Xi also said that world affairs should be discussed by all, and international norms should be set by all.
"The authority and vitality of the United Nations need to be restored. Multilateral mechanisms, global and regional, should enhance their coordination and improve their efficiency," he said.
"We should focus on the development agenda, uphold openness and cooperation, and bridge the digital and AI divides, so that technological revolution and development achievements can benefit all nations," Xi added.
Xi noted that after a 25-year journey, the SCO has successfully set a stellar example in conducting relations among big countries, among neighbors, and among countries of different sizes.
The SCO, Xi said, has successfully brought together half of the world's population and a quarter of the global economy, generating strong driving forces for development, adding that a more united and vibrant SCO is fully capable of making greater contributions to a multipolar world.
"It is important that SCO member states and partners ride the trend of history and shoulder the responsibility of our times. Let us take the people-centered and action-oriented approach, jointly advocate an equal and orderly multipolar world, make global governance more just and equitable, and build a community with a shared future for humanity," Xi said.
To further enhance the SCO's role, Xi called for advancing common prosperity in the vast continent straddling Asia and Europe with the SCO Strength.
"We should continue to leverage our strengths, unlock our potential, and connect the multiple growth poles across the continent through high-quality Belt and Road cooperation. We should empower each other, help each other succeed, and work together to create new opportunities and promote shared prosperity," Xi said.
"We should promote the development and rise of the Global South through the SCO Wisdom," Xi said, calling on various parties to "carry forward the Shanghai Spirit, strengthen and expand the SCO Plus partnerships, and jointly speak up for peace, foster synergy for development, build bridges for cooperation, and pave the way for win-win outcomes."
Xi also proposed that the SCO countries should guide the reform and improvement of global governance through the SCO Action.
"We should stay committed to building partnerships rather than alliances, and engaging in dialogue rather than confrontation," he said.
Xi also called for sticking to the principle of "planning together, building together and benefiting together" to encourage equal participation in global governance by all countries and ensure all will benefit from it.

U.S. Army delegation visits Korea’s K9 howitzer production line

2026-09-02

- A U.S. Army delegation led by Brent G. Ingraham toured Hanwha Aerospace's Changwon production facilities on August 26.
- The visit included demonstrations of the K9MH, K9A1 and Chunmoo systems as Hanwha expands U.S.-based howitzer production in Opelika, Alabama.
A senior U.S. Army acquisition delegation toured Hanwha Aerospace’s production facilities in Changwon, South Korea, on August 26 to review the company’s manufacturing capabilities across artillery, rocket systems and other land defense platforms.
The delegation was led by Brent G. Ingraham, Assistant Secretary of the Army for Acquisition, Logistics and Technology. The visit included a tour of the K9 self-propelled howitzer production line, where K9MH systems are currently in production, along with a look at automated manufacturing processes including robotic welding that Hanwha uses to support high-volume output.
The delegation also watched live mobility demonstrations of the K9MH and K9A1 howitzer variants, along with a demonstration of Hanwha’s Chunmoo multiple rocket launch system, before viewing the company’s broader land systems portfolio. The visit ended with discussions between Hanwha and the delegation on the company’s manufacturing capabilities and the Army’s modernization priorities.
“Hanwha brings proven manufacturing capabilities and global production experience that will strengthen deterrence and support the U.S. industrial base,” said Michael Coulter, CEO of Hanwha Defense USA. “For more than seven decades, the U.S.-Korea alliance has been a cornerstone of peace and security, and defense industrial cooperation is an increasingly important pillar of that alliance.”
The Changwon complex serves as the production base for Hanwha’s K9 family of howitzers, supplying concurrent production programs for South Korea, Poland, Australia, Egypt and other allied nations. Hanwha said the manufacturing capacity built through those programs will inform how the company scales up its U.S. operations.
Hanwha is expanding its U.S.-based production of the K9MH variant as part of what the company calls a phased localization strategy. Hanwha Defense USA’s integration and test facility in Opelika, Alabama, currently serves as the company’s U.S. artillery manufacturing hub, with additional production phases under evaluation as the company works to scale output to meet Army requirements.
Hanwha’s Changwon visit follows the company’s recent K9 export agreement with Spain, signed with Indra Sistemas on August 31, which made Spain the 11th country to operate the howitzer.

The shifting ties in Australia's backyard as 'deep pockets' beckon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:56:09 UTC
16:56:09 KST

in brief
- Geopolitical tensions over Taiwan are hanging over the annual Pacific Islands Forum in Palau.
- However, island leaders insist local climate threats and rising drug crime take priority.
China and Taiwan's diplomatic tug-of-war is casting a shadow over the ongoing Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) as a handful of national leaders declined to attend — however, experts on the ground caution that a geopolitical focus risks ignoring the core priorities of Australia's neighbours.
The annual 18-member gathering in the Taiwanese-allied nation of Palau opened on Monday with climate change, economic security, and the rising influence of the transnational drug trade top of the agenda.
China has said it has "serious concerns" that Taiwan was invited to attend in its own right, while questions have been raised about whether China has influenced five of 18 national leaders from the forum (those of Kiribati, Fiji, Vanuatu, Samoa and Solomon Island) not to attend.
The cornerstone regional political forum began this year with a pointed message from Palau's President Surangel Whipps Jr, who urged nations to adhere to this year's theme of unity and reminded outside partners that they "do not choose our destination".
This year's PIF takes place as Kiribati moves to constitutionally restrict diplomatic recognition to UN member states only — thus excluding Taiwan — while China actively seeks to strip Taiwan of its 'development partner' status in the forum. This comes nearly two months after a Chinese ballistic missile test in the Pacific Ocean.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Taiwan, a self-governing democracy, broke away from mainland China in 1949. China views it as Chinese territory that must be brought under its control by force if necessary.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has made strengthening regional ties a key focus of his administration's foreign policy, signing multiple bilateral agreements with countries like Fiji, Vanuatu, and Tuvalu.
But despite the noise around China, "leaders have made it clear they're here to work" Tess Newton Cain, principal consultant at Asia-Pacific strategic firm Sustineo, told SBS News from Koror.
"The issue of the China-Taiwan tussle is largely a distraction, and one that they try to minimise."
On Wednesday, $600 million in Australian funding was announced to tackle transnational drug smuggling from South America that is increasingly causing harm across the Pacific.
Cautions against Pacific chess games
China has made the PIF something of a battleground, maintaining that Taiwan ought to be sidelined during talks, as it is not technically a "dialogue partner" due to a difficult compromise that PIF members have reached over its status for the past three decades.
Palau, one of the few nations that maintains official diplomatic ties with Taiwan, has accused China of running a coercion campaign against it after travel warnings were issued to Chinese citizens looking to visit Palau.
Australia, which maintains a flexible approach to the 'One China' policy by recognising Beijing and maintaining informal economic and security ties with Taiwan, is better able to weather such geopolitical storms in part owing to its size.
Yet, as Pacific island nations increasingly turn to China for economic support, experts caution that for Australia to treat the Pacific as a geostrategic game would be a mistake, as that is "certainly not" how Pacific leaders see their own relationships.
"It's not appropriate that Australian officials or politicians are shaking hands with members of the Pacific while looking past them to see what China may or may not be doing," Newton Cain said.
Professor Dave Peebles, director of the Pacific Security College at the Australian National University, agrees that the Taiwan question is not the focus of relations in the Pacific.
Issues of Taiwanese sovereignty are "not something" Australia is seeking to influence in its dealings with island nations, he told SBS News, as those decisions are for democratically elected governments of Pacific Island countries to make.
"Some Pacific Island countries do have similar relationships with Taiwan as Australia does," Newton Cain said. "Others are possibly just too small to be able to justify that and to have to wear the tussle and competition that comes with that."
However, she dismissed fears that Kiribati's current domestic push to change its constitution in a way favourable to China — making it far more difficult for successive governments to switch alliances back — is a blueprint for a wider Pacific pressure campaign.
Whether a country recognises Taiwan can have significant domestic impact on small island nations.
In 2024, after decades of support, the Pacific Island nation of Naoero (formerly Nauru) abruptly severed diplomatic ties with Taiwan and formally recognised the People's Republic of China as "the only legitimate government of China and Taiwan" — leaving the latter with just a handful of diplomatic partners, including just three in the Pacific.
Diplomats and technical staff were forced to rapidly leave the country as it moved to deepen economic ties with the economic superpower, which has developed a "very strong portfolio" of investment in regional countries that do make the switch.
"It's often quite evident to see at a fairly early stage the impacts of having a partner that comes with deeper pockets than Taiwan," Newton Cain said.
Bigger issues at hand
While the threat of a hostile takeover of the region that the Chinese Communist Party views as an "inalienable part of China" simmers in the minds of policymakers across the globe, the threat of regional intervention from the United States and its allies has thus far kept the cross-strait conflict tense but cool.
As such, analysts argue that, while military conflict in the region and its impact on the economy is a genuine concern for Pacific nations, there are more immediate problems to deal with.
"There's no getting around the fact that the global and regional order is changing and the Pacific isn't immune from that," Peebles said. "But I think too that the Pacific is confronting this poly-crisis and geopolitics, though very important, is but one of the issues."
The PIF is expected to produce a joint shared position from all members, including Australia, on climate, which will be taken to the pre-Conference of the Parties meeting in Fiji in October before COP31 in Türkiye in November.
For low-lying Pacific nations, rising sea levels are considered an existential threat, one that Australia recognised with the landmark 2023 Falepili Union treaty that would allow a third of the 11,000 people living in Tuvalu to immigrate and escape increasing flooding.
"This is a serious gathering of serious people to discuss serious issues," Peebles said, also speaking from the forum in Koror. "There is a lot going on at this meeting, happily, that has nothing to do with geopolitics and is setting the region up for success."

Chevron set to expand in Venezuela as US energy secretary lands in Caracas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:55:38 UTC
16:55:38 KST

Chevron announced a $7 billion expansion deal for its Venezuelan operations on Wednesday, hours after the country's parliament approved handing Washington control over a fifth of its oil reserves.
America's second-largest oil company has announced it will develop two additional oil fields in Venezuela's Orinoco Belt, more than doubling its output in five years, in a deal worth $7 billion.
The joint venture between Chevron and Petroindependencia, in which Chevron has a 49% stake, will develop two greenfield sites near existing work and lift output to around 600,000 barrels per day, according to a company press release.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright landed in Venezuela late Tuesday to unveil fresh investments, with Chevron making the first corporate move to follow the agreement that just cleared Venezuela's National Assembly.
Chevron is the only major American producer to have stayed in Venezuela since Hugo Chávez completed the nationalisation of the industry in 2007, a move that drove Exxon and ConocoPhillips out.
After landing in Caracas, Wright immediately addressed the media and stated that "as large investments flow into this country that creates more jobs which pushes wage pressure up and creates opportunity for Venezuelans' prosperity."
A vote and an argument about the fine print
The announcement lands alongside a much bigger prize, a separate deal giving Washington control of a fifth of Venezuela's oil through a different operator entirely.
Venezuelan lawmakers approved the agreement by a show of hands late Tuesday, though some opposition members abstained, saying they had not seen the terms.
"We need and are obliged to know what is written in the fine print," said opposition lawmaker Luis Emilio Rondón.
"Who benefits from this oil if it stays underground?" argued the National Assembly chief Jorge Rodríguez in return.
Speaking in Spanish for an interview posted online on Tuesday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio described the arrangement in blunt terms.
"Essentially, this is now an agreement with the US government, specifically involving the Defense Department, which holds a special account allowing it to take possession of a certain percentage of these assets," Rubio said, adding that American backing would help the company attract the private investment needed to develop the fields.
The "vast majority" of the 17 fields had been in Chinese and Russian hands, Rubio pointed out, as the White House has also cast the agreement as a reassertion of the Monroe Doctrine.
Those fields come with 100-year rights for North American Blue Energy Partners and hold 65 billion barrels. A new company will be created in which the US Department of War's Office of Strategic Capital takes a 35% stake, with the US State Department entitled to buy 20% of output at production cost.
US citizens must form a majority of the board, and Washington holds a veto over appointments.
NABEP is owned by Alejandro Betancourt, who has faced investigations over alleged money laundering in Spain and Switzerland without charges being filed and has been accused of involvement in a corruption scheme at state producer PDVSA.
An unnamed US official called him a "proven operator" while conceding that geopolitics sometimes means dealing with imperfect figures.
"I'm not nominating anyone for sainthood here," the official said. "What I am telling you is that this is a person that, in the past, has been helpful to the United States government."
What the deal has not settled
Analysts remain sceptical that output can be revived quickly, with estimates ranging from one to ten years before new barrels reach the market. Washington is not investing money in the venture, officials say, arguing its backing alone will attract the capital needed.
US President Donald Trump suggested on Monday that others would follow Chevron.
"We have Exxon going in, we have Chevron going in. We have our big oil companies going in," Trump stated.
However, Exxon's position appears unchanged as a spokesman said on Tuesday that "nothing has changed" after CEO Darren Woods also called Venezuela "uninvestable" earlier this year.
For the US administration, the urgency is domestic.
US President Donald Trump just met oil executives at the White House on Tuesday as petrol prices climbed because of new US strikes on Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz, posting afterwards that "we are unleashing American Energy Dominance!"
Cheaper fuel is a priority before November's midterm elections, in which Republicans could lose control of both the House and the Senate.

Explosives experts from the Bavarian State Criminal Police Office are on the scene, according to police. The cause of the explosion is still unknown.
Police are also investigating suspected sabotage at an Amprion power substation in Bergheim, in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia, public broadcaster WDR reported.
A short circuit knocked several power lines out of operation, but the wider electricity supply was unaffected.
Police suspect the incident was deliberate rather than the result of a technical fault. Investigators are examining whether it could be connected to suspected sabotage in Brandenburg.
Suspected sabotage at Brandenburg power plant
The incident in Bergheim came after unidentified suspects carried out a sabotage attack on an electrical facility at a major power plant in the eastern state of Brandenburg on Tuesday, according to authorities.
Brandenburg Interior Minister Jan Redmann said the suspects used projectile devices to cause a short circuit in an extra-high-voltage line near the Jaenschwalde power plant.
“We cannot currently confirm that an explosive device detonated there or anything of that sort,” Redmann said.
Police earlier said devices apparently made from pyrotechnics had been found at an electrical substation, although reports differed over whether any of them exploded.
Bild reported that police had confirmed an explosion and discovered several improvised incendiary and explosive devices, not all of which detonated.
Public broadcaster RBB, however, quoted police spokesperson Stefanie Pilz as saying that no explosion had occurred.
Grid operator 50Hertz said unknown perpetrators damaged several transmission lines, briefly interrupting operations. All lines were later restored, and the public electricity supply was unaffected.
The Jaenschwalde facility near the Polish border is one of Germany’s largest lignite-fired power stations.

German Navy tests Israeli LORA ballistic missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:52:55 UTC
16:52:55 KST

- Germany's Navy conducted a successful dual firing trial of IAI's Naval LORA ballistic missile under its OPEX testing program.
- Germany is reportedly moving forward with plans to procure the missile system, which has a range of more than 500 kilometers.
The German Navy successfully completed a dual firing trial of Israel Aerospace Industries’ Naval LORA ballistic missile, launching the weapon from an operational German vessel and hitting its target with precision in both test scenarios, IAI said.
The trial was conducted as part of the German Navy’s Operational Experimentation program, known as OPEX, a testing initiative the service launched to support its “Marine 2035 and Beyond” plan. IAI said the missile was launched from a configuration comprising a command trailer and a launcher aboard the German vessel, and that the weapon system met all the trial’s objectives in both scenarios.
Separately, Reuters reported that a German frigate tested the Lora system in the North Atlantic, between Ireland and Iceland, in a previously undisclosed operation. According to that report, Germany now plans to move forward with preparations to procure the missile, which has a range of more than 500 kilometers (311 miles).
LORA, short for Long Range Artillery, is a quasi-ballistic missile developed by IAI’s MLM Division that can be launched from land-based mobile launchers or naval vessels. The missile has a publicly listed operational range of 90 to 430 kilometers (56 to 267 miles) and uses a combination of GPS and inertial navigation for guidance, with a circular error probable of 10 meters (33 feet), according to IAI’s own published specifications. It is unclear whether the range Reuters cited reflects an upgraded or export-specific configuration.
The missile has seen combat use by Azerbaijan, which deployed the system during the 2020 Nagorno-Karabakh conflict against Armenia.
“This is an unprecedented achievement for IAI and the Israeli Ministry of Defense,” said Boaz Levy, IAI’s Chairman. “The successful trial of the LORA missile, launched from a naval vessel and striking its target with exceptional precision, took place overnight in Germany, the country where the world’s first ballistic missile was developed. This trial demonstrates Israel’s technological strength and the unique cooperation between Israel and Germany. It marks another significant achievement alongside the deployment of the Arrow 3 system on German soil, further strengthening Germany’s defense and deterrence capabilities and deepening the strategic partnership between our two countries.”
“Israel Aerospace Industries is proud to take part in strengthening the strategic cooperation between the State of Israel and the Government of Germany,” said Guy Bar Lev, IAI’s CEO. “This significant milestone is underscored by the operational live-fire exercise (OPEX) of the LORA system, one of the world’s most advanced and combat-proven ballistic missile systems.”
Germany separately fields IAI’s Arrow 3 missile defense system, which has been operational on German soil as part of the country’s broader air and missile defense buildup.

Because complaints get made! We’re living in a complainant society.

Zelensky Claims Ukrainian Drones Have ‘Effectively Closed’ Russian Airspace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:51:56 UTC
16:51:56 KST

Russian transportation authorities on Wednesday vowed to prevent any disruptions to domestic air travel after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned the day before that Kyiv's drone attacks were making Russian airspace too dangerous for flying.
Transportation Minister Andrei Nikitin said that civil aviation authorities are "constantly improving flight safety and airport security requirements, and we have solutions for all of this," as quoted by the news agency Interfax.
"We are working in close contact with the Defense Ministry and the Russian National Guard. And I believe that we will not allow any significant disruption to civil aviation," Nikitin added.
Following Zelensky's warning, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Kyiv had officially notified the International Civil Aviation Organization that Russian airspace is unsafe for commercial flights.
Those comments appeared to have an almost immediate impact on air travel inside Russia. On Wednesday, Moscow's Sheremetyevo airport showed 21 canceled flights and 235 delays, while Vnukovo airport saw 22 canceled flights and 94 delays, according to the flight tracking service Flightradar24.
Turkish carrier Pegasus Airlines said it had canceled some flights to Russia for "technical and operational" reasons but did not provide further information.
Vnukovo airport said Pegasus Airlines had canceled six arriving and six departing flights at the hub on Tuesday. The carrier said overnight flights into Wednesday would be impacted, but other ongoing flights were "operating as scheduled."
Aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions said in an alert to clients that while the majority of Ukraine's drone and missile strikes were likely to occur within 300 kilometers (186 miles) of the border, daily attacks deeper inside Russia were near-certain through 2026, including near Moscow and St Petersburg.
"There is also a realistic possibility that the frequency of Ukrainian strikes will continue to increase in the short term deep inside Russian territory," the alert said. "It is assessed that miscalculation and/or misidentification is likely in areas related to the Ukraine conflict."

Ireland foreign minister dodges question over Russian-owned alumina plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:51:17 UTC
16:51:17 KST

Editor's note: this article was updated to include Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha's perspective on alumina exports to Russia.
Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee would not commit to including Ireland's alumina plant, whose products reportedly ended up in Russian weapons in Ukraine, in an upcoming EU sanctions list, during remarks made ahead of a meeting of the bloc's foreign ministers on Sept. 2.
The Irish Times published data in May showing that the Aughinish Alumina plant, owned by Russian company Rusal, exports overwhelmingly to Russia, with the material reportedly being found in weapons Moscow uses against Ukraine.
The Irish government initially argued that sanctioning the plant would cause more harm to the EU than to Russia. However, Dublin later agreed to an investigation, which "has not found concrete or definitive evidence linking the alumina to a weapons manufacturer in Russia," said Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin.
"Look, you'll know that the report was recently provided to the (European) Commission in relation to Alumina," the Irish foreign minister said when asked about sanctions against the plant ahead of a ministerial meeting in Wicklow, Ireland.
"We've also provided it to our colleagues in Ukraine and we will work with them."
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha posted on X that he reiterated his call for Ireland to halt its alumina trade with Russia during the meeting of EU foreign ministers.
"We urge a complete EU embargo on Russian alumina, stricter crackdowns on the shadow fleet, a ban on Rosatom and Roscosmos, and severe travel restrictions on Russian nationals to counter acts of sabotage across Europe," Sybiha wrote.
The topic is back on the table because the EU is considering its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia, which is set to include some 1,600 listings, the highest number ever.
"Ireland has supported every single package of sanctions that has been put forward. We have worked over the last number of months with colleagues to ensure that the 21st (package passes)," McEntee said.
However, Estonia's Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna revealed that he had proposed the inclusion of alumina in the 21st package of sanctions, passed in July.
It did not feature, meaning an EU member state had vetoed its inclusion. All EU sanctions require unanimity among the 27 member states.
Ireland has never admitted to vetoing the plant's inclusion, but it is the only country with an obvious interest in doing so.
Just after McEntee spoke, her Finnish counterpart Elina Valtonen said Finland remains "open to sanctioning aluminum."
"Russia is a war economy... everything is going directly or indirectly towards the war," Valtonen said.
"I think we really need to explore all the options on the table."

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.

Open-source intelligence analyst ASTRA later geolocated eyewitness footage, confirming that the fire occurred on the grounds of Proton-PM.

Where else there are outages due to enemy attacks

Will there be power outages across Ukraine
The use of restrictions is not forecast today, the ministry reported.
It also urged people today, September 2, where possible, to shift active electricity consumption to daytime hours — from 10:00 to 16:00 — and limit the use of powerful electrical appliances from 18:00 to 22:00. This helps reduce the load on the power system.
According to Ukrenergo, electricity consumption has decreased. Today, September 2, as of 09:30, it was 6.8% lower than at the same time the previous day — Tuesday. The reason for the change was clear weather across almost the entire territory of Ukraine, which resulted in high efficiency of household solar power plants and a corresponding decrease in the volume of electricity consumption from the grid. Another factor was the significant number of consumers disconnected from power as a result of the nighttime missile-and-drone attack on the energy infrastructure.
Yesterday, September 1, the daily peak in consumption was recorded in the evening. It was 3.4% lower than the peak of the previous day — Monday, August 31. The reason was a decline in the heat in most regions of Ukraine and a reduced need for widespread use of air conditioners.

The collision occurred 18 nautical miles (33 kilometres) off the Silivri district on the western edge of Istanbul province, the governor's office said on X.
A Turkish cargo ship carrying 10 crew members sank on Wednesday after colliding with a tanker off the coast of Istanbul, with no immediate signs of survivors, Turkish authorities said.
A lifeboat and other debris from the Tugberk Imamoglu have been found, but there has been no sign of the crew, Turkey's General Directorate of Maritime Affairs said in a statement.
“There are 10 seafarers on board, including the captain,” Transport Minister Abdulkadir Uraloglu said. “They are all Turkish. We can say that the sinking occurred rapidly in 11 minutes. No one has been found alive.”
Two helicopters and 12 search and rescue vessels were searching the area.
The ship collided with the Turkish-flagged tanker Alsu in the Marmara Sea at around 3 am (2 am CEST), according to the General Directorate of Maritime Affairs. An emergency signal was received from the Tugberk Imamoglu, with the first rescue vessel reaching the area at around 4:10 am (3:10 am CEST).
“It is assessed that the Tugberk Imamoglu vessel sank, because it did not respond to any calls and the mobile phones of the personnel on board went unanswered,” the maritime directorate said.
The Alsu's captain had reported the collision as happening at 3:15 am, with 14 search and rescue vessels dispatched to the area backed by a helicopter, it said.
What do we know so far?
The directorate's head, Unal Baylan, said the ships had been communicating with each other by radio immediately prior to the collision indicating “that the two captains saw each other and were talking to each other to adjust their routes,” he told a news conference.
The owner of the Tugberk Imamoglu said the ship's captain had contacted the Alsu before the collision, warning that the tanker was entering the cargo vessel's shipping lane.
“Despite this, according to our initial findings, the collision occurred as a result of M/T Alsu’s navigational movements and our ship sank shortly afterward,” the statement from Imamoglu Denizcilik said.
Turkish news agency DHA reported that radio recordings showed the Tugberk Imamoglu's captain warning the Alsu to steer to port in an attempt to avoid the collision.
The Alsu's owners did not immediately respond to the claim.
The 90-metre cargo ship was travelling from the Mediterranean port of Iskenderun to Eregli on the Black Sea. The 91-metre Alsu, an oil or chemical tanker, was sailing from Kocaeli, east of Istanbul, to Aliaga on Turkey's Aegean coast, according to MarineTraffic.
The Silivri Public Prosecutor’s Office said it had launched an investigation into the sinking.

2026-09-02

Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
A shootout between two branches of Ukraine's security services broke out on the morning of Sept. 2 during an investigation into an alleged Russian terrorist plot against a Russian opposition figure.
Earlier, a source in Ukraine's Defense Forces told the Kyiv Independent that the target of the plot was Stepan Kaplunov, deputy commander of the Russian Volunteer Corps (RVC) that fights alongside Kyiv.
Kaplunov had been in Ukraine for Independence Day celebrations on Aug. 24 but was "abducted by unknown individuals in the courtyard of his home," the RVC wrote on Telegram on Sept. 1.
As authorities announced that the alleged plot had been thwarted, reports of a shootout in Kyiv began to emerge.
According to Ukraine's Prosecutor General's Office, Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) officers were attacked by "one of the units of the Defense Forces of Ukraine" while conducting an investigation into the alleged plot.
"During the investigative actions in the proceedings regarding the terrorist act of the FSB of the Russian Federation, an armed attack occurred on SBU officers," it said in a post on Telegram.
"During the cessation of armed resistance, law enforcement officers used weapons," it added.
Speaking to journalists, Presidential Adviser Dmytro Lytvyn said the two units involved were the SBU and Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR). He added that President Volodymyr Zelensky had "called out" the heads of both and ordered them to inform the public about what was happening.
Zelensky later called the incident "an absolutely disgraceful situation" involving SBU and HUR units and said Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko and the State Bureau of Investigation would determine what happened.
The president said those responsible must be held accountable, including through possible personnel decisions by the heads of the security services and internal investigations by both agencies.
"Here in Ukraine, one can shoot only at the Russian occupiers in defense of Ukraine," Zelensky said. "No other shootout will ever be perceived by our state as something that anyone is allowed to do."
Taras Borovskyi, a lawyer representing Kaplunov, told Ukrainian TV that HUR service members were injured in the shootout, two of them seriously.
"One was shot in the leg and had an artery severed, and he was bleeding out. He is in very serious condition in a medical facility. The second is also in serious condition in hospital. The third is more lightly wounded," Borovskyi told Ukrainska Pravda.
Borovskyi, who said he was at the scene, also alleged that SBU officers had carried out an emergency nighttime search of Kaplunov's apartment without allowing his lawyer inside and without a court warrant.
He questioned why the search was carried out on Sept. 1 if Kaplunov had already been detained on Aug. 23, and said he still had not been told why his client was detained.
The lawyer also rejected the SBU's claim that it had foiled an assassination attempt against Kaplunov, calling it an attempt to justify what he described as an extrajudicial detention and a "PR move."
The commander of HUR's so-called "Timur" special unit was also present during the investigative actions and conducted negotiations between representatives of the two security services, according to Kaplunov's lawyer.
Kaplunov has since been released, the lawyer said.
President's Office Head Kyrylo Budanov called for a "thorough and impartial investigation," RBC Ukraine reported.
Violent incidents involving HUR and the SBU are rare but not unheard of.
In March 2022, the body of banker Denys Kireyev was thrown from a van in central Kyiv with a gunshot to the head.
Kireyev had been working for HUR and was credited with obtaining information about Russia's full-scale invasion plans that helped Ukraine to defend against the Kremlin's initial plans to take Kyiv.
He was subsequently involved in the ultimately fruitless peace talks between Kyiv and Moscow in 2022, but fell under suspicion of treason and accusations of being a double agent working for Russia.
In 2023, Budanov, then-head of HUR, denied Kireyev was working for Russia and claimed he had been killed by members of the SBU.
"I share the opinion and believe the facts that Mr Kireyev was killed in the SBU car when they conducted an operation against this person," he said.
The President's Office, in a 2023 statement, said Kireyev's death was "connected with the poor coordination of the Ukrainian special services at the beginning of the war."

Fake 10 Downing Street listing on Booking.com highlights security failures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:45:12 UTC
16:45:12 KST

Successive politicians have clawed their way past colleagues over the years to call the residence home. Yet in an offer that probably seemed too good to be true, the property site Booking.com has been accused of “systemic security failures” after it was able to set up and accept payment for a fake listing for 10 Downing Street.
A property listed as a “1 bedroom apartment in the heart of London” – with the exact address and a picture of the prime minister’s home – was listed on 18 June by researchers from the consumer watchdog Which?.
The listing, which promised a four-minute walk to the Houses of Parliament, was set up so that users had to request a stay and were unable to reserve and pay automatically.
The booking window opened briefly and closed so that a test could be carried out by a researcher from Which?. The consumer watchdog said a payment for a week-long stay had been processed by the digital travel site that enables users to book hotels and other accommodation as well as flights and car rentals.
The money had still not been refunded more than six weeks after it had been set up, according to Which?, which is associated with the Consumers Association charity.
A fake review was also uploaded to the site, describing the stay as “exceptional” and enjoying the experience of “hanging out with Larry the cat”, in a reference to Downing Street’s resident feline.
Despite Booking.com sending a message saying the review would be checked by a team of moderators, the consumer watchdog said it had been added almost immediately.
The team of researchers were also said to have used Booking.com’s mailing system to send an external URL asking the representative for credit card details to confirm the booking, Which? said.
The watchdog claimed the travel site had told them it had the ability to block URLs being sent through the messaging system if it suspected fraudulent activity, but it had not done so.
The listing was finally removed on 27 August, six weeks after it went live.
Rory Boland, the editor of Which? Travel, said: “If Booking.com’s so-called sophisticated AI systems can’t spot that 10 Downing Street is not a holiday rental, then it’s no wonder scammers can exploit the platform so easily.”
The watchdog said its investigation had “uncovered systemic security failures across the platform” and urged Ofcom, the UK’s communications regulator, to investigate.
A Booking.com spokesperson said: “This limited test is not a true reflection of the experience of millions of listings on our platform. The property added by Which? was not visible to customers or ‘live’ for the time period referenced.
“We use a range of checks, verification measures and artificial intelligence, which help us detect and remove the majority of fraudulent listings within 24 hours.”
It said that as the property was not open and bookable, some of its automatic fraud controls were not triggered to completely remove the fraud listing.
An Ofcom spokesperson said platforms have legal duties obliging them to take down illegal content generated by users once it is known. “Booking.com is not in scope of future rules that will apply to paid-for fraudulent advertising, and any change to that would be a matter for government,” they said.

Europe's August LNG imports among lowest for month in five years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:44:04 UTC
16:44:04 KST

MOSCOW, September 2. /TASS/. Europe imported one of its lowest volumes of liquefied natural gas (LNG) for the month of August in the past five years amid intense competition with Asia for available supplies on the market due to the Middle East crisis, according to TASS calculations based on data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE).
In August, LNG flows from European terminals into the EU gas transmission system totaled only around 9.1 billion cubic meters, up 8% from July but down 6% from August 2025. Over the past five years, Europe purchased a lower volume of LNG in August only in 2024, when imports totaled 7.3 bln cubic meters.
In January-August 2026, LNG flows from terminals into Europe's gas transmission system slowed to around 90.3 bln cubic meters, already 2.8% lower than in the same period of 2025.
LNG supplies accounted for the largest share of Europe's gas supply sources in January-August at 42.5%, according to data from the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas (ENTSOG) as of August 28. Supplies from the North Sea, primarily Norwegian gas, ranked second with a 37.5% share, followed by supplies from North Africa at 9.2% and supplies from the east at 6%, including Russian gas, gas supplied from Ukraine, as well as withdrawals by European companies of their own gas from Ukrainian underground storage facilities.
This exceeded the share of withdrawals from underground gas storage facilities, which stood at 1.5%. Gas supplies from Azerbaijan accounted for 3.4%.

New photo shows Wolf XM30 hidden under tarp
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:43:53 UTC
16:43:53 KST

- General Dynamics Land Systems released the first photo of its Wolf XM30 prototype, shown wrapped in a tarp during transport following its August 21 delivery to the U.S. Army.
- The vehicle's design remains concealed as it competes against American Rheinmetall's Lynx XM30, with the Army expected to select a winner in 2027.
General Dynamics Land Systems released the first publicly available photo of its Wolf XM30 prototype in transit this week, showing the vehicle wrapped entirely in a black tarp and strapped to a flatbed trailer.
The image follows the company’s confirmation that it delivered the prototype to the U.S. Army at Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland, on August 21, a delivery The Defence Blog previously reported based on a social media post from Geoffrey Norman, a retired Army brigadier general who now serves as director of strategy at General Dynamics Land Systems.
The tarp keeps the vehicle’s actual shape and design details concealed. General Dynamics has not released an uncovered photo of the Wolf XM30 or said when the vehicle’s full appearance will be shown publicly. The transport photo is the closest look the public has gotten so far at the physical hardware behind the program.
Norman, who spent 30 years in the Army as a tanker and cavalryman before joining General Dynamics two years ago, worked on the Next Generation Combat Vehicle Cross Functional Team at Detroit Arsenal before leaving the service. In his earlier post announcing the delivery, he said the Wolf uses what the company calls a Modular Open Systems Architecture, intended to let new software and hardware be added to the vehicle without a full redesign, a “born-digital” approach he said was built specifically for future upgrades.
Norman said the August 21 delivery is the first of several Wolf XM30 prototypes General Dynamics plans to complete and hand over to the Army. Additional vehicles are expected to go to Fort Hood, Texas, where the Army will run them through an evaluation process that could lead to a full-rate production decision. General Dynamics has credited teams across six sites, Sterling Heights, Lima, Scranton, Tallahassee, Grand Rapids and London, with building the vehicle.
The Wolf XM30 is one of two competing designs in the Army’s program to replace the M2 Bradley Infantry Fighting Vehicle, which has been in continuous service for more than 40 years. American Rheinmetall Vehicles is building the program’s other entrant, the Lynx XM30, and delivered the first of eight Lynx prototypes to the Army within days of General Dynamics’ Wolf delivery. That delivery put the Lynx into government-led developmental and performance testing under the program’s Phase 3/4 Engineering and Manufacturing Development contract, worth approximately $764 million. Rheinmetall has said it will deliver its remaining seven prototypes later this year for use in operational unit training, running in parallel with technical evaluation as part of the Army’s Transformation in Contact 2.0 initiative.
Both companies are developing and testing their prototypes in Michigan, drawing on the state’s concentration of Army ground-vehicle expertise centered on Detroit Arsenal, home to the Army’s Tank-automotive and Armaments Command and the Combat Capabilities Development Command Ground Vehicle Systems Center.
The Army is expected to select a winning XM30 design in 2027, with the design and prototype phase of the program alone valued at $1.6 billion.

The absence of Western sanctions and the shorter distance make the Northern Sea Route along Russia’s Arctic coast attractive to India, the CEO of a logistics company has said.
”The key factor is the absence of problems related to sanctions restrictions, which allows us to insure cargo against transport risks at very favorable rates,” Y&H Cargo CEO Rakesh Mishra said at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok on Tuesday.
The four-day annual event is being attended by officials, businessmen, experts, and researchers from 80 countries.
Mishra said the Arctic route is shorter for Indian shippers and will also provide a boost to trade with Southeast Asia, the world’s largest manufacturing hub. “Overall, this trade route is more efficient than the western route,” TASS cited him as saying.
The 5,600 km Northern Sea Route (NSR) from Vladivostok to Murmansk runs off Russia’s Arctic coastline and is the shortest shipping route between East Asia and Europe. For India, the route can save up to 40% in distance and around two weeks in travel time to most European ports.
Mishra added that the Middle East conflict leaves India, which has traditionally relied on the Suez Canal route, with “no choice but to develop the eastern route.” India is the second-largest importer of Russian oil and the two countries have set a bilateral trade target of $100 billion by 2030.
India plans to send its first commercial ship along the NSR next year, an official said at the Arctic-Regions Forum in Arkhangelsk last month.
State-owned conglomerate Rosatom is the designated operator and coordinator of the NSR and also manages Russia’s nuclear-powered icebreaker fleet, which is keeps the shipping lane navigable.
Shipping traffic along the Chennai-Vladivostok corridor – also known as the Eastern Maritime Corridor – has seen a 70% jump in cargo movement.

Gaza's fishermen face shrinking fishing grounds and arrests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:36:52 UTC
16:36:52 KST

Breadcrumb
Gaza's fishermen face shrinking fishing grounds and repeated arrests by Israel
For fishermen in the Gaza Strip, the sea has become increasingly difficult and dangerous to access, as Israeli naval forces continue to restrict their movement, open fire on fishing boats, and arrest fishermen, according to local fishermen's representatives.
On Tuesday, Israeli naval forces arrested 10 fishermen off the coast of al-Zawayda in central Gaza and Sheikh Ajlin, southwest of Gaza City, according to the Union of Fishermen's Committees.
In a press statement, the union said Israeli forces opened fire on the fishermen's boats before taking the detainees to the Israeli port of Ashdod.
Seven of the fishermen were later released, while three remained detained at an unknown location at the time of reporting, the union added.
"The arrest of these 10 fishermen adds to a series of daily violations, including killing, arrest, and the destruction of fishing boats and equipment, in addition to preventing fishermen from accessing the sea for more than three years," Zakaria Bakr, an official with the Fishermen's Committees, told The New Arab.
"The arrests were part of broader restrictions and violations affecting Gaza's fishing sector, including the destruction of boats and fishing equipment and restrictions on access to fishing areas," he said.
The number of Palestinian fishermen arrested by Israel since the Israeli genocidal war began on October 2023 had reached about 150, he explained.
Under constant fear
For fishermen who continue to venture into the sea, each trip has become a source of uncertainty.
"We go to sea not knowing if we will return," Salim Hamouda, a Gaza-based fisherman who has worked in the profession for years, told TNA.
Hamouda said the sea had previously provided his family with a stable source of income but had now become associated with fear and insecurity.
"We go out to sea not knowing what will happen to us. We might return with some fish, or we might lose our nets or boats, or we might be shot at or arrested. The sea has become a path to death for us, not a path to livelihood," he added.
Hamouda noted that the decline in fish stocks, rising fuel prices, and the high cost of fishing equipment had further undermined the profession.
Many fishermen and their families were now dependent on debt and humanitarian assistance, according to Hamouda.
"No one asks about us. Organisations talk about farmers, displaced people and workers, but fishermen have been forgotten," Hamouda lamented. "We have families and children who need food, medicine and education, and we have no other source of income."
Mohammed Saadallah, another fisherman from Gaza, said the fishing community had been living under a constant sense of fear and uncertainty, while many fishermen had lost their boats and nets during the war.
"We used to live off the sea, but today we cannot work," Saadallah told TNA, "A boat that used to support an entire family can be destroyed in minutes, while nets that we buy at great expense can be lost in an instant."
"We are not asking for the impossible. We simply want to work safely and return to our families. But even this right has been denied to us," he said.
Heavy losses
The restrictions have affected not only fishermen but also thousands of people who depend directly or indirectly on fishing for their livelihoods.
According to the Union of Fishermen's Committees, around 4,000 fishermen in Gaza work on more than 700 boats, while around 70,000 people rely on fishing and the sale of fish for income.
Bakr estimated that the fishing sector had suffered direct losses of about 120 million US dollars, with around 95 per cent of its infrastructure damaged or destroyed through bombardment, fires and the destruction of fishing equipment.
He estimated indirect losses at approximately 7 million dollars per month, as the fishing catch has fallen to about 2 per cent of its pre-war level.
Bakr described the restrictions and attacks on fishermen as violations of international humanitarian law and the Fourth Geneva Convention.
He also said the ceasefire had failed to provide meaningful protection for fishermen, as restrictions and attacks continued.
He called on the international community and relevant countries to pressure Israel to halt violations against fishermen, ensure safe access to fishing areas and support the rehabilitation of Gaza's fishing sector.

Belgians’ commute to work longer than an hour a day for the first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:35:56 UTC
16:35:56 KST

For the first time, we are spending more than an hour each day travelling to and from work. This emerged in an international study by HR services provider SD Worx, the findings of which appeared in Flemish daily Het Laatste Nieuws. The average Belgian worker’s commute takes 61 minutes a day, which is well above the European average of 48 minutes.
Belgians’ commute to work longer than an hour a day for the first time
With an average commute of 61 minutes a day, Belgians are Europe’s commuting champions. Sweden (57 minutes) and Ireland (56 minutes) complete the top three.
Part of the explanation lies with ‘long-distance commuters’, says SD Worx. More than one in eight Belgian workers (13 per cent) commute for two hours or more a day – the highest proportion of all the countries surveyed. This group often travels more than 120 kilometres a day. The international average is 8 per cent.
“Belgians live quite a long way from work, but traffic jams undoubtedly play a role too,” says Veerle Michiels, a mobility expert at SD Worx. The majority of Belgian commuters travel to work by (company) car.
The study reveals that public transport remains an area for concern: only 25 per cent of women and 28 per cent of men find public transport convenient, reliable and easily accessible. This is lower than the European average of 36 per cent across the countries surveyed.
A symbolic threshold crossed
“The one-hour mark is more than just a symbolic threshold,” emphasises Michiels. “It crosses the line that employees themselves still consider acceptable.”
Nevertheless, Belgians seem to have largely accepted long journey times as part of the job. One in three Belgian employees (34 per cent) say that their commute takes up a significant amount of their working time, which is barely above the average of 32 per cent across the countries surveyed.
Men’s commute longer, women prefer to work from home
The SD Worx study reveals clear differences between men and women. For instance, men spend longer travelling to work (65 minutes) than women (56 minutes). There are also twice as many men (23 per cent) as women (12 per cent) who commute more than 100 kilometres a day.
Women live closer to work, and they also have a lower threshold for acceptable commuting time (47 minutes) than men (67 minutes). They are also more likely to say they would prefer to work from home more often (35 per cent compared with 28 per cent of men).

Apple joins Google in renaming Lake Ontario 'Lake America'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:35:37 UTC
16:35:37 KST

Apple Maps now shows Lake Ontario as "Lake America" for US users, following Google's lead in complying with US President Donald Trump's order as trade talks with Canada sour.
Apple has become the latest company to adopt US President Donald Trump's new name for Lake Ontario — Lake America — on its Apple Maps platform.
The move came less than a week after Trump formally ordered the change in an executive order. Lake Ontario is one of North America's five Great Lakes, alongside Superior, Michigan, Huron and Erie.
The name change was driven largely by the collapse of trade talks between the US and Canada at the end of August, after the US imposed new 50% tariffs on around $20 billion (€17.3bn) worth of Canadian goods.
Apple Maps users based in the US will see the lake as Lake America, while those in Canada will still see the original Lake Ontario. According to US Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, Trump personally approached Apple and urged it to implement the change on its navigation platform.
Trump has since posted a number of AI-generated social media videos, including one showing him kicking over a Lake Ontario sign and replacing it with one reading "Welcome to Lake America".
At the lake itself, however, Canada has installed a new sign reading "Lake Ontario. Now and Always."
"Long before President Trump, this lake was called Lake Ontario. Long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario," Ontario Premier Doug Ford said, according to the BBC.
Canada has also said it will implement "dollar-for-dollar" counter-tariffs in response to Trump's new levies.
Google under fire
Google made the same move over the weekend, drawing significant criticism on social media, with users accusing the tech giant of capitulating to the Trump administration.
This is despite the fact that while the US president can dictate how the federal government refers to geographic features, he has no authority to force private companies, foreign governments or even US states to do the same.
"The US Geographical Names Information System has formally changed the name for 'Lake Ontario' to 'Lake America' in the United States," Google said in a blog post.
"Since we update Google Maps to reflect name changes in official government sources, which is GNIS for the US, people using maps in the US will see 'Lake America', those in Canada will continue to see 'Lake Ontario', and those outside of the US and Canada will see both names."
However, other map services such as MapQuest have refused to change the lake's name. Last year, MapQuest also declined to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.
The latest stand has driven MapQuest to the number one spot on the US Apple App Store's top charts, as of 1 September, ahead of even long-time favourite ChatGPT.

He said there were an estimated 400,000 drug users in the island nation of 22 million people.

Why Greece is betting on Israel’s Achilles Shield
The defence deal between the two countries fits into a larger shift in regional alliances amid the US-Israel war on Iran.
On Monday, Greece and Israel signed a $3.5bn defence deal to build an integrated, multilayered defence network to protect Greek territory dubbed the Achilles Shield. The package brings together the David’s Sling and Spyder interceptors, the Barak air and missile defence system and multimission radars, alongside a separate deal adding Drone Dome systems to protect strategic sites from UAVs.
It is the largest defence deal ever concluded between the two countries. It is also one of the most significant export agreements in Israel’s recent history.
What makes the agreement particularly striking is that it comes as Israel’s global standing is at one of its lowest points in decades. And Greece is no outlier, given that 65 percent of its citizens now view Israel unfavourably. Why, then, has Athens now chosen to openly deepen its ties with Israel in the most politically sensitive of areas: defence and military technology?
Firstly, the shadow of Israel’s conflict with Iran looms large. In early March, an Iranian drone struck Cyprus, Greece’s neighbour and close partner. This likely reinforced anxieties that were already visible in 2024. After Israel, with the help of the United States, downed approximately 300 Iranian drones and missiles, Greek Defence Minister Nikos Dendias called on Athens to develop its own antidrone “dome”.
The deal is therefore partly the product of pragmatic necessity as countries scramble for military solutions to growing drone threats. Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, for example, are acquiring antidrone technology from Ukraine, another country able to market its products as battle-tested.
Despite its political disadvantage, Israel has a practical head start, given that it has long practised “arms diplomacy”, using its defence industry as a springboard to cultivate deeper bilateral ties with prospective buyers.
The second factor driving the Achilles Shield deal is another longstanding tenet of Israeli grand strategy: the “periphery doctrine”. This advocates that Israel develop ties with non-Arab states and peoples on the periphery of the Levant to counter the hostility between Israel and its immediate neighbours. It is a recognition that shared threats can produce strategic partnerships. And in the case of Israel and Greece, that shared threat is Turkiye.
The irony is that Turkiye – as a non-Arab state and the gateway between the Middle East and Europe – was Israel’s close partner in the early days of the periphery doctrine. In 1949, Turkiye was the first Muslim country to recognise Israel. In subsequent years, Ankara and Tel Aviv developed robust but clandestine security ties.
This worked as Israel intended in that it opened the door to increasingly public and broader bilateral relations, which continued even after the Islamist-oriented AK Party, or Justice and Development Party, came to power in Turkiye in 2002.
But both sides fell out in late 2008 after Israel launched an offensive on the Gaza Strip. Subsequent divergences over Israeli policies towards the occupied Palestinian territory have gradually unravelled their deep ties.
Bilateral trade has collapsed since Ankara imposed an embargo on Israel in 2024. There are no longer direct flights between the two countries. In June, US President Donald Trump claimed that US pressure stopped Turkiye from joining the war on Iran, on Tehran’s side. This may sound far-fetched, yet it illustrates how Israel and Turkiye not only disagree on many geopolitical issues, but increasingly see each other as rivals and even threats.
What is remarkable is how quickly Greece has filled the void. In previous years, Tel Aviv’s partnership with Ankara precluded closer ties with Athens. But no more: in late 2025, Israel, Cyprus and Greece signed a “Joint Action Plan” that mandates enhanced military cooperation.
Energy has reinforced this strategic convergence. The discovery of substantial gas reserves in the eastern Mediterranean encouraged Israel, Greece and Cyprus to cooperate on pipelines and maritime security.
And, as was the case with Turkiye, more extensive bilateral ties followed security cooperation: some 744,000 Israelis visited Greece in 2025, compared with the peak of 558,000 Israeli tourists who travelled to Turkiye in 2008.
The increasing regional division into competing blocs has also driven the burgeoning Israel-Greece relationship. In February, Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu floated a “hexagon alliance” of Israel, Greece, Cyprus, India and unnamed Arab and African countries.
Six months later, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement. This alliance broadly overlaps with what commentators earlier labelled the “Islamic coalition”.
This is an evolving dynamic and inter-bloc collaboration is as common as intra-bloc divergences. But it demonstrates that the crisis of confidence in the US as a security guarantor extends beyond the Gulf states and predates the recent war on Iran. It also portends headaches for Washington’s policymakers, given that these increasingly competing states are all US allies.
The Achilles Shield deal is therefore the new manifestation of an old Israeli strategy that has been accelerated by the US-Israel war on Iran. Public scepticism may complicate Greece-Israel relations, but Israeli-Turkish ties deepened for decades despite similarly unfavourable public attitudes.
In short, in the eastern Mediterranean and elsewhere, growing popular outrage at Israel’s policies will continue to coexist uneasily with deepening security cooperation at an elite level. The irony is that the same conflicts that have damaged Israel’s international standing have also increased the value of its military experience and defence technology.

- Work is being performed in Beavercreek, Ohio, under Air Force Research Laboratory management, with completion expected by February 2028.
The U.S. Air Force has added $11.2 million to a contract with BlueHalo LLC for a program called Aiman Improved Readiness, bringing the deal’s total value to $41.2 million, up from $30 million, according to a Department of War contract announcement.
The modification adds scope to a cost-plus-fixed-fee contract Air Force Research Laboratory originally awarded to BlueHalo. Work will be performed in Beavercreek, Ohio, near the lab’s headquarters at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base. The contract is expected to be completed by February 13, 2028.
Fiscal 2026 research, development, test and evaluation funds totaling $32,147 will be obligated at the time of this modification. Air Force Research Laboratory at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, is the contracting activity managing the award.
BlueHalo, based in Huntsville, Alabama, and Arlington, Virginia, is a defense technology company that works across space superiority, directed energy, counter-drone systems, autonomy, radio frequency and signals intelligence programs. The company has held multiple prior contracts tied to the Wright-Patterson research ecosystem.
In February 2026, the Department of War awarded BlueHalo a separate sole-source contract worth up to $19.95 million to develop AI-enabled frameworks for human biological modeling, work performed in nearby Dayton, Ohio, and managed through the same Wright-Patterson contracting activity. That program focuses on integrating large-scale biological data with artificial intelligence to support monitoring of warfighter health, performance and exposure risks, with work running through February 2029 and options extending to 2031.
BlueHalo has separately built up a portfolio of space technology work. In March 2025, the company said it successfully demonstrated a long-haul, two-terminal laser communication system designed to simulate conditions across low-Earth, medium-Earth and geosynchronous orbit, advancing the technology to Technology Readiness Level 6, a designation indicating the system has been proven in a relevant environment and is ready for accelerated development.
The Air Force has not disclosed the specific technical scope of the Aiman Improved Readiness program, what capability or system it supports, or how this funding increase changes the program’s objectives beyond the added dollar value.

Germany does not currently have ballistic missiles, which fly at much higher speeds than the cruise missiles in its arsenal. The Israeli-built system has a range of up to 500 km (310 miles), Germany's defence ministry said.
Berlin is engaged in a number of multinational collaborations aimed at developing long-range missiles, and also looking at options to buy such weapons.
Navy chief Jan Christian Kaack said the test was a success.
"Our units can successfully deploy the system, and its potential range exceeds anything we have seen before," he said in a statement. "In terms of protecting Germany and our allies, this test marks a new chapter in deterrence and maritime defence readiness."
Germany is also working on an upgraded version of its Taurus cruise missile, currently its only weapon with a range of several hundred kilometres, with production scheduled to start in 2029.
The upgraded Taurus NEO missile will feature an extended range, improved shielding against interference, and advancements in navigation and seeker head technology, according to a budget document.
German forces have about 600 Taurus missiles with an official range of more than 500 km (310 miles) in their inventories, that can be launched from fighter jets such as the Tornado, the F-15 or the F-18.
The weapon, built by European defence company MBDA,,, is designed to destroy targets behind enemy lines such as command bunkers, ammunition and fuel dumps, airfields and bridges. REUTERS

Defense Minister Israel Katz said Wednesday that Israel is preparing for the possibility of an Iranian attack during the Jewish holiday period and is ready to respond with significant force if targeted.
Speaking at the “Decision Time: Democracy and Society” conference hosted by ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth in cooperation with the Israel Democracy Institute, Katz said Iran “likes to attack on holidays” and stressed that Israel was prepared.
Asked whether the current exchange of strikes between Washington and Tehran could spill over into Israel, particularly ahead of the Jewish holidays, Katz said Israeli leaders were monitoring developments continuously.
“The prime minister and I are following this on a daily basis together with the IDF, sometimes in the middle of the night on the red phone,” he said. “We are not taking any information lightly. We do not want to be surprised. We are prepared.”
Katz said the IDF, including the Israeli Air Force, was ready to strike Iran if necessary.
“If they attack us, we will respond with great force, independently of anyone else,” he said.
Katz said Israel was currently allowing the United States to take the lead in strikes against Iran because of American interests involving the Strait of Hormuz and energy security.
“For now, they are striking throughout the region except us,” he said. “But there is a possibility that they will attack us. We are prepared for that defensively.”
He added that Iran had a history of timing attacks around Jewish holidays.
“They like to attack on Jewish holidays because they hate Jews,” Katz said. “Look at many things that happened in the past. But we are prepared both defensively and offensively, in coordination with the United States in this area.”

“If they attack because of Lebanon, because of the West Bank, because of Gaza, or simply because they feel like it, our planes are ready to take off,” he said.

“We destroyed it, the entire production process, all of it,” he said. “There was an active program. We destroyed it.”

“Since then, the nuclear program has not been renewed, and we are monitoring these developments,” Katz said. “Now we need to make sure they do not regain the ability to return to it and that they do not go back to it.”
He said Israel’s policy remained unequivocal.
“We will not allow Iran to have nuclear weapons,” Katz said. “If something like that happens, and President Trump says the same thing, then we will likely attack together.”
Katz argued that Israel’s campaign had significantly weakened Iran.
“We removed an existential threat from Iran, eliminated Khamenei, thwarted their strategic capabilities and set them back by decades,” he said.
He added that Israel had also benefited strategically despite casualties on the home front.
“There were casualties, but when you look at the overall balance, there could have been many more,” Katz said. “We neutralized their launch capabilities. Against Iran, we achieved an enormous gain. Our most dangerous enemy was struck and is now significantly weaker than us.”

Pearl Liang brings Hong Kong dining memories to Taipei
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:30:19 UTC
16:30:19 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — From baskets of dim sum to steamed fish for the family table, some of Hong Kong’s most familiar food memories have made their way to Taipei.
Pearl Liang is bringing them to life through Sept. 30 with a 10-dish selection created with guest chef Chan Hon Cheong (陳漢章), executive Chinese chef of Michelin-recommended One Harbour Road. The offerings draw on three sides of Hong Kong’s food culture — tea-house dim sum, banquet cuisine, and home-style cooking.
The journey starts with dim sum, a dining tradition that took root in Hong Kong after spreading from Guangzhou during the late Qing Dynasty (1850 to 1910). Tea houses became gathering places for generations of diners, who came together over tea and small dishes, with siu mai and fun guo becoming staples of the Cantonese table.
One dumpling takes inspiration from the Qing Dynasty dish “scrambled crab.” Instead of crab, it combines egg white with grass shrimp, atrina, carrot, coriander and scallions, wrapped in pumpkin and red rice powder that turns translucent when steamed and finished with flying fish roe.
Another dish puts a different spin on traditional fun guo. Coriander is incorporated into the wrapper, while the filling combines deep-sea Chilean seabass, shrimp and water chestnut. The dumpling is steamed and finished with flying fish roe.
The menu then moves from the everyday tea house to the more elaborate world of banquet dining, which became increasingly popular in Hong Kong from the 1950s onward. Such dishes are traditionally judged not only by flavor but also by the skill and preparation behind them.
The four-treasure soup is served inside a hollowed-out papaya filled with a broth made from Jinhua ham and chicken, along with crab meat, roast duck, bamboo fungus and Chinese violet. The filled papaya is then steamed, allowing its natural sweetness to blend into the rich broth.
Another banquet-style dish, stuffed crab shell, is a classic Cantonese preparation. It combines crab meat with coconut milk and onion before being fried. The result pairs the sweetness of crab with the creamy aroma of coconut.
Wok hei takes center stage in the fried rice with duck liver, beef and mushrooms. The term refers to the smoky aroma that develops when ingredients are quickly cooked over high heat in a wok.
The dish combines Thai rice, beef, egg and Yunnan termite mushrooms with duck liver. Unlike the goose liver traditionally used in Hong Kong, the lower-fat duck liver is used to better suit local tastes, with crispy garlic added on top.
The final part of the menu turns to the family table, where steamed fish has long been a familiar Cantonese staple. Rather than relying on elaborate sauces, the preparation centers on fresh fish and a handful of ingredients.
The fish is marinated for 24 hours before being steamed with preserved mustard greens, scallions and lotus leaf. It is finished with a sauce made from soy sauce, fish sauce, and rock sugar.
Dessert brings the meal back to another set of familiar Hong Kong flavors. The almond tart takes inspiration from almond tea and steamed milk custard, combining almond paste, egg white and milk in a flaky tart shell.

For the heathens amongst you, the Vulcan salute is the gesture made famous by Leonard Nimoy's character Spock. It involves raising your hand, palm forward, with the middle and ring fingers parted. Europe ends summer with lowest gas inventories on record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:30:01 UTC
16:30:01 KST

MOSCOW, September 2. /TASS/. Gas inventories in European underground storage facilities (UGS) are at their lowest level since records began in 2011, with one month to go before the traditional start of the heating season, posing a risk to gas supplies in the region, according to TASS calculations based on data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE).
Gas withdrawals from European storage facilities in August were the highest in five years at 771 mln cubic meters, up 11% from last year. At the same time, injections into UGS facilities fell by 8% to 10 billion cubic meters. As a result, total net injections, the difference between injection and withdrawal volumes, were 9% lower in August than a year earlier and among the lowest in 12 years at just 9.2 bln cubic meters.
At the end of August 2026, European UGS facilities were 65.39% full, 16.76 percentage points below the average for that date over the past five years, compared with 77.7% a year earlier. This was the lowest level for that date since records began in 2011. At the end of the month, EU storage facilities held around 71.5 bln cubic meters of gas, 14 bln cubic meters less than a year earlier and the lowest level since 2013. Gazprom forecast that gas inventories in European UGS facilities might not even reach 75% by the next heating season.
TASS previously reported that Europe risks entering the heating season with record-low gas inventories. The average pace of replenishment at EU storage facilities in July was among the lowest since records began in 2011 and accelerated only slightly in August. At the current pace, Europe may have its storage facilities only 70-75% full by the start of the fall-winter period, which would be the lowest level ever recorded at the beginning of a heating season.
Under European Commission requirements, EU countries must ensure that their gas storage facilities are 90% full at some point between October 1 and December 1 each year. A 10% flexibility margin is allowed in the event of difficult storage-filling conditions. Accordingly, net injections into European storage facilities must total at least 68 billion cubic meters by the start of the 2026-2027 fall-winter period to meet the storage target. So far, Europe has injected only 60% of the volume needed for the coming winter, or 41 bln cubic meters.
The pace of storage filling this year has been significantly affected by Europe's loss to Asia in the competition for available LNG supplies during the Middle East conflict, higher fuel prices and extreme heat in June and July. During such hot summer periods, demand for electricity to power cooling and air-conditioning systems rises sharply. Gas is one of the main sources of electricity generation, alongside nuclear, wind and solar power.
LNG supplies to Europe
Europe imported one of its lowest volumes of liquefied natural gas (LNG) for the month of August in the past five years amid intense competition with Asia for available supplies on the market due to the Middle East crisis.
In August, LNG flows from European terminals into the EU gas transmission system totaled only around 9.1 billion cubic meters, up 8% from July but down 6% from August 2025. Over the past five years, Europe purchased a lower volume of LNG in August only in 2024, when imports totaled 7.3 bln cubic meters.
In January-August 2026, LNG flows from terminals into Europe's gas transmission system slowed to around 90.3 billion cubic meters, already 2.8% lower than in the same period of 2025.
