‘I want to live’: the disabled people unable to go abroad because of care funding refusal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
05:00:24 UTC
14:00:24 KST

Disabled people are being blocked from travelling abroad by NHS care boards and local councils that refuse to let them use their care funding outside the UK, the Guardian has learned.
Campaigners warn of a “postcode lottery” in England where the right of a disabled person to travel overseas depends on where they live or the whim of local officials – even when there is no extra cost to the taxpayer.
Disabled care users report having to abandon travel plans at the last minute, or go for years without a break, when authorities refuse to pay for their care abroad, even though they have agreed to meet all the travel expenses.
The Guardian is aware of instances where individuals have had requests for care and support for overseas travel turned down by NHS officials – only to have the decision reversed when they threatened legal action.
Lucy Robinson, 38, told the Guardian she had been prevented from attending international work events and going on a holiday because health officials in Oxfordshire had refused to allow her to use her care package abroad.
Robinson, who is quadriplegic and has a team of 24-hour personal assistants, is often required to travel in her role as the president of the European Spinal Cord Injury Federation. She has received NHS support for some trips.
She said the experience had caused huge stress: “Travel is one of the things that defines my life, in terms of most of the work I do, but also because I like travelling. My quality of life is based around that. I want to live, not just to exist.”
The cases have led to calls for national guidance amid concerns there are no clear or consistent NHS or council-wide rules clarifying the right of disabled people to take their carers abroad. Their care packages typically provide them with personal assistants for help with dressing, movement and night support.
Campaigners have emphasised this is not about “holidays on the NHS”. There is no extra cost for the health service or local authorities, which are already paying for the care. In almost all cases, the care recipient is expected to pay for their assistant’s expenses and arrange their insurance.
“Refusing to pay for care and support abroad does not deliver any financial savings for the taxpayer,” said Carol Barraclough, the advocacy and support manager at the Spinal Injuries Association. “We’d like to see national guidance on this that is effective and clear on the rights of all disabled people to take their carers outside the UK.”
Robinson said the Thames Valley NHS integrated care board (ICB) told her in April it had rejected her care request to attend a conference in Germany because “NHS funding responsibilities cease at the UK border”.
As a result, she was forced to abandon planned work events in Norway and Albania. She was able to go to Germany only because her 69-year-old mother stepped in as her 24/7 carer.
The care board made a rapid U-turn in June when Robinson threatened the health board with legal action, arguing it was acting unlawfully. It then agreed to fund her care overseas on condition she dropped plans for a judicial review.
Analysis by the Guardian shows a wide variety of policies across councils and the NHS. Some are explicit that overseas care is possible, while some agree in principle but attach a string of conditions. Others say overseas travel is allowed only at the discretion of their officials.
“There’s a postcode lottery in NHS care and support policy to allow recipients of funding to take their assistants with them outside the UK,” said Barraclough, who added she was aware of several cases where disabled individuals had been turned down for care abroad.
Giselle Hoad, the founder of the Adult Social Care Warriors campaign group, said: “There’s a concern that cultural prejudice about disability – that we don’t have families, partners, or jobs – means the care system sometimes assumes disabled people should be satisfied with opportunities closer to home.”
Disabled people in England can get care funding through two main sources: NHS continuing healthcare, which provides support for daily living for people with the highest needs, and social care paid for by local councils.
 Anne-Marie Irwin, a solicitor at Rook Irwin Sweeney who represented Robinson, said NHS care boards had a legal duty to meet a disabled person’s assessed needs. As long as the care user remains a resident of the ICB’s area this duty does not stop if they temporarily leave the UK.
Thames Valley said it did not comment on individual cases. It added that where a patient requested temporary travel abroad an ICB “may consider if it’s appropriate to continue commissioning care to meet their assessed health needs while they are outside the country”.
It said its decisions were informed by considerations of patient safety, practical care delivery factors and risk assessment and insurance issues.
Local authorities hold a similar duty to ICBs, previous court judgments suggest.
Chelsea Pettitt, 25, and her parents, have been in dispute with Lancashire council over her entitlement to care on holiday.
Chelsea, who has cerebral palsy, quadriplegia and learning difficulties, wants to return to Spain where she had a week-long break in 2022 accompanied by two assistants. Like other twentysomethings, she loved the sun, the swimming, food and culture. “I felt like I belonged there,” she said.
But her parents, Barbara and Alison Pettitt, said they were told by a social worker that she was no longer eligible for care abroad as she now lived in supported accommodation.
Her care plan specifies two-to-one care for seven nights a year for trips outside Lancashire – but the council stipulates the care must be used by Chelsea to “maintain … important relationships” with her birth family and friends.
A lack of national guidelines means the family is unsure where this leaves Chelsea’s right to choose whether – or where – to travel. All Chelsea can do is savour her memories of Spain. “She had an absolute blast,” said Barbara, “and she’d like to do it again.”
The council said it did not object in principle to Chelsea using her care package on a holiday abroad and it was “working closely with the individual, their family and care provider to understand the issues that have been raised and support a positive resolution”.
A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “This government is committed to making sure all those who are eligible for NHS continuing healthcare receive the support they need to live independent and fulfilling lives.
“Integrated care boards are responsible for planning a package of care that meets each individual’s needs. We expect them to fulfil this duty in line with national policy and legislation.”

Poppy O’Toole’s midweek timesavers: spicy chicken and baked rice, and Thai-style lemongrass fishcakes – recipe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
05:00:24 UTC
14:00:24 KST

I’ve called this spicy chicken and baked rice “midweek”, but you can enjoy this baby all week long. Juicy, spiced chicken, fluffy baked rice and enough flavour to make you bin that takeaway menu and raid your cupboards instead. Then some fragrant, delicate fishcakes with a lovely, bouncy texture, which are such a winner for the freezer. Taking only 10-ish minutes to cook from frozen, they save you from hunger and distraction on a busy WFH day.
Midweek spicy chicken and baked rice
Prep 10 min
Marinate 1 hr
 Cook 45 min
 Serves 8
200g Greek yoghurt 
  Zest and juice of 1 lemon 
  50g harissa paste 
  1 tbsp garlic granules 
  1 tbsp dried oregano 
  2 tsp ground turmeric 
  1 tbsp ras el hanout 
  2 tsp ground coriander 
  2 tsp ground cumin 
  Salt and pepper 
  16 skinless, boneless chicken thighs 
  Olive oil 
3 red onions, peeled and roughly chopped into large pieces 
2 red peppers, deseeded and roughly chopped into large pieces 
4 garlic cloves, peeled and minced or grated 
2 tbsp tomato puree 
  400g basmati rice 
  1 400g tin crushed tomatoes 
800ml chicken stock
Serving suggestions (optional) 
Sliced or pickled red onion 
  Crumbled feta 
  Flat-leaf parsley leaves
In a bowl, combine the yoghurt, lemon zest and juice, harissa, garlic granules, dried oregano, ground turmeric, ras el hanout, coriander and cumin with a large pinch each of salt and pepper. Add the chicken thighs, give them a good mix to coat, then pop them in the fridge to marinate for at least an hour.
Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Meanwhile, put a glug of olive oil in an oven-safe saute pan on a high heat. Chuck in the onions and peppers, fry for two to three minutes, until colooured and slightly blackened, then add the garlic and fry for a minute more, until fragrant.
Turn down the heat to medium, squeeze in the tomato puree and cook for one minute, until the mix darkens. Season generously, then tip in the rice and toast for a minute. Pour in the crushed tomatoes and chicken stock, and bring to a bubble.
Put the chicken thighs on top of the rice – you want about half of each chicken thigh sitting above the level of the stock – then put the pot in the oven for 30 minutes, until the chicken is slightly charred and cooked through and the rice is tender. Serve immediately, piping hot, with the pickled red onion, feta and parsley, if you like.
To eat later, freeze in an airtight container for up to three months. To reheat from frozen, heat the oven to 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5 and reheat for 45–50 minutes, until piping hot throughout. Or defrost fully in the fridge overnight, then heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6 and reheat for 25–30 minutes, again until piping hot throughout.
Lemongrass and ginger Thai-style fishcakes
Prep 5 min
Chill 1 hr
 Cook 15 min
 Serves 8
500g skinless, boneless cod, or haddock 
  200g shelled raw king prawns 
  3 tbsp green Thai curry paste 
  2 lemongrass stalks, bashed and roughly chopped 
50g fresh ginger, peeled and roughly chopped 
4 garlic cloves, peeled 
1–2 tbsp fish sauce, to taste 
2 tsp palm sugar 
  1 tbsp light soy sauce 
  2 eggs 
  About 200g cornflour 
Olive oil
To serve (optional)
Sweet chilli sauce 
  Pickled veg 
  Cooked rice noodles 
  Thai basil and mint leaves 
  Lime wedges
Tip the fish, prawns, curry paste, lemongrass, ginger, garlic, fish sauce, palm sugar and soy sauce into a food processor. Crack in the eggs, then blitz to a paste. Tip the mixture into a bowl and stir through enough cornflour to make a wet dough (you may not need all of it, so add the cornflour in batches).
Wet your hands so the fishcake mixture won’t stick to them, then weigh out 16 equal balls of about 70g each. Shape these into 2cm-thick patties, then arrange on a well-oiled baking tray – they will feel really wet, but that’s normal! - and refrigerate for at least an hour, to firm up.
Put a little olive oil in a frying pan on a medium heat, then, working in batches, fry the fishcakes for three to four minutes on each side, until cooked through, piping hot and golden. Serve with sweet chilli sauce, rice noodles, herbs and lime, if you like.
To eat later, freeze the raw fishcakes on a tray until solid, then transfer to an airtight container and freeze for up to three months. To cook from frozen, put a little olive oil in a frying pan on a medium-low heat, then fry the fish cakes in batches for about five to six minutes on each side, turning carefully, until cooked through, piping hot and golden.
- 
  These reccipes are edited extracts from Poppy Cooks: The Actually Delicious Batch Cookbook, by Poppy O’Toole, published by Bloomsbury Publishing at £22. To order a copy for £19.80, visit guardianbookshop.com

====================================================================================================

Andy Burnham has already made a mistake that will cost him his premiership: he lost his nerve over political donations | George Monbiot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
05:00:23 UTC
14:00:23 KST

Damn the electorate. They’re so impatient. No sooner do they get a new leader than they want another one. Those ingrates are already starting to grumble about Andy Burnham. Maybe the country is becoming ungovernable. Perhaps it’s social media. Or a consumerist culture, always picking the next shiny thing. Perhaps we’re addicted to drama. As we’re on our sixth prime minister in 10 years, and as similar levels of discontent surface in many other countries, these claims are recited across the media. What’s wrong with us?
Yet our disgruntlement is entirely rational. We give up so quickly on our prime ministers because they give up so quickly on us. Though it may involve different issues, it is always the same betrayal: the public interest is sacrificed for the sake of a tiny number of immensely wealthy people. And it tends to happen almost immediately.
The latest example, which has triggered both fury and grim resignation, is Burnham’s backtracking on his intention to cap political donations. It was hardly a radical policy: he proposed that no person would be able to give more than £500,000 to a political party in one year. That would still have granted the very wealthy disproportionate influence over our politics. I have long believed that the only fair system is one in which there should be no private donations at all beyond a standard, fixed membership fee. Otherwise voters will always take second place to money. But at the moment there is no cap, which ensures that billionaires can buy political parties and their platforms. So a £500,000 maximum, pathetic as it is, is at least a start. In a subsequent pledge, Burnham suggested that it could gradually be lowered.
Now, we are told, even this high cap has been abandoned: the representation of the people bill will concentrate instead on introducing Keir Starmer’s risible proposals, which are intended to limit donations sent from abroad but not from within the UK: as if billionaire donors and their wealth managers have no expertise in transferring money from one account to another. The loopholes are designed in.
Burnham’s buckling on this issue is not a small matter. It cuts to the quick of what this country is and how it works. It has immense implications for democracy, for policy formation and for every other aspect of civic life. What it means is that the ultra-rich will continue to own our politics and our country. Succumb to the power of money and you will find yourself, like Starmer, tongue-tied and immobilised, unable to rise to any challenge that requires a confrontation with oligarchic might. In other words, get this wrong and every other wrong thing follows.
The official reason for Burnham’s U-turn is that trade unions objected: they have long channelled large sums into the Labour party. I doubt this is the real explanation; most of the donations Burnham received for his leadership campaign came from large private donors. Almost half was supplied by Lord Sainsbury, who was also a major funder of the Starmer project. Union money scarcely featured.
But even if Burnham has retreated from his promise for the sake of the unions, I believe trade union funding is also problematic. It ensures that sectoral interests are elevated above the general interest. For example, Labour governments know they can safely bash benefit recipients, who aren’t unionised, while they tread very carefully – far too carefully in my view – around the interests of oil workers. And if the unions believe that an uncapped system works for them, they are deluded. They can never match the spending power of billionaires, whose interests in most cases are diametrically opposed to those of their members.
The power of the ultra-rich is now manifest in every policy governments do adopt and the policies they don’t. We see it in the new protest laws and their applications, which become more absurd by the week. Labelling protesters “terrorists” is part of a long-running programme to ensure that no one dares protest about anything any more. This programme has been rolled out across the world, through model legislation drawn up by junktanks funded by some of the richest people on Earth. Just as it did in the 18th century, an ever more extreme defence of property keeps pace with a growing concentration of wealth.
We see it in the way that datacentres have been labelled “critical national infrastructure”, enabling the government to bypass the usual planning process and impose them on communities, regardless of their impacts on local people’s quality of life, on water resources, energy supply and climate breakdown. Again, similar measures are being imposed in other countries at the behest of the same billionaire-funded groups. The role of governments appears to have been reduced to nodding them through.
We see it in the Burnham government’s insistence this summer, in the midst of shattering droughts, heatwaves and fires, on launching a consultation that proposes radically curtailing the transition to electric vehicles. I believe there is only one possible explanation for this policy: lobbying by corporations and their shareholders. Their interests appear to outweigh those of the living planet and its 8 billion people.
If our country and many others are becoming ungovernable, it is not because of the people. It is because the ultra-rich have smashed the system. The electorate and the MPs who might seek to represent us pull the political levers, but nothing happens. They might replace the leader, but the new one promptly repeats the “mistakes” that caused the eviction of the old one. It makes you wonder: what threat do the oligarchs present that outweighs even the threat of losing power?
Whatever the reason may be, disillusionment is an inevitable result of such betrayals. I think most people want stability. I think most people want to be able to trust their governments. We don’t like in-built obsolescence in our leaders any more than like it in our phones. I don’t want to see Burnham go the way of Starmer. But I know he will succeed only if he defends the public interest against the power of money. So what’s stopping him?
- 
  George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist

‘It smelled like dead people’: the plan to tackle England’s illegal waste problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
05:00:23 UTC
14:00:23 KST

“There were parents dropping their children off and then heaving from the smell,” says Liz Thompson, 45, who runs Blessings Nursery in Bradford, West Yorkshire.
During the recent heatwaves, the smell from an illegal waste dump on Midland Road, just metres from the nursery, became so unbearable that staff had to keep the doors and windows shut and the children couldn’t play outside.
“It smelled like dead people, like really bad rotten food. It was horrible,” she says.
The smell, which lingered for weeks, started to impact Thompson’s business, with prospective parents put off from enrolling their children at the nursery. “It was embarrassing,” she says.
The situation Thompson faced is far from a one-off. The Environment Agency received 10,238 reports of suspected waste crime in England in 2025.
Yorkshire is a particular hotspot, with a new heatmap showing 1,068 reports in 2025, second only to the West Midlands, where a record 1,542 reports of waste crime were filed. These figures are probably underestimated, with just 27% of waste crimes thought to be reported.
It’s a problem that particularly exercises the public and it’s striking that in one of his first moves as prime minister, Andy Burnham visited the Midland Road waste dump, declaring that the “days of making easy money out of waste are over”.
The dump, which first came on to Bradford Council and the Environment Agency’s radar in June after reports of foul smells, had been building for months. HGVs had been entering the site in the dead of night and early hours, with a large excavator unloading and dumping thousands of tonnes of waste.
“There are really clear signs that this is linked to organised criminality,” says the Environment Agency’s area environment manager, Ben Hocking. Waste crime is profitable for the criminals involved, but costly for the public; approximately 20% of the waste in circulation in England is managed illegally, at a cost to the economy of about £1bn a year.
The clean-up is particularly expensive. Burnham has earmarked three illegal sites where waste needs to be removed: Power Station Road, on the Isle of Sheppey, Kent; Aymer Close, in Runnymede, Surrey; and Midland Road. But Hocking estimates the cost to the taxpayer of cleaning up the Midland Road site alone will be upwards of £250,000. The cost of cleaning up the Hoads Wood illegal waste dump in Kent came to £15m.
“The aim is to recoup the costs through the courts, but whether that will be possible for this site remains uncertain,” says Hocking. Criminal investigations are still taking place.
As part of Burnham’s plans to tackle waste crime, Tracy Brabin, the mayor of West Yorkshire, will be appointed to take a new region-led approach to the problem.
“We are cracking down on the criminals behind it and giving the Environment Agency the tools it needs to go further and faster,” said the environment secretary, Angela Eagle.
But just how well equipped mayoral authorities and the Environment Agency are to tackle organised criminality at this scale remains up for debate, with the House of Lords recently accusing the agency of “incompetence” when it comes to waste crime.
“We could always do with more funding,” says Hocking, “but we’re also looking to be more effective with the people that we have. We are really looking to get a better intelligence picture of what’s happening and where.”
With no set timeline for when the clean-up of the Midland Road waste dump will begin, one woman who works at a nearby youth centre but asked to remain anonymous worries that more hot weather could bring more devastating smells.
“It was really hard for us to work,” she says. The centre had to cancel its youth cooking and exercise classes because the flies and smell made working unbearable.
“Whoever did this wasn’t thinking about the local people and how it’s affecting them and their businesses,” she says. “It’s really unfair. Whoever dumped this waste needs to be held responsible.”

Mohe-Nayba international transport corridor to be built in Russian Far East
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
04:58:52 UTC
13:58:52 KST

VLADIVOSTOK, September 2. /TASS/. The Mohe-Nayba international transport corridor will be built in the Russian Far East, providing the shortest route between China's northeastern provinces and the Arctic coast, a TASS correspondent reported. The relevant agreement was signed at the Eastern Economic Forum.
"The Mohe-Nayba international transport corridor is a project capable of fundamentally reshaping the transport geography of northeastern Russia. The new corridor will connect the largest markets in the Asia-Pacific region with Yakutia, the Magadan Region and the Transarctic Transport Corridor. The project involves the construction of more than 2,900 km of new railway infrastructure, a deepwater port and a new border crossing with China. This will provide the infrastructure needed to develop mineral deposits, launch new production facilities, expand the freight base and bring products from the Russian Far East to international markets," Nikolay Zapryagaev, CEO of the Far East and Arctic Development Corporation, said.
The project includes the creation of a combined international border crossing with China, the construction of the deepwater port of Nayba, a new railway line of around 1,300 km from Nizhny Bestyakh to Nayba with access to the port, as well as a roughly 1,670-km railway line to Magadan.
The Mohe-Nayba corridor is expected to handle around 2 mln metric tons of freight per year, Head of Yakutia Aysen Nikolayev noted.
The Eastern Economic Forum is being held on September 1-4 in Vladivostok on the campus of Far Eastern Federal University. The forum is organized by the Roscongress Foundation with the support of the Russian government. TASS is the general information partner.

NASA awards Blue Origin contract to develop Mars telecommunications network
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:52:57 CST
13:52:57 KST

LOS ANGELES, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- American private aerospace company Blue Origin was awarded a contract by NASA on Tuesday to develop the agency's Mars Telecommunications Network, a next-generation communications system designed to provide reliable, high-bandwidth communications and navigation services for current and future Mars missions.
The firm-fixed-price contract has a maximum potential value of approximately 700 million U.S. dollars. Under the contract, Blue Origin will deliver a high-performance telecommunications orbiter for Mars to NASA no later than Dec. 31, 2028, according to NASA.
Blue Origin will design, develop, integrate, launch, and operate the network as part of NASA's broader space communications and navigation infrastructure.
The network will include a high-performance telecommunications spacecraft orbiting Mars to transmit science data, imagery, navigation information, and critical mission communications for spacecraft operating on and around the planet.
The network, managed by NASA's Space Communications and Navigation program, is expected to be operational at Mars by 2030 and will support both current and future missions to the Red Planet, according to NASA.
NASA said the contract award marks a milestone in its strategy to expand communications and navigation services beyond Earth and the Moon, laying the foundation for sustained exploration of Mars in the coming decades. ■

Booze at young age linked to lasting brain changes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
04:52:02 UTC
13:52:02 KST

Binge drinking during adolescence may cause lasting changes to brain structure and function, including disrupted communication within the brain, according to a new study.
Repeated alcohol exposure during adolescence disrupted communication between astrocytes — brain cells increasingly recognised for their role in neural signalling — and synapses – tiny contact points where neurons communicate with each other – in the hippocampus, a region important for learning and memory, researchers at Marshall University’s Joan C. Edwards School of Medicine found.
The changes were still present after prolonged abstinence and were associated with altered fear-related behaviour in adulthood, researchers found in a preclinical rat model.
"Understanding why binge drinking specifically during adolescence worsens mental health outcomes and reduces overall quality of life is the goal of this research," Mary-Louise Risher, associate professor at the Joan C. Edwards School of Medicine, said in a press release. "From these studies, we aim to increase public awareness and develop new therapeutic approaches to alleviate the long-term consequences of adolescent binge drinking.”
The findings suggest that astrocytes may play a larger role in the long-term effects of adolescent alcohol exposure than previously understood. They also raise the possibility that targeting astrocyte function could eventually help address some of the persistent behavioural effects associated with alcohol exposure and substance use.
Researchers used a model of adolescent intermittent ethanol exposure to examine how repeated alcohol consumption during adolescence affected the brain following a period of abstinence and into adulthood.
“Growing evidence in recent years has highlighted a promising new role of astrocytes in the modulation of synaptic activity and behavioral outcomes,” said Olivia Coulter, first author of the paper and doctoral candidate at the Joan C. Edwards School of Medicine.
Coulter said the findings could contribute to the development of astrocyte-targeted approaches to improving brain health, although further research is needed.

New Zealand central bank raises interest rate to 2.75 pct as inflation rises
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:51:59 CST
13:51:59 KST

WELLINGTON, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand's central bank on Wednesday raised its official cash rate by 25 basis points to 2.75 percent as annual inflation rose to 4.1 percent in the June quarter, driven by higher fuel prices arising from the Middle East conflict.
The Reserve Bank of New Zealand's Monetary Policy Committee said in a statement that gradually removing monetary stimulus was appropriate to return inflation to its 2 percent target midpoint while supporting growth and employment.
New Zealand's economic recovery has most likely resumed but remains uneven after lackluster growth in the June quarter, the committee said, noting that resilient demand from trading partners and strong export prices are supporting income growth and investment in export-exposed sectors and regions of New Zealand.
In contrast, weak income growth, job insecurity and flat house prices continue to weigh on household spending and residential investment, particularly in Auckland, the country's largest city, and the capital Wellington, the statement said.
The committee expects the recovery to strengthen and broaden, with the export sector remaining resilient and household spending gradually increasing.
Conditions in the labor market should improve as the recovery gathers pace, and purchasing power will increase as inflation returns to the 2 percent target midpoint, it said, adding that future policy decisions will depend on the committee's judgement of the balance of risks to medium-term inflation.
"Unlike some previous upturns, this recovery is being driven by the export sector rather than rising house prices. That augurs well for the future," Finance Minister Nicola Willis said in a statement. ■

S. Koreans' overseas card spending falls 4.2 pct in Q2 amid lower outbound travelers
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:51:59 CST
13:51:59 KST

SEOUL, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- South Koreans' overseas plastic card spending fell in the second quarter due to a sharp decline in outbound travelers that outweighed steady growth in direct foreign online shopping, central bank data showed Wednesday.
Overseas spending by domestic residents through credit, debit and prepaid cards totaled 5.85 billion U.S. dollars in the April-June quarter, down 4.2 percent compared to the previous quarter, according to the Bank of Korea.
The quarterly fall was driven by a slowdown in travel-related expenditures. The number of outbound South Korean travelers plunged 20.4 percent over the quarter to 6.63 million in the second quarter.
The lower travel demand eclipsed the expansion in online direct purchases from foreign websites, which gained 4.3 percent to 1.41 billion dollars during the second quarter.
The number of plastic cards used abroad shrank 3.3 percent to 18.16 million in the cited quarter, while the average spending per card ticked down 0.9 percent to 322 dollars.
Meanwhile, plastic card spending by foreign visitors to South Korea surged 36.1 percent from three months earlier to hit an all-time high of 4.86 billion dollars in the second quarter.
The previous record high of 3.79 billion dollars was set in the second quarter of 2025. ■

MOSCOW, September 2. /TASS/. Russia's hard-to-recover gas reserves and resources have an estimated potential of around 30 trillion cubic meters, Russian Natural Resources Minister Alexander Kozlov told TASS in an interview ahead of the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF).
"We estimate the potential of such hard-to-recover gas reserves and resources at around 30 trillion cubic meters," he said.

Oleg Kazanov, head of Russia's Federal Agency for Mineral Resources (Rosnedra), said earlier that hard-to-recover reserves account for more than 30% of production and that their share will continue to increase.

Apple's top job has changed hands for the first time in 15 years, with John Ternus succeeding Tim Cook, the man who built the iPhone maker into a wildly successful tech giant.
Apple has a new boss for the first time in 15 years — and he is stepping into some famously large shoes.
John Ternus took the helm from Tim Cook on Tuesday, who hands over a company worth $4.6 trillion (€4tn) after growing it from less than $350 billion during his tenure — a run that turned him into one of the most consequential CEOs in tech history.
The transition comes at a pivotal time for Apple.
Artificial intelligence has triggered one of the biggest upheavals in the industry since Steve Jobs unveiled the first iPhone in 2007, and Apple has got off to a rough start, stumbling in its efforts to deliver new AI features it promised nearly two years ago.

Ternus faces challenges that will push him well outside his comfort zone in hardware engineering.
Beyond keeping Apple competitive in the AI race, he will need to navigate supply chain questions and relationships with figures such as US President Donald Trump, who publicly praised Cook on Tuesday.
Cook cultivated ties with Trump while steering the company through Trump's trade and tariff war targeting countries in Asia, where Apple has extensive manufacturing supply chains.
Although he is handing over the CEO role, Cook is widely expected to help Apple maintain its relationship with Trump in his new role as executive chairman.
Ternus worked on some of Apple's signature products under Cook, including the Apple Watch, AirPods and Apple Vision Pro.
He will headline next week's launch of the latest iPhone at Apple's Cupertino, California, headquarters.

Mass burials of unidentified victims continue in Nepal as death toll exceeds 1,000 one week after flash floods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
04:45:28 UTC
13:45:28 KST

Many were outraged and expressed their disapproval after the government revealed it intended to carry out mass “temporary” burials of the deceased. Nepal’s largely Hindu community objected to the measure which they say goes against religious traditions.
Nepali families were holding symbolic funeral ceremonies to "liberate the souls" of loved ones missing since deadly flash floods swept away their villages and homes in the Himalayan region a week ago.
Emergency teams have recovered more than 1,100 bodies, as nearly 4,000 people remain missing after the gigantic wave of freezing water, rocks and debris triggered by a high-altitude glacial collapse roared down the China-Nepal border on 26 August, causing grave damage to much of what was in its path.
After days of searching shelters and mortuaries, relatives of some of the missing lost hope and began conducting last rites.
"We had to do this to set his soul free, so that he is at peace and happy wherever he is," said Dolma Newar Tamang, flanked by her sobbing son, at a funeral for her husband.
He had been en route to China when the disaster struck. "I saw the news and called him," she said. "I called repeatedly, but he never picked up."
A week after the colossal disaster, Nepali rescuers remained hopeful about finding survivors, particularly in multiple tunnels of hydropower plants across the region. So far, rescuers have recovered only bodies from tunnels blocked by sludge, but teams were still digging, drilling and blasting through debris in the hopes of reaching any potential survivors.
Nepal's Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said he still hoped some of the thousands of people still reported missing could be alive.
"Miracles do happen," he said in an interview. "At this point, I do not want to completely give up hope."
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah said the catastrophe was "a serious indication that the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing alongside climate change".
"Climate change is a global contribution, and disaster response is also a global responsibility," he wrote in a post on Facebook.
Scientists say the Himalayas, the world's highest mountain range, are warming rapidly as global temperatures rise, accelerating glacier melt.
Glaciers in the wider Himalayan and Hindu Kush ranges are a crucial water source for around 240 million people in the mountainous regions, as well as for another 1.65 billion people in the South and Southeast Asian river valleys below.
There is growing anger at the scale of destruction to hit Nepal, a largely rural nation of 30 million people. The country has contributed little to the greenhouse gas emissions driving global warming, but is among those suffering its consequences.
Kathmandu has warned reconstruction costs could run into the "billions of dollars". Nepal's economy is already strained, with limited resources to respond to a disaster of this scale.
With mortuaries overflowing in Nepal, authorities have had to bury hundreds of unidentified bodies after DNA sampling in mass graves, sparking major uproar from the country’s largely Hindu community, who accused the government of ignoring religious burial rites.
The total number of confirmed deaths as of Wednesday morning sat at 1,114. The latest figures also show 3,916 people still missing.

The possible cost of Australia's stronger-than-expected growth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
04:41:57 UTC
13:41:57 KST

in brief
- Australia's GDP grew by 2.1 per cent in the last financial year.
- An economist said the fresh data alone does "not compel" the RBA to raise rates.
Australia's economy is "resilient and robust", Treasurer Jim Chalmers says, after fresh data showed stronger growth, though the figures may also add to pressure on the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) to raise interest rates again.
Australia's gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 2.1 per cent — a sign of increased economic activity — in the last financial year, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) reported on Wednesday.
A growing GDP suggests more business activity and can lead to more jobs being created as demand for goods and services rises.
Chalmers described the results as positive for the nation.
"Growth is as strong, if not stronger, than every major advanced economy," he said in a video posted to social media.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
But increases in spending can also mean demand for goods outpaces supply, leading to price increases and contributing to inflation.
The hot GDP result could therefore add more pressure on the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) to raise interest rates again as it struggles to close the gap between supply and demand.
Australia's cash rate target is currently 4.35 per cent following three rate hikes this year.
What does the data show?
Despite the impact of higher interest rates and the United States-Iran war, GDP growth accelerated on a quarterly basis from 0.3 per cent in March.
While the 2.1 per cent annual growth rate is faster than the RBA's assumed speed limit of 2 per cent, it was a subdued result by historical standards, as households continued to behave cautiously, ABS head of national accounts Grace Kim said.
"While increased spending and business investment occurred in pockets of the economy, imports supported much of the growth, moderating its contribution to overall GDP growth," she said.
Imports of goods rose 2.4 per cent, driven by increased purchases of cars and planes.
Meanwhile, services imports fell 4.9 per cent as Australians' travel plans were disrupted by war in the Middle East.
"The number of Australians travelling overseas for the northern hemisphere summer fell for the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic, significantly reducing international travel expenditure," Kim said.
Household consumption rose 0.4 per cent, with falls in fuel consumption and travel due to higher fuel prices.
But the oil crisis also supported growth as consumers flocked to electric vehicles. EV purchases rose 10.3 per cent.
"The rise in electric vehicle purchases may have reflected households taking a longer-term approach to cost-of-living pressures, with some choosing EVs to help reduce ongoing expenses," Kim said.
Meanwhile, private business investment declined 0.5 per cent, due to a pullback in data centre investment.
GDP per capita was flat over the quarter, growing by 0.7 per cent over the 12 months to June.
Productivity was likewise flat but fell 0.2 per cent over the year.
Real unit labour costs — a measure closely watched by the Reserve Bank for signs of cost pressures on businesses — rose 0.9 per cent.
Impact on RBA
David Bassanese, chief economist at financial firm Betashares, said the "jury remains out on a September rate decision".
He described Wednesday's figures as slightly better than market expectations but still leaving Australia's economy "in a rut".
"The saving grace from the economic rut revealed by these numbers is they do not compel the RBA to raise rates, but they also do not rule out a hike in the future," he said in a statement.
"My base case is that September will not bring a rate increase, as the RBA will want to see more evidence on inflation and the moderation in house prices."
The RBA will next meet to discuss any changes to the cash rate target on 29 September.
— With additional reporting by the Australian Associated Press.

Their son fell in Lebanon. Now a court has allowed his sperm to be used to have a child
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
04:39:53 UTC
13:39:53 KST

The parents of a Golani Reconnaissance Unit company commander who was killed nearly two years ago in battle against Hezbollah terrorists will be allowed to use his sperm to have a child, the Rishon Lezion Family Court ruled Sunday. With no objection from the attorney general’s office, Judge Rivka Makayes granted the parents’ request.
Their son was appointed company commander in the elite unit in September 2024, and about a month later was killed along with four other soldiers in a battle in the village of Ayta ash-Shab in southern Lebanon. He was 24.
Immediately afterward, his parents signed authorization forms for the retrieval of his sperm and the donation of his organs. Twelve sperm samples were extracted and frozen, and one of his corneas was transplanted into a patient, restoring the recipient’s sight.
In December 2025, the parents filed a petition seeking permission to use his sperm in order to continue his lineage. His father testified that during a brief respite trip the two took to Greece, his son had asked him to have children from his sperm if he were killed.
The father recalled his son telling him: “If I don’t come back from the war, take good care of Mom and of [my two siblings], and make sure I have children. I trust you to choose the right mother.”
Friends who had previously served with him in the Egoz Unit also said he told them he wanted to have descendants after his death, and that he wished to name a future child after his commander and friend, Maj. Shilo Har-Even, who was killed in the fighting on October 7.
According to them, the deceased soldier had stressed that if he fell in battle, he wanted his parents to make sure he had children, and even joked that his mother would know how to choose the most suitable woman for him.
A representative of the attorney general’s office did not oppose the parents’ request and left the decision to the court’s discretion.
Judge Makayes granted the parents permission to use their son’s sperm and wrote: “After reviewing their affidavits and hearing the testimony of the plaintiffs and two of the deceased’s close friends, the court was persuaded that the plaintiffs proved that the deceased’s ‘presumed’ wish was to have continuity even after his death.”
She stressed that these were not merely general remarks, but “very specific conversations” in which he clearly expressed his wishes.
“Although there is no doubt that he was fully aware of the dangers he faced as a combat soldier and commander, the deceased chose, in an altruistic and admirable manner, to put his life at risk for the defense of the state, its security and the safety of its citizens, while making clear to those close to him his desire for continuity if the worst should happen and he were killed,” she wrote.
Under those circumstances, the judge approved the parents’ request to use their fallen son’s sperm to have a child, subject to court approval of any future agreement reached with the intended mother.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
04:36:50 UTC
13:36:50 KST

A British-Australian couple will be allowed to spend more time with their three children after the youngsters were removed from the family’s off-grid woodland home in central Italy last year, their lawyer said on Tuesday.
The juvenile court of L’Aquila in Italy has approved a staged process under the supervision of social services that could ultimately allow the children to leave the residential care facility where they have been living since November.
Under the court’s plan, British father Nathan Trevallion and Australian mother Catherine Birmingham will gradually be able to spend more time with their children in a home environment.
“The ruling partially revises previous court decisions and sets out a gradual reunification process, allowing the children to return home for daytime visits immediately and, from October, for weekend overnight stays with their family,” lawyer Simone Pillon said.
The decision marks a significant turning point in a case that sparked a national debate in Italy over alternative lifestyles and state intervention in family life.
Social services will monitor the process and assess the children’s reintegration before any permanent reunification can take place.
Pillon said the family planned an appeal in order to pursue a more rapid and complete process to bring the family back together.
The court suspended the couple’s parental responsibility in an order issued on 20 November last year.
Since then, the couple’s three children, a nine-year-old girl and twin boys aged seven, have been housed in a residential care facility.
Birmingham remained with the children until March when she was ordered to leave under a new court ruling based on recommendations from social services.
The case first drew public attention last year after Italian authorities examined the family’s living conditions in a remote farmhouse in the Abruzzo region.
A court ruling issued in November said the family had no significant social interactions, no stable income and lacked adequate sanitary facilities. The children were being homeschooled.
The family’s situation first came to the attention of authorities after all five family members were taken to hospital following mushroom poisoning.

UN says world must navigate ‘reality’ of 1.5 deg C overshoot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
04:31:00 UTC
13:31:00 KST

UN says world must navigate ‘reality’ of 1.5 deg C overshoot
- The UN report confirms the world will surpass the 1.5°C warming limit and must now focus on managing and reducing this overshoot.
- Policymakers need to adapt climate strategies to handle warming beyond 1.5°C, emphasising rapid emissions cuts and carbon removal.
- Climate activists warn overshoot is not a reason to abandon the 1.5°C goal and stress urgent action over reliance on unproven technologies.
AI generated
PARIS – The United Nations outlined on Sept 2 how the world might bring global temperatures back to 1.5 deg C once the milestone target is breached in a first-of-its-kind assessment that drew criticism from climate activists.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres in 2025 acknowledged the inevitability of overshooting 1.5 deg C, but this is the first time a UN agency has addressed this head-on in a dedicated report.
Scientists agree that warming above 1.5 deg C relative to pre-industrial times poses grave risks and nearly 200 nations committed in 2015 to try and keep global temperature rises to this safer threshold.
But the world is expected to blow past 1.5 deg C in a matter of years and attention has pivoted to making any “overshoot” as brief and contained as possible.
In a much-anticipated report, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) stated unequivocally that 1.5 deg C would be surpassed and “the challenge has shifted from avoiding overshoot to navigating it”.
“It’s a reality check. We have to live with this warmer world... but there’s still a lot we can do to limit warming,” said report co-author Richard Betts from the University of Exeter.
The report “was about responses rather than just sort of saying it is happening”, he told journalists.
Fellow author Debra Roberts said it was important for policymakers “to realise the rules of the game are now changing”.
“I think for me that’s the clarion call... we now have to reconfigure our climate governance around dealing with an overshoot pathway. None of our plans are prepared for that,” said Roberts from the University of KwaZulu-Natal.
The report’s stark language alarmed climate campaigners who have rallied around 1.5 deg C since it was affirmed as the more ambitious goal of the Paris Agreement a decade ago.
“This is a heartbreaking moment, but overshoot is not the reason to give up and surrender 1.5 deg C,” said Jasper Inventor, deputy programme director at Greenpeace International.
Bill Hare, a climate scientist and chief executive of policy institute Climate Analytics, slammed the report and said it risked becoming “a call to apathy rather than a call to arms”.
Small island nations threatened by rising seas have been particularly vocal defenders of the 1.5 deg C target and have urged wealthier countries not to abandon the milestone even as it slips out of reach.
The world has already warmed roughly 1.4 deg C since 1850-1900, mostly from the burning of fossil fuels, and the last three years have been the hottest on record.
Scientists say any overshoot of 1.5 deg C threatens more extreme weather and pushes the planet closer to tipping points like the collapse of ice sheets and loss of coral reefs.
UNEP executive director Inger Andersen said there “are no good outcomes if we remain above 1.5 deg C”.
“Let’s be very clear – that 1.5 deg C target is still the goal. But now, we need to approach it differently: from above,” Andersen told journalists.
Guterres said it was possible to bring warming back below 1.5 deg C by the end of the century.
“The fight for 1.5 deg C is the fight for humanity,” he said.
To achieve this, carbon dioxide removal – the process of pulling carbon from the air and storing it – would be essential alongside deep and rapid cuts to greenhouse gas emissions, the UNEP report said.
At present, carbon removal plays a vanishingly small part in addressing climate change and is strongly opposed by many activists pushing for a faster phase out of coal, oil and gas.
“The only way to minimise harm is to cut emissions now... not to delay action with speculative techno-fixes,” said Lili Fuhr from campaign organisation Centre for International Environmental Law. AFP

====================================================================================================

Country diary: The rain has come, and suddenly the land looks (and smells) different | Nicola Chester
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
04:30:22 UTC
13:30:22 KST

After an entire heat-baked summer without rain, the land looks strange and unlike itself. Fields, banks and grassy margins are the lurid yellow ochre of climate fiction – the mise en scène captured with eerie relevance in the recent BBC TV drama The Rapture.
There are cracks so deep in Weaver’s Field that the farmer can push his arm in up to his elbow. Spots of bird’s-foot trefoil and sky-blue chicory (the latter on uncannily short stems) polka-dot the otherwise dead pasture. Sentinel field oaks seem unaffected, but shallow-rooted beech trees, familiar in giant caterpillar shapes on the downs, shed shrivelled brown leaves and a poor, early beechnut mast. Gnarly field maples are almost leafless, while sycamores bracket the green with their browning leaf-curl. Even in the keepered woods, laurel has wilted.
For a week, skeins of black smoke drift from the field fires at Enham Alamein, from the eastern end of Greenham Common, and from the New Forest further south. But over the nearby border into Wiltshire, it is white smoke that veils Salisbury Plain all the way to Avebury and its village in the stones. The Westbury White Horse, of Eric Ravilious’s 1939 painting, is on fire – or the down and iron age Bratton Camp next to it is. Probably carved from the chalk in the late 1600s, it is surrounded by an apocalyptic vision.
The smell of smoke lingers long after a fire is out. Dad was a fireman who fought the New Forest conflagration in 1976, and Windsor Castle’s blaze in 1992. For me, the smell of burning evokes heightened awareness, comfort and safety, an olfactory memory of him coming home from work in damp, sooty uniform, and the alarm bell that rang in my childhood home whenever he was needed.
The rain teases us for a few more days, as towering piles of cumulus sail north like galleons. When it comes, it darkens the down to an unfamiliar moorland brown. The heat rises again afterwards, and with it the strong scent of ammonia from sheep’s urine. The only thing to wet the ground all summer, it had remained undiluted and on the surface. Reanimated, mingled with damp dust and baked grass, it’s a heady, confusing new scent.

Earth may have lost the Sun’s protective shield millions of years ago
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
04:25:48 UTC
13:25:48 KST

Earth may have lost the Sun’s protective shield millions of years ago
- Date:
- September 2, 2026
- Source:
- NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center
- Summary:
- NASA-funded studies suggest Earth’s climate has been influenced by both the Sun’s travels through dense regions of the Milky Way and the violent superflares of its youth. Those events may help explain ancient ice ages as well as how early Earth stayed warm enough for liquid water when the Sun was much dimmer.
- Share:
The Sun does far more than provide Earth with light and heat. Two recent NASA-funded studies suggest that events from the Sun's distant past may have influenced Earth's climate in unexpected ways, from helping drive ancient temperature shifts to keeping the young planet warm enough for liquid water and possibly life.
One study from NASA's SHIELD (Solar Wind with Hydrogen Ion charge Exchange and Large-Scale Dynamics) center, one of NASA's DRIVE (Diversify, Realize, Integrate, Venture, Educate) Science Centers, examines how the heliosphere moved through the Milky Way over time. The heliosphere is the vast protective bubble produced by the Sun that surrounds the solar system. Researchers found that changes in the galactic environment around this bubble may have affected conditions on Earth.
A separate study led by a NASA scientist explores another ancient puzzle: how a much dimmer young Sun could have kept Earth warm. The findings suggest that powerful solar eruptions may have helped generate strong greenhouse gases in Earth's early atmosphere.
The Sun's Journey Through the Milky Way
Earth's climate has changed dramatically over tens of millions of years. At various points, major ice ages temporarily lowered global average temperatures by several degrees, while other periods brought repeated swings between warmer and colder conditions.
Scientists have traditionally investigated changes in Earth's orbit, greenhouse gas levels, ice coverage, and other planetary factors to understand these shifts. New research now suggests that changes in the space environment surrounding the Sun may also have played an important role.
The solar system is enclosed within a protective region created by the Sun, somewhat like the way Earth is surrounded by an atmosphere. This region, called the heliosphere, forms as charged particles in the solar wind continuously stream outward from the Sun in every direction.
Reconstructing the Sun's Galactic Path
The entire heliosphere travels around the center of the Milky Way. During the Sun's 4.6-billion-year lifetime, the solar system has moved through many different galactic environments.
In a study published on Aug. 21 in Annual Review of Astronomy and Astrophysics, researchers with NASA's SHIELD center used computer simulations to reconstruct the heliosphere's past trajectory through the galaxy. Their results suggest that some of the regions the solar system encountered may have produced measurable changes on Earth.
Merav Opher, SHIELD's principal investigator at Boston University, and her colleagues simulated encounters between the solar system and extremely cold regions filled with gas and dust. Their work indicates that the Sun passed through such environments at least three times during the past several million years.
During these encounters, enormous interstellar "cold clouds" may have pressed against the heliosphere with enough force to dramatically compress it. According to the simulations, the heliosphere may at times have shrunk to a size smaller than Earth's orbit, temporarily leaving our planet outside the Sun's protective bubble.
When Earth May Have Lost Its Solar Shield
The modeled encounters occurred approximately 2 to 3 million years ago, 6 to 7 million years ago, and 13 to 14 million years ago. If the heliosphere contracted as the simulations suggest, Earth's atmosphere would have been directly exposed to a very different interstellar environment during those periods.
The timing also lines up with geological evidence. Elements commonly associated with interstellar dust have been found in deep-sea sediment cores, Antarctic snow, and samples from the Moon that correspond to these time periods.
These episodes of heliosphere collapse may also help explain some ancient climate patterns.
In the simulations, exposing Earth's atmosphere to a dense, cold cloud of galactic hydrogen increased atmospheric water vapor and changed conditions in the upper atmosphere. Those effects eventually influenced conditions closer to Earth's surface.
The results raise the possibility that the solar system's passages through colder parts of the Milky Way contributed to some long-term climate changes on Earth, potentially including ice ages.
Building a Digital Twin of the Heliosphere
NASA funds SHIELD as one of several centers designed to advance the study of heliophysics. As a DRIVE Science Center, SHIELD brings together researchers with different areas of expertise, methods, and scientific perspectives.
One of the center's goals is to build a detailed model, or "digital twin," of the heliosphere. This model could help scientists better understand how the Sun's protective bubble responds when it encounters features such as dense interstellar clouds.
Studying the history and structure of our habitable solar system could also provide clues about how life evolved on Earth. In the future, that knowledge may help researchers identify other star systems capable of supporting habitable worlds.
The Mystery of the Faint Young Sun
A second study focuses on a different problem involving the Sun's early history.
Vladimir Airapetian, a scientist at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, and his collaborators investigated how early Earth managed to remain warm enough for liquid water when the young Sun produced much less energy than it does today.
About three billion years ago, the Sun was only 70% as bright as it is now. Based on that reduced output, Earth should theoretically have been frozen solid.
Geological evidence tells a different story. Stable liquid water existed on Earth long before then. The contradiction between a relatively warm early Earth and a cooler, dimmer Sun is known as the Faint Young Sun paradox.
A Violent Young Sun May Hold the Answer
Scientists may find clues by examining young stars elsewhere in the Milky Way that resemble the early Sun.
These "toddler" stars are far more active than mature stars. Observations from NASA's retired Kepler space telescope show that young Sun-like stars can produce enormous superflares on a daily basis, sending high-energy particles racing outward through space.
If the young Sun behaved in a similar way, Airapetian proposes that these energetic particles could have triggered chemical reactions in Earth's atmosphere that helped warm the planet.
To test that idea, Airapetian's team recreated conditions thought to resemble the atmosphere of early Earth inside a sealed chamber. The researchers combined molecular nitrogen, ammonia, carbon dioxide, and carbon monoxide.
They then bombarded the gas mixture with protons to imitate the stream of energetic particles generated by solar superflares.
Superflares Could Have Created a Powerful Greenhouse Gas
The simulated particle bombardment produced several chemical changes, including the formation of nitrous oxide. Nitrous oxide is a greenhouse gas roughly 300 times more potent than carbon dioxide. The study was published in Astrophysical Journal Letters.
That nitrous oxide could have helped early Earth retain heat.
Not all of the gas would have remained in the atmosphere, however. Intense ultraviolet radiation from the young Sun would have broken down some nitrous oxide molecules, separating them back into nitrogen and oxygen.
Even so, the researchers found that relatively little nitrous oxide may have been needed.
Computer simulations showed that if just 10% of the nitrous oxide produced in the laboratory experiment survived, it could have raised temperatures near Earth's equator to around 41 degrees Fahrenheit (5 degrees Celsius). That would have kept temperatures above the freezing point of water.
Conditions That May Have Favored Early Life
A cooler but unfrozen Earth may have offered another advantage.
The smaller surviving amount of nitrous oxide could have supported prebiotic chemical reactions. Research has found that temperatures only slightly above freezing can be more effective than warmer conditions for assembling complex chains of amino acids.
That means the young Sun's violent activity may have done more than prevent Earth from freezing. It may also have helped create environmental conditions favorable to the chemistry that preceded life.
How the Sun Helped Shape Earth
Together, the two studies highlight how deeply Earth's history is connected to the Sun.
The solar system's movement through the Milky Way may have exposed Earth to changing interstellar environments capable of influencing its climate. Billions of years earlier, intense activity from the young Sun may have helped warm the planet when sunlight alone should not have been sufficient.
Earth is unusual in many ways, but it has never existed in isolation. It formed within a larger star-planet system and has remained closely connected to the changing behavior and environment of the Sun throughout its history.
Understanding that relationship could reveal new clues about Earth's climate, the evolution of life, and the conditions that might make other planetary systems habitable.

From delivering food to retrieving bodies, drones take new role in Nepal's disaster response
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
04:25:31 UTC
13:25:31 KST

Amir Latif Arain
02 September 2026•Update: 02 September 2026
As search and rescue operations continue in flood-hit areas of Nepal, drones have taken a new role from delivering food to retrieving bodies, the Kathmandu Post reported Wednesday.  
Residents of Dhading, one of the areas devastated by last week’s floods, witnessed an unusual scene in the skies when an unmanned aircraft flew overhead carrying a human body.
The drone had been deployed to retrieve the body from an area rescuers found difficult and dangerous to navigate.
Seven bodies were airlifted by drones from the area.
Barely a decade ago, drone technology was largely associated with international search and rescue teams responding to disasters in Nepal.  
International relief agencies brought drones to help search for survivors, assess damage and support recovery after a 7.8-magnitude earthquake struck Nepal in 2015, killing thousands and destroying large parts of Kathmandu and other areas.
The technology, however, is now being used far beyond aerial photography and mapping, in search-and-rescue operations.
Drone operators said despite restrictions in terms of payload capacity, range and weather conditions, the effect of drones can be disproportionate to their size where conventional transport is impossible.
The eight-member drone team has been using the Chinese-made DJI FlyCart 100, a heavy-lift industrial cargo drone capable of carrying logistics weighing up to 85 kilograms (187 pounds) and operating a range of up to 4 kilometers (2.5 miles).
Other drones have been deployed to inspect rivers and their banks in the search for missing people.  
Thermal drones can detect signs of living people, potentially allowing rescuers to locate survivors in areas that are inaccessible or too dangerous to enter.
Drone operators have used unmanned aircraft inside the tunnel of the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project, where scores of workers are believed to have been trapped following the floods.
The technology is also being used to deliver food in several affected areas.
Around1.6 million people have been affected by last week's devastating flash floods, which have killed nearly 1,100 and left nearly 4,000 missing in Nepal.
At least 16 people were killed on the Chinese side of the border, with 546 missing, including 261 foreigners.

Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong pleads guilty in second national security case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
04:23:43 UTC
13:23:43 KST

Joshua Wong, one of Hong Kong’s most prominent pro-democracy activists, pleaded guilty on Wednesday to conspiring to seek foreign sanctions against Hong Kong and China, a national security charge that carries a maximum life sentence.
Prosecutors have accused Wong, 29, of working with the exiled Hong Kong activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against China.
The court heard that Wong had visited foreign countries and met foreign politicians to lobby for sanctions against Hong Kong and China.
The prosecution said he had continued to call for sanctions on Hong Kong and China after the implementation of the national security law and that he had posted meetings on his social media accounts.
Wong has been continuously imprisoned since November 2020. He has spent nearly six years in detention and had been due to be released in January 2027.
In 2022 he pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit subversion for his role in an unofficial primary election. In November 2024 he was sentenced to four years and eight months in prison.
Wong waved at supporters as he entered the dock. He wore a blue shirt and black-rimmed glasses. He stood with his arms behind his back as he pleaded guilty to the charges.
Wong is expected to be sentenced later. The offence is punishable by a prison term of three to 10 years, or up to life imprisonment if the offence is deemed to be “of a grave nature”. Pleading guilty could typically result in a reduced sentence.
Outside Hong Kong’s high court, people queued overnight to secure a seat at Wednesday’s hearing.
One supporter who attended the court criticised the proceedings.
“Under a compromised judicial system with zero space for a fair trial, Wong’s plea is a forced reality,” they said, asking not to be named. “This is not justice, but Beijing’s absolute eradication of Hong Kong’s dissident voices.”
In 2014, the then teenage Wong became the international face of the Umbrella Movement, when thousands of protesters occupied major roads across Hong Kong for 79 days demanding greater democracy. In October 2014 he appeared on the cover of a Time magazine under the headline: “The Face of Protest”.
When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the movement and immediately joined calls for the bill to be withdrawn.
In 2020 Beijing imposed a wide-ranging national security law on Hong Kong after a year of anti-government protests. The authorities said the law was needed to restore stability to the international financial hub. Critics say six years on the law is continuing to expand in scope.
Wong is the only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under the law. Supporters say the prosecution heavily relied on his advocacy before the national security law was enacted and argue his case has been applied retroactively.
“It’s obvious that the government wants to keep him behind bars for as long as they can, so as to isolate him and not to let him become a visible symbol of resistance.” said Frances Hui from the Committee for Freedom in Hong Kong Foundation.
Wong’s case has attracted widespread condemnation from global rights organisations.
“By stacking one charge after another against Joshua Wong, the authorities are ensuring that the democracy icon stays behind bars, silencing him and the Hong Kong pro-democracy movement he helped lead and inspire,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch.
“Conflating promoting democracy and free speech with undermining national security is a favourite dodge for authoritarians. Beijing also likes blaming ‘hostile’, but unspecified foreign forces,” said Sophie Richardson, a longtime China rights advocate.
On Tuesday the former Conservative leader Iain Duncan Smith urged the UK government to raise Wong’s case with Beijing, saying: “Enough is enough. It’s time to stop chasing peaceful protesters.”
With Associated Press

Zelensky says airlines should avoid Russian airspace as Ukraine escalates drone operations
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
05:23:23 BST
13:23:23 KST

Zelensky says airlines should avoid Russian airspace as Ukraine escalates drone operations
- Published
Ukraine's president has told airlines that Russian airspace will be "effectively closing" as his country escalates its drone strikes.
"We want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, everyone who still uses key Russian airports: the Russian sky is becoming completely dangerous," Volodymyr Zelensky said. Ukraine has since formally notified the UN of the risks to civilian aviation.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said the comments amounted to a "declaration of state terrorism".
Most Western commercial airlines do not fly over Russia because of the ongoing Russian invasion of Ukraine, but carriers in countries like Turkey and China do.
Explaining the elevated airspace risk in his nightly video address on Tuesday, Zelensky said that "Ukraine does not threaten civilian aviation as such - not a single civilian aircraft" and did not want the loss of innocent lives.
"There will simply be drones in Russia's skies on a scale that has to be taken into account," he said.
Zelensky directed the warning to airlines continuing to operate flights to Russian airports, especially in major cities like St Petersburg and Moscow.
In a statement on X, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said that Ukraine had officially notified the International Civil Aviation Organization that Russian airspace was not safe for civilian aviation.
"We want to prevent unintended incidents," he said, adding: "The war is returning home to Russia."
On Wednesday afternoon, flight tracking website FlightRadar24 showed many planes flying over Russia, including arriving and departing from the two main airports, which had some delays, but few cancellations.
Several airlines that fly through Russia told the BBC that they were carefully monitoring the situation.
Qatar Airways, which flies into Moscow and travels through Russian airspace to get to the US west coast, said its flight planning was "guided by rigorous and continuous monitoring of airspace security, safety assessments, and geopolitical developments".
Turkish low-cost airline Pegasus cancelled its flights to Russia on Tuesday and Wednesday, citing "technical and operational reasons", but said future flights "are operating as scheduled".
FlyDubai, an Emirati government-owned carrier, told the BBC that it would "closely monitor the evolving situation in the region and adjust our flight schedules and routings as necessary".
- Rosenberg: Putin's veiled threat to UK part of Russia's campaign against West 
  - Published7 hours ago
Ukraine has targeted energy facilities deep inside Russian territory and there have been repeated attacks on depots belonging to Russia's two biggest online retailers, Wildberries and Ozon.
Its drone attacks have for months led to disruption at some of Russia's biggest airports, especially in Moscow where at times all four major airports have been forced to halt arrivals and departures.
Several cancellations were reported on Wednesday.
Ukraine does not have to target airports to cause disruption.
Under Russia's air defence "Kovyor" (carpet) plan, flights are suspended if a drone is detected in the relevant area.
Aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions said in an alert to clients that while the majority of Ukraine's drone and missile strikes were likely to occur within 300km (186 miles) of the border, daily attacks deeper inside Russia were almost certain to continue this year.
"There is also a realistic possibility that the frequency of Ukrainian strikes will continue to increase in the short term deep inside Russian territory," the alert added. "It is assessed that miscalculation and/or misidentification is likely in areas related to the Ukraine conflict."
Speaking to reporters at the Shanghai Co-operation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan, Putin said: "They are asking us to resume negotiations... but you don't negotiate with terrorists."
His comments come as Russia's attacks on Ukraine continue, with heavy strikes killing 12 people on Tuesday and further attacks on Odesa, Sumy and Kyiv on Wednesday. Russia's military has said it is preparing to carry out "massive" strikes on Ukrainian power stations.
The Ukrainian capital and its surrounding region have come under attack for seven days in a row.
A few weeks ago, Zelensky said Russia was attacking Ukraine every day, and Ukraine's military had "begun the process of bringing the war back to Russia". At the weekend he said the same, that Russia had to feel the war was "returning to where it came from".
Putin acknowledged that Ukrainian strikes had damaged infrastructure inside Russia, while insisting that "only 10%" of oil refineries were left to repair.
Chinese, Turkish and Gulf state airlines are among those using Russian airspace, with savings in time and fuel on routes between Asia and Europe.
Other carriers have largely avoided the eastern European region since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion in February, 2022.
Ukraine has closed its airspace to civilian aircraft throughout that period.
The risks of civil aviation during a war are clear. A few months after war broke out in eastern Ukraine in 2014 between Russian-backed separatists and the Ukrainian military, a Russian-made missile brought down a passenger plane, killing all 298 people on board.
Last year, the UN aviation agency ruled that Russia was responsible for the downing of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17 over eastern Ukraine in July 2014.
The Kremlin has always denied any responsibility for the air disaster.
In 2024, Putin apologised to the president of neighbouring Azerbaijan over the downing of a commercial airliner in Russian airspace, in which 38 people were killed.
He said the "tragic incident" had occurred when Russian air defence systems were repelling Ukrainian drones.
