US Congress seeks to identify foreign countries behind scam calls
Inquiry comes as US government reports tying much of the financial damage from scams to Chinese criminal networks based in Southeast Asia
The inquiry follows a string of US government reports tying much of the financial damage from scams to Chinese criminal networks based in Southeast Asia.
“Everyone with a phone has received a robocall or scam call,” said Representative Tom Kean Jnr, a Republican from New Jersey. “Robocalls originating from overseas pose an especially nefarious threat. Congress has taken strides to identify and to trace back illegal robocalls.”
Under the House bill, the task force would study the volume of unlawful robocalls originating inside and outside the US and determine which foreign countries serve as the main departure points for the most calls entering the country.
It would also assess the financial losses and identity theft associated with foreign-originating robocalls, examine how countries could work together to authenticate international calls, and consider incentives for foreign governments to cooperate with US law enforcement.

The two-day meeting of finance chiefs in Asheville, North Carolina, came amid a global bond market selloff on worries over growing debt levels and inflation pressures.

“And unfortunately, I was right. They have – and the rest of the world probably needs to take a hard look at what they should be doing to protect their citizens’ jobs,” he told the meeting.
“We’re seeing a lot of non-market economies with these big imbalances that are sucking growth from the rest of the world,” Bessent told reporters.
Joint communique unclear
China’s massive export push has pressured economies across the globe, especially as the US has imposed high tariffs on Chinese goods and outright bans on some products, such as Chinese vehicles.
With chronically weak domestic demand, China has doubled down on exports of electric vehicles, semiconductors and other goods. Its total exports rose 23.9 percent in July year-on-year, prompting growing calls in Europe for tougher curbs on Chinese imports.
At the same time, the Trump administration’s tariff policies have been criticised by economists and politicians for raising costs for US consumers and, in many cases, for punishing allies.
The Tax Foundation, an independent think tank, found that the tariffs imposed by the Trump administration throughout 2025 raised the overall retail price of imported consumer goods by roughly 7 percent relative to pre-tariff trends.
European Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis agreed that China is a major source of economic imbalances, but said that the US and Europe also had roles to play in evening things out.
In more direct comments, German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil noted that the US-Israel war on Iran, together with ongoing US tariff disputes, were also major causes of uncertainty holding back the global economy.
“Uncertainty is poison for economic growth,” he said. “The tariff conflicts being pursued by the US, such as the current dispute with Canada, destroy trust.”
It remains unclear whether the US will be able to bring the diverse forum together to agree on a joint communique on how to reduce global imbalances.
G20 member China has shown little interest in longstanding calls for it to reduce industrial subsidies and rebalance its economy, while its yuan currency remains significantly undervalued by most measures.
Beijing has also exploited its dominance in processing critical minerals by placing export restrictions on rare earths in April 2025, a response to Trump’s tariffs that have also hit non-US companies.

Tropical Storm Edouard moves ashore Gulf Coast near Texas-Louisiana border
Sept 1 - Tropical Storm Edouard churned out of the Gulf of Mexico and sloshed ashore near the Texas-Louisiana border on Tuesday, packing sustained winds of up to 60 miles per hour and unleashing soaking downpours.
According to the National Hurricane Center in Miami, Edouard made landfall near Johnson Bayou in the southwesternmost corner of Louisiana at about 2:20 p.m. Central time (1920 GMT), and veered west, spreading heavy rains and gale-force winds into southeastern Texas.
Forecasters say Edouard is expected to weaken rapidly as the storm center moves farther inland, diminishing to a tropical depression by early on Wednesday.
Still, the storm was carrying a substantial load of moisture siphoned up from warm Gulf waters, with as much as 9 inches of rain expected to fall along the storm's inner path from the coastline into east-central Texas, the hurricane center said.
Forecasters warned that heavy downpours could spawn local flash flooding.
The storm disrupted electricity supplies for more than 4,000 homes and businesses in southeastern Texas, according to utilities.
Little if any consequence to Gulf Coast oil and gas production was reported, though people familiar with regional energy plant operations said East Texas refineries took steps to secure their facilities ahead of the storm.
"We are closely monitoring Tropical Storm Edouard," Shell said in a statement ahead of the storm's landfall. "At this time, we do not anticipate weather impacts to production or drilling."
Edouard is the fifth named storm of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season, which officially began on June 1 and runs to November 30, though none have reached hurricane strength. REUTERS

Belgian court orders trial for corruption, money laundering linked to Congo passport deal

Belgian court orders trial for corruption, money laundering linked to Congo passport deal
LONDON, Sept 1 - A Brussels court has ordered Belgian biometrics company Semlex and 13 other defendants to stand trial over alleged corruption, money laundering and tax fraud linked to a contract to produce passports in the Democratic Republic of Congo, civil parties involved in the case said.
A spokesperson for the Belgian Federal Prosecutor's Office confirmed that Semlex and an unspecified number of employees were among those referred by the prosecutor to the criminal court, without giving further details.
The civil parties, including 51 Congolese citizens and anti-corruption groups who filed a suit in 2020 to join an ongoing criminal investigation, said the decision by Brussels' Council Chamber on Monday would lead to the first trial of a Belgian company over alleged bribery of foreign public officials. Reuters could not immediately confirm the trial would be the first. The allegations have not been proven in court.
Reuters reported in 2017 that millions of dollars from the production of Congo's biometric passports were being channelled offshore, including to a company linked to a relative of then-President Joseph Kabila. Authorities have not conclusively linked the company to the president's relative.
“We have a right to know where our money went. This trial will finally shed light on the matter,” Fred Bauma, a Congolese human rights activist and a claimant in the civil suit, said in a statement after the decision.
The Council Chamber did not respond to a request for comment.
Semlex did not respond to an emailed request for comment. Francois Koning, a lawyer who has previously represented Semlex, declined to comment. Semlex said in a 2017 statement that it was the target of a smear campaign.
A person close to Kabila said the former president did not have any comment as he was not directly associated with the case. Kabila's relative did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Reuters could not find contact information for the company.
Reuters could not determine when a trial might take place.
SCHEME LED TO $60 MILLION DIVERSION: CIVIL PARTIES
Semlex produced passports for Congo, the Central African country of 116 million people, between 2015 and 2025. Congo is one of the world's poorest countries by GDP per capita, despite its abundant mineral reserves.
In 2017, Reuters reported the Semlex deal led to the cost of Congo's passports nearly doubling to $185 each and that $60 from the fee for each document issued went to the company owned by Kabila's relative.
At the time, Reuters was unable to determine how much money the Gulf company was paid.
The civil parties said on Monday the scheme is alleged to have resulted in the diversion of nearly $60 million, without giving further details.
The court referral follows years of criticism from activists and the Paris-based Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development over Belgium's limited enforcement of overseas corruption cases.
The civil parties, who did not name the defendants other than Semlex, said the referral to court marked a significant step for the Belgian justice system, which they said had previously failed to sufficiently enforce anti-bribery laws. REUTERS

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Sept 2, 2026
US strikes Iran in latest tit-for-tat attacks
US forces launched fresh attacks on Iran on Sept 1, including one that the Iranian Red Crescent said left four people dead at a wedding celebration, with Tehran vowing “severe punishment” in response.
Washington hit Iranian targets on Aug 30 in its first known strikes in several weeks, after which Tehran’s forces targeted US troops in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates, and projectiles struck two oil tankers in unclaimed attacks.
More US strikes came on Sept 1, with Iranian state television reporting that explosions were heard in the country’s south along the strategic Strait of Hormuz waterway and on an island in the Gulf, and that US forces hit an airport in the southern province of Kerman.

Germany blames airport drone ‘hybrid attack’ on Russia
Germany on Sept 1 blamed Russia for an attempted “hybrid attack” involving an explosive-laden drone at a strategic airport in August and announced diplomatic counter-measures.
The European Union expressed “full solidarity” with Germany, NATO assured that it would defend its members and countries including Britain, Estonia and Poland offered strong backing.
Germany will close Russia’s consulate in the former capital Bonn later this month, and cancel the contract for the Russian House, a cultural centre in Berlin, said Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul.
China’s Xi arrives in Egypt
Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Egypt on Sept 1 on a rare trip to the Middle East as both countries face the threat of US sanctions over financial links to Iran.
Xi and his wife were greeted on the tarmac by Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi and the first lady, as well as a performance by an Egyptian folk dance troupe.
The two-day visit comes as both countries seek to manage the fallout of the months-long Middle East war, which began when the United States and Israel launched strikes against Iran on Feb 28, throwing the crucial trade region into crisis.
Bank of America V-P killed in Times Square stabbing

Piacenti, 32, was a vice-president in BofA’s business selection and conflicts unit, according to her LinkedIn profile.
“We are shocked and deeply saddened by the tragic loss of our colleague. She was a valued teammate who will be greatly missed. Our hearts go out to her family and all of her loved ones,” the US banking giant said, in an emailed statement to Reuters on Sept 1.
Cobolli claws out 5-set victory at rain-delayed US Open
Fifth-seeded Flavio Cobolli rallied from two sets down to beat Francisco Comesana at the US Open on Sept 1, where top-seeded Alexander Zverev and No. 4 Coco Gauff were finally slated for first-round action.
Italy’s Cobolli, runner-up to Zverev at the French Open, shook off an erratic start to triumph 3-6, 2-6, 6-3, 6-4, 6-4, dropping to his knees and raising his arms in celebration after closing out the four-hour, 13-minute marathon.
“In a Grand Slam it’s never done,” Cobolli said. “You have to fight to the last point.”

What's behind France's plan to survey school children on sexual violence?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
22:07:25 UTC
07:07:25 KST

For the first time, France's annual school questionnaire on bullying — which has been handed out to pupils since 2023 — will include questions on sexual violence. Pupils will be able to choose whether or not they wish to remain anonymous in this questionnaire, to be distributed in November.
Ringing school bells marked the start of the new year academic year in France on Tuesday. This year, the government has introduced a string of unprecedented measures, including a ban on mobile phones in primary and secondary schools, as well as new steps to tackle sexual violence.
For the first time, France's annual school questionnaire on bullying — which has been handed out to pupils since 2023 — will include questions on sexual violence. Pupils will be able to choose whether or not to they wish to remain anonymous in this questionnaire, which will be distributed in November.
Speaking to French broadcaster BFMTV on 25 August, France's education minister Édouard Geffray, said that around 10 million pupils, ranging from primary to secondary school, would complete the form, designed "with school staff, parents' associations and a committee of experts, including child psychiatrists". According to the minister, the results could be "seismic".
Teachers will collect the forms first. If any responses raise concerns, school leaders are then expected to step in, either by reporting the case to the relevant regional education authority or, in more serious situations, referring it to the justice system.
This initiative comes in the wake of numerous child sexual violence scandals in France, particularly in supervised childcare services. In Paris alone, there are 203 criminal investigations underway into alleged acts of violence, including sexual violence, in schools and in after-school settings, according to the latest official figures dated 26 August.
Despite these alarming figures, schools are still the main place where child sexual abuse reports are filed, with on average 80,000 reports a year, according to France's education minister.
Estimates made in 2023 by the CIIVISE (the Independent Commission on Incest and Sexual Violence against Children) assessed that around 160,000 children are victims of sexual violence every year in France, with 77% of this abuse occurring in a family environment. That amounts to one child being raped or sexually assaulted every three minutes.
Parents divided on the matter: "School must be a sanctuary"
According to France's education minister, questions about sexual violence will be tailored to pupils' ages. Despite this, parents have mixed feelings.
For Samuel Bougnat, a father of a three-year-old, the measure is a step in the right direction, "I think school has a role to play in providing support and in reporting possible violence, because school should be a sanctuary, a place where children can feel confident enough to talk about things that may be happening at home"."
Another father of two young children who preferred to remain anonymous also backed the measure, "personally, I think it is pragmatic given that all children are supposed to go through school at some point; so if there is one place where we can spot things that are problematic and dangerous for children, it is there."
"As a parent, I will be paying close attention to how these forms are rolled out through, especially to ensure that they are appropriate for younger children", he added.
Others, like Caroline Varas, who has a four-and-a-half-year-old son, are less convinced. "I am not entirely sure that school should be responsible for this. I think it should be collaborative work: with independent parents' associations, the local council and the school."
"If it is only the school dealing with it, they will cover themselves, protect themselves. I found out afterwards that there had been violence – not sexual violence, but violence – in my child's school. There is a missing intermediary between the school and parents", she added.
Child protection organisations express concerns
Laura Morin-Baudet, who heads L'Enfant Bleu, a Paris-based non-profit that fights child abuse, says she "welcomes" the fact that the education ministry is taking up the issue of child sexual violence, but also voiced doubts about the practical side of things.
"It all depends on the conditions children answer these questions in. If the child feels comfortable, has the feeling that their friend sitting next to them cannot necessarily see their answers, then perhaps, indeed, they will end up saying something. But on the other hand, if they have the slightest doubt, if they are afraid, if they are unsure where these documents will go, we unfortunately know that they will not necessarily confide."
For Laura Morin-Baudet, alongside any such questionnaires, it is still key to carry out prevention and raise awareness in schools.
"We know just how poorly trained teachers and childcare professionals are in this area. Our organisation regularly receives calls from professionals who tell us: 'I have observed this and that, what can I do, how should I act?' So we know there is that need."
"Sometimes signs can manifest themselves through words, but it can also be through behaviour. It may be a child who suddenly becomes very agitated when they were not before, or conversely a child who withdraws completely. And that is where an adult's gaze can interpret things and build upa relationship of trust."
Differing stances from teachers' unions
According to Jean-Rémi Girard, president of the National Union of Lycées and Collèges, schools and higher education (SNALC), "the vast majority" of teachers support the initiative.
"For us, the most important thing is that school should be a safe place for our pupils and, in fact, for everyone. That does not mean we are the ones who will do the work of the justice system, quite clearly. But we are nonetheless able to talk to pupils, to go and see a little what is happening, to take an interest in children's living conditions and to gather information so that we can then pass the baton to the police and the justice system."
"Sometimes very young children are not aware of how serious what has happened to them is. With the form, very simple questions will allow us not to make a diagnosis, but at least to identify a first point that needs attention."
For her part, Béatrice Laurent, secretary of the education union UNSA Éducation, speaks of a "dilemma".
"We cannot be against a programme that allows children to report violence they may have suffered. But the immediate question is whether a written questionnaire is the right format."
"Our concern also relates to how these questionnaires will be processed. Is there enough staff in the education system to deal with the reports that children are going to make? It would be truly tragic for children to disclose what has happened to them and for nothing to happen afterwards."
France's education ministry did not respond to Euronews' questions about the specific details of the questionnaire, or about how the justice system would intervene if the results turned out to be "seismic", as the country's minister has suggested.
The ministry said that work to prepare the questionnaire is underway and that it was therefore premature to provide more precise answers.

Supreme Court Tuesday sought Centre's response to the use of a 'totaliser' mechanism to mix votes
NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Tuesday sought Centre's response to the use of a 'totaliser' mechanism to mix votes from different EVMs before counting, to prevent any backlash from candidates by preserving voter anonymity.Petitioner advocate Ashwini Upadhyay said a totalisation system hides booth-wise voting patterns by mixing up votes from multiple electronic voting machines (typically around 14) before displaying the count, which helps protect voters from post-poll violence and political victimisation.
Election Commission, through senior advocate D Seshadri Naidu, said the issue was referred by EC to govt, which consulted stakeholders and found it inadvisable to employ the 'totalisation' mechanism, mainly because of staunch opposition by political parties. He said a switch to this method would require changing the statute which the commission could not bring about.When Upadhyay pointed out that the totalisation mechanism was adopted by EC to count paper ballots, a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana asked Centre to respond on why the same mechanism could not be adopted for EVMs. Upadhyay also said in Jan 2018, EC itself had told the court that the "time had come" to introduce the totaliser to "protect secrecy of the ballot and privacy of the individual".
It had said that "the right of the people staying in a particular locality should not be exposed, and any kind of prejudice or discrimination because of the voting pattern should be avoided".In a U-turn, EC in its affidavit filed on Aug 31 said, "Experience of litigations has revealed that the present system which includes a simultaneous audit by the candidates is necessary to ensure that frivolous and baseless allegations do not cloud the outcome..." It said the introduction of the totaliser system would give fresh anxieties, misgivings and allegations regarding data, machine tampering and transmission glitches.

Mainland China stepping up preparations for Taiwan blockade, report says
Defence ministry says PLA exercises are increasingly focused on plans to cut off the island and control air and sea routes
The assessment was made in the ministry’s “2026 China Military Power Report”, which was submitted to the legislature this week along with its five-year force development plan and next year’s proposed defence budget.
The report said recent PLA exercises were increasingly focused on the “joint blockade and control” of the island’s external air and sea routes.
“Combined with annual PLA training, the exercises have increasingly focused on maritime and air blockades or quarantines, joint firepower strikes, seizure of comprehensive battlefield superiority and joint amphibious landing operations,” it said.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and has never ruled out the use of force to reunite it with the mainland.

Authorities have arrested 34 people, including French, Belgian and Algerian nationals, after a person died in a pre-dawn shootout in a Dutch village reportedly linked to a notorious drug lord.
Police urged people in Overasselt, near the German border, to stay indoors with doors and windows shut in case further suspects were on the loose.
At about 4am on Tuesday, a group of heavily armed men in balaclavas approached a house in Overasselt and shots were fired, resulting in the death of a 51-year-old, reportedly a security guard.
Police responding to the scene immediately came under fire, with two officers sustaining non-life-threatening injuries, police spokesperson Jolanda Aalbers said. Several weapons, data storage devices and vehicles were also seized, she said.
According to local media, the shootout was likely connected to the criminal underworld of Dutch drug lord Jos Leijdekkers, also known as Bolle Jos (fat Jos).
Leijdekkers is one of the Netherlands’ most wanted criminals and has previously been convicted for his role in international cocaine trafficking.
He has lived in Sierra Leone for at least three years and is reportedly in a relationship with the daughter of the country’s president, Julius Maada Bio.
The Het Parool newspaper said the gunfight resulted from a conflict over several hundred kilograms of cocaine thought to have been trafficked by Leijdekkers’ gang.
Deputy chief prosecutor Monique Vinkesteijn said there had been a shooting at the same house last year related to a “longstanding conflict” but did not reveal further details.
“We know that the group currently in custody is international in nature,” Vinkesteijn said. “It includes French and Belgian nationals, people from Algeria, and also individuals from the Netherlands.”
The prosecutor said the suspects faced a variety of charges ranging from murder to manslaughter to preparing a kidnapping and that it was possible further arrests would follow.
Local mayor Joerie Minses said the whole community was shocked by the violent events.
“What happened in Overasselt crosses all boundaries. This is un-Dutch … Overasselt has been shocked by a form of extreme violence that is totally unacceptable,” he said.

Finland drops planned financial support for data centers
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
05:58:07 CST
06:58:07 KST

HELSINKI, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- The Finnish government has decided to drop plans for new public financial support for data centers, Finance Minister Riikka Purra said on Tuesday following coalition talks on the 2027 state budget.
Public support for data centers in Finland has mainly taken the form of tax relief. A preferential electricity tax rate for data centers ended in June, and the government had planned to replace it with a new support scheme in the 2027 budget.
Purra said the new support was no longer necessary because Finland's attractiveness as a destination for data center investment did not depend on tax subsidies.
Finnish national broadcaster Yle reported that the previous tax support cost about 47 million euros (54.5 million U.S. dollars) annually, while the proposed replacement scheme would have cost around 30 million euros (34.8 million dollars) a year.
The decision comes amid growing public debate over Finland's rapid expansion of data centers. Dozens are currently under construction, while around 100 more are being planned, according to media reports.
The boom has raised concerns about pressure on the country's electricity grid and its potential impact on electricity prices.
Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said on Tuesday that Finland remained "a very attractive country" for data centers, but added that sufficient electricity supply also had to be taken into account. ■

2026-09-01

Russian President Vladimir Putin said Tuesday that Moscow is not attacking Ukraine's military-political leadership because it will need negotiators from Ukraine if Kyiv is to engage in dialogue. 
“We need some people for negotiations ... if they understand that they want to resolve issues peacefully,” Putin said at a news conference in Bishkek after the Shanghai Cooperation Organization. 
He said Russia would respond if Ukrainian authorities continue what he described as terrorist actions. 
On Ukraine war 
Putin said that Moscow had given military instructions to prepare for and carry out massive strikes against Ukrainian energy facilities in response to what he described as continued Ukrainian attacks on Russian civilian infrastructure and fuel and energy facilities. 
“They strike ours, they will receive a response,” he said, adding that a large number of drones attempted to breach air defenses in Moscow and St. Petersburg overnight and struck civilian targets, including oil refineries. He said three refineries were targeted. 
Given the situation on the battlefield in Ukraine, Putin said Russian forces were increasing the pace of their advance. 
He claimed Russian forces captured 270 square kilometers (104 square miles) of territory and 15 settlements in Ukraine’s Donetsk region in August. 
Putin also said Russian forces captured nine settlements in the Zaporizhzhia region last month and were fighting in the central districts of the city of Orikhiv. 
He also criticized Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s warning that civilian aviation was unsafe in Russian airspace, saying that if the statements were intended as threats, they amounted to “a claim to state terrorism.” 
“And I'd like to point out that they're asking us to resume negotiations, asking for personal meetings with terrorists, but they're not negotiating,” he said. “But that's the first point. And secondly, in the same section, if, God forbid, such tragedies occur, we'll find a way to respond.” 
Putin said Russian forces have suffered damage to about 100 vessels during Ukrainian attacks in the last 40 days, including deaths of foreign sailors. He said the attacks caused economic damage, but it is not a critical threat to Russia. 
"And the total damage, according to our preliminary estimates, was quite significant, about 1% of GDP. This is not critical damage for us," he said. 
He said before Moscow launched retaliatory strikes against Ukrainian exports, Kyiv received $3 billion per month from the sale of grain and other agricultural products. 
He warned that a loss of export revenues could trigger three crises in Ukraine -- currency, budget and banking. 
Asked about allegations of the upcoming massive mobilization, Putin dismissed the claims, calling such reports an “information attack” against the country. 
On possible peace talks 
Putin said Russia is open to expanding peace talks if new participants could make a concrete contribution to the process, which he said was currently largely frozen. 
“If anyone makes or can make a concrete contribution to this process, we are all for it. The only thing is, I wouldn't want everything to spin in a senseless manner,” he said. 
Putin said Russia is comfortable working with people it knows and trusts, citing US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, whom he described as sincere and committed to giving the process substantive content. 
Commenting on Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s proposal in July to freeze the Ukraine conflict, Putin said, “Of course, we want that too.” 
“Only not to freeze it. We want to end the war and achieve lasting, absolute peace in Ukraine and in Europe,” he added. 
On Russia's foreign policy 
Speaking about relations with Yerevan, Putin said Russia will leave its military base in Armenia if Yerevan decides it is no longer needed. 
“If Armenia considers that the Russian base in Armenia is not needed militarily, we will leave tomorrow,” he said. 
Putin also addressed Armenia’s plans to pursue European Union membership, saying that Yerevan cannot simultaneously belong to the EU and the Eurasian Economic Union due to incompatible rules and standards. 
“If you have decided to move toward the EU, please, this is the sovereign decision of any country,” he said, while urging a calm dialogue with Yerevan on future relations. 
On Germany’s allegations that Russia was involved in an attempted drone attack at Leipzig Airport, Putin said Berlin’s accusations were primarily linked to the country’s domestic political situation. 
Regarding the UK, Putin said any British military facilities in Ukraine would be legitimate targets for Russia. 
Asked whether military-industrial facilities in Britain could become Russian targets, Putin stressed, “It’s a secret, a military secret.” 
He also blamed Japan for the deterioration in Russian-Japanese relations, saying Moscow had taken no steps, and that Russia is open to dialogue on a peace treaty and humanitarian issues. 
“The deterioration of our relations is entirely the responsibility of the Japanese government,” he said.

United States Energy Secretary Chris Wright is set to travel to Venezuela, after the South American country has approved a deal that will see the US seize effective control of a large portion of its oil reserves.

“First and foremost, it furthers the national interest of the United States,” the official said, adding that it is “critically important” for the US to be able to “to buy oil at cost reliably”.
Details are still emerging about the arrangement, likened by critics to deals imposed by colonial powers.
Still, the interim government of Venezuelan President Delcy Rodriguez has defended the agreement as a boon to her country’s beleaguered economy. The National Assembly, led by her brother Jorge Rodriguez, voted to back the measure on Tuesday.

Asked about the possibility of democratic elections in Venezuela, the official said they were not feasible in the immediate future.

Separately, oil giant Chevron is expected to sign an agreement to expand operations in Venezuela on Wednesday.
Venezuela’s energy sector has become dilapidated, with critics blaming heavy US sanctions and government mismanagement.
While the Trump administration has pushed for greater international participation in Venezuela’s oil sector, some companies have expressed scepticism about investing there.
The 65-billion-barrel oil deal was announced on August 27 in a post on Trump’s Truth Social platform.
His administration has exercised increasing influence over Venezuela’s government, since it launched a January 3 military operation to abduct and imprison Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.
Trump and Maduro had frequently clashed. In the wake of Maduro’s abduction, Trump backed the socialist leader’s vice president, Rodriguez, to take over Venezuela’s government, holding her up as a model of cooperation.

Latvia banned the import of Russian books on September 1. That won’t get them off the shelves: booksellers say shipments will just clear customs elsewhere in the EU.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
21:50:07 UTC
06:50:07 KST

Latvia banned the import of Russian books on September 1. That won’t get them off the shelves: booksellers say shipments will just clear customs elsewhere in the EU.
A Latvian ban on imports of certain goods from Russia and Belarus took effect on September 1. The restrictions cover not only clothing and children’s toys but also books. Latvian authorities say the ban is meant to sever economic ties with Russia and Belarus: Latvia intends to deprive both countries of some export revenue. The ban is also aimed at combating Russian propaganda in a country where nearly 38% of the population considers Russian their native language. At Meduza’s request, Latvian journalist Roman Shmelev examines how the new law will affect Latvia’s Russian-language bookstores, which were already hit earlier this year by an increase in the value-added tax on Russian-language books.
On the last weekend of summer, one of Riga’s bookstores has few customers. A boy of about 9 walks along the shelves, reading passages to his mother from a Russian-language book on the history of ancient Rome.
“Should we get it?” the mother asks.
“Wait,” the son says. “I’m choosing between the book on Byzantium and the one on Rome. This one has a lot about politics and history; that one has more about monuments and art.”
The boy says he wants to think carefully about how to spend his savings. He offers his mother a deal: “Let me buy the book about Rome with my own money, and you buy me the one about Byzantium.”
The book on the Eastern Roman Empire costs almost 50 euros; the one on Rome is half the price. After talking it over, the family decides to put off the pricier one “until next time.” They are sure they will still be able to buy books printed in Russia after September 1.
“Why would they disappear?” asks a salesperson at MnogoKnig, Latvia’s largest bookstore chain, sounding surprised. “Selling them isn’t banned.”
How Latvia is trying to stop imports from Russia and Belarus
The book ban is part of a broader push to reduce economic ties with Russia and Belarus. In addition to European Union sanctions, Latvia has already banned imports of vegetables, fruit, grain, and animal feed.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began, imports of all goods from Russia and Belarus into Latvia have fallen by more than 90%. Imports totaled 2.13 billion euros in 2022; in 2025, they came to just 193 million euros, or 0.8% of Latvia’s imports.
Latvia still imports some Russian and Belarusian food and drinks, but the authorities plan to extend the ban to these products as well. Cookies, candy, beer, and soft drinks could be next.
Latvian authorities began cutting imports from Russia and Belarus in 2024. But goods made in those countries still turn up on store shelves, brought in through other EU countries that have no such bans. The same will probably happen with books.
Even as they impose the bans, Latvian officials acknowledge that they will not make Russian and Belarusian goods disappear from shelves altogether. One of the main goals is to signal to the public that the state considers it unethical to support producers in aggressor countries.
To push businesses to drop Russian and Belarusian suppliers on their own, Latvian authorities decided to publish a list of the companies still trading with them. The hope is that those companies’ customers will take their business elsewhere.
According to Latvia’s Central Statistical Bureau, the list currently runs to 170 companies.
Will Russian and Belarusian books really disappear from stores?
Russian-language books can be found in many bookstores across Latvia — not only in Riga, but also in Jurmala, Daugavpils, and Liepaja, cities where Russian speakers make up a significant share of the population.
Rihards Jerums, who owns the small Riga bookstore Intellectual Book (Intellektualnaya Kniga), is convinced the new ban will not change his selection at all. He buys his stock from a wholesaler operating under the MnogoKnig brand, one of the biggest importers of printed matter from Russia.
The chain’s mascot is a cartoon bookworm named Fedya, whom the company’s website calls “the true guardian of the Russian word in Europe.” That’s partly true: MnogoKnig stores operate in Latvia, Lithuania, Estonia, Germany, and Cyprus, and legal entities with similar names are registered in Germany and Poland. Alexander Korabelnikov, a Latvian citizen, founded those companies.
Another major importer of Russian books in Latvia operates under the Polaris brand. Representatives of both companies declined to comment.
Asked by a Meduza correspondent whether shipments of Russian books would continue, employees at stores in both chains were evasive, saying the companies were “looking for a way.”
“They’ll simply clear customs in another country instead of Latvia. It’s already happening. It’s easier that way,” says Jerums. He thinks the ban “makes no sense at all”:
The European Union is a city. There’s a wall around it, and gates in the wall. One gate is called German, another Swedish, another Estonian, another Latvian. But once goods are inside the city, they travel completely freely. You can bring them in through Estonia, clear customs in Spain, and sell them in Latvia.
Arina Lindanen, who owns the Riga bookstore Vilki Books, says the ban will not change what she stocks but will complicate logistics for bookstores, since they will have to source books in other European countries. She expects prices to rise “by about 1–2%” as a result:
As far as I know, everything sold on the EU market goes through a single Latvian company. We’re all hooked up to the same pipeline. That’s bad for the market, but it’s how things turned out because of the war. I had other suppliers, but they left Russia in 2022, so we have no choice.
Lindanen says Latvian policy on Russian-language books is having a serious impact on her business: after the reduced value-added tax rate on such books was scrapped, prices rose and sales fell. “We would have had to close the store if we hadn’t found an investor,” the Vilki Books owner says.
Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braže has acknowledged that the import ban could push prices higher, but she is confident that books once brought in from Russia and Belarus can be replaced with products from other countries. Booksellers are certain she is wrong: outside Russia and Belarus, they say, Russian-language classics are not printed.
“In Europe, they publish émigré literature that can’t be published in Russia. But they don’t publish the classics at all. It isn’t profitable,” Jerums says.
Lindanen says she already leans toward cheaper editions when deciding what to stock: “We’re trying to get better at choosing — to find editions where the price, the paper quality, the design, and the notes balance out so that they aren’t too expensive. Nobody is going to buy The Master and Margarita for 40 euros.”
Both Lindanen and Jerums say Russian-language classics are in high demand at their stores. “People buy a lot of Dostoevsky and Bulgakov — they’re evergreens. It’s like bread,” Jerums says. “People buy it every day — and they buy The Master and Margarita, too.”
How Latvian booksellers, readers, and security services are fighting Russian propaganda
In the early 2010s, Russian books offering “alternative” versions of history were easy to find in Latvian stores. That began to change after Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014, when new Russian children’s atlases started disappearing from bookstores — atlases in which state borders could be made out among the descriptions of animals and plants.
In 2024, Latvia’s State Security Service publicly acknowledged that it had held “conversations” with bookstore managers and asked them to “review the selection of books they offer.”
Jerums says customers police the shelves themselves and take action if they see books that could pass for propaganda.
“People report us to the police. There’s an anti-Putin book by Olaf Kühl, Z: A Short History of Russia, Seen From Its End. A customer saw the letter Z on the cover and filed a complaint. We had to explain ourselves to the police,” Jerums says.
The reverse happens, too: sometimes customers “ask us to order books by Margarita Simonyan or a biography of Viktor Bout.” “I wouldn’t bring those in now,” the bookseller says.
He says a bookseller cannot always keep track of everything the publishers he buys from put out, and that this sometimes leads to trouble. “Say I want to order psychology books, but that publisher might also put out Z-poetry about the Donbas. Those books automatically end up on the price list and on our website. And they shouldn’t be there,” he says.
To avoid such situations, Jerums and his colleagues at the store have had to compile their own list of “undesirable literature” to hide those books on the website. The list already runs to 470 titles, Jerums says.
Lindanen says her store, too, has deliberately cut certain Russian authors from its shelves: “I was never a fan of [the propagandist] Zakhar Prilepin, and even if I had been, we’re crossing this author out. Neither his early nor his later novels will be on our shelves.”
Meduza checked the catalogs of Latvia’s major bookstore chains and found no titles by Prilepin listed.

ICYMI: The KPMG scandal
What's it all about?
I get asked a lot about the KPMG scandal and why it's important. Here's a short recap of some of the issues.
KPMG Australia is a consulting firm, linked to a global parent.
There are four large ones in a similar model - EY, PwC and Deloitte - and like our major banks, they are known as the "big four".
There is a smaller tier of even fancier and more expensive ones: Bain, Boston Consulting Group, McKinsey & Company.
The big four have two key roles: audit and consulting. In consulting, they solve business problems.
KPMG Australia has almost 10,000 staff, and if you were a business with an issue, you could go to them or rivals to seek a solution to problems like these:
- How do we crack the Indonesian market?
- We've got immense turnover and low morale in our X division. What's going on?
- We need to get our company's emissions down. How should we do that?
The firms have lots of smart people, with experience in diverse fields.
Audit asks the hard questions
The other part of the big four is audit.
It's very important.
Auditors go into companies and government agencies and certify that the financial numbers are solid.
They ask searing questions, interrogate the spreadsheets and the staff and eventually "sign off" that the published accounts are credible and reliable.
So when you see a profit announcement, a revelation of a cost blowout on a project or an annual report, there will almost certainly be a page with the logo of a big four firm and the auditor's signature and name on it.
Weirdly, a lot of our economy runs on trust. You have to be able to trust the numbers, and auditors give you that assurance.
What went wrong at KPMG?
Well, we can't go on all day....
Essentially, a whistleblower who worked at KPMG raised serious allegations about the misuse of confidential information by extremely senior partners of the firm.
Despite raising the allegations through all the appropriate channels, the whistleblower was treated poorly. Eventually, having failed to get the allegations investigated seriously, the claims made their way to Labor senator Deborah O'Neill, who read them out in Parliament - allowing the media to report them.
What were the allegations?
They might seem minor, but the allegations were around the storage and sharing of confidential information:
- A laptop left open in a boardroom, a joke that the owner was going to lunch and another person could look at it
- A report printed off and stored in a locker, with an executive assistant being compelled to give another executive access to the documents
The best way to describe it is probably a singular example. Staff at KPMG used the confidential internal financial information from telecommunications company Optus to try and win the more lucrative account of Optus's direct rival, Telstra.
The issue is that these were the most senior leaders at the firm, who set the culture. It also trashed the reputation of the auditors and the broader firm and consulting industry, even though the overwhelming majority of people at the firms have had nothing to do with it.
What's happened since then?
After searing hearings exposed the issues, and the firm's attempt to minimise them, lots has gone on.
- The CEO, chair and a swathe of senior executives have gone
- A new CEO from a different division, John Sams, has taken over
- New chair Michael Ebeid is in place (although controversial because he was a director when the firm was busy not doing enough about the allegations - which have since been proven out)
- Hundreds of staff have been sacked, with KPMG facing a grim outlook at clients leaving or not starting congrats
- The Department of Finance has banned government agencies from new contracts with the firm until a report is completed, due this month
I hope that explains some of how we got here. Drop a comment if you have more questions.
The next hearing of the committee examining KPMG is on Friday.
We'll have more then.

It's ostensibly about the "Oversight of ASIC, the Takeovers Panel and the Corporations Legislation" but let's be real: it's The KPMG Show at the moment, with the consulting firm in the frame over the misuse of confidential information and woeful treatment of a whistleblower who brought it to light.
The hearing will be in Sydney, in the Masonic Centre Corinthian Room at 66 Goulburn Street.
At this stage I do not believe there will be an internet feed, but we'll bring you the best bits.
The program for this hearing has not yet been released. We know regulator ASIC got pushed out due to the last hearing running overtime, so expect them.
Beyond that? Anyone's guess.

Economy slowing down, but will RBA be satisfied?
When it comes to GDP and inflation data, some analysts make the point that, since both sets of data are backward-looking, it can be a bit misleading to speak about them in annual terms because growth rates from a year ago don't provide much information about what's happening today.
They say one solution is to take the last six months of data and annualise it, because that gives us a better idea of what's happening right now, and Westpac's economics team has done that with today's GDP data.
For example, the data show that Australia's economy expanded 0.4% in Q2 2026, with annual growth slowing to 2.1%.
But it's a different story when you look at the last six months:
"Despite the slight upside surprise, the economy is losing momentum, with growth running at around 1.5% on a six-month annualised basis over the first half of 2026, down from around 2.8% in the second half of 2025," they say.
Having said that, they say the economy is still running a touch firmer than expected by the RBA at this point in the economic cycle.
And they say unit labour costs ticking higher in the June quarter will likely add to the RBA Monetary Policy Board's unease leading into its September meeting.

Russia is secretly helping Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles capable of targeting US aircraft carriers - report

Russia is secretly helping Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles - report
The FT report indicates that the support continued throughout the US war with Iran, as Tehran intends to develop a new class of weapon capable of threatening US aircraft carriers
Russia has been secretly supporting Iranian missile development since 2023, according to a report in the Financial Times on Tuesday.
The goal of the program, codenamed C430L, was to help Iran develop missiles capable of taking out US Navy aircraft carriers in the Middle East.
In particular, they aimed to develop a ramjet propulsion system that would allow Iranian missiles to fly at several times the speed of sound.
Fast, low-flying missiles would give Western air defences less time to react increasing the impact of such an attack.
The transfer of advanced missile technology would have required approval from the highest political echelons in Russia, amid speculation that this was a technology exchange. Iran supports Russian drone development, and Russia supports Iranian missile development, in addition to the already existing intelligence cooperation between the two.
Leaks seen by the Financial Times showed that preparations for the deal were underway before the deal was signed in November 2023, only a month after October 7.
"Russia is trying to broaden the Ukraine war and draw the US into different theatres," said Nicole Grajewski, a professor at Sciences Po University in Paris.
The investigation also showed that the support continued throughout the war with Iran in February, and provided significant assistance to Iran during its attacks on the Gulf states.
Iran has long sought to develop a ramjet propulsion system, as far back as 2019, when then supreme leader Ali Khamenei was seen inspecting development sites. Iranian media also reported the testing of ramjet prototypes in August 2023.

As my awareness of self and world expands and deepens, I begin to better understand the sources and…
Unknown

As my awareness of self and world expands and deepens, I begin to better understand the sources and scope of my suffering. I gradually become more aware of the simple fact that much of my ordinary experience includes various forms of suffering.
When the world seems to contradict and oppose me, I suffer from frustration or anger. When I compare my life to the lives of those who seem to be doing better than me, I suffer from envy. When memories of what I’ve lost spring to mind, I suffer from grief. When my present circumstances feel stagnant and hopeless, I suffer from despair. When I feel overwhelmed by demands and obligations, I suffer from stress. When the dangers of an uncertain future are approaching, I suffer from anxiety.
As I look more carefully at the particular forms of suffering I experience, I also start to see how these forms depend on my attachments. This is frequently a distressing process, because it means coming to terms with the broad reach of suffering. Discovering that suffering arises merely from my way of life and the structure of the society in which I live can be painful.

Second drone brigade in two months: Ukraine is forming the 446th Unmanned Systems Brigade. It is the second brigade of this level stood up in 2026, following the 445th, and recruitment is already underway, per unofficial sources.
Drone attack damages Russia's Baltic oil port as drone crosses Latvia into Estonia. Finland separately restricted air and maritime traffic in the eastern Gulf of Finland. No drones entered Finnish territory.
Russia's 6-day attack on Kyiv that started two days after CIA head's visit to Moscow, culminates with massive ballistic missile strike on eve of school year. Three children were among the injured. Civilian infrastructure was damaged in five of Kyiv's ten districts.
800 jet drones in four days: Russia is now firing type Ukraine's interceptors cannot catch. Of more than 1,500 drones launched over four days, about 800 have been jet-powered.
"In intercepts, they're screaming": Russia occupied this spit to control Ukraine's ports. Military says it has now isolated 2,500-strong grouping and destroyed all its artillery. Drone strikes and remote mining have cut supply, the Ukrainian soldiers say.
Intelligence and technology
Russia's Starlink rival falters as latest satellite batch stalls in low orbit, ISW says. None of the 16 spacecraft launched in July reached the 550-kilometer benchmark, while two may reenter the atmosphere and be lost.
Fired Ukraine defense chief Fedorov launches defense-tech company with Palantir CEO backing. After leaving government, Mykhailo Fedorov has moved deeper into defense technology, raising money in the US and pitching new ways to turn Ukraine's battlefield experience into weapons and military systems.
Russia promised a scramjet superweapon. Ukraine says Zircon runs on solid fuel. Ukraine's military intelligence puts Zircon's highest recorded speed at Mach 6.8, below Moscow's Mach 9 claim, and says both its motors are solid-fuel. Its component catalogue also names two US-manufacturer chips inside.
Ukrainian company builds single device that detects FPV drone, reads its video feed, and jams it. Brama has passed lab and combat testing and is now going through codification.
About $150 for airframe, about $875 for finished glider: Ukraine's BlueBird is selling its drone at every stage of assembly. Units pick the control system, camera, and electronics themselves; the bare airframe starts near $150.
Fired Ukrainian minister offers to help build America's drone army— for Patriot missiles in return. Mykhailo Fedorov is courting US investors for a fund that would build defense tech companies itself, not just back them.
International
Germany blames Moscow for Leipzig drone attack, closes consulate and cultural center among sweeping diplomatic measures. One of three drones linked to the incident reportedly struck a Ukrainian Antonov without detonating. Berlin also plans tighter entry controls for Russian nationals and additional EU sanctions.
German politician wants to send Taurus missiles to Ukraine after Russian drone attack in Leipzig airport. Wolfgang Kubicki wants Berlin to warn Moscow that further sabotage in Germany could unlock long-range cruise missiles for Ukraine.
US welcomes Russia back to G20 but rules out economic relief, source says. Washington tied any economic relief for Moscow to the end of the war, while European officials resisted Russia's return to the G20.
Armenia drops Russia's 'strategic partner' label, but foreign minister says alliance remains. The comments come after Armenia's new five-year government program changed how it describes ties with Moscow.
Latvia blocks Russian and Belarusian books, clothes and toys. The national measure goes beyond EU sanctions, covers goods worth €12.5 million in 2025, and limits the entry of propaganda materials.
Indonesia is examining whether traffickers put its citizens into Russia's war on Ukraine. The country's Foreign Ministry has put its overseas missions on establishing how one of its nationals came to serve Moscow's forces.
Someone placed funeral wreaths near defense companies in Lithuania and Czechia. The head of a Lithuanian defense company called it "ordinary intimidation" by Russians.
The US built itself a Russo-Ukrainian drone-war drill—Poland is the first ally in. A Green Beret officer expects most of NATO's 32 members to want a look, as Ukraine's war experience reshapes how the alliance trains.
Russia's shadow war on Europe is widening—NATO still sees no attack coming. A Polish warning, a US spy chief's Moscow trip, and an explosive drone found beside a cargo plane at a German airport all preceded the alliance's assessment.
Humanitarian and social impact
Russian air attack interrupts lessons on first day of school in Ukraine. Around 240,000 Ukrainian children entered first grade, 10% fewer than last year. 200,000 students near the front will study entirely online.
UN counted 183 Ukrainian children killed or wounded in July, the highest since 2022. The Ukrainian military released the breakdown on the day many schools across the country stayed shut because of Russian strikes.
Russian drone struck a Ukrainian fire truck on its way to a house fire—four rescuers injured. The crew was answering a call in a village outside Zaporizhzhia, and all four men went to hospital with injuries of differing severity.
Political and legal developments
"Russian airspace will effectively be closing": Zelenskyy warns airlines Russian skies are no longer safe. Ukraine says civilian aviation is not a target, but warns airlines can no longer assume Russian skies are safe.
Former Ukrainian president has made offer to Zelenskyy amid Russia's new type of war on Kyiv. Petro Poroshenko has tabled a five-point plan for how the capital survives permanent air raid alerts.

Honduran court drops charges against former president pardoned by Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Honduran court drops charges against former president pardoned by Trump
TEGUCIGALPA, Sept 1 - A Honduran court has dropped charges against former President Juan Orlando Hernandez over fraud and money laundering, judiciary authorities said on Tuesday, nine months after he was freed from U.S. prison where he was serving a lengthy sentence for drug trafficking charges.
Judiciary spokesperson Carlos Silva told local media the judge concluded Hernandez was not responsible for budgetary decisions at the time of the crime and it could not be confirmed that embezzled funds had been channeled into his 2013 presidential campaign.
"Of course we expected this outcome because the case had no basis," Hernandez told supporters outside the court. "The ruling is clear. Today, this chapter of political persecution has ended."
"Those who orchestrated this operation not only wanted to see me banished from Honduras forever, never to return, but they were determined to leave my family on the street," he added, pointing to assets seized by Honduran authorities. "It was utter vandalism."
Hernandez spoke alongside his wife Ana Garcia, who sought their party's presidential nomination in 2025.
Even as Hernandez's supporters celebrated the ruling, anti-corruption groups warned the outcome could further erode Hondurans' trust in the courts and pointed to the absence of a key witness for the prosecution whose release from prison was confirmed just hours before the ruling.
Silva said prosecutors could still appeal the case.
Hernandez had returned to the Central American nation in late July, after being extradited to the U.S. in 2022 on drug trafficking charges. Two years later, he was convicted and sentenced to 45 years in U.S. prison, but was then pardoned by U.S. President Donald Trump late last year.
Trump's pardon of Hernandez was announced two days before Honduras' November presidential vote, in a move widely seen as an effort to influence the country's election. Trump also said at the time he would cut funding to Honduras should the candidate for Hernandez's right-wing National Party — now President Nasry Asfura — not win the election.
After being freed from U.S. prison, Hernandez continued to face charges of fraud and money laundering in Honduras as part of a sprawling corruption investigation, known as Pandora II.
Prosecutors had accused Hernandez and other high-profile officials of diverting nearly $11 million in state funds to political campaigns between 2010 and 2013. Some of this money allegedly was used for Hernandez's first presidential campaign.
Charges have also been dropped against other high-profile officials, including former President Porfirio Lobo and ex-finance minister Wilfredo Cerrato.
Hernandez led Honduras from 2014 to 2022, a period during which the Central American nation served as a major drug trafficking route, and hundreds of thousands of Hondurans fled drug-related violence and extortion.
During that period, Hernandez abused his position as president and ran the country "as a narco-state," allowing drug traffickers to operate with "virtual impunity," according to U.S. prosecutors.
Hernandez told Reuters in an interview in late July he had no immediate plans to seek public office in Honduras but wanted to support the new government. REUTERS

Dell surges 9% after lifting fiscal 2027 forecast on AI server strength
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
21:40:18 UTC
06:40:18 KST

Dell Technologies shares moved 9% higher in extended trading on Tuesday after the computer maker reported results and a forecast that easily cleared Wall Street expectations.
Here's how the company did relative to LSEG consensus:
- Earnings per share: $7.04 adjusted vs. $4.92 expected
- Revenue: $46.97 billion vs. $44.92 billion expected
Revenue came in higher than every estimate, growing about 58% year over year for the fiscal second quarter, which ended on July 31, according to a statement. Net income of $4.13 billion, or $6.34 per share, increased from $1.16 billion, or $1.70 per share, in the same quarter a year ago. Adjusted earnings exclude impact from stock-based compensation.
For the fiscal third quarter, Dell called for $6.50 in adjusted earnings per share on $49.0 billion in revenue, which implies 81% growth. Analysts polled by LSEG had anticipated $4.49 per share and $41.42 billion in revenue.
Dell ratcheted up its full-year view. The company now sees $25.50 in adjusted earnings per share on $192 billion in revenue. Analysts surveyed by LSEG were expecting $18.92 per share and $172.67 billion in revenue. As of May, the company's 2027 guidance included $17.90 in adjusted earnings per share, with $165 billion to $169 billion in revenue.
Price increases brought on by climbing input costs factor in to the elevated revenue guidance, Jeff Clarke, Dell's operating chief, said on a conference call with analysts.
As of Tuesday's close, Dell shares had gained 236% year to date, while the wider S&P 500 index is up 11% over the same period. The stock has become a popular choice for investors who want to bet on the continuing growth of artificial intelligence infrastructure. In July President Trump, who has bought Dell shares since returning to office last year, again recommended buying Dell computers.
Michael Dell, the company's founder, chairman and CEO, is now the world's fifth richest person, according to Bloomberg calculations.
"There's an old Texas saying I may have just made up...," Michael Dell posted on X after the results became available. "If you keep growing EPS 200%+ y/y something good will happen."
The company's Infrastructure Solutions Group targeting data center hardware posted $31.78 billion in fiscal second-quarter revenue, up 89% and more than the $29.61 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount. In that segment, Dell generated $16.40 billion in revenue from AI-optimized servers. The sum was above StreetAccount's $16.07 billion consensus.
Storage revenue, at $4.85 billion, went up almost 26%. Revenue from traditional servers and networking equipment jumped 122% to $10.53 billion.
"We are seeing a growing trend of customers that require meaningful CPU compute capacity to support AI and agentic workflows," Clarke said. "These workloads are creating incremental demand for traditional servers."
Dell's Client Solutions Group, which sells PCs and accessories to consumers and commercial clients, contributed $15.03 billion in revenue. The number was up 20% but slightly lower than StreetAccount's $15.08 billion consensus.
"One of the things that we did earlier this year is we saw the PC market showing signs of softening in the second half," Clarke said. "We optimized the bits and bytes we have towards the infrastructure business."
During the quarter, Dell received a $9.7 billion contract to provide software to the U.S. military, and AI-centric cloud infrastructure provider Iren said it agreed to buy $1.6 billion in Dell hardware, including servers that contain Nvidia chips.
Dell now foresees $74 billion in AI-optimized server sales for the fiscal year, which would be up 200%. Just six months ago, the company had predicted 103% growth.

Nepal-China floods highlight a growing front of the climate change crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
21:30:07 UTC
06:30:07 KST

Advertisement
Opinion
Nepal-China floods highlight a growing front of the climate change crisis
Rising sea levels, extreme weather and drought all remain concerns, but destabilised ice and snow at high altitudes is increasingly a threat
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Dr Zhengxu Wang is a distinguished professor at the School of Public Affairs, Zhejiang University. 
On August 26, a section of glacier collapsed at an altitude of more than 5,000 metres on the Nepalese side of the Himalayas. The falling ice and rock accelerated down a steep valley at about 50 metres per second, scouring debris and transforming into a high-speed mudslide that slammed into Gyirong Port on the Chinese side just seven minutes later.
The force of the flow largely buried and obliterated the border facilities. Hundreds of people, many of them travellers, remain missing on the Chinese side. Across the border in Nepal, entire villages were swept away, leaving hundreds dead and thousands unaccounted for.
For decades, the defining image of climate vulnerability has been the low-lying island nation, where rising seas threaten to erase entire communities from the map. That threat is real, urgent and unfinished business. However, the catastrophic mudslide that tore through the China-Nepal border forces us to look beyond the waterline and consider a more complex, multidimensional map of climate risk.
The iconic risk remains sea-level rise. It is slow, inexorable and already under way. Coastal megacities from Shanghai to Mumbai to New York are investing heavily in sea walls and surge barriers. Small island states are exploring relocation treaties and purchasing land abroad as a form of climate insurance. The very predictability of this threat has allowed societies to develop institutional responses.
The second most immediately felt climate risk is extreme rainfall and the catastrophic flooding it brings. For several years, traditionally drier places such as Beijing and large swathes of inland China have suffered disastrous floods that overwhelmed infrastructure, affecting millions and exposing the limits of urban drainage systems never designed for the intensity of rain now falling from a warmer atmosphere.
The third risk is drought. This summer, a severe and persistent drought, coupled with record-breaking heatwaves, created a crisis across much of Europe. The prolonged lack of rainfall pushed major waterways, including the Rhine, Danube and Loire, to historically low levels, disrupting river transport and forcing cargo vessels to reduce their loads. France alone faces an estimated €10-15 billion (US$11.6-17.4 billion) in heat-related losses and a projected 35 per cent drop in maize yields.
Across Europe, low river levels and wildfires have exposed unexploded ordnance from World War II that had long been submerged or buried – another stark reminder of how climate change is already profoundly affecting our lives.

Urgent need for access to Iranian sites, cautions UN nuclear watchdog
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
21:28:00 UTC
06:28:00 KST

IAEA calls for access to Iran nuclear sites over proliferation concerns
UN watchdog says lack of information and access to facilities to verify Iran’s nuclear material is a proliferation concern.
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has called for “utmost urgency” to address the lack of access to Iran’s nuclear sites.
In a quarterly report seen by news agencies on Tuesday, the United Nations nuclear watchdog labelled its “lack of information about this nuclear material and access to facilities to verify it is a matter of proliferation concern”.
The US has claimed preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon – an ambition that Tehran continues to deny – as the motivation for the war that it launched in March. However, Tehran has been successful in shifting the focus of the hostilities to control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz waterway.
In particular, the IAEA report raised concerns over the lack of access to the Isfahan plant, which was targeted several times by the US and Israel over the past year or so.
In the report, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi expressed his “conviction that the long-standing problems and recurrent crises surrounding these issues must be resolved through a long-lasting, verifiable diplomatic agreement”.
However, Iran has said that access to the sites that have been struck by military action must be arranged via special arrangement.
The head of Iran’s Atomic Energy Organization, Mohammad Eslami, said on August 26 that the IAEA “cannot seek to inspect these centres until it develops specific criteria and protocols for inspecting sites targeted by military attacks”.
Tehran suspended cooperation with the UN nuclear watchdog following US and Israeli attacks on Iran in June 2025 that included strikes on nuclear sites before saying in September 2025 it would allow the UN agency’s inspectors to return.
However, access to the nuclear sites that have been bombed has not yet been granted. Despite US President Donald Trump having claimed last year that the US had destroyed the facilities and crippled Tehran’s nuclear programme, Iran’s stores of enriched uranium remain unaccounted for.
Tehran has repeatedly denied any military ambition linked to its nuclear programme, insisting on its right to the technology for civilian purposes.
However, the IAEA, whose latest report will be discussed at its board of governors meeting from September 21-25, has reported in the past that the level of Iran’s enrichment of its uranium reserves is well above that needed for civilian purposes, although neither is it at the level of weapons grade.

Australians accused of involvement with IS look set to face trial in Iraq
In short:
About a dozen Australians accused of involvement with the failed Islamic State are set to face trial in Iraq.
Local Iraqi authorities say they have finished interrogating more than 5,700 prisoners transferred from Syria earlier this year.
What's next?
Iraq's Supreme Judicial Council said the next phase was "their referral to the trial court, each according to the evidence and facts established in his or their case".
About a dozen Australians accused of involvement with the Islamic State group are set to face trial in Iraq, after local authorities said they had finished interrogating more than 5,700 prisoners transferred from Syria earlier this year.
The man known as "Dr Jihad", Perth-born paediatrician Tareq Kamleh, is likely among the group, given previous comments by Iraqi authorities about his involvement with Islamic State going beyond providing medical services.
That is despite his insistence in a recently resurfaced interview that he never pledged allegiance to the so-called caliphate.
Another member of the group may be Yusuf Zahab, now in his early 20s, who was taken to Syria at age 12.
He was captured and separated from his family after the battle of Baghuz in March 2019, when he was still a teenager, and disappeared into the Syrian jail system.
Members of his family, including his mother, were among the women who returned home to Australia in May this year, after spending years in the al-Roj refugee camp in north-eastern Syria.
Iraq's Supreme Judicial Council issued a statement on Tuesday, local time, announcing interrogations of "5,704 defendants who are members of the terrorist ISIS gangs" had been completed.
It said the next phase was "their referral to the trial court, each according to the evidence and facts established in his or their case".
Evidence of crimes against Yazidi community
For the first time, the Judicial Council provided a rough breakdown of the nationalities of those involved.
It said there were prisoners from 67 different countries who were being held: 16 were nationals from Arab states, 19 from European Union members and 32 from other countries.
The bulk of the prisoners came from Syria, with 3,497 detained, while there were 474 Iraqis.
"The investigations, evidence collection, and analysis resulted in the identification of several highly dangerous individuals who had held leadership, security, religious, military, media, or other positions, or who had been involved in high-profile operations and crimes of an international dimension, including first-tier leaders within the terrorist ISIS gangs," the Judicial Council said in a statement.
"The investigations also revealed the multiplicity of roles within the organisation, which were not limited to combat activities, but also included military, security, financial, logistical, administrative, medical, technical, and media activities."
Iraqi authorities said it had uncovered evidence of crimes against the Yazidi community, a Kurdish-speaking minority IS has been described as committing genocide against.
"Six defendants were identified whose case files indicated roles directly connected to the enslavement of Yazidi women, or to their detention, transportation, sale, supervision, or benefiting from the system of enslavement established by the terrorist ISIS gangs," the Judicial Council said.
In July, the Albanese government said it would not provide assistance to "any Australian who made the horrific choice to join a dangerous terrorist organisation".
Regarding the reports about Tareq Kamleh, cabinet minister Clare O'Neil said he could "rot in jail".
Diplomats, consular staff allowed to visit citizens
The Judicial Council said it had allowed diplomats and consular staff from "several countries" to visit their citizens in jail during the interrogation process, as well as the International Committee of the Red Cross.
The ABC has contacted the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, and the office of Foreign Minister Penny Wong, for details of what contact Australian officials have had with the group.
The ICRC has also been contacted for comment.
The Judicial Council said there had been insufficient evidence in some cases, leading to some prisoners being released: one Finnish national, one American citizen and seven Iraqis.
Another 457 Syrians will also be released, given a lack of evidence tying them to their alleged crimes.
The US military began transferring Islamic State prisoners held in facilities controlled by Kurdish forces in north-eastern Syria to Iraq earlier this year.
It followed moves by Syria's new president, Ahmed al-Sharaa, to take back control of large swathes of the country which had been controlled by the Kurds for the best part of a decade, during Syria's bloody civil war.
Iraq's Supreme Judicial Council revealed interrogations began in February this year, and said a special courtroom had been established to allow trials to happen remotely via video link to avoid risks of transporting high-security prisoners.

Social media empires are being put on notice for content that promotes controlling, violent sexual acts.
Big tech companies are radicalising young men into harmful sexual acts, the founder of education and advocacy organisation Teach Us Consent is expected to tell the National Press Club on Wednesday.
Chanel Contos will say the content is pushed by bad actors who share commercial infrastructure and have identified male psychology as a market — together, they make up the "manosphere".
"Young men online seeking community, belonging, and self-improvement advice are targeted with content that blames women for their misfortune and reinstates harmful and outdated gender roles," she is expected to say.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Contos will say that boys aged between 16 and 18 are likely to be fed misogynistic content less than 25 minutes after signing up to social media.
That was true even if preferences were set to try and exclude it, according to research from Teach Us Consent.
Teens are regularly fed content suggesting women should not leave the house alone, should not work and should not be in charge of their own money.
Most harmful content starts in the wellness landscape through gym videos or motivational content.
They then promote good looks and dominance over women as markers of male worth.
Contos will tell the Press Club men who subscribe to those ideals are twice as likely to binge drink and eight times as likely to have suicidal thoughts as their peers.
They are also 17 times more likely to have hit their partner.
Australian teenage boys aged 16 to 18 are committing sexual assault against children more frequently than adults are, the Australian Child Maltreatment Study found in 2023.
Contos has previously cited media content as a driver, noting her organisation had found an explosion in peer-on-peer teen sexual violence in the past five years.
Sexual choking sparks calls for action
The federal government is currently exploring whether Australians should be able to opt out of algorithmically curated social media feeds, Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek told ABC Insider's program on Sunday.
The announcement came after a 16-year-old Sydney girl's death was linked in media reports to a suspected sexual choking act — a behaviour often promoted to teenage boys through pornography and social media content.
Contos will tell the Press Club that, while the change would be positive, harsher crackdowns are needed.
She will suggest feeds should only show posts from people users follow, unless users explicitly opt out, to circumvent harmful content. Such a move would revert social media algorithms to how they were a decade ago.
"(The change) would fundamentally make the transition onto social media for 16-year-olds and other children safer, and it would bring the principle of affirmative consent to our screens," Contos will say.
"It is too easy for big tech to design schemes that appear as structural reform but actually suit them just fine."
Teach Us Consent has been running a campaign promoting the change since 2025.
An open letter to the prime minister requesting an end to algorithmic feeds without an opt-out choice has been signed by more than 13,000 Australians.

US may require parents to prove citizenship to get passports for their children
