West lacks adequate defence against drone swarms
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
20:30:49 BST
04:30:49 KST

Western militaries do not currently have an adequate defence against the autonomous drone swarms that could emerge as unmanned warfare moves beyond systems requiring individual human pilots, General David Petraeus has warned in an address to the House of Lords, the UK Defence Journal understands.
Speaking on 1 September, Petraeus argued that the war in Ukraine is demonstrating a change extending well beyond the adoption of drones themselves. He described a battlefield in which large numbers of relatively expendable unmanned systems are linked with sensors, software, electronic warfare, artificial intelligence and increasingly rapid targeting processes, while military technology and tactics are being modified continuously during combat.
Petraeus said: “Much of the discussion has understandably focused on individual technologies—unmanned systems, artificial intelligence, electronic warfare, cyber capabilities, precision strike, battle management systems, and others. Each matters. But the principal lesson is larger: the very concept of warfare is changing.”
He continued: “We are witnessing the convergence of technological, operational, industrial, and organizational change into an entirely new way of conducting war. Information is collected, analyzed, disseminated, and acted upon at unprecedented speed. Sensors and battle management systems are connected to vast numbers of attritable unmanned systems capable of precision effects across every domain.”
Petraeus said commercial innovation was also moving directly onto the battlefield, with software, hardware and operational methods adapted during fighting and an increasingly close relationship developing between military operations and the industrial base.
The former US commander said remotely controlled systems are already changing the role of conventional formations by taking over tasks previously performed by personnel in some of the most exposed parts of the battlefield.
He said: “And remotely operated unmanned systems on the ground, in the air, and at sea are increasingly displacing humans from many of the most dangerous functions of front-line combat and profoundly changing the role of traditional combined-arms formations.”
Petraeus also made a strong claim about the scale of drone employment in Ukraine, telling peers that remotely piloted systems now account for the overwhelming majority of Russian casualties and that established land systems are operating under persistent threat from surveillance and precision weapons.
He said: “Those changes will encounter fierce resistance from advocates of existing force structures and legacy systems, many of which are becoming extraordinarily vulnerable on the battlefield we see in Ukraine. Remotely piloted systems, employed there in enormous numbers, already inflict the overwhelming majority of Russian casualties. Tanks and artillery increasingly operate only under extraordinary threat from ubiquitous surveillance and precision strike.”
His warning went further with the development of fully autonomous systems. Petraeus argued that removing the requirement for an individual human pilot for each platform would allow unmanned formations to increase dramatically in size, potentially producing swarms considerably larger than those possible with today’s remotely operated systems.
He said: “And the advent of fully autonomous systems in the months and years ahead will represent another profound development. Removing the constraint imposed by the number of human pilots will make possible unmanned operations at vastly greater scale—including swarms for which we presently possess no adequate defense.”
Petraeus argued that military advantage would consequently depend on institutional adaptation as well as technical development, particularly the ability to incorporate battlefield lessons rapidly into doctrine, force design, training and acquisition.
He said: “In this environment, decisive advantage will belong not simply to those who innovate technologically, but to those whose institutions learn faster than their adversaries. Warfare is becoming a continuous competition in institutional learning and adaptation—the ability to identify lessons, incorporate them rapidly into doctrine, force design, procurement, training, and leader development, and repeat the process before the adversary catches up.”

Burnham promised hope. Reality is already getting in the way
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
19:30:27 UTC
04:30:27 KST

LONDON — Britain’s new prime minister spent his first statement to parliament promising to “bring back hope.” Over 204 minutes he demonstrated just how many of those hopes could ultimately be dashed.
Taking 125 questions in the Commons Tuesday, Andy Burnham made, hardened or reiterated a dizzying flurry of commitments that would radically alter the British state — if he manages to see them all through.
The man who became PM just 43 days ago suggested he will scrap Britain’s first-past-the-post voting system before 2034 if a majority of parties pledging reform — such his own Labour Party plus the centrist Liberal Democrats — win “consensus” at the next general election, due by 2029. He hinted that he could cap individual U.K. donations to political parties or block those from abroad entirely in future (though as POLITICO revealed, he has declined to do either in the short term).
Advertisement
He pledged to shake up England’s privatized water sector as part of a “10-year plan” this fall. He promised to impose his predecessor Keir Starmer’s social media ban on under-16s “at pace.” He repeated his long-held vows to radically reform the social care system, move powers and officials out of Whitehall, release public land for a wave of house-building and “end” rough sleeping — while still bringing down the welfare bill. “Working together to build a new sense of optimism around the country, we can make this next decade better than the last,” he said.
The parliamentary chamber began to empty, MPs turning to other duties and their bladders, as the hardiest stayed behind in the hope they would extract yet another commitment from the prime minister.
As the session wore on, Burnham hinted he could one day scrap England’s system of local taxation, which is based on property valuations from 1991. In the third hour he even promised to save Jodrell Bank, a locally-beloved cluster of deep space radio telescopes near Manchester that has had its funding cut.
The new prime minister was not offering a free-for-all and, like any minister, swerved more invitations to commit policy than he accepted. He insisted he will make tough choices.
Yet he is also enjoying a practical by-effect of being a new leader: He hasn’t yet had to disappoint all the people he will eventually disappoint.
Rhetoric vs. reality
The 125 questions he took showed that the difficulties and trade-offs that come with power are already coming into view.
Advertisement
Burnham dropped a hint that he could raise defense spending to 3 percent of GDP by 2030 — a key demand of his chief finance minister, John Healey, when he quit Starmer’s government earlier this year as defense minister. Burnham said he had appointed Healey “precisely because” of his arguments on defense.
Yet both men have pushed back any decision to a spending review in 2027, and will not face easy choices; the U.K.’s long-term borrowing costs are their highest since 1998, and Burnham declined to rule out tax rises in Healey’s fall budget. On paper, the position did not move on Tuesday.
The tension was summed up in Burnham’s promise to bring “much more substantial change as promised in [our] 2024 manifesto.” Healey last week put the same thing very differently, saying it was a “continuity of a Labour government with a change of leader.”
Contradictions are already emerging within Burnham’s approach.
The new prime minister wants to keep his focus more domestic than Starmer’s, but said he will head to the COP31 climate summit this November. He also promised a statement “very shortly” responding to Israel’s E1 settlement project in the West Bank, which he said “could imperil, if not end, the two-state solution.” That statement will strain relations with Israel and could do so too with Donald Trump, who Burnham is hoping to meet on a U.S. trip in late September.
He said the recent mass fatalities in Nepal, caused by falling glacier ice, were “what the climate crisis looks like.” But with energy prices rising, Burnham hinted his government will soon approve at least one of the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas projects in the North Sea.
Advertisement
Not even the Commons theatrics were immune. Moments after he pledged to avoid point-scoring, Burnham pointed some jabs at the 49-day premiership of former Tory PM Liz Truss.
Past is precedent
Elsewhere, Burnham’s promises to change the way things are done in Britain are butting up against reasons why they were done that way in the first place.
The PM told MPs that Brexit had inflicted “a decade of low growth” and promised to get closer to Brussels ahead of an EU-U.K. summit in the fall. Yet like his predecessor he will be bound simultaneously by the EU’s red lines and his own. Burnham has chosen to continue Labour’s 2024 pledge not to rejoin the single market or customs union.
He appeared tearful when he promised to invest “all” his political capital into reforming the social care model, but even that cannot happen fast thanks to the complexity of the system; his intervention has been to bring forward a review from 2028 to 2027.
He promised to be “relentless” in bringing in more “public control” of the water industry, but as POLITICO reported, his officials are still wading through all the ownership models and could apply several at the same time.
He left the door open to banning all overseas donations to U.K. political parties (saying “we can come back to these issues” before 2029), and to imposing a cap on individual donations (“we do need to go further,” he added). But unions worry their donations to Labour would be imperiled by a cap, and Burnham punted any action to an ongoing taskforce on democracy rather than accepting amendments to a bill this week.
Advertisement
He also left the door open to reforming the council tax system, but made clear that he already knows the danger in expending too much political capital. (When Conservative PM Margaret Thatcher last tried major reforms in 1990, there were riots in the streets; the successor system dating to 1991 has remained ever since.) “I don’t think I can go all that way today [… but] a council tax system based on 1991 valuations is not going to deliver fairness across the country,” he said. “We need to proceed with consensus if we can.”
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused Burnham of presiding over “a government swerving all over the place” that is obsessed with Thatcher’s legacy of privatization. “He is living in the past and he wants to take us back to the 1970s,” she said.
For many of his own Labour MPs, Burnham is saying what they want to hear — at least for now. “The grasp of detail is impressive,” said one, granted anonymity to speak candidly.The statement was “good,” said another. (The adulation is not universal; a third Labour MP confessed: “I’ll be honest, I was doing emails and forgot.”)
But as Starmer retreats from parliament — the former PM announced Tuesday that he will stand down from the Commons entirely — MPs are turning their full focus to his successor. At some point, they and the public will expect the many promises to be fulfilled. The question is when they decide that point has arrived.

South Korean company Hanwha Aerospace has signed a contract with Spain’s Indra Sistemas to supply K9 Thunder self-propelled artillery systems.
The agreement provides for localized production of the howitzers in Spain, rather than direct import of finished equipment, according to Maeil Business.
The Korean side will provide the platform and key technologies, while Indra will manufacture the chassis, control systems, and components at its plant in Gijón.
The cost and timeline of the contract have not been officially disclosed due to commercial confidentiality, but the deal is estimated to be worth over €450 million.
The procurement is part of a large-scale program to modernize the Spanish Army’s self-propelled artillery, with a total value of €4.5 billion, which includes the purchase of 128 tracked and 86 wheeled self-propelled howitzers.
News of the development in Spain of a new wheeled self-propelled howitzer based on components from the South Korean K9 Thunder first emerged this past spring.
Spanish experts plan to borrow the main components of the loading and fire-control systems, which have already been tested on the tracked prototype. The vehicle’s primary armament will be a 155-mm gun with a 52-caliber barrel. This will allow for the standardization of ammunition use with allies.
To achieve a firing range of over 40 km, the military is considering options for using an even longer barrel.
Due to the integration of Korean automation technologies, the crew size for each vehicle will be reduced to three service members.
Instead of a specialized chassis, the developers will use a military truck platform with an 8×8 or 10×10 wheel configuration.
Militarnyi previously reported that the U.S. subsidiary Hanwha Defense USA, signed an agreement with the U.S. Army to supply a prototype of the K9MH wheeled self-propelled howitzer.

Spanish government approves €309 million aid package for Ceuta amid migrant crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
19:27:31 UTC
04:27:31 KST

Spain's Economy Minister said the aid package represents a 'shock response' designed to meet the demands of social organisations and the city government.
The migrant crisis in Ceuta continues to dominate Spain's political agenda.
The Council of Ministers on Tuesday approved an extraordinary funding package worth €309 million for the autonomous city, aimed at safeguarding jobs, supporting businesses, strengthening security and ensuring public services.
Government spokesperson Elma Saiz presented the measures alongside First Vice-President Carlos Cuerpo and Territorial Policy Minister Ángel Víctor Torres. The announcement came on the eve of a demonstration in the city that has exposed divisions in the PSOE and prompted Podemos to call a separate anti-racism rally.
The package, Cuerpo explained, amounts to around 16% of the city's GDP over the four remaining months of 2026.
The money is divided into four areas: €21 million for healthcare, education, justice and water treatment; more than €90 million for defence and the national security forces; €118 million for humanitarian care of unaccompanied migrant minors; and €80 million in direct support for businesses, incentives for trade and tax cuts.
Cuerpo, who also serves as Economy Minister, said the aid package represents a "shock response" designed to meet the demands of social organisations and the city government.
He said that the main aim of the decree was "to give confidence" to both companies and workers.
Cuerpo also stressed that, before the migration crisis, Ceuta was going through a "period of economic dynamism" that had helped to correct some of the "structural deficits" the city had struggled with for decades.
Direct aid for businesses and the self-employed
Of the €80 million allocated for businesses, €36.6 million is earmarked for direct support: €5,000 per self-employed worker and between €10,000 and €150,000 per company, depending on turnover.
Applications can be submitted from Monday 14 via the Tax Agency website, with the first payments aiming to arrive in early October.
The government has estimated that the measure will benefit 2,600 self-employed workers and 1,400 companies. This is supplemented by €14 million in consumer and tourism vouchers, €1 million for the Plan Ceuta Exporta, and another €1 million to promote the city as an international tourist destination.
The package also includes permanent measures: Corporation Tax relief rises from 50% to 60% for companies in Ceuta and Melilla that maintain their activity and jobs, alongside improvements to personal income tax (IRPF) for the self-employed, totalling €12 million.
Employers' Social Security contributions are to be subsidised from 50% to 75% for permanent contracts linked to training, at a cost of €12.2 million over four months.
The government will also set up an ICO-backed loan guarantee scheme worth up to €50 million, introduce exemptions for companies that make use of the job retention scheme (ERTE) and provide an extraordinary benefit for self-employed workers who are forced to stop working.
The president of the Ceuta, Juan Jesús Vivas, warned of the seriousness of the situation a month ago, when the Government approved a first package of €168 million euros for the territory.
Vivas reiterated this in a new text, published by PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, in which he denounced an "attack on its territorial integrity" and described a city "overwhelmed and on the brink of collapse."
Vivas calls for Spanish unity on Ceuta Day
Vivas has also addressed Spaniards across the country in a message marking Ceuta Day, which is celebrated on 2 September, amid the fallout from the migrant crisis.
In his letter, Vivas called for national unity and solidarity and thanked people for the support shown to Ceuta in recent weeks.
"Ceuta has lived through its toughest month this August," he added in the text, in which he described recent events as "an unprecedented outrage" against the territory.
But whatever happens, he insisted that the city would "never" be abandoned.
A Ceuta Day overshadowed by crisis
Vivas also acknowledged that this year's 2 September celebrations would be different from those of previous years.
However, in his view, the situation the city is facing has made this day "particularly significant" and has presented an opportunity to strengthen ties and unity among Spaniards.
The president also referred to the rallies scheduled for 8 pm in municipalities across Spain following a call by the Spanish Federation of Municipalities and Provinces (FEMP).
He stressed that these demonstrations were not intended to serve partisan interests and are "not marked by political colours or ideologies."
Their purpose, he said, was to send a message of unity and support to Ceuta.
Another of the key messages in the letter is that the defence of Ceuta goes far beyond the territory itself.
"The cause is not exclusively Ceuta's; it is the cause of all Spain," he said, linking the defence of the city to protecting territorial integrity and democratic values.
"We have never stopped feeling you at our side," Vivas continued, while also expressing gratitude for the support shown towards the city during "its most difficult moment."
He added that such displays had been "a source of encouragement and hope" and had helped send Ceutans a clear message: "We are not alone".

The Georgian authorities must also ensure that Denis Kulanin can effectively seek international protection, including to leave voluntarily for a safe third country
Denis Krivosheev, Amnesty International’s Eastern Europe and Central Asia Deputy Director

IAEA urges access to Iran's nuclear sites with 'utmost urgency'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
19:25:16 UTC
04:25:16 KST

The UN nuclear agency has said in a confidential report that the lack of access to key nuclear sites in Iran "needs to be addressed with the utmost urgency".
"The agency's lack of information about this nuclear material and access to facilities to verify it is a matter of proliferation concern," the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said in the report, according to AFP on Tuesday.
The IAEA has not had access to some key nuclear facilities in Iran since Israel, joined by the United States, launched a 12-day conflict in June 2025 that included strikes on nuclear sites.
Nuclear facilities have also been hit in the latest war, which erupted on February 28. The IAEA has repeatedly urged access.
IAEA head Rafael Grossi "again expresses his conviction that the long-standing problems and recurrent crises surrounding these issues must be resolved through a long-lasting, verifiable diplomatic agreement", the report said.
‘Widespread impression’
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian on Tuesday vowed to match any US move to return to a June deal aimed at ending their war.
The deal, meant to set the stage for final peace talks, has collapsed as both sides accused each other of violating its terms.
Prior to US strikes in June 2025, the IAEA calculated that Iran possessed approximately 440 kilogrammes of uranium enriched to 60 percent, which is close to the 90 percent needed to make a bomb and well above the 3.67-percent limit set by a 2015 now-defunct agreement with Iran.
Since June 2025, the fate of this stockpile has remained uncertain.
Grossi said in June that the "widespread impression" was that the stockpile remains where it was before June 2025, near to the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant.
In the report, to be discussed at an IAEA board of governors meeting next week, the IAEA said it was "concerned" about the lack of access to the Isfahan plant.
Israel and the United States have long accused Iran of wanting to build a nuclear weapon.
Tehran has repeatedly denied having any military nuclear ambitions, insisting on its right to the technology for civilian purposes.

Pentagon Issues Contracts to Boost Manufacturing Capacity for Space Systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
19:17:45 UTC
04:17:45 KST

The Pentagon is moving forward with plans to invest in manufacturing capacity for the space industrial base, awarding multiple contracts in recent weeks to companies who supply key space components and subsystems as well as firms with innovative manufacturing technology that’s ready to scale.
The Defense Innovation Unit, a Pentagon technology hub designed to help funnel promising commercial capabilities to the military at scale, awarded other transaction agreements in July and August to two companies through its Adaptive Space Manufacturing and Integration Scale project. The effort aims to leverage commercially available tools and adaptive manufacturing processes to kick-start higher production rates across the space industrial base.
ALL.SPACE, a firm owned by York Space Systems, was one of those recipients. The company said in an Aug. 31 statement that it will demonstrate on-demand production of its Hydra satellite communications terminal with the goal of producing hundreds of units per month and potentially thousands per year.
“This award reflects a fundamental shift in how defense capabilities are being fielded,” ALL.SPACE Chief Operating Officer Rod McCurdy said in a statement. “Hydra was designed to deliver resilient connectivity across multiple networks and orbits, and this effort provides an opportunity to demonstrate how those capabilities can be delivered at the pace required by next-generation space and defense architectures.”
A second company, Freeform Future Corp., received a contract in July to scale its production of key propulsion and structural hardware. Earlier this year, the company unveiled a laser-based additive manufacturing platform called Skyfall, which it says will significantly expand its production.
Separate from the DIU awards, the Pentagon announced Sept. 1 it would invest $11.4 million in Stellant Systems, a company that makes vacuum tubes that can amplify certain radio frequency signals. In a statement, the Pentagon said it would use Defense Production Act funds to support qualification of the company’s space-based amplifier and to boost production rates, which it says “will greatly reduce schedule, cost, and performance risks to U.S. government satellite programs.”
The Space Force is preparing for a sizable increase in the number of satellites it operates. Deputy Chief of Space Operations for strategy, plans, programs, and requirements Gen. David N. Miller Jr. said in May that the service’s five-year budget projection includes “thousands” of satellites. Those will fall across a number of mission areas, including space-based moving target indication, data transport, missile warning, and space domain awareness.
In May, the Space Force awarded more than $4 billion to SpaceX to build out a new Space-Based Air Moving Target Indicator constellation and another $2.3 billion contract to field satellites as part of its Space Data Network program. It’s also planning to launch new fleets of surveillance and reconnaissance satellites starting in 2029. The service hasn’t said how many spacecraft these constellations will include, but officials have said hitting these numbers will require significant expansion of current production capacity.
“If a company is nominally making 10, we want you to be prepared to make 40,” Space Systems Command Commander Lt. Gen. Philip Garrant said in April. “We want industry to make the investments in capitalization and facilitization, and in return you’re going to get these large production contracts.”
Air Force Secretary Troy Meink has said he’s interested in awarding multiyear procurement contracts for both aircraft and satellites. He told Air & Space Forces Magazine in July the goal is to give industry the demand signal it needs to make investments in its manufacturing capacity.
“When the future is uncertain, it’s hard for industry to make those investments to either modernize their facilities or do what they need to do to get to the production capacity we need,” Meink said. “So those long-term deals are a huge part of that.”

Penn. Gov. Shapiro says too many data center developers 'don't care about our communities'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
19:17:43 UTC
04:17:43 KST

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said Tuesday that "too many" data center developers don't care about the communities where they are building those artificial intelligence-sector projects, which have met with growing opposition nationwide.
Shapiro's comments to CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" came a day after President Donald Trump said the only reason American communities should not want AI data centers "is if they want to end up being backwards and poor."
"The reality is, I want CEOs that give a damn about the community where they're going to be," said Shapiro, who appeared on CNBC with Chobani CEO Hamdi Ulukaya to talk about the Greek yogurt maker's planned $1.2 billion investment in a new Lehigh Valley, Pennsylvania, dairy manufacturing hub.
"Unfortunately, we've seen too many developers who don't care about our communities, who are trying to run roughshod over our communities, and those are the kinds of data center projects we don't want here," Shapiro said. "We want to work with people that want to work with local communities."
The governor, who is considered a potential contender for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination, on Aug. 18 signed an executive order aimed at controlling data center development, mandating that any proposals for centers comply with the Governor's Responsible Infrastructure Development, or GRID, Requirements, and removing all AI data center projects from a fast-track approval program.
"This executive order represents the most stringent requirements in the entire country," Shapiro said when he signed the order. "And my word to developers is you better follow these requirements. Otherwise you shouldn't plan to do business here."
Shapiro's order came as he seeks reelection as governor against the Republican nominee, state Treasurer Stacy Garrity.
He cited that order during his appearance with Ulukaya on Tuesday.
"That's why I put those regulations in place through my executive order that says you've got to earn local support before you can even come to the state for permitting," Shapiro said. "We want to frankly knock out the people who don't view the world the way Hamdi and Chobani do, that they're partners with the community."
Asked what that means, Shapiro said data center developers have to earn local support before seeking permits from the state.
"No. 2, you've got to generate your own power, and you got to pay for the power," he said. "You can't saddle local homeowners and businesses with that. No. 3, you've got to protect our water supply and our air quality.
"All of those things are common sense, and you are now legally bound to those standards."
Shapiro is one of several governors who have imposed new restrictions or called for greater scrutiny of data center development amid widespread public opposition to the projects, which has become a political flash point in the upcoming congressional and state elections.
Opponents to AI data centers, which house computing equipment used to train and operate artificial intelligence models, say they can boost electricity demand and utility costs and strain local water resources.
In June 2025, Shapiro had touted Amazon's announcement that it would spend at least $20 billion to build two data center complexes in Pennsylvania as the biggest private investment in state history.
"It's important to note that this is just an initial investment coming from Amazon, so this is going to grow," Shapiro told CNBC's "Squawk Box" that month. "Pennsylvania is going to be better off. I think America is going to be better off because we're going to win the battle of AI supremacy and it's going to be done right here in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania."
Shapiro's challenger, Garrity, in response to his executive order in August, released a video calling it "damage control."
"Josh Shapiro spent the last year rolling out the red carpet for massive data center development in Pennsylvania," Garrity said in the video. "He celebrated it, he promoted it, he said he was proud of it."
Garrity said that if she is elected, "I will pause data center development in Pennsylvania."
But Garrity, in a radio interview a year earlier, had said "Ohio is kicking our butt" in having more than double the number of data centers that Pennsylvania has.
"We could be doing so much more in that space," she said.
A Gallup survey released in May found that "seven in 10 Americans oppose constructing data centers for artificial intelligence in their local area."
On the same day Shapiro signed his order in August, the National Republican Senatorial Committee issued a memo warning voter backlash to data centers has put Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, at risk of losing a special election to Democratic nominee Sherrod Brown, himself a former senator.
"If Husted loses because of data centers, the industry will be blamed, and elected officials of both parties will learn a cautionary lesson," the NRSC said.
David Sacks, who is co-chair of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, in a separate interview later Tuesday on "Squawk on the Street," said "there is a good deal to be made here between local communities and data centers and the AI companies."
"You educate the average residential consumer and voter, that actually there's a way for these data centers to bring down their electricity costs," Sacks said.
"That actually the data center operators are willing to fund grid upgrades. That actually data centers don't use a lot of water now because the water recirculates," he said. "When you actually educate them about the issue, the poll numbers change dramatically, and you'll see that a majority of voters will actually support data centers."

Ukraine seeks to strengthen the liability of organizers of fraudulent call centers — Zelenskyy will submit a bill to the Verkhovna Rada tomorrow
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
22:17:22 EEST
04:17:22 KST

Ukraine seeks to strengthen the liability of organizers of fraudulent call centers — Zelenskyy will submit a bill to the Verkhovna Rada tomorrow
Kyiv • UNN
Zelenskyy said that on September 2 he would submit to the Verkhovna Rada a bill targeting the organizers of fraudulent call centers. As of the evening of September 1 , the new presidential bills were not present in the Verkhovna Rada database.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that on the morning of September 2 he would submit to the Verkhovna Rada draft laws providing for tougher criminal liability for organizers of fraudulent call centers. The Head of State has not yet disclosed details of the forthcoming changes, reports UNN.
Details
Zelenskyy announced preparations for the legislative initiatives in his evening address on September 1.
Tomorrow morning, I will submit to the Verkhovna Rada draft laws on strengthening criminal liability for those who organize fraudulent call centers. This issue must be resolved. Law enforcement agencies are taking the appropriate steps. Legislative steps are needed. All organizers of call centers must be held accountable
It should be noted that as of the evening of September 1, the new presidential draft laws were still absent from the Verkhovna Rada's database. Therefore, it is currently unknown which specific articles of the Criminal Code the Ukrainian leader proposes to amend, to what extent the sanctions are to be strengthened, and whether separate liability will be provided for creating and managing fraudulent call centers.
At the same time, current legislation already provides for severe punishment for fraud committed by an organized group. Under Part 5 of Article 190 of the Criminal Code, such actions may be punishable by imprisonment for a term of five to twelve years, with confiscation of property.
Thus, the strengthening of liability announced by Zelenskyy may concern not only increasing prison terms, but also introducing a separate criminal offense for persons who create, finance, or manage fraudulent infrastructure. This will become clear after the texts of the presidential draft laws are published.
How lawmakers have already proposed combating call centers
A draft law No. 10190 on establishing liability for electronic communications fraud, registered back in October 2023, has already been registered in parliament.
In May 2024, the Verkhovna Rada adopted it in the first reading; however, as of September 2026, the document is still being prepared for the second reading.
The draft law, in particular, proposes supplementing the Criminal Code with separate articles concerning electronic communications fraud, the creation and management of an electronic communications fraud organization, as well as the involvement of people in its activities.
For creating or managing such an organization, as well as participating in it, imprisonment for seven to twelve years with confiscation of property was proposed.
At the same time, there is currently no official confirmation that the new presidential draft laws will be directly related to document No. 10190 or repeat its provisions.
Scale of the problem
Zelenskyy's announcement came amid large-scale law enforcement operations against fraudulent call centers.
In August, the National Police reported that, together with the Security Service of Ukraine and the Prosecutor General's Office, it had conducted more than 400 searches and shut down the operations of 94 fraudulent call centers. Nearly 1,800 equipped workstations were identified, and 26 suspects were notified of suspicion. Law enforcement officers seized more than 3,300 pieces of computer equipment, over 1,300 phones, thousands of SIM cards, bank cards, access credentials to crypto wallets, cars, and significant amounts of cash.
The fraudsters posed as employees of banks, brokerage companies, or law enforcement agencies; created fictitious investment and cryptocurrency platforms; used remote-access programs; and obtained victims' banking details.
In addition, on September 1, law enforcement officers reported that they had shut down the operations of new fraudulent call centers in Dnipro and Kharkiv, as well as exposed a network of fictitious investment platforms through which citizens of more than 20 countries were defrauded.

Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov has announced the launch of a new defense technology company, with Palantir CEO Alex Karp set to become its first major investor.

From digital minister to defense reformer

Before becoming defense minister, he served as minister of digital transformation, where he helped build Ukraine’s digital government infrastructure and became closely associated with the country’s rapid adoption of drones and other military technologies.
He became defense minister in February 2026 and spent roughly five months in the post before President Volodymyr Zelenskyy dismissed him on 15 July as part of a broader government reshuffle. The dismissal reportedly followed a prolonged conflict between Fedorov and then-Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrskyi over the direction of Ukraine’s military. Zelenskyy later said the relationship between the two had broken down.
Fedorov had pushed for a more technology-driven military, including greater use of drones, robotics, artificial intelligence and data-based decision-making. During his tenure, his team also pursued changes to defense procurement and logistics.
His dismissal triggered rare wartime protests across Ukraine. Demonstrators in Kyiv and several other major cities demanded his reinstatement, arguing that his removal threatened the military-technology reforms they credited with improving Ukraine’s ability to fight Russia.
The protests continued for roughly a month but failed to reverse the decision. Parliament approved Yevhenii Khmara as defense minister on 19 August.
The movement later lost momentum after Fedorov called for wartime elections, a position that protesters rejected amid the ongoing war. The episode nevertheless made his dismissal an unusually public political dispute, with supporters defending his record while Zelenskyy and others pointed to disagreements over military leadership and policy.
The Fedorov protesters lost. But they backed a man for what he built, not what he promised—and that may be new in Ukraine.
What Fedorov did after leaving office
Since leaving the Defense Ministry, Fedorov has remained focused on defense technology rather than returning to another Ukrainian government position.
In late August, Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto said he had offered Fedorov a position as an adviser on modern warfare and defense innovation. Fedorov agreed to provide advice remotely and on a non-staff basis, while keeping his main work focused on Ukraine’s defense-tech sector.
Fedorov has also been working to establish a defense-tech investment fund and has been seeking US investors for it. During a working trip to Washington in August, he pitched a fund that would not only invest in existing Ukrainian defense-tech companies but also build new ones around technologies he considers critical to the war.
He identified three priorities: battlefield robots that can replace soldiers in the most dangerous positions, jet-powered interceptor drones capable of countering Russia’s faster attack drones, and inexpensive AI-enabled missiles.
Fedorov also proposed helping the United States develop an attack-drone fleet in exchange for additional Patriot interceptor missiles for Ukraine. He described the idea as a potential trade, but it is his own proposal rather than an agreement with the US government, and he no longer holds a government position that would allow him to negotiate such a deal.
In a recent Reuters interview, Fedorov also emerged as a more outspoken critic of Ukraine’s wartime trajectory, saying that “it looks as though we’re gradually, slowly losing.” His comments came after his dismissal and amid his continuing disagreements with the military leadership over the direction of Ukraine’s war effort.
The new company announced on 1 September appears to build on this work, moving from plans to invest in and create defense-tech companies toward establishing a company of Fedorov’s own.
Why Palantir matters
Karp’s involvement connects Fedorov’s new venture to one of the world’s largest defense and intelligence technology companies.
Palantir develops software for large-scale data analysis, artificial intelligence and military and government operations. Its products are used to integrate data from different sources and support operational planning and decision-making. Palantir has also worked with Ukraine during the full-scale war, including on AI and data-analysis initiatives.
The company has become increasingly involved in military technology, while also facing criticism over its work with governments and armed forces. Its ties to Israel and its role in military applications, particularly in relation to the war in Gaza, have generated protests and scrutiny over the use of AI and data technologies in warfare.
Palantir has faced separate concerns in the UK over its access to sensitive government and health data, with critics questioning how effectively safeguards around such information can be independently verified.
For Fedorov, the partnership marks a shift from trying to change Ukraine’s military from inside government to building defense technology outside it. For Karp and Palantir, the investment offers a direct connection to a former Ukrainian defense minister whose team worked on military technologies during a war that has rapidly changed how drones, AI, robotics and data are used on the battlefield.

US Chargé d’Affaires Joshua Harris is ending his year-long appointment in Baghdad. He was appointed last August.
Asharq al-Awsat noted that “political circles expect former US ambassador to Yemen Steven Fagin to become Washington’s new chargé d’affaires in Baghdad. Many describe him as an expert on Iraq and the wider region, particularly Iran.”
The change in diplomats in Baghdad comes at an important time. US troops who are part of the anti-ISIS coalition are expected to complete their withdrawal by September 30, which would be at least the second time the US has left Iraq since 2003.
The US left in 2011, and the ISIS invasion in 2014 led to its return. Now the US is leaving again. This is concerning for US friends in Iraq, particularly in the autonomous Kurdistan Region.
Meanwhile, the US is also in a conflict with Iran. The US has been pressuring Iraq to rein in Iranian-backed militias, which are supposed to disarm. However, the militias continue to put up roadblocks.
Militias continue to hold up roadblocks, won't disarm without concessions
Kataib Sayyid al Shuhada has created a list of conditions before it disarms. The head of the Badr Organization, one of the most powerful militias, has said that Iraq won’t confront the militias, but instead the arrangement will continue peacefully.
This likely means Baghdad won’t disarm the groups.
On August 27, Iraq’s new prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi, met with Harris.
“The prime minister, Mr. Ali Falih al-Zaidi, received Mr. Joshua Harris, chargé d’affaires of the United States Embassy in Iraq, on the occasion of the conclusion of his tenure,” Zaidi’s office said.
“During the meeting, the bilateral relations between Iraq and the United States were reviewed, along with ways to enhance joint cooperation in various fields and expand the fruitful partnership, in a manner that serves the mutual interests of the two countries and their friendly peoples.”
Iraq’s Prime Minister’s Office noted that he “expressed his appreciation for the efforts exerted by the American chargé d’affaires during his tenure in Iraq, wishing him success and achievement in his forthcoming duties.”
The statement went on to say that “for his part, Mr. Harris expressed his thanks and appreciation to the prime minister and the efforts of the Iraqi government in developing joint economic cooperation and supporting the consolidation of security and stability in the region, affirming his country’s keenness to continue developing relations with Iraq, in a way that enhances the common interests between the two countries.”
A diplomatic downgrade
Asharq al-Awsat noted that “Harris took over after former US ambassador Alina Romanowski, ushering in a diplomatic downgrade in a country that hosts one of Washington’s largest embassies, sprawling for nearly two kilometers along the Tigris River in Baghdad.
“Iraqi officials and experts told Asharq al-Awsat that Baghdad-Washington ties could take a different course in the next phase, particularly as they become linked to US-Iranian relations.”
The US is monitoring the disarmament of the militias and whether their weapons will be under state authority.
“Despite optimism about the new prime minister and the clear support for him, Washington has concluded that the factions are not serious about handing over their weapons and are merely playing for time,” the report quoted a source as saying.
According to the US Department of State, Ambassador Steven Fagin has been the US ambassador to Yemen since 2022. He was deputy chief of mission at the US Embassy in Baghdad (2020-21) and also the principal officer at the US Consulate General in Erbil (2018-20).
As such, he has extensive experience in Iraq. He also served as the main US diplomat at the Civil-Military Coordination Center - now known as the International Gaza Support Center (IGSC) - established in October 2025 as part of the US-backed peace plan for Gaza.
He also served briefly as chargé d’affaires in Baghdad from May to August 2025. In June, reports said he was wrapping up his role as ambassador to Yemen.

The Board of Peace plan for Gaza: Will it really disempower Hamas? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
19:14:57 UTC
04:14:57 KST

Sunday, November 15, 2026, is a date to circle in your diary. By then – precisely 90 days since a meeting in Jerusalem on August 17 to discuss the Board of Peace’s plan for Gaza – Hamas should be demobilized and the IDF should have begun withdrawing from the Gaza Strip.
That August 17 meeting brought Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu together with the three-man team of Jared Kushner, Nickolay Mladenov, and Sir Tony Blair. They had just returned from an unprecedented negotiating session in Egypt with Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya.
The significance of November 15 lies in what was agreed in Cairo – a handover by Hamas of weaponry and tunnels within 90 days.
As Kushner told Fox News, following the meeting: “For Israel, we think this is a win-win situation, because if Hamas actually gives over the weapons and the tunnels willingly over the next 60 to 90 days, that obviously would be the elimination of a huge security threat for Israel, almost an unthinkable achievement.”
To advance the Board of Peace’s aim of reconstructing Gaza, the August meeting agreed to set up two working groups. One would facilitate the disarmament and demilitarization process, which, according to a statement from Netanyahu’s office, “both Israel and the Board of Peace are determined should be prompt and completed before any reconstruction happens.”
The second would focus on sanitation, clean water, and public health in Gaza.
While Israel has consistently supported the 20-point peace plan produced by US President Donald Trump and endorsed by the Board of Peace, there seemed to be a problem regarding sequencing.
The plan requires both the disarmament of Hamas and the withdrawal of the IDF from Gaza, and for a time both Hamas and Israel were asserting that they would indeed act, provided the other party acted first.
Initially, the Board of Peace planned to connect incremental disarmament with gradual Israeli withdrawals. The August meeting seems to have established a way through the impasse. It now seems there will be no IDF withdrawal until Hamas has disarmed.
The IDF’s withdrawal is linked to agreed standards, milestones, and timeframes as the International Stabilization Force (ISF) establishes control and stability, although an Israeli security perimeter may remain until Gaza is judged secure.
Under the UN-endorsed Trump peace plan, the ISF is envisaged as a temporary multinational security force, operating alongside Israel, Egypt, and a newly trained and vetted Palestinian police force.
Its mandate includes helping to secure borders, supporting Gaza’s demilitarization, dismantling military and terrorist infrastructure, permanently decommissioning non-state armed groups’ weapons, and protecting civilians.
At Israel’s request, the parties agreed that in the initial stage of disarmament Hamas’s weapons would not be turned over to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza.
Why did Israel make this a condition? Because the National Committee is a wholly Palestinian body – and even though it is specifically apolitical, Israel was taking no chances. Concerned principally with civil administration, it is led by Dr. Ali Shaath, a civil engineer and former deputy minister, and composed of independent Palestinian technocrats and experts.
The future of Gaza
Israel and the US are reported to have agreed that Hamas weapons surrendered during the opening phase would be placed under the control of the ISF for destruction. Maj.-Gen. Jasper Jeffers, the US commander of the ISF, would oversee the process. Precise operational details and sequencing remain for the moment unresolved.
However, the viability of the ISF as a credible military force is far from assured. Five countries have made provisional commitments to provide troops to the ISF: Albania, Indonesia, Kazakhstan, Kosovo, and Morocco. These commitments are at different levels of firmness, and some have subsequently been delayed or narrowed.
Indonesia offered up to 8,000 troops but subsequently put the commitment on indefinite hold. Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev publicly committed the country to fully supporting the ISF.
Subsequent reports, however, indicate that Kazakhstan does not envisage its contribution as a combat contingent, but primarily as a humanitarian component, including medical units and a field hospital.
As for Kosovo and Albania, though they both committed to contributing troops, as yet no figures for their contingents have been released and no troops have been sent.
On August 6, Uganda’s parliament approved the potential deployment of Ugandan forces to Gaza as part of the US-backed ISF, if required. The size, timing, command arrangements, and final operational deployment of any Ugandan contingent have not been publicly settled.
Burundi, too, has been engaged in active preliminary discussions – including a reported pre-deployment site survey – but has not publicly made a final commitment to contribute troops.
Around the time of the August 17 meeting, senior military officers from Uganda and Burundi are reported to have visited the Civil-Military Coordination Center (CMCC) in Kiryat Gat to prepare for the deployment of hundreds of troops in the Gaza Strip as part of the ISF. They met with officers from the IDF and the US Army, who presented the operational plans to them.
In late July, Israel authorized the entry into areas of Gaza outside its control of an initial multinational contingent of approximately 200 personnel, reportedly from Morocco and Uganda. Despite the international commitments, that appears to be the current extent of the ISF – namely 1% of its projected strength of 20,000 troops.
All the same, the Board of Peace says recruitment and deployment efforts are “well advanced.”
Meanwhile, the ISF is functioning primarily as a command, planning, liaison, force-generation, and limited pilot-deployment operation.
The 200 personnel are, among other tasks, reported to be establishing the first ISF headquarters, securing a limited humanitarian zone, and preparing the logistics and command infrastructure for subsequent troop arrivals.
One report says a 150-person Moroccan military outpost is being constructed in Gaza as an initial facility which will eventually be substantially larger.
There is evidence that the ISF infrastructure is beginning to materialize. A US funding notification reported by Reuters on August 19 commits $200 million for ISF equipment, vehicles, and operations, plus about $6 million to adapt US armored vehicles for the force.
Surely the troops themselves will have materialized by November 15.
The writer, a former senior civil servant, is the Middle East correspondent for Eurasia Review. Follow him at: www.a-mid-east-journal.blogspot.com.

Putin, Xi attempt to rally SCO leaders behind a new multipolar world order in Kyrgyzstan - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
19:14:54 UTC
04:14:54 KST

Seven years after similar meetings took place in Central Asia, Russian and Chinese leaders are back again for a familiar meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization. Meeting in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, the Russians and Chinese are seeking to push for a post-American world order.
These leaders have been doing this for a while. Back in 2019, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) held a summit in Bishkek. At the time, some of the officials flew to Tajikistan’s capital, Dushanbe, for the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia. Taken together, the leaders were lifting the curtain on their push for a multipolar world order.
Much has changed since 2019. Russia had already invaded part of Ukraine in 2014, but in 2022 it launched a major new invasion. The US left Afghanistan. A civil war broke out in Sudan. The Assad regime was overthrown in 2024. Hamas attacked Israel on October 7, 2023, creating a multi-front war. The US and Israel attacked Iran in February 2026. Russia and China are watching.
The SCO is one vehicle they use to discuss with non-Western powers the new world order that Moscow and Beijing want to create.
Back in 2019, there were eight member countries attending the SCO, and numerous other countries were attending as observers and partners. Russia’s TASS news agency said on Tuesday, “Russian President Vladimir Putin said the potential of the United Nations (UN) remains untapped and called for improving its effectiveness at the SCO Plus meeting.
'Building a fair multipolar world order is irreversible'
China’s President Xi Jinping, who is set to visit Egypt soon, said the world must reject the “law of the jungle.” Clearly, this was a reference to the US war with Iran.
Putin said Russia is not fully satisfied with the UN, but that is nothing new: “We do not always like or are satisfied with everything the UN does. At the same time, I must note that, to be honest, this has always been the case, practically since its creation.”
Putin called for the SCO to work more closely at the UN and also have broader representation from countries of the Global South and East. Overall, the organization should adapt to the changing realities and fundamental shifts emerging in global politics and the economy.
Xi Jinping said the emergence of a multipolar world “is now an irreversible historical process,” TASS noted. Xi said the SCO “has become one of the key platforms for joint development and addressing challenges facing Eurasian countries.”
SCO summit highlights growing challenge to US-led world order
Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko also spoke. Tajikistan President Emomali Rahmon said the UN and SCO can play a greater role in building a fair and inclusive world order, TASS noted. Kyrgyzstan’s President Sadyr Japarov also noted this multipolar theme.
Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev made an interesting reference to the current world order. He said that it should not be a “cult of force,” essentially arguing that it shouldn’t be one of “might makes right.” He added, “Our common strategic task is to build a world order in which a cult of force and confrontation gives way to mutual responsibility, joint development, and long-term cooperation.”
Photos from the event appeared to show leaders from 25 countries attending. China’s state news agency Xinhua noted that Xi said, “The meeting today focuses on strengthening the role of the United Nations and building a multipolar world, and it demonstrates SCO’s commitment to reforming and improving global governance as required by our times.”
He added that there are many changes that are “accelerating across the globe. Hegemonism, unilateralism, and protectionism are resurging against historical trends.” In essence, this was a critique of the US. He argued that the rise of the Global South is reshaping the world order.
“What kind of multipolarity does the world need? How will countries take part in and promote it? The international community should build consensus and make the right choice that can stand the test of practice and history,” Xi said, according to Xinhua.
“Major countries in particular should take the lead in observing international norms and honoring the rule of law and work together to tackle global challenges,” he added.
The SCO meeting matters because it brings together so many countries that apparently agree on confronting the US-led world order that began at the end of the Cold War.
Many of these countries are now advancing new ideas on how to shape the world order. The origins of the SCO date from 1996, when China, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, and Tajikistan met to discuss closer cooperation. A charter was signed in 2002. As such, the current SCO is very much a legacy of the long-term leadership of Putin, Xi, and several other leaders who have been around for decades.
Much has changed in the last decade. As things change, the SCO continues to expand. India, Pakistan, Iran, and Belarus have joined. More dialogue partners and observer states have also joined. These include Turkey, Azerbaijan, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Egypt, and others.
'Hide your strength, bide your time'
What matters at the SCO today, as it did in 2019, is that these countries are openly talking about supplanting the US and creating a new world order. What does this mean for countries such as Pakistan, which work with the US but also formed a new alliance with Turkey and Saudi Arabia? Turkey and Saudi Arabia are both close friends of the US.
Turkey is a member of NATO. However, more and more countries want to hedge and keep a foot in several camps. SCO, BRICS, and other groupings provide that opportunity.
India, for instance, has mastered this balancing act. It has been since the era of the non-aligned movement during the Cold War. In those days, some countries wanted to balance between the Soviets and the Americans. Now the game afoot is to balance between the US and the rest. This is because the US remains the most powerful and influential country in the world.
Beijing has pursued a policy of “hide your strength, bide your time.” As China expands globally and increases the size of its navy, it is no longer hiding. It is now taking a more aggressive stance. However, it doesn’t want direct confrontation yet.
Russia has been willing to directly confront the West over Ukraine. This has led to a long and difficult war. It remains to be seen how Russia will behave as the war appears to sap its strength.
However, for now, Putin continues to put on an image of moving forward with his war in Ukraine.
What that means for the Middle East, Asia, and other areas is not yet clear. China’s outreach to Egypt this week, for instance, is a key example of how Beijing is exerting its influence in the Middle East.

Israeli army ‘kills first, then seeks justification’ for Gaza strikes, says veterans group chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
19:11:53 UTC
04:11:53 KST

The Israeli army “kills first, then thinks and tries to find a reason” afterward to justify strikes on the Gaza Strip, said the executive director of Israeli veterans' group Breaking the Silence.
In an interview Friday with France 24, Nadav Weiman said the army and Israeli authorities seek to “retrospectively” legitimize attacks by attempting to establish links between victims and Hamas or Palestinian Islamic Jihad after strikes have taken place.
“In cases like this Nasser hospital or the 15 paramedics that were killed by IDF (Israeli army) soldiers in Rafah, or air strikes that are killing three-digit numbers of civilians in Gaza ... suddenly the IDF spokesperson in the state of Israel needs to explain to the international community what we did over there and who are the targets for the attack,” Weiman said.
On Aug. 25, 2025, an Israeli attack on the Nasser Medical Complex in the southern Gaza Strip killed at least 20 Palestinians, including patients, health workers, civil defense personnel, and press crews, while several others were injured in the attack, according to the enclave’s Health Ministry.
On March 23, 15 emergency and civil defense workers, who were protected by international law, were killed by the Israeli army in Rafah, southern Gaza.
Weiman said that intelligence personnel compile the names of those killed and then search for evidence that can establish a connection, such as having a relative linked to Hamas or the Palestinian Islamic Jihad movement, being near a building identified as belonging to Hamas or having once been on a payroll.
“Then the IDF (Israeli army) tries to build a case around certain individuals to say we attacked because there were Hamas members over there,” he said.
He questioned how the military could have identified the victims as targets in advance, particularly in the Nasser Hospital attack, where he said a second shell struck the site and killed most of those present.
“This is something that we do after we shoot,” he said, accusing the army of the deadly attacks. “First we shoot, we kill, and then we think and try to find a reason why it happened.”
“I don't think that the tank that fired the tank shells at the hospital had a booklet with 25,000 Hamas members and looked photo after photo and said, 'Ah, there are Hamas members over there,’” he added.
Weiman said the practice was not unique to the Nasser Hospital incident and cited the 2018 Gaza border protests, when more than 200 Palestinians were killed by Israeli forces.
On March 30, 2018, the Great March of Return and Breaking the Siege began with Palestinians gathering along the barrier between the Gaza Strip and Israel to demand the right of return for Palestinian refugees and an end to the Israeli blockade of Gaza. The protests also coincided with the anniversary of Land Day. Israeli forces killed 215 Palestinians.
“Back then it was the same on the evening news in Israel: 'We killed this and that amount of terrorists,’” Weiman added.
He said Breaking the Silence has received testimonies from soldiers in the current Gaza war confirming that “if we shot and killed someone, he would be listed as a terrorist.”
An operations officer from a major battalion that participated in the Gaza genocide told the group that “every night he had to count all of the numbers of the Palestinians they shot at and listed all of them as terrorists. Doesn't matter if they're civilian or not," Weiman said, adding that this happened “because that's the assumption" in the Israeli army.
He also slammed the Israeli army's internal investigations into wrongdoing, saying they rarely result in meaningful accountability.
“Almost none,” he said when asked how often such investigations lead to charges or disciplinary action.
According to Weiman, military investigations generally focus on lower-ranking officers rather than examining who “gave the command, authorized rules of engagement or approved the number of civilian deaths considered acceptable as collateral damage.”
He said the focus should instead be on policy “and that's something that the IDF (Israeli army) cannot investigate because a situation like this where it is out in the world and outside of regulation is wrong, obviously.”
“The problem is what the state of Israel and the IDF (Israeli army) see as legitimate — as okay commands, as crucial commands — and those are the places that we want investigation,” he said.
Israel launched its genocide on Gaza on Oct. 8, 2023. More than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 174,000 wounded, most of them women and children, according to Palestinian figures.
Despite the ceasefire in effect since Oct. 10, 2025, Israel continues to violate the agreement, with attacks that have killed 1,320 Palestinians and wounded 4,385 others, mostly women and children, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.

"Severe punishment awaits the aggressors; the United States will regret its new attacks," said IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebi in a post on X on Tuesday.

“If Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level,” he said.
Trump added that a larger attack was “waiting in the wings” and claimed it would leave “very little” of Iran.
Trump described the strikes as “large and powerful” and said they were retaliation for what he called Iran’s “failed attempt” to plant sea mines in the strait.
“The United States is, as we speak, striking Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
He also cited an Iranian missile attack on a US base in Jordan, saying Iran had fired eight missiles and that they were “all successfully knocked down.”
Earlier, the US Central Command said the US military began striking IRGC targets in Iran at 1600 GMT.
"The strikes follow recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region," the US military's Central Command said in a statement on X.
Tensions between Tehran and Washington have remained high since the war began with strikes on Iran in late February.
A framework deal was signed in June through Pakistani and Qatari mediation.
The US began a two-week bombing campaign in July and reimposed a naval blockade after differences over navigation in the strait.

Govt Tuesday halved sugar stock holding limit for dealers to 2,000 quintals
NEW DELHI: Govt Tuesday halved sugar stock holding limit for dealers to 2,000 quintals from Sept 15 till Nov 30, in its bid to ensure adequate availability in the domestic market and prevent hoarding and speculative trading. The move comes as retail prices have moderated to around Rs 63 a kg, but still remain elevated even as ex-mill prices have crashed by more than 20% after govt took a series of steps.At present, stock holding limit for sugar dealers across the country is 4,000 quintals. Meanwhile, govt has undertaken intensive monitoring and physical verification of sugar stocks, covering sugar mills, dealers and traders.

Petraeus says Afghanistan withdrawal was unnecessary
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
20:00:50 BST
04:00:50 KST

General David Petraeus has said the United States and its allies did not need to withdraw from Afghanistan when they did, arguing that the Western military commitment had reached a sustainable level and that the loss of coalition support helped undermine Afghan forces, the UK Defence Journal understands.
Petraeus, who commanded NATO and US forces in Afghanistan before later serving as Director of the CIA, made the comments during the Lord Speaker’s Lecture at the House of Lords on 1 September. He rejected the argument that the length of the conflict itself meant involvement had to end, saying the relevant question was whether the continuing human and financial cost remained proportionate to the interests involved.
He said: “And here, allow me an aside to observe that I do not believe we had to leave Afghanistan when we did. Nor do I believe we should have done so.”
Petraeus continued: “For years I disagreed with the increasingly fashionable argument that we simply had to ‘end endless wars.’ That formulation asks the wrong question. The issue is not how long a conflict has lasted. It is whether the commitment required to sustain it remains proportionate to the interests being protected and the costs being borne.”
He contrasted Afghanistan with Vietnam, which he said had become unsustainable in terms of lives and expenditure. Afghanistan, he argued, had by 2020 reached a comparatively modest level of Western involvement.
Petraeus said: “We obviously have to end wars that are not sustainable. But sustainability should be measured principally by the expenditure of our blood and our treasure. Vietnam, by those metrics, clearly became unsustainable. By contrast, the effort in Afghanistan by 2020 had become sustainable at a relatively modest level.”
He cited approximately 2,500 American troops and 8,500 coalition personnel remaining by the time of the final withdrawal and said Western forces were no longer engaged in front-line combat. Their principal role, according to Petraeus, was advising and assisting Afghan forces and providing capabilities which those forces could not yet supply themselves.
He said: “The Taliban controlled no major population centers, and our forces were no longer engaged in front-line combat. Their principal role was to advise, assist, and enable Afghan partners and provide capabilities the Afghan security forces had not yet developed for themselves.”
Petraeus also criticised the requirement for the Afghan government to release Taliban prisoners during the process leading to the withdrawal. He said: “Nor should we have required the Afghan government to release some 5,500 Taliban detainees merely to secure from our adversary an agreement confirming what it already wanted us to do—to leave.”
A central part of his argument concerned the withdrawal of civilian contractors alongside military personnel. Petraeus said more than 15,000 Western contractors departed, removing specialist support required to maintain American-supplied Afghan aircraft and helicopters.
He said: “The consequences of withdrawal should have been foreseeable. It removed not only American and coalition forces, but also more than 15,000 Western contractors who were indispensable to maintaining the sophisticated American aircraft and helicopters we had provided the Afghan forces.”
Those aircraft had provided mobility for around 35,000 Afghan commandos who were used to reinforce conventional forces facing Taliban attacks around the country. Petraeus argued that the disappearance of aviation maintenance support consequently affected the ability of those commandos to move rapidly between areas of fighting.
He said: “As that maintenance capacity disappeared, so did the mobility upon which some 35,000 exceptionally capable Afghan commandos depended to respond to attacks around the country.”
Petraeus continued: “Without that air mobility, those commandos could no longer reinforce front lines held by much less capable conventional soldiers and police. The essence of the Afghan strategy was therefore fatally undermined—and once that capability eroded, the collapse accelerated.”
He used Afghanistan to make a wider point about how military capability should be assessed, arguing that personnel and equipment numbers alone provide an incomplete measure of combat effectiveness.
Petraeus said: “Military effectiveness cannot be measured simply by counting soldiers, aircraft, ships, or weapons. It depends upon the institutions, logistics, intelligence, technology, industrial capacity, and professional relationships that enable those capabilities to function.”

A sell-off of bonds from key countries worldwide has deepened, sending government borrowing costs soaring and equities lower as investors fretted over US-Iran war and that energy-driven inflation would force central bankers to hike interest rates.
The latest bout of fighting between the United States and Iran on Tuesday pushed oil prices higher, stoking fears of tighter monetary policy that could weigh on economic growth.
Heavy bond selling sent the interest rate on 30-year UK government bonds to the highest since 1998, while the 10-year yield surged to a level not seen since the global financial crisis of 2007-08.
Japan's 10-year bond yield touched a 30-year high of three percent, reflecting worries about plans for massive government spending.
The yield on the 30-year US Treasury bond stood at just under 5.3 percent, not far from levels last seen in 2007, while the 10-year yield rose to its highest level since January 2025.
"The bond sell-off has... been a global affair," said Deutsche Bank's Jim Reid.
He said the "main culprit was the weekend escalation in the Middle East that saw the US and Iran exchange strikes for the first time since late July".
But Patrick O'Hare at Briefing.com pointed to underlying fears about inflation and government deficits.
"The result has been a steady uplift for sovereign bond yields that has stirred competition concerns for stocks, as well as general growth concerns," he said.
Oil prices up as US resumes attacks on Iran
Wall Street's main stock indices were firmly in the red in late morning trading.
European stocks ended lower, with sentiment hit by official data showing that eurozone inflation hit a three-year high at 3.3 percent in August, cementing expectations that the European Central Bank would raise interest rates next week.
Oil prices jumped over two percent on Tuesday as traders continued to react to the US resuming military attacks on Iran for the first time in weeks and US President Donald Trump threatened to hit Iran "hard".
After six months of war, the conflict remains at an impasse, with Tehran keeping the strategic Strait of Hormuz closed and Washington maintaining a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
"With Trump now threatening further action against Iran, including against Kharg Island, Iran's key oil export hub, supply worries are once again front and centre," said Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club.
Traders are now awaiting key economic data ahead of the US Federal Reserve's policy meeting on September 16.
The jobs and consumer price index reports could play a major role in whether the bank lifts rates, with bets on an increase surging after Fed chair Kevin Warsh gave a hawkish speech on Friday.
Data released on Tuesday showed slowing US manufacturing growth and jobs openings figures came in below expectations.
Asian stock markets were also lower on Tuesday, with Tokyo, Hong Kong and Shanghai all falling.
The yen weakened against the dollar despite US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent telling CNBC he expected Japan to support the currency, which has lost half the gains made in a historic joint intervention after it hit a 40-year low.
The comments were seen as a signal for the Bank of Japan to tighten monetary policy when it meets this month.

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01

Aamir Latif
01 September 2026•Update: 01 September 2026
Around 1.6 million people have been affected by the devastating flash floods, which have killed 1,050 people and left nearly 4,000 missing in Nepal, local media reported, citing the government’s preliminary situation report released Tuesday.
The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) identified Rasuwa and Nuwakot as the worst-affected districts. Dhading, Gorkha and Chitwan were listed as moderately affected, the local English daily Kathmandu Post reported.
The highest number of bodies, 321, were recovered in Chitwan, followed by Nawalparasi East with 216, Nawalparasi West with 170 and Nuwakot with 142.
Some 3,916 people have been reported missing from 62 districts across the country.
Of those reported missing, 62% were Nepali nationals traveling in groups, including domestic tourists, while 17% were employees of government agencies and 15% were foreign nationals.
About 43,000 women and girls in Nepal urgently need humanitarian assistance following the flash floods that swept through parts of the country last week, according to UN Women.
The disaster, the UN agency said, has disproportionately affected women and girls, particularly those who were already vulnerable because of poverty, disability, pregnancy, limited access to information and a lack of resources.
“Pregnant women, lactating women, people with disabilities, the people we would normally support – are gone, washed away, because they could not run to higher ground,” one women-led organization working in affected communities told UN Women.
Massive floods have directly or indirectly affected an estimated 157,050 women and girls living in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts.
The overall death toll from flash floods and mudslides in the Himalayas reached 1,066 on Tuesday, a week after the disaster struck the border region between Nepal and China, according to official data.
Data from Nepal and China showed that some 4,462 people, including 844 foreigners, remained missing.
Chinese authorities confirmed 16 deaths, while the search continued for 546 people reported missing, including 261 foreigners.

What do Canada and Iran have in common? The US bullies both
